0.title: 2 Corinthians: Strength in Weakness
0.overview:
Second Corinthians is the most autobiographical of Paul's letters and, by many measures, the most emotionally raw document in the New Testament. Where Romans is a theological treatise and Galatians a polemical defence of the gospel, 2 Corinthians is a window into the interior life of an apostle under siege — attacked by opponents, misunderstood by the very church he founded, exhausted by suffering, and yet mysteriously sustained by a grace he cannot fully explain. It is the letter in which Paul most fully exposes the paradox at the heart of the Christian life: strength made perfect in weakness, treasure carried in jars of clay, life produced through death.

The letter was written from Macedonia, probably in AD 55–56, after a painful sequence of events: a “painful visit” to Corinth that went badly (2:1), a severe letter that followed (2:3–4; 7:8), anxiety about how the Corinthians would respond, and then the relief of Titus's report that most had repented (7:6–7). Paul writes in the aftermath of that partial reconciliation, addressing a church that has largely come back to him — but not entirely, since a group of opponents (often called the “super-apostles” or “false apostles”) still commands a following and challenges his authority.

How many letters did Paul write to Corinth? At least four. An early letter, now lost, warned against associating with the sexually immoral (1 Cor 5:9); then came 1 Corinthians; then a painful visit (2:1); then a letter written with many tears (2:4; 7:8); and then this one. Many scholars think chapters 10–13 are part of that tearful letter, or a later one, because the tone changes so sharply at chapter 10. But no manuscript ever divides the letter; the tearful letter was written to grieve them over an offence, which chapters 10–13 never mention; and the change of tone is explained by Paul turning from the repentant majority (chapters 1–9) to the false apostles still at work. The more likely reading is that 2 Corinthians is one letter, and the tearful letter is lost.

The letter falls into three broad movements. Chapters 1–7 address the ministry of suffering and reconciliation: Paul defends the authenticity of his apostleship by pointing to suffering as its credential, not its disqualification, and unfolds a breathtaking theology of the new covenant ministry. Chapters 8–9 address the collection for the Jerusalem church — a sustained theology of generosity rooted in the self-giving of Christ. Chapters 10–13, which contain the “fool's speech,” are Paul's sharp and ironic defence of his apostleship against the super-apostles, climaxing in the account of his thorn in the flesh and the word that defines the entire letter: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”

The letter's central theological contribution is its theology of weakness and glory. Paul's opponents measured apostleship by rhetorical skill, impressive presence, and spiritual fireworks. Paul measures it by the cross: authentic ministry looks like dying and rising, like carrying in the body the death of Jesus so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested. This is not merely Paul's personal psychological coping; it is a fundamental claim about how the kingdom of God advances — through the cruciform shape of those who carry it.

1.title: The God of All Comfort and the Yes of Christ
1.overview:
Some background makes this letter far clearer. Corinth was a rich, proud, commercial city on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, refounded by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony in 44 BC and full of ambitious freedmen on the way up. Status, eloquence and success mattered enormously there. Paul founded the church around AD 50 (Acts 18) and later wrote 1 Corinthians. Things went badly afterwards: he made a short “painful visit” in which someone in the church publicly opposed him (2:1–5), then wrote a severe letter “with many tears” (2:4), and changed his plan to visit again. Meanwhile visiting preachers, impressive speakers with letters of recommendation, were telling the church that Paul was weak, unreliable and second-rate. 2 Corinthians is Paul’s reply, written from Macedonia once Titus brought news that most of the church had repented (7:5–7).

Chapter 1 sets the theme of the whole letter: God’s power shows up in weakness. Paul begins by blessing the God of all comfort, who comforted him in an affliction so crushing he despaired of life, so that he can comfort others and learn to rely on God who raises the dead. Then he answers the charge that his changed travel plans prove he is fickle. His message is not “Yes and No”, because in Christ every promise of God is “Yes”; God has anointed and sealed his people with the Spirit as a down payment. He stayed away to spare them, not because he wants to lord it over their faith.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The God of All Comfort
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul opens by naming himself an apostle by God’s will, the very point his critics dispute. Then, instead of complaining about a terrible year, he praises God as the Father who shows compassion and gives strength in every kind of trouble. The comfort he receives is not for himself alone: it equips him to strengthen others in their troubles. His sufferings and the Corinthians’ are bound together, and so is the comfort. He tells them frankly that in Asia he was crushed beyond endurance and expected to die, and he sees the purpose: to stop relying on himself and rely on the God who raises the dead. That God rescued him and will do so again, helped by their prayers, so that many will give thanks.
verseByVerse.theology:
The phrase “Father of mercies and God of all comfort” (v. 3) is a carefully constructed title. “Mercies” is plural, and it echoes the Hebrew word for the deep, gut-level compassion that is related to the word for womb. “Comfort” shares its root with the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit, the Helper (John 14:16). God himself, through the Spirit he sends, is the source and supply of all genuine comfort. No human comfort is ultimate; all genuine comfort is God’s own comfort mediated through creaturely means.

The suffering-comfort dynamic in vv. 4–7 is the pastoral theology of the cross applied to ministry. The wound is the credential. Those who have been comforted in their own affliction have something to give that those who have only known ease cannot supply. This is not a glorification of suffering for its own sake but a recognition that God wastes nothing — not even the darkest experiences of his servants.
verseByVerse.examples:
A pastor who has gone through a severe depressive episode returns to ministry and finds that his counselling of those suffering from depression has taken on a different quality. He is not simply applying techniques; he is giving what he has received. His people sense it. This is the dynamic Paul describes — not therapeutic expertise but the transferable comfort of one who has been there and been comforted by the God who is there.

And v. 11 puts the same dynamic in reverse. A member of the congregation who has never taught, never led and never travelled prays through the week for a missionary she has met once. Paul’s sentence says that her praying is not a gesture of support alongside the real work; it is a shoulder genuinely under the load. Churches that publish requests and never report the outcomes rob such people of the best half of it — the thanksgiving that Paul says was the point of the rescue in the first place.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians is Paul’s most personal letter. Since 1 Corinthians, his relationship with the church had been through a crisis: a painful visit, a severe letter, an attack on his authority by some in Corinth, and later the arrival of rival teachers whom he calls super-apostles. Now, having heard from Titus that most of the church has repented, he writes with relief, love and warning. The whole letter answers one question: what does true Christian ministry look like? Paul’s answer is that it looks like the cross: strength in weakness, comfort in suffering, glory in jars of clay. Chapter 1 begins with a blessing of the God of all comfort, who comforts Paul in his afflictions so that he can comfort others, and who delivered him from a deadly peril in Asia to teach him to rely on the God who raises the dead (vv. 3–11). Then Paul defends himself against the charge of being fickle for changing his travel plans: his word is reliable because the God he preaches is faithful, and all God’s promises find their Yes in Christ. God has anointed, sealed and given his Spirit as a guarantee. Paul changed plans not from weakness but to spare them pain (vv. 12–24). A letter that begins in a defence of one man’s diary ends up at the summit of the Bible: every promise God ever made, answered Yes in his Son.

The setting. Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–56, about a year after 1 Corinthians. The events in between, pieced together from the letter: Paul made a second, painful visit to Corinth (2:1; 13:2), where someone attacked him publicly (2:5–8; 7:12). He then wrote a severe, tearful letter (2:3–4; 7:8), now lost, sent by Titus. Anxious, he left Ephesus after the riot there, waited for Titus in Troas, then went on to Macedonia, where Titus finally met him with good news (2:12–13; 7:5–7). Chapters 10–13 deal with false apostles who had arrived in Corinth.

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God. Every letter Paul wrote begins by naming himself, and the words he chooses are never decoration. Here they are the thesis of the whole letter compressed into a single phrase. Picture the room. The letter is being read aloud in a rented hall in Corinth, and the people listening are not united about the man who wrote it. Some love him. Some have been told, persuasively, by teachers with better credentials and a better manner, that Paul is unimpressive in person, weak, inconsistent, possibly a fraud. And the first thing they hear is a claim about where his commission came from. Not from a committee. Not from the church at Jerusalem. Not from the Corinthians themselves, who might therefore withdraw it. From the will of God.

Authority his critics cannot reach. That is not vanity. It is the only ground on which a servant of God can stand when the people he serves are weighing him. If his standing came from their approval, their disapproval would end it. Paul is about to spend thirteen chapters being misunderstood, and he begins by putting his authority somewhere his critics cannot reach it (Galatians 1:1). There is a practical edge to this that reaches well beyond apostles. Anyone who has served in a church for long has felt the ground move: the elder who is quietly criticised, the Sunday school teacher who overhears what a parent thinks, the pastor who discovers that a group has been meeting to discuss him. The temptation in that moment is to build a case: to gather evidence, to win the argument, to reclaim the room. Paul will do some of that later and hate every minute of it. But he starts somewhere else, and it is the right place to start. If God put you where you are, the room does not have the authority to remove you from it, and the room’s good opinion was never what was holding you up.

And Timothy our brother. Not my assistant. Timothy had been with Paul since the second journey (Acts 16:1–3), had visited Corinth before (1 Corinthians 4:17; 16:10), had been sent into the hardest situations, and is here given a name that levels rather than ranks. The man defending his own apostolic authority does not use that authority to raise himself above the young man standing beside him.

To the church of God that is at Corinth. Read that slowly, because the possessive is startling. This is the congregation that had split into factions, tolerated incest, sued one another in pagan courts, got drunk at the Lord’s Supper and quarrelled over spiritual gifts. It is the church of God. It belongs to him. It is at Corinth the way a ship is at anchor: located there, not owned there. Whatever a congregation is like on a bad Sunday, its title deed is not in the hands of the people who spoil it.

With all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia. Achaia was the Roman province covering southern Greece: Athens, Cenchreae (Romans 16:1), and the scattered believers in between. The letter was meant to travel. That is worth knowing when the tone gets sharp in chapter 11: Paul knew that his most personal, most wounded words would be read out in villages he had never visited.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. A greeting so familiar that it slides past the ear. Slow it down. Grace is God giving what was not earned; peace is what grace produces when it lands: the war over, the account settled, the relationship restored. And they come from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, from both, out of one source, as naturally as water comes from a spring. Only God gives grace, so the Son is named beside the Father as its giver without a word of explanation. Paul is about to write a letter soaked in tears. He opens it by wishing on his critics the two things he most needs himself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is writing to a perfect church. He writes to a church still struggling, and still the church of God. Nor does “saints” mean an elite of unusually holy Christians. It is Paul’s ordinary word for every believer, set apart by God for himself, in Corinth as in Rome.

Should I leave a church that has hurt me, or that is in a mess? Not simply because it is a mess. Every church is made of sinners, and Paul did not abandon Corinth when it divided, misjudged him and listened to his rivals; he wrote, prayed, wept and waited. Ordinary failures, poor leadership, hurt feelings and disagreements over secondary matters are reasons to work and pray for repair, not to walk away. But there are real reasons to leave: where the gospel itself is denied, where open sin is defended and never disciplined, or where abuse is covered up and victims are silenced. Abuse must never be tolerated, and no one is bound to sit under it. If you go, go honestly, without slander, and join another faithful church rather than none.

In a sentence. From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by God’s will, and our brother Timothy, to God’s church in Corinth and all his people throughout Achaia: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Relationships in the church can go through painful seasons, and Paul’s did. Think of the person in your congregation with whom things are strained. Before you rehearse your case against them, say this sentence about them to God: they belong to you, not to me. Then wish them, in prayer and if possible in person, the two things you most need yourself: grace and peace. And if you serve in the church and feel the ground moving under you, ask who gave you the work. If it was God, the opinion of the room is not your foundation, and you can afford to be gentle with it.

For worship. The God who owns the church at Corinth has never once signed it over to the people who spoil it. He calls a quarrelsome, sinful congregation his own, sends them his apostle and his grace, and stands beside his Son as the single fountain from which the peace flows. He does not wait for a church to deserve his name before he writes it on the door.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–56, after a painful visit to Corinth and a severe letter written “with many tears.” Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Paul has just been through the worst year of his life. He will describe it in a few verses as a burden beyond his strength that left him despairing of life itself. And the first thing out of his mouth is not a complaint. It is a blessing. “Blessed” (eulogētos) is the language of Jewish prayer, which began this way: barukh attah Adonai, blessed are you, Lord (Ephesians 1:3; 1 Peter 1:3). Paul takes the ancient opening and fills it with the name of Jesus. The God he blesses is identified by his relationship to the Son. There is no access to the Father that goes round Christ, and no comfort in this chapter that is not finally the Father’s comfort reaching us through him. Then come two titles, and they are worth taking apart because they are the ground the entire chapter stands on.

The Father of mercies. The Greek is oiktirmoi, plural, mercies, compassions, standing behind the Hebrew rahamim, which comes from the word for a womb. It is not a legal term. It is the word for what a mother feels when her child is hurt: the involuntary lurch in the stomach, the movement toward the pain before any decision has been made. As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Psalm 103:13). To call God the Father of mercies is a Hebrew way of saying the merciful Father, and more: compassion is not something God occasionally does. It is something God fathers. Every genuine mercy in the universe traces its paternity back to him.

And God of all comfort. The word is paraklēsis, and it or its verb will appear ten times in five verses. English has weakened it. We hear comfort and think of a warm drink and a soft chair, something that takes the edge off. The Greek is built from para (alongside) and kaleō (to call): to be summoned to someone’s side. It is the word for what a defence counsel does in a courtroom, what a friend does when he sits down on the edge of your bed at two in the morning, and it carries strengthening and encouragement as well as consolation. Its cousin is paraklētos, the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit in the upper room (John 14:16). Comfort in this sense does not remove the trouble. It puts someone beside you in it, and the someone is God. Isaiah heard the same note at the turning point of his prophecy: comfort, comfort my people, says your God (Isaiah 40:1), and later, I, I am he who comforts you (Isaiah 51:12).

All. Notice the reach of the word. Not the God of some comfort, or of religious comfort, or of the comfort that arrives once the crisis is over. Every real consolation you have ever received, the friend who said the right thing, the sleep that finally came, the verse that surfaced from nowhere at four in the morning, the hand on your shoulder in the corridor outside the ward, came out of his treasury. There is no other supplier. Those were not distractions from God while you waited for him to act. They were God acting.

Found out in the field. This is why the verse is a blessing rather than a complaint. Paul is not thanking God for suffering. He is blessing God for who God turned out to be inside it. A man can only write this sentence on the far side of something. The titles are not from a textbook; they are from the field. He found out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God removes all suffering. It means he comforts us in it. Nor does it mean that every comfortable feeling is from God: the comfort of a lie, of a drink, of a sin that numbs the pain for an evening, is counterfeit. God’s comfort always leaves you nearer to him and more truthful about your life, not further away.

What if I do not feel comforted? Then you are not alone, and you have not been passed over. Comfort in this chapter is not first a feeling but a presence: God summoned to your side. Feelings of consolation often come late, sometimes long after the worst is over, and Paul is writing from the far side. In the meantime, go where God has promised to meet you: his word read and heard, the prayers of others, the Lord’s Supper, the friend who will sit with you without fixing anything. Tell God plainly that you do not feel him; the Psalms do it constantly (Psalm 13:1; 88). The God of all comfort is not offended by the honesty. He is the one who prompted it.

In a sentence. Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father who is full of compassion and the God from whom all comfort comes.

On a Tuesday. Make a list of the comforts of the last month: a meal someone brought, a conversation that helped, a line of a hymn that held you, a good night’s sleep after a bad week. Write the name of the God of all comfort at the top of the list, because that is whose they were. Then begin the next hard conversation with God the way Paul begins this letter: not with the complaint, which you may certainly bring, but with a blessing of who he is.

For worship. Blessed be he. Not because the affliction was light, for it was not, and Paul will say so. But because when the strength ran out there was Someone already alongside, whose compassion is not a decision he makes but a nature he has, and whose supply of consolation has no visible floor. The Father of mercies. The God of all comfort. He has never once been found to be less than his names.

parallels.desc: I, I am he who comforts you

verseByVerse.quote: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.

Who comforts us in all our affliction. Here is the sentence that governs the letter, and its most important words are the little phrase in the middle: so that. Affliction is thlipsis, from a verb meaning to press or crush: the pressure of a weight, not the sting of a scratch. And the preposition matters. God comforts us in affliction, not only by taking us out of it. The comfort is delivered inside the pressure.

So that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction. Read it as a chain and count the links. God comforts us. That comfort makes us able. What we then give away is not our own invention but the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God: the same substance, handed on. Comfort in this verse behaves less like a private consolation and more like water in a bucket line. It is given to you in order to be passed along, and the God at the head of the line has more.

All and any. Notice the two adjectives Paul pairs. God comforts us in all our affliction so that we can comfort those in any affliction. The comfort received in one kind of trouble is transferable to another kind. The woman who was carried through a bereavement is not disqualified from sitting with the man losing his business. What she has to give is not a technique specific to grief. It is God. Which answers the objection almost every Christian raises at this verse, usually silently: I have nothing to offer; I have never been through what she is going through, and the people who have will do it better. Paul’s logic dismantles that. The qualification is not that you have suffered the same thing. The qualification is that you have been comforted by God, and the currency you hand over is his, not yours. You are not being asked to be wise. You are being asked to be there, with what you were given.

With the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God. Here is a test you can run tonight. Think of the hardest stretch you have lived through: the diagnosis, the redundancy, the marriage that nearly went, the year you could not pray. Now ask: who got the benefit of it? If the honest answer is nobody, this verse says something has been left in the bucket. God did not comfort you merely so that you would feel better. He comforted you so that you would be able, and the ability he built in you may be sitting unused while somebody two rows behind you on Sunday is going through it now.

Nothing wasted. There is a hard implication in the other direction too, and it is worth naming honestly. If comfort is given to be passed on, then some of what God allows into your life is allowed for someone else’s sake. That is a costly thought and Paul does not soften it; he will say it outright in verse 6. It does not mean your suffering is only instrumental, as though you were a training exercise for somebody else’s benefit. God loves you for your own sake. It means that nothing in it will be wasted: not the sleepless nights, not the questions you could not answer, not even the months you handled it badly. God is not merely repairing you. He is equipping you.

The wound is the credential. And this is precisely what Paul’s opponents could not see. They looked at a beaten, imprisoned, shipwrecked man and concluded that God was plainly not blessing his ministry. Paul looks at the same evidence and says: this is not the damage to my ministry, this is the making of it (12:9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean only those who have suffered the exact same thing can comfort others. It means God’s comfort in any trial equips us for any trial. Nor does it mean you must wait until your own trouble is over before you can help anyone. Some of the most strengthening comfort is given by people still in the middle of it.

What do I actually say to someone who is suffering? Often less than you think. Go, and stay; presence is most of it. Say that you are sorry and that you are praying, and then pray, sometimes with them if they welcome it. Listen more than you speak, and do not rush to explain why it happened or to tell them it will be all right; Job’s friends did best in the week they said nothing (Job 2:13). Offer specific help rather than a general “let me know”: a meal on Thursday, a lift to the hospital, an hour with the children. When the moment is right, share briefly what God was to you in your own dark place, and point them to his promises rather than to your story. Then keep coming back after everyone else has stopped.

In a sentence. God comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort others in any trouble with the same comfort God has given us.

On a Tuesday. Think of a hard season God brought you through. Now think of one person around you who is going through something, not necessarily the same thing. Comfort them this week, concretely: a visit, a message that names their trouble, a meal, a prayer said aloud with them. Do not wait until you feel qualified. You were qualified when God comforted you.

For worship. The God of all comfort could have consoled each of his children privately and left it there. Instead he has built his family so that his comfort travels from hand to hand, and the weakest believer who has been held by him becomes a carrier of his consolation to another. He wastes nothing, not even our worst year. Out of the darkest places he has brought us through, he makes ministers of his mercy.

parallels.desc: as one whom his mother comforts

verseByVerse.quote: For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.

For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings. Paul now tells us where the comfort of verse 4 comes from, and the answer raises a question every careful reader ought to ask. Literally, the sufferings of Christ overflow to us. In what possible sense does a Christian share in the sufferings of Christ? Did the cross leave something outstanding?

The atonement is finished. Take the hard question head on, because a vague answer here does real damage. The New Testament is emphatic that the atoning work of Christ is finished and unrepeatable. He offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins (Hebrews 10:12, 14); at the end he said, It is finished (John 19:30). Nothing you suffer adds a gram to the payment for your sin, and any teaching that suggests otherwise has cut the ground from under the gospel. When Paul speaks elsewhere of filling up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions (Colossians 1:24), he is not topping up the atonement. He is saying that the sufferings of the Messiah continue to spill over into the age of the church through the people who carry his message (Philippians 3:10; 1 Peter 4:13).

Why are you persecuting me? So what is being shared? Look at how the risen Christ addressed Saul on the Damascus road: not why are you persecuting my followers, but why are you persecuting me (Acts 9:4). The Head feels what happens to the body. When Paul is flogged for preaching Jesus, the blows fall on a member of Christ, and Christ counts them as his own. That is the sharing. It is not that our pain completes his; it is that his life has been so joined to ours that our pain is drawn inside his.

So through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too. Two things follow, and both are what a suffering believer needs at three in the morning. First, the measure is exact. The word rendered share abundantly is used on both sides of the sentence: the sufferings overflow, and so does the comfort. Whatever the measure of the one, the other is poured at the same rate. That is not a promise that the pain will be small. It is a promise that it will never outrun the supply. If the flood rises, so does the boat. Second, the channel is named: through Christ. The comfort does not arrive from a distance, dispatched by a God who has only heard about suffering. It comes through the one who was in it: whose friends fell asleep while he prayed, who was misrepresented at his trial, who was abandoned by the people he had healed, and who cried out that God had forsaken him. There is no experience of yours that he learned about second-hand.

Which sufferings count? Not every hardship is in the first place a sharing in Christ’s sufferings; Paul is speaking chiefly of what comes upon a person for the sake of Christ and his gospel. But do not draw that line too tightly. Paul is not building a hierarchy of holy pain. He is telling a church that despises weakness that the sufferings of their apostle are not evidence against him. They are the family likeness. And every trouble borne in faith by someone joined to Christ is borne in fellowship with him, who is touched with the feeling of our weakness (Hebrews 4:15).

The shape of the cross. And look what that does to the cross. It was an event that happened once and is never to be repeated as a payment. But it is also a shape, and the Lord who bore it has bent the whole life of his people into conformity with it, so that dying and rising is not an interruption of the Christian life but its rhythm. He goes first into every dark place his people are asked to enter, and he comes out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean our sufferings add to Christ’s atoning work. That was finished once for all (Hebrews 10:14). It means we share in the pattern of his sufferings as his followers, and in the comfort that flows from his risen life.

Should a Christian go looking for suffering? No. Paul never sought pain for its own sake, and he used lawful means to escape danger: he was lowered over a wall in a basket (11:33) and appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25). Suffering is not a merit badge, and inflicting it on yourself has no value before God (Colossians 2:23). What Paul did refuse was to avoid suffering at the cost of faithfulness. Do not court it; do not dodge it by denying Christ. When it comes because you belong to him, receive it as fellowship with him, and expect his comfort to overflow in proportion.

In a sentence. For just as Christ’s sufferings spill over into our lives, so through Christ our comfort spills over too.

On a Tuesday. If you are carrying something now because you are a Christian, the colleague who freezes you out because you would not shade the truth, the family member who mocks your faith, the opportunity you lost because you would not compromise, name it before God as what it is: a share in the sufferings of his Son. Then ask him for the matching share of comfort, by name, and expect it. And if your suffering is of the ordinary kind, illness, grief, weariness, remember that the Lord who comforts you was a man of sorrows who knows it from the inside.

For worship. He went first. Into the garden, into the trial, into the darkness of the forsaken cry, into the grave, the Son of God went ahead of every one of his people, and he came out the other side alive. Now there is no affliction of a believer in which he is not present, counting the blows as his own, and no flood of trouble that his comfort does not rise to meet. The overflow of his sufferings has become the overflow of his consolation.

verseByVerse.quote: If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.

If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation. This is one of the strangest sentences in the letter, and if it does not stop the reader it has not been read properly. Paul says that his afflictions are for the Corinthians. Not merely useful to them afterwards. For them. Aimed at their benefit. Stand it up next to what was actually happening. The Corinthians were sitting in relative comfort, comparing their apostle unfavourably with more impressive teachers, and complaining about his travel arrangements. Paul was in Asia being crushed to the point of despair. And his reading of the situation is that the crushing was on their account.

How can that be? The verse gives two ways. The first is the one we have already met: what he receives in affliction he hands on. He is being taken through it so that he will have something real to give them, which is why the sentence works just as well the other way round. And if we are comforted, it is for your comfort. Both halves of his experience are theirs. His bad years are their supply. The second is nearer the surface than we notice. A watching church learns what the gospel can carry by seeing what it carries a man through. Doctrine held under no pressure teaches nothing. When the Corinthians heard that Paul had been beyond his strength and had not let go of Christ, they were being handed evidence about the strength of the one he was holding. Paul’s sufferings also brought them the gospel in the first place, for he preached it at Corinth through opposition and fear (Acts 18:6–10; 1 Corinthians 2:3).

And salvation. Not that his suffering saves them: only Christ’s suffering does that. But it is part of the means by which God brings the gospel to them and keeps them in the faith they were saved into. God preserves his people to the end, and he does it through means: through preaching, example, encouragement, warning, and the sight of other believers holding on.

Which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer. The last clause does not flatter them. There is a condition here. The comfort is not received by studying Paul’s hardships from a safe distance. It is received in the place where the same pressure is bearing on you. A spectator gets nothing from this verse. A sufferer gets everything. The word for patiently endure is hypomonē, literally a remaining under. Not gritted teeth and not resignation, but staying put under a weight instead of crawling out from under it. The comfort of God is not found by the man who has arranged his life to avoid all pressure. It is found by the one who stayed.

The same sufferings. There is a quiet dignity being handed to ordinary Christians here, and it deserves saying plainly. Most believers will never be flogged for the gospel. They will be passed over at work for being honest, or lose a friendship over what they believe, or carry a chronic illness for thirty years without much notice being taken. Paul’s phrase is the same sufferings. He does not put his own trials in one category and their smaller griefs in another. Whatever is borne under the pressure of belonging to Christ belongs to the same stock, and draws on the same comfort.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s suffering saves them. Christ’s suffering saves. Paul’s suffering serves their salvation as he brings them the gospel and shows them how to endure.

Is it wrong to pray for my suffering to end? No. Paul himself asked three times for his thorn to be removed (12:8), and Jesus prayed, if it be possible, let this cup pass. Asking for relief is not a failure of faith; it is a child speaking to his Father. What Paul adds is that while the answer is not yet, the suffering is not empty. Pray for healing, for rescue, for the trouble to lift; and pray too that while it lasts it will do its work, in you and in those who are watching you.

In a sentence. If we are in trouble, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which helps you endure the same sufferings we go through.

On a Tuesday. Your suffering, borne in faith, can strengthen others; do not waste it by hiding it altogether. Somebody is watching how you carry the illness, the loss, the long wait. You do not have to perform cheerfulness for them. But you can let them see where you go with it: that you still pray, still come to worship, still say that God is good while the tears are real. That is the evidence the next sufferer will need.

For worship. In God’s family nobody suffers alone and nothing is borne for nothing. The Lord has arranged his church so that the trials of one become the strength of another, and the comfort that reached an apostle in Asia reached a church in Corinth and reaches us still. Behind it all stands the one whose sufferings alone purchased our salvation, and whose comfort flows out through every one of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.

Our hope for you is unshaken. Paul has been describing what suffering does. Now he says what he expects it to produce in them, and the word he reaches for is startling. The Greek is bebaia: firm, secured, the word used of a legally binding contract or an anchor that holds. His hope for this church is not a wish. It is a settled expectation.

Who he is talking about. This is the congregation of 1 Corinthians. He has had to write to them about lawsuits, incest, drunkenness at the Lord’s table and factions formed around preachers. Since then there has been a visit so painful he cannot bring himself to repeat it, and a letter written out of much affliction and anguish of heart. If any pastor ever had grounds for saying I have lost hope for that church, it is this one about this church. And his hope for them is unshaken. Not because he has revised his opinion of their behaviour, and not because he is being polite.

For we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort. Read the reason he gives. His confidence is not in their track record. It is in the settled pattern of how God deals with his people: he never takes anyone into the affliction without taking them through to the consolation. Paul is sure of them because he is sure of God. And notice the word for share, koinōnoi: partners, people in a common enterprise. There is one experience running through apostle and church, and no clean line between the man in the pulpit and the people in the seats.

Who have you written off? That is a lesson for anyone who has given up on someone. Hope that rests on a person’s performance is shaken every time they fail, which is why so much Christian hope for other people is exhausted by about the third disappointment. Hope that rests on God’s character survives the failures, because it was never resting on the record in the first place. The question is not whether they deserve better. It is whether the God who has not finished with you has finished with them.

The order of the clauses. There is also a searching implication in the order, and it should not be smoothed over. The sharing in comfort is promised to those who share in the sufferings. If a person has arranged a Christianity that costs nothing, he should not be surprised that it consoles nothing. The deepest comforts of God are not stored where the weather is fine.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering will end soon. It means comfort will come with it. Nor is Paul assuming that every person in the Corinthian church is a true believer; he will warn them to examine themselves (13:5). His confidence is the confidence of love that hopes all things, grounded in what God does for his own.

What if the comfort has not come and it has been a long time? Then hold to the tense Paul uses: you will share. It is a certainty about the future, not a description of how you feel tonight. Some comfort comes quickly; some comes in small portions that only add up in hindsight; and some of God’s comfort is kept for the morning of the resurrection, when he will wipe away every tear. Meanwhile do not suffer in secret. Tell a pastor or a trusted friend, let the church carry you, and keep putting yourself where God speaks. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning (Psalm 30:5). The night has an end, and the one who promised it is faithful.

In a sentence. Our hope for you stands firm, because we know that just as you share our sufferings, you also share our comfort.

On a Tuesday. Think of one person you have quietly given up on: a wayward child, a cold friend, a struggling church member, a believer who keeps falling. Move the ground of your hope from their record to God’s character, and pray for them today on that basis. And if you are the one suffering, thank God for the partners he has given you in it, and tell one of them how you are actually doing.

For worship. The one who has never yet brought a child of his into affliction and left him there is not going to begin with you. His comfort is not may but will. He binds his people together so that their sufferings are shared and their consolations are shared, and over the whole fellowship he stands as the anchor that holds, the God whose faithfulness makes hope for the worst of us unshakeable (Romans 8:18).

verseByVerse.quote: For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.

For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. Of all the sentences Paul wrote, this is among the ones the church has most needed and least expected. The apostle who wrote that we are more than conquerors, who told the Philippians to rejoice always, who sang hymns at midnight with his back opened by rods (Acts 16:22–25), here says in plain words that he came to the point of despairing of life itself. Asia is the Roman province around Ephesus, and “brothers” includes the sisters of the church.

For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength. Take the words as they stand. Burdened is bareō, weighed down, crushed under a load. Utterly renders kath’ hyperbolēn, beyond all proportion, the phrase our word hyperbole comes from. Beyond our strength is hyper dynamin: past the limit of what he could carry. God let his apostle be given more than he could handle in his own strength.

That we despaired of life itself. The verb is exaporeomai: literally to be without a way out, at the end of every road, no exit visible in any direction. He is not saying that things were difficult. He is saying he could see no way he was coming out of it alive, and he stopped expecting to.

What was it? He does not tell us. The riot in Ephesus recorded in Acts 19:23–41 is the usual guess; some think of a near-fatal illness, others of an imprisonment or a plot we have no record of. The silence is frustrating and it may be a mercy, because a named crisis would let the reader file it under somebody else’s category. As it stands, whatever is crushing you fits the gap.

Oxygen for the despairing. Now hold this verse where it will do the most good, because there are readers for whom it is oxygen. There are Christians who have come to a place where they no longer wanted to be alive, and who have carried, on top of that darkness, the private conviction that a real believer could never get there. They have heard that despair is unbelief, and have concluded that whatever it is they have, it disqualifies them. This verse takes that conclusion away from them. The man who despaired of life itself is the man who wrote Romans 8. He was not backslidden when it happened; he was in the middle of the most fruitful ministry in Christian history. He was not weak in faith; he was an apostle. And he was not ashamed of it afterwards. He wrote it down, in a letter, to a church that already thought he was too weak, knowing they would read it aloud.

The saints have been here. Scripture has more of this than we usually admit. Elijah sat under a tree and asked to die (1 Kings 19:4). Jeremiah cursed the day he was born (Jeremiah 20:14). Job did the same (Job 3:1–3). The psalmist ended a psalm with darkness as his closest friend (Psalm 88:18), and God put it in the hymnbook. And in Gethsemane the Lord himself said that his soul was very sorrowful, even to death (Mark 14:34). The Bible does not hand us a faith that floats above the water. It hands us a faith that has been to the bottom.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul lost his faith. It means he lost hope in himself. And it does not contradict 1 Corinthians 10:13. That verse is about temptation to sin: God will never put you in a place where obedience is impossible and sinning is your only option. It is not a promise that you will never be given more suffering than you can carry. Paul says here that he was. The point of that weight is the next verse.

Is depression a sign of weak faith, and should a Christian get help? Darkness of mind is not in itself a sign of weak faith; Paul, Elijah and the psalmists knew it. Sometimes it has spiritual causes that need dealing with, such as unconfessed sin or bitterness, but often it has causes in the body, in grief, in exhaustion or in trauma. Seek help, as you would for any illness. Tell your pastor and a trusted friend. See your doctor, and do not be ashamed of medicine or counselling; using means is not distrusting God, any more than Paul’s advice to Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach was (1 Timothy 5:23). And if you are thinking of ending your life, tell someone today and contact emergency help now. You are not a burden to God’s people. You are one of them.

In a sentence. We want you to know, brothers and sisters, about the troubles we went through in Asia. We were under such crushing pressure, far beyond what we could bear, that we gave up hope of surviving.

On a Tuesday. If you feel crushed beyond your strength, you are not a failed Christian. Paul felt that too. Be honest with God about it, in words as plain as these, and be honest with one other believer. And if you are the one who is well, look around. Somebody in your church may be carrying a weight like this with a smile on Sunday. Ask them how they actually are, and wait for the answer.

For worship. The Lord of glory does not ask his people to pretend. He let his apostle go down to the very bottom, and then had him write it in Scripture, so that no believer who goes down there would ever think he was the first. And beneath the deepest place any of us has fallen lies the Son, who went lower still, into a sorrow even to death, so that the bottom of the pit would be a place where Christ has already stood.
verseByVerse.note: Paul does not say what the danger in Asia was; it may have been the riot at Ephesus, severe illness or another threat.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.

Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. The first sentence darkens the picture before the second lifts it. The sentence of death is to apokrima tou thanatou, and apokrima is a legal word: the official answer of a court, the verdict handed down. This is not a mood. It is a man who has heard the judgment read out and knows the appeal has failed. Inside himself, the case was closed.

But that was to make us rely not on ourselves. Then comes the word that turns the whole letter, and it is one of the smallest in the sentence: but that was to. There was a purpose. The thing had a design. This is the point at which honest readers need care taken with them, so let it be said carefully. Paul is not saying his suffering was pleasant, or light, or that he understood it at the time. He is not saying that every affliction comes with an explanation attached, and he is certainly not handing us a sentence to say breezily at a funeral. He is saying, looking back, that the crushing was not random. It was aimed, and the target was his self-reliance.

The end of himself. Consider what it takes to reach that target in a man like this. Paul was formidable. He had the training, the languages, the stamina, the courage, the intellect, the personal history with the risen Christ. If anyone had resources to fall back on, he did. And that is exactly the problem, because a man with resources will use them, and will keep on using them, and will never discover what God can do at the point where the resources are gone. Even an apostle can drift into trusting his own strength. There was no way to teach Paul this except to take him past the end of himself.

Where does your confidence rest? Not the answer you would give in a Bible study: the answer your body gives at three in the morning. When the letter arrives, what do you reach for first? The savings, the contacts, the plan, the argument you have rehearsed? There is nothing wrong with any of those, and God gave them. But if you have never once been past the end of them, then you do not yet know from experience whether the God you profess actually holds. Paul knows. It cost him everything he had to find out.

But on God who raises the dead. Notice the name he gives God at the moment of extremity: not the God who prevents death, not the God who explains death, but God who raises the dead. That is a very deliberate title. If the verdict of death has been passed and cannot be appealed, then what you need is not a rescuer who gets you off the charge. You need a God whose power operates on the far side of the sentence being carried out. And that is the God Christians have. Abraham trusted him when his own body was as good as dead, believing in the God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17), and he reasoned that God was able even to raise Isaac from the dead (Hebrews 11:19). Paul is not comforting himself with the thought that he will probably survive. He is resting on the fact that whether he survives or not, the God he serves has already emptied one tomb and has publicly committed himself to emptying the rest (1 Corinthians 15:20).

The ground floor. That is the ground floor beneath every Christian who has run out of options. When there is nothing left to rely on, there is still the God who raises the dead, and he does his best work precisely there. He did not begin the world’s salvation from a position of strength but from a sealed grave in a garden, with the case closed and the verdict carried out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God causes suffering carelessly or enjoys it. It means he uses it purposefully, and that the purpose is loving: to bring us to lean our whole weight on him.

Does God send my suffering, or only allow it? Scripture speaks of God as truly sovereign over our troubles, not a bystander who reacts to them. Nothing reaches his child by accident; even what others mean for evil, God means for good (Genesis 50:20), and he works all things together for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28). Yet he is never the author of sin, and the cruelty of people or of Satan remains theirs, not his. Scripture holds both together without explaining every case. For the sufferer the comfort is this: what is happening to you is not meaningless and not out of control. It is in the hands of a Father whose purpose for you is to bring you to rely on him, and finally to raise you from the dead.

In a sentence. In fact, in our hearts we felt we were under a death sentence. But this happened so that we would stop trusting ourselves and trust God, who raises the dead.

On a Tuesday. Name the thing you are relying on most to hold your life together: your health, your income, your competence, your reputation, a person. Thank God for it, and then hand it to him in words. Tell him that if it went, he would still be the God who raises the dead. If you are past the end of yourself already, you are standing exactly where Paul learned to trust.

For worship. Death is not the place where his power stops. It is the place where it was displayed. The Father let the verdict fall on his own Son, let the sentence be carried out and the stone rolled across, and then raised him on the third day, so that every one of his people who hears the sentence of death passed on himself would know whose hands he is in. The God of the empty tomb is the God of every believer at the end of his strength.

verseByVerse.quote: He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.

He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. The same verb three times in one short verse: he delivered, he will deliver, he will deliver again. Past, future, and future once more, as if Paul cannot say it enough times. The word is rhyomai: to snatch out, to drag someone clear of danger. It is what a man does when he pulls a child out from under a falling wall.

Memory and hope wired together. Notice that Paul’s memory and Paul’s expectation are joined. Because God did it, God will do it. The past tense is not nostalgia; it is evidence, and the evidence is what his hope is built on. This is one of the most practical habits in the Christian life and one of the most neglected. We are creatures with astonishingly short memories for mercy. We can be delivered in March and be certain by August that God has abandoned us, because we never wrote March down. Israel did this as a nation: they forgot his works and the wonders that he had shown them (Psalm 78:11). Paul does the opposite. At the moment he most needs confidence about the future, he goes back and looks at what has already happened.

What about the times he does not deliver? The harder question must not be dodged, because a reader will hit it within seconds. Paul, writing this, had perhaps a decade left before a Roman sword ended his life. The deliverance he is so sure of did not, in the end, keep him out of Nero’s hands. The answer is in the title he used one verse earlier. The God he is trusting is God who raises the dead, and a God like that has a wider definition of rescue than we do. Paul says as much to Timothy at the end, writing from prison: the Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom (2 Timothy 4:18). He did not mean he expected to be released. He meant that the sword would be the last thing that ever happened to him, and that on the far side of it he would be safe. Deliverance is not always deliverance from; sometimes it is deliverance through. Not one child of God has ever failed to arrive.

On him we have set our hope. The verb is in the perfect tense: a decision made that is still standing. Not a hope he feels when circumstances allow, but a stake driven into the ground, still there in the morning. Paul’s hope rests on God, not on circumstances. He had put his weight on God before the crisis and he has not shifted it since.

What has changed. It is worth seeing what has happened to a man over three verses. He began crushed beyond his strength and expecting to die. He ends certain that he will be delivered again. Nothing in his circumstances has changed between verse 8 and verse 10. What has changed is what he is looking at.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul would never die, or that the scan will be clear or the job saved. He was eventually martyred. But even then God delivered him, into his presence and to the resurrection. Read this verse as the promise it actually is: that nothing will take you out of his hand, and that whatever it costs to get you home, he will pay it (John 10:28).

How do I build this kind of memory? Keep a record. Write down, in a notebook or at the back of your Bible, the specific things God has carried you through and the prayers he has answered, with dates. Tell them to your children and to younger believers; Israel was commanded to do exactly this (Psalm 78:4). Sing hymns and psalms that rehearse God’s past faithfulness, because they train the memory. And when a new trouble comes, read the record before you decide what God is like. The facts on that page are part of your evidence, and they are admissible.

In a sentence. He rescued us from mortal danger, and he will rescue us again. We have set our hope on him to keep on rescuing us.

On a Tuesday. Remember one time God rescued you, in detail: where you were, what you feared, how it turned out. Write it down today. Then set it next to the thing you are afraid of now, and tell God that the one who did that will do this, whether by deliverance from it or deliverance through it.

For worship. He delivered, he will deliver, he will deliver again. The God of Israel, who snatched his people from Egypt and from Babylon, snatched his apostle from death in Asia and at last from death itself. No grave is the end of his rescue. Every deliverance in a believer’s life is a small rehearsal of the final one, when he who raised Jesus will raise us also and bring us with him into his presence (4:14).

verseByVerse.quote: You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.

You also must help us by prayer. Paul has just described a deliverance so far beyond his own resources that he had already written himself off. And then he tells a distant church that they have work to do in it. The verb translated help is a vivid one, synypourgeō, to work underneath alongside: the picture of several people getting their shoulders under the same load. It is not a request for good wishes. Paul is treating the prayers of ordinary Corinthian believers as genuine labour applied to his actual survival.

If God has decided, what does prayer change? It is the question every thinking Christian asks and seldom hears answered. If God had already decided to deliver Paul, what did the praying change? And if the praying changed it, is God being steered by us? The answer Scripture gives is not that God is persuadable but that he is generous. He ordains the end and he ordains the means to it, and he has chosen to make the prayers of his people one of the means. A father who could carry the box himself asks the four-year-old to take the other end, and the child really is carrying it. Nothing is being pretended. The father has arranged a world in which the child’s effort genuinely bears weight, because he wants the child in the work and not merely watching it. So here: the deliverance was God’s from first to last, and it came through the prayers of many, and both halves of that sentence are true.

So that many will give thanks on our behalf. Paul’s reason for wanting their prayers is not the one we would give. He does not say so that I will be delivered. He says so that many will give thanks. The point of the rescue, in his mind, is the volume of worship it will generate. Every person who prayed for him becomes a person who will hear that it was answered, and every one of those becomes a voice raised in thanksgiving. He wants the prayer list long because he wants the choir large.

For the blessing granted us through the prayers of many. The word for blessing is charisma, a gift of grace. Even the answer to prayer is grace, not wages. That reorders something in most of us. We tend to ask for prayer so that our situation will improve; the thanksgiving afterwards, if it happens at all, is a private postscript. Paul is thinking the other way round. God’s answer to a request is not the end of the transaction. It is the raw material of praise, and the more people involved in the asking, the more glory comes back to God in the getting.

No bystanders. Notice, finally, what this does to the smallest member of that church. Somewhere in Corinth there was a believer with no gift anyone could name, no money, no standing, who had never travelled further than the harbour. Paul’s sentence puts that person’s shoulder under an apostle’s survival in Asia. There are no bystanders in the kingdom.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is reluctant until enough people pray, as if answers were won by a petition with the most signatures. It means God has chosen to work through the prayers of his people, and loves to be thanked by many.

Does it matter how many people pray? Yes, but not because God is out-voted. The number matters because Paul wants many to share in the work and many to share in the thanks. God hears the single prayer of a lonely believer as surely as the prayer of a thousand (James 5:16–18). But he has made us a body, and he loves to answer in a way that draws many into the asking and many into the praise. So do ask others to pray for you; it is not weakness or self-importance. And when you are asked, pray, and later ask how it turned out.

In a sentence. And you help us by praying for us. Then many will thank God for the gracious answer he gives to the prayers of many.

On a Tuesday. Two things follow for ordinary church life. First: tell people what to pray for, and then tell them what happened. A congregation that hears the requests and never hears the outcomes is being robbed of the best half. Second: if you have prayed for someone and never learned the result, you have a thanksgiving still owed. Pray today for a missionary or pastor in danger or difficulty, by name; then find out how God answers, and give thanks aloud.

For worship. The God who could do everything alone has chosen not to. He invites the least of his people to put their shoulders under his work, and then he answers in such a way that the praise comes back from a multitude. The work of the church is done by people whose names are not recorded, and the God who keeps the record has never once mislaid one of them. Every answered prayer comes home to him as thanksgiving, which is where every blessing was always meant to end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–24 — The Yes of God in Christ and Paul’s Changed Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul defends his integrity. His conscience is clear: he has dealt with them openly and sincerely, by God’s grace rather than clever technique, and his letters mean what they say. His critics say his changed travel plans prove he is unreliable. Paul answers by pointing to God’s faithfulness: the message he preached was not a mixture of yes and no, because every promise God has made is confirmed in Christ, and the church says its Amen to that. It is God who keeps them firm, who has anointed and sealed them and given the Spirit as a first instalment. Paul stayed away to spare them a painful confrontation, not to dominate them; he wants to serve their joy.
verseByVerse.theology:
“All the promises of God find their Yes in him” (v. 20) — This is the hermeneutical key to the entire OT: every promise — to Abraham, to Moses, to David, through the prophets — is fulfilled in Christ. This does not mean every OT text is directly about Jesus; it means the entire trajectory of divine promise reaches its destination in him. The “Amen” that believers add in worship is their ratification of what God has already declared: yes, it is so, in Christ.

The Trinitarian shape of vv. 21–22 is worth noting: God establishes (the Father), anointed (chrisas — sharing the root with Christos), and sealed with the Spirit, giving the Spirit as a deposit (arrabōn — the down payment guaranteeing the full inheritance, as in Eph. 1:14). The three persons are active together in the believer’s assurance.
verseByVerse.examples: A church member accuses her pastor of inconsistency when he changes a ministry plan he had announced. He is tempted to defend himself by cataloguing the reasons. This passage suggests a different approach: the goal is not to vindicate the decision but to demonstrate that the change came from genuine care for those affected — the same reason Paul stayed away from Corinth. Integrity is not the absence of changed plans; it is the transparent, godly motivation behind all decisions, including the changes.

verseByVerse.quote: For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you. For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand— just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you. For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand—just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.

For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience. The tone changes here. Paul turns from what God has done in his suffering to what his critics have been saying about his character, and the charge behind these verses is that he is a man who cannot be trusted: that his letters say one thing and his intentions are another, that there is a hidden Paul behind the written one. His answer begins with a word that ought to make us uneasy: boast. It will run through the whole letter and turn into open, painful irony in chapters 10 to 12. Paul knows perfectly well that boasting is a sickness; he has already told this church that if anyone boasts he should boast in the Lord. But when a minister’s integrity is being publicly dismantled, silence is not humility. It leaves the people he serves with no ground to stand on. So he speaks, and he is careful about what he claims.

The testimony of our conscience. What he claims is the witness of his conscience. Not the verdict of the Corinthians, which is currently divided, and not his own self-assessment, which he elsewhere says proves nothing: I am not aware of anything against myself, but I am not thereby acquitted (1 Corinthians 4:3–4). Conscience is the internal witness that watches what we actually do when nobody is looking, and Paul’s is not accusing him.

That we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity. Two words describe how he has lived. Simplicity is haplotēs: singleness, the state of being one thing rather than two. Its opposite is the double life: the man in the pulpit and the different man in the car afterwards. Some manuscripts read holiness here instead, as the ESV notes, and the sense is close. And godly sincerity is eilikrineia, a word the ancients liked to explain as judged by sunlight: something held up to the light to see whether it is flawed all the way through. Paul is saying: hold my ministry to the light; it will bear inspection. No hidden agendas.

Not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you. Then the crucial qualifier, which keeps this from being self-congratulation. Not by worldly cleverness, manipulation or self-interest, but by God’s grace. He does not claim to have generated his own integrity. He is boasting about something he received, and especially in his dealings with the Corinthians themselves.

For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand. Here is the specific accusation answered. Some said Paul’s letters had hidden meanings. There is nothing between his lines. What the letter says on the surface is what he means underneath, with no code, no manipulation, no second layer for the initiated. Anyone who has been on the receiving end of a message that had to be decoded, from a colleague, a relative, a leader, knows what a rare and restful thing this is. Plain speech is a form of love, because it refuses to make the other person guess.

That on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you. Notice how far ahead he is looking. Partially they understand him now, and that partial understanding is painful; but he sets his hope on the day of our Lord Jesus, when the misunderstanding will be finished on both sides. On that day they will boast of him and he of them: mutual rejoicing, each as the fruit of God’s work in the other, all the accusations dissolved (Philippians 2:16; 1 Thessalonians 2:19–20).

When you cannot clear your name. That is worth holding if you are living inside a relationship where you have been misjudged and cannot fix it. Some misunderstandings do not get resolved in this life; some people will go to their graves with the wrong idea of you, and no amount of explaining will shift it. Paul, an apostle, could not clear his name in Corinth by writing about it. What he does instead is put the date of the hearing in the future and leave it there. There is a day coming when the Lord will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness (1 Corinthians 4:5), and on that day the vindication will not be yours to arrange, which is precisely what makes it worth waiting for.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was sinless. It means he had been honest and sincere in his ministry to them. A clear conscience is not a claim to perfection; it is the absence of known, unconfessed double-dealing.

What is conscience, and can it be wrong? Conscience is the inner sense, given by God, that judges our own actions as right or wrong (Romans 2:15). It is a real witness, and going against it is sin (Romans 14:23). But it is not infallible. It can be too tender, condemning what God allows, or too dull, excusing what God forbids, and it can be seared by repeated sin (1 Timothy 4:2). So a conscience must be taught by Scripture and kept clean by confession. A clear conscience does not make you right; only God’s word decides that. But a guilty conscience should never be ignored: take it to Christ, whose blood purifies the conscience (Hebrews 9:14), and put right what can be put right.

In a sentence. This is what we take pride in: our conscience tells us that we have lived in the world, and especially toward you, with integrity and God-given sincerity, relying not on worldly wisdom but on God’s grace. We write nothing you cannot read and understand. And Paul hopes that, as you have understood us in part, you will come to understand fully that on the day of the Lord Jesus you will be proud of us just as we will be proud of you.

On a Tuesday. Can you say with Paul that your conscience is clear in your dealings? Think of one place where you have been one person in public and another in private, or where your words have carried a hidden meaning: the email with a barb in it, the promise made to keep someone quiet, the reason you gave that was not the real reason. Put it right today, plainly. And if you have been misjudged and cannot fix it, stop rehearsing your defence and leave the hearing with the Lord.

For worship. There is one Judge before whom every heart is open, and on his day nothing hidden will stay hidden. For those who are in Christ that day holds no terror, because the one who searches the conscience is the one who washed it. He gives the grace that makes his servants sincere, he will bring every true thing to light, and on that day his people will rejoice in one another as his workmanship, and all the boasting will be in him.

verseByVerse.quote: Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace. I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea. Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace. I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea. Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?

Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first. Now we get the actual grievance. It sounds almost too small to have generated so much self-defence: Paul had announced a travel plan and had not kept to it. His original plan (1 Corinthians 16:5–7) had been to come through Macedonia to Corinth. He then changed it to a double visit, and then changed it again.

So that you might have a second experience of grace. The new plan was generous: Corinth twice, on the way north to Macedonia and again on the way back, instead of the single visit they had expected. He calls it a second grace, a second benefit, which tells us what he thought a visit from an apostle was for: not an inspection, a gift.

I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea. The plan: Corinth, Macedonia, Corinth again, then Judea with the collection for the poor saints in Jerusalem. Then the itinerary changed, and by the time this letter is written the double visit has not happened at all.

A small brick for a large case. It seems trivial. It was not, and it is worth understanding why, because the same dynamic operates in churches now. Paul’s opponents were not really interested in his diary. They were building a case about his character, and a broken travel plan was the most available brick. The pattern is familiar: a small verifiable failure is seized on, not for its own sake, but because it can be made to stand for a large unverifiable one. He changed his plans, therefore he is unreliable; he is unreliable, therefore his gospel cannot be trusted either.

Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Two questions, both expecting the answer no. Vacillating translates elaphria, lightness: the flightiness of a man whose word weighs nothing. Did I make plans carelessly?

Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time? According to the flesh does not mean sinful appetite here. It means deciding the way a person decides who has no reference point beyond his own convenience: for selfish reasons, to suit myself. The doubled Yes, yes and No, no is the picture of a man saying both at once to different audiences, agreeing with whoever is in the room, with no real commitment.

Is it a failure of integrity to change your mind? Clearly not, or Paul is condemned by his own defence. Scripture nowhere requires that a plan once announced must be carried out regardless of what has happened since. What it requires is that the reason be honest. The sin is not the changed plan; it is the changed plan made for self-serving reasons and then dressed up as principle. Paul will tell them in verse 23 exactly why he stayed away, and the reason turns out to be mercy toward them, the very people now complaining. So when a commitment has to be dropped, do not ask, can I justify this?, since almost anything can be justified given a few minutes. Ask instead: if the person affected could see my actual reasoning, would it look like care for them or convenience for me? That is the line between Paul and the man he is accused of being.

Explaining to people who have not earned it. The remarkable thing is that he takes the accusation seriously at all. He could have dismissed it as beneath him; an apostle does not owe the Corinthians his itinerary. Instead he explains himself, at length, to people who have not earned the explanation. That is what pastoral love looks like when it is inconvenient.

What it does not mean. It does not mean changing plans is always wrong. Paul changed his plans for good reasons (v. 23). Plans are made under God, if the Lord wills (James 4:15), and a Christian who changes course for love, wisdom or new light has not broken faith.

What about a promise that has become costly to keep? Then, as far as it is lawful, keep it. Scripture praises the one who swears to his own hurt and does not change (Psalm 15:4). Inconvenience, a better offer or a change of mood are not reasons to break your word. A promise may be set aside only if keeping it would mean sinning, if the other person releases you, or if circumstances genuinely make it impossible. In those cases, go to the person, explain honestly and early, apologise for what it costs them, and make it up to them where you can. Do not let them find out by your silence.

In a sentence. Because Paul was confident of this, he planned to visit you first so that you might be blessed twice: once on his way to Macedonia and again on his way back, so that you could send him on to Judea. Was he fickle when he planned this? Does he make plans in a worldly way, saying yes and no in the same breath?

On a Tuesday. Think of a commitment you have recently dropped or are about to drop: a meeting, a visit, a task you volunteered for.
