Apply Paul’s test: would your real reason look like care or convenience if they could see it? If it is convenience, keep the commitment. If it is a good reason, say so out loud to the person affected rather than letting them discover it, which is exactly what Paul is doing here, in writing, to a church that has every reason to read it uncharitably.

For worship. Behind every unreliable word of ours stands a God whose word has never once weighed nothing. He does not say Yes to please us in the morning and No in the evening. He makes his plans in perfect wisdom and love, and when his ways seem to change they are only unfolding what he purposed from the beginning. And he is patient with servants who must explain themselves, because he is the one making them people whose word can be trusted.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had changed his travel plans, and some at Corinth accused him of being unreliable.

verseByVerse.quote: As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.

As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. Watch what Paul does here, because it is one of the most audacious turns in his letters. He is defending a change of travel plans. Within two sentences he is describing the character of the eternal Son of God. That is not evasion; it is the recognition that the two questions are finally one. A messenger’s reliability is not a private matter about his diary. The people who heard the gospel from his mouth cannot easily hold that the man was double-tongued and the message was not. So he stakes the answer on something larger than himself, with what amounts to an oath: as surely as God is faithful. God does not say one thing and mean another, and Paul’s word, above all his preaching, rests on that.

For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I. Silvanus is Silas, who worked with Paul at Corinth when the church was founded (Acts 18:5). Three named men preached, so this is not one man’s word, and the message they preached was Christ himself.

Was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. Christ is not uncertain or contradictory. He is God’s definitive Yes, and the Greek tense says it has become Yes and stays Yes.

For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. Here is one of the great summits of the New Testament, often quoted without anyone noticing what it claims. All of them. Not most, not the obviously messianic ones, not the ones about a coming king while the rest are left in the file. Every commitment God has ever made to his people has arrived at its destination in Jesus Christ.

The outstanding balance. Set that against the Old Testament and see the scale of it. God promised Abraham a land, a seed and a blessing that would reach every nation on earth, and centuries later Abraham’s descendants were a small, conquered, disappointed people, and the nations were not blessed. He promised David a son whose throne would never end, and the throne of David ended with a blinded king led away in chains to Babylon (2 Kings 25:7). He promised through the prophets a new covenant, a cleansed heart, a shepherd, a return, a servant who would be pierced for transgressions. Century after century the promises accumulated and none of them were fully paid. Anyone reading the Old Testament and stopping at Malachi is looking at four hundred years of silence and an enormous outstanding balance.

Settled in one Person. Paul says the account was settled in one Person. The seed, the blessing to the nations, the throne, the covenant, the cleansing, the shepherd, the servant: every one of them says Yes in Jesus Christ. He is not merely the recipient of the promises; he is the fulfilment of them, and the God who made them has never once gone back on them.

That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory. This is why the church says Amen, and why the word is more than a signal that the prayer has stopped. Amen is a Hebrew word meaning it is firm, it is so, and it was said in worship to affirm what God has said. It belongs on the human side of the transaction. God says Yes; the church says Amen. He makes the commitment; we countersign it. And even the countersigning is through him: we do not have the standing to say it on our own. The whole exchange ends where it began, for his glory.

Does this mean I can claim any promise in the Bible, health or wealth, for myself? The promises find their Yes in him: they come to us through union with Christ and on his terms. The great promises of the gospel, forgiveness, the Spirit, adoption, the resurrection, are certain for every believer. Promises given to particular people in particular settings, such as the land to Israel or long life to the obedient, are not blank cheques for health and prosperity now. The promise that is ours in every case is that all things work together for good for those who love God (Romans 8:28), and he decides what that good is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every promise we want to claim is ours. It means every promise God made to his people is secured in Christ, and that none of them is provisional or waiting on our performance.

What if a promise seems unfulfilled in my life? Then read the promise carefully, and read the calendar of God. Some promises are already fully yours in Christ, such as forgiveness and adoption, whatever you feel. Some are being kept now, slowly, such as your growth in holiness. And some are kept in full only when Christ returns: no more tears, a resurrection body, the new creation. The saints of Hebrews 11 died not having received the things promised, but having seen and greeted them from afar (Hebrews 11:13). An unfinished promise is not a broken one. God’s Yes in Christ has already been spoken; the rest is delivery.

In a sentence. As surely as God is faithful, our message to you has not been yes and no at once. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom Silas, Timothy and Paul preached among you, was not yes and no; in him it has always been yes. However many promises God has made, they are yes in Christ. And so through him we say Amen, to the glory of God.

On a Tuesday. The promise that God works all things for good, that nothing separates you from his love, that he will never leave you, that he who began a good work will complete it: on a hard Tuesday every one of those can feel provisional, pending your performance. Pick one of them today. Write it down, read it aloud, and say Amen to it, deliberately, as your countersignature on what God has already said Yes to in Christ. The answer was given before you were born and does not come up for review.

For worship. Every hope God ever raised in a human heart, every altar, every sacrifice, every prophecy, every unfinished story in the Hebrew Scriptures, was reaching toward someone. It reached him. There is no promise of God anywhere in the Bible that terminates somewhere other than in Jesus Christ; he is where the whole thing was always going. God has spoken his final Yes, and it has a face and a name. To him, therefore, the Amen, and the glory, for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is Silas, who worked with Paul at Corinth. “Amen” means “it is true, so be it.”

verseByVerse.quote: And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.

And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ. Paul has just said that God’s promises are all Yes in Christ. The obvious question follows: how does an ordinary believer know that the Yes includes him? These two verses are the answer, and they are among the clearest statements of Christian assurance in the New Testament. Notice first who is doing the work. It is God who establishes: every verb in the sentence has God as its subject and believers as its object. Nobody here is establishing himself. And notice the little phrase with you: Paul puts himself and his critics inside the same sentence, held by the same hands. Whatever else is unresolved between them, this is not. Four things are said, and they build.

Establishes. The verb is bebaioō, the same root as the unshaken hope of verse 7: a legal and commercial word for confirming a contract so that it will stand up in court. It is in the present tense: not a thing God did once, but something he is doing continually. Your standing in Christ is being actively maintained, today, by someone other than you.

And has anointed us. In the Old Testament, oil was poured on the head of a prophet, a priest or a king to mark him out as set apart for God’s work. The word here is chrisas, from the same root as Christos, the Anointed One. Paul is saying that believers share in the anointing of the one they are named after. As Christ was anointed with the Spirit, so are those in him (1 John 2:20, 27). The anointing is no longer for a select few; every Christian has been marked out for God’s service. There is no second-class member of the body of Christ.

And who has also put his seal on us. A seal in the ancient world did two jobs. It marked ownership, as sacks of grain and jars of wine were stamped with the merchant’s sign, and it guaranteed that the contents had not been tampered with in transit. Both meanings apply. The Holy Spirit in a believer is God’s stamp saying this one is mine, and his guarantee that what he has sent will arrive intact (Ephesians 1:13–14; 4:30).

And given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee. The word is arrabōn, a commercial term, and it is startlingly concrete. It means the down payment: not a sample, not a gesture of goodwill, but the first instalment of an agreed price, which binds the payer to hand over the rest (5:5; Ephesians 1:14). In modern Greek the same word is used for an engagement ring. Sit with that, because it changes what the Christian life feels like. Whatever you have known of God, the moments when Scripture came alive, the peace that arrived from nowhere, the love for people you used to have no time for, the strange homesickness for a country you have never seen, is not the whole payment. It is the deposit. And a deposit is not merely a promise of more; it is the same currency as the rest, paid early. What awaits you is not different in kind from your best hour with God. It is that, without the interruptions, for ever.

Where Christians differ: assurance of salvation. Some teach that believers cannot be sure of their final salvation in this life, or that a true believer may finally fall away. Verdict: God himself establishes, anoints, seals and gives the Spirit as a guarantee. These are God’s acts, not ours, and they make the outcome certain. Believers can have a well-founded assurance, resting on God’s promises, the inner witness of the Spirit (Romans 8:16), and the evidence of his work in their lives (Westminster 18.2).

The weakest witness in the room. So here is the question to put to yourself when assurance is thin, and it is not the question we usually ask. We ask, do I feel saved?, which is asking the weakest witness in the room. Ask instead: has God established, anointed, sealed and paid a deposit on someone he intends to abandon? The security of a Christian does not rest on the strength of his grip on God. It rests on four actions of God on him, and every one of them was taken while he was still at his worst.

The whole Trinity in one sentence. See the whole Trinity at work here. The Father establishes; the anointing and the standing are in Christ; the Spirit is given as the deposit and the seal. Three persons, one operation, one purpose: that the people God has claimed should certainly arrive.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every believer always feels assured. Assurance can be weakened by sin or trial, and a true believer may wait long and struggle hard before he has it (Westminster 18.3–4). But God’s seal does not break. Nor does it mean that a person who lives in settled, unrepentant sin may comfort himself with the seal; the Spirit who seals is the Holy Spirit, and his presence shows itself in a growing hatred of sin.

When are we sealed: at baptism, or in a second experience? The seal is the Holy Spirit himself, given to every believer when he first trusts Christ: in him you also, when you heard the word of truth and believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit (Ephesians 1:13). It is not a later blessing reserved for some Christians, and it is not conferred by the water of baptism. Baptism, which this app holds is for believers, is the public sign that declares the Spirit’s work already done; many of our paedobaptist brothers call the sacraments seals as well, and we share with them the conviction that the sign does not save without faith. If you trust Christ, you have been sealed.

What about “anointed” leaders and special anointings today? The New Testament never divides Christians into the anointed and the ordinary. Every believer has the anointing of the Spirit (1 John 2:20). So be wary of anyone who claims a special anointing that places him beyond question or correction. God does gift and call particular men to preach and lead, and they deserve honour, but their teaching is tested by Scripture like everyone else’s (Acts 17:11). The anointing that matters is the one every humble believer already has.

In a sentence. Now it is God who makes both us and you stand firm in Christ. He anointed us, set his seal of ownership on us, and put his Spirit in our hearts as a deposit, guaranteeing what is to come.

On a Tuesday. You carry God’s seal and his down payment. When doubts come today, do not begin by taking your spiritual temperature. Say the four verbs to yourself: God establishes me, God anointed me, God sealed me, God gave me his Spirit as a pledge. Then live as one who belongs to him: the seal means ownership, and an owned life is spent on its owner’s business.

For worship. The Father has signed the contract, the Son has paid the price, and the Spirit has been given as the deposit and the ring. He has never lost one whom he sealed, and he has staked his own name on the delivery. What we have tasted of him now is the first instalment of the same glory, and the full sum is certain, because the one who owes it is God.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership. The word for “guarantee” was used in business for a first instalment or deposit, pledging that the full payment will follow.

verseByVerse.quote: But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.

But I call God to witness against me. At last the real reason. Paul stayed away, and it was not weakness, and it was not indifference. It was mercy. He introduces it with an oath, which is not something he does lightly: inviting divine scrutiny on his own motives, staking his life on what he says next and accepting the consequences if he is lying. The Corinthians could not see inside him. God could. It is a solemn way of saying: the reason I am about to give is the true one.

But did Jesus not say, Do not take an oath at all (Matthew 5:34)? He was condemning the casual and evasive swearing of his day, oaths used to make some promises binding and leave others loose; that is why he goes on, Let what you say be simply Yes or No (Matthew 5:37). He was not forbidding a solemn, truthful appeal to God. Paul makes such appeals (Romans 1:9; Galatians 1:20), God himself swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13–17), and Jesus answered when put under oath (Matthew 26:63–64). A Christian may take an oath in court or make marriage vows; what he may not do is need an oath to be believed.

It was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth. A visit would have been a confrontation. There had already been one painful visit, and another would have meant discipline exercised in person on a church only half repentant, coming with a rod (1 Corinthians 4:21). He did not want that for them. So he stayed away to give them time to repent, and wrote instead (2:1–4). The man accused of being unreliable turns out to have been protecting the very people who were filing the complaint, and could not say so at the time without making it worse.

The slower road. There is a whole ministry philosophy buried in that. It is often easier to confront than to wait. Confrontation feels decisive, and it discharges the tension in the person doing it. Paul chose the slower, more humiliating road: absorb the criticism, let them think what they will, and give the situation time to ripen. Anyone who has held back a hard conversation for the sake of the other person, and been thought cowardly for it, is standing where Paul stood.

Not that we lord it over your faith. He seems to catch himself. Talk of sparing them could sound like a man describing the punishment he graciously withheld, so he corrects the impression immediately, and in doing so gives the New Testament one of its sharpest statements on spiritual authority. Lord it over is kyrieuō: to exercise dominion, to rule as master. Jesus used the related word of the kings of the Gentiles when he told his disciples that it would not be so among them (Luke 22:25–26), and Peter tells elders not to be domineering over those in their charge (1 Peter 5:3). Note carefully what Paul disclaims dominion over: your faith. He has apostolic authority; he does not pretend otherwise, and he will use it in chapter 13. But it does not extend to standing between a believer and God.

The thing Paul refuses. This needs saying plainly, because it has been ignored with great damage. There are churches where a leader’s approval functions as the measure of a member’s standing with God; where questions are treated as rebellion; where major life decisions require clearance; where people are told that to leave is to leave the Lord. Every one of those is the thing Paul is refusing here. A minister who makes himself the gatekeeper of another Christian’s relationship with God has taken a place that is not his, and the New Testament calls it lording it.

But we work with you for your joy. What is offered instead is startling. Work with is synergoi, fellow workers: on the same side of the table, and the goal is not compliance but gladness. Ministers are helpers of believers’ joy. Any authority in the church that produces fear rather than joy has misunderstood its own job description.

For you stand firm in your faith. And the reason he gives is the most generous line in the chapter. This is the church of the factions and the lawsuits, the one that has been listening to men who despise him. And his verdict on them is that they are standing. Their faith rests on God, not on Paul. Not because they are impressive, but because they are held: the Master is able to make him stand (Romans 14:4).

Where Christians differ: church authority over conscience. Some churches claim authority to bind believers’ consciences in matters beyond Scripture. Verdict: Church leaders have real authority to teach Scripture and to discipline, but no authority to rule over faith or bind the conscience beyond what God’s word requires. God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster 20.2). Leaders serve believers’ joy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church leaders have no authority. Paul used his authority. It means authority serves, not dominates. Believers are still told to obey their leaders and submit to them, so that their work may be a joy and not a groan (Hebrews 13:17).

How do I tell faithful leadership from lording it? Faithful leaders point you to Scripture and let it bind your conscience, not their preferences. They welcome questions, explain their decisions, and can be corrected. They care about your joy in Christ more than your loyalty to them. They exercise discipline for open sin according to the word, not for disagreement with them. Lording it looks different: control over personal decisions the Bible leaves free, punishment of questions, secrecy, isolation from family and other churches, fear. And where there is abuse of any kind, it must never be tolerated or covered up. Speak to other elders or leaders outside the situation, report crimes to the authorities, and know that leaving such a church is not leaving Christ.

In a sentence. Paul calls God as his witness, and stakes his life on it: it was to spare you that he did not return to Corinth. Not that we rule over your faith; we work alongside you for your joy, because it is by faith you stand firm.

On a Tuesday. If you have any authority over others, as a parent, an employer, a small group leader, an elder, ask whether the people under you are more joyful in Christ because of you or more afraid of you. Ask one of them, and listen. And if you are holding back a hard conversation for someone’s sake, examine your motive: is it mercy, giving them time, or is it fear? Mercy waits with a purpose; fear only postpones. Pray today for your pastors, that they will lead as helpers of your joy, and pray for your own faith to stand firm in God.

For worship. That is where the chapter comes to rest. Paul does not need to control them, because their faith was never resting on him. He planted, he wrote and he wept, and the one who keeps them upright is Christ, the only Lord of the conscience, who has never yet let a believer fall out of his hand. The Chief Shepherd rules his flock not by fear but by love, laying down his life for the sheep, and every under-shepherd who works for their joy is only reflecting the gentleness of his King.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia:<sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>3</sup>Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,<sup>4</sup>who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.<sup>5</sup>For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.<sup>6</sup>If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.<sup>7</sup>Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.<sup>8</sup>For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.<sup>9</sup>Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.<sup>10</sup>He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.<sup>11</sup>You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.<sup>12</sup>For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you.<sup>13</sup>For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand—<sup>14</sup>just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.<sup>15</sup>Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace.<sup>16</sup>I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea.<sup>17</sup>Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?<sup>18</sup>As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No.<sup>19</sup>For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes.<sup>20</sup>For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.<sup>21</sup>And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us,<sup>22</sup>and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.<sup>23</sup>But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth.<sup>24</sup>Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.

2.title: Forgiveness, the Aroma of Christ, and the Triumph of God
2.overview:
Paul continues to explain why he did not come back to Corinth. After the “painful visit”, in which one man publicly wronged him, he chose to write a tearful letter instead of returning to discipline them in person. The letter worked: the church disciplined the man. Now Paul’s concern is the opposite danger. The punishment has been enough. They must forgive him, comfort him and reaffirm their love, or Satan will take advantage, whether by crushing the man with excessive grief or by splitting the church.

Then Paul tells of his anxiety at Troas, where he could not wait for Titus’s news and left an open door to go to Macedonia. Before finishing the story (it resumes at 7:5), he bursts into thanks. God leads his servants in a Roman triumphal procession, captives of Christ on display, and through them spreads the fragrance of Christ everywhere: to some a smell of death, to others of life. Who is adequate for that? Not those who peddle God’s word for profit, but those who speak sincerely, as sent by God, in his sight.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Severe Letter and Forgiveness of the Offender
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why he wrote a severe letter instead of making another painful visit: he did not want to grieve the very people who give him joy, and he wrote in anguish and tears, out of love. The man who caused the trouble has wronged the whole church, not just Paul, and the church has now disciplined him. That is enough. Paul urges them to forgive, comfort and openly welcome him back, so that he is not crushed by sorrow, and so that Satan does not exploit the situation. Their response will show whether they obey in everything, including restoration.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage teaches that church discipline has a defined goal: restoration, not condemnation. This is the consistent NT pattern: Matthew 18:15–20, Galatians 6:1, 1 Corinthians 5. Discipline protects the community and pursues the restoration of the erring member. When the discipline has achieved its purpose, continuing to withhold forgiveness becomes its own sin — a sin that Satan is actively happy to see, because it fractures the community and communicates to the world that the church’s gospel of forgiveness does not apply internally.
verseByVerse.examples: A church elder who was removed from office after a moral failure has spent two years in genuine repentance and restoration. The leadership has quietly re-engaged him in limited service; but a vocal minority insists that any restoration is a betrayal of those he hurt. This passage does not minimise the hurt — Paul explicitly says the offender has caused grief to some extent (v. 5). But it insists that the goal of discipline is always restoration, and that the refusal to forgive when repentance is genuine is not faithfulness; it is a gift to the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained?

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 2 continues Paul’s explanation of his change of plans and then opens the great theme of the letter: the nature of gospel ministry. First, he explains that he did not come because he did not want another painful visit; instead he wrote a tearful letter out of love (vv. 1–4). Second, he addresses the man who had caused the trouble. The church has disciplined him and he has repented; now they must forgive, comfort and reaffirm their love for him, so that Satan does not gain an advantage through excessive severity (vv. 5–11). Third, Paul recalls his anxiety waiting for Titus, and then bursts into thanks: God leads his servants in Christ’s triumphal procession and spreads the fragrance of Christ through them, a fragrance of life to some and death to others. No one is sufficient for that, but Paul speaks sincerely, as one sent by God, not as a peddler of God’s word (vv. 12–17). A chapter that begins with tears and a disciplined sinner ends with the whole world smelling of Christ’s victory.

For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. The word another carries a whole episode in it. Somewhere between the writing of 1 Corinthians and this letter, Paul went to Corinth and it went badly: so badly that he cannot bring himself to describe it, and so badly that he will not risk repeating it. “Painful” is lypē, grief, sorrow. The Acts narrative says nothing about this visit. We know of it only because of the scar tissue it left in these chapters.

Piecing the story together. Put the sequence together and the letter makes far more sense. Paul planted the church. He wrote 1 Corinthians. Then he made a short, unplanned crossing from Ephesus, the painful visit, during which someone in the congregation confronted and humiliated him publicly, and the church did not defend him. He went back. He then wrote a letter out of tears, which we no longer have, calling them to deal with the man. Titus carried it. Paul then waited, in agony, for news of how they had taken it. That waiting is what he is writing out of. So the changed travel plans of chapter 1 turn out to have this behind them. He did not stay away because he was avoiding trouble. He stayed away because a second confrontation, arriving before they had had time to respond, would have destroyed something.

For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained? This is one of the most disarming sentences in Paul, and it is worth reading twice, because what it exposes is that the apostle needs them. His argument is simply this: you are my joy. There is no reserve supply. If I come and wound you, I have wounded the only people who can make me glad, and I will go home emptier than I came. A man who did not care could confront them and feel nothing. Paul cannot confront them without paying for it himself, because the people he would have to hurt are the people his happiness depends on. Love makes the pastor’s happiness depend on his people’s well-being.

Not the man they had been told about. Notice what that does to the picture of authority the Corinthians had been forming. They had been told he was a domineering figure who wrote fierce letters from a safe distance and was unimpressive in the room. Here he is telling them that they hold his gladness in their hands.

Will this cost me anything? There is a searching question in this for anyone who has to speak hard truth to another person: a parent, an elder, a friend, a manager. Not, am I right? Usually you are, and being right is the cheapest part of it. Ask instead: will this cost me anything? If a rebuke costs the person delivering it nothing, something has gone wrong upstream. It has become an exercise of position rather than an act of love, and the one receiving it can always tell the difference. Real correction is expensive at both ends. That is why so little of it is done well, and why the little that is done well is remembered for a lifetime by the person who received it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul avoided confrontation. He confronted in writing. It means he chose the way and the time that would cause least harm and do most good.

Should a hard conversation be in person or in writing? Usually in person, where tone can be heard, questions asked and misunderstandings corrected on the spot; Jesus’ pattern begins with going to your brother (Matthew 18:15). But Paul shows there are times when writing is wiser: when a meeting would inflame things, when the other person needs time to think before responding, or when you need to choose your words with great care. Whichever you choose, never use writing to hide, to fire a parting shot, or to say what you would not say to the person’s face. Write as if you were sitting across the table, and re-read it the next morning before you send it.

In a sentence. So Paul decided not to make another painful visit to you. For if he grieves you, who is left to make him glad except the very people he has grieved?

On a Tuesday. When you must confront someone, ask God for wisdom about the best way and time, and then ask whether you love the person enough for it to cost you. If you would feel nothing about wounding them, wait and pray until you would. If you dread it because you love them, that dread is often a sign you are the right person to go.

For worship. The God who must sometimes wound his children never does it from a distance. The Father of mercies takes no pleasure in grieving those he loves; he does not willingly afflict (Lamentations 3:33). And when the greatest wound had to fall, he gave his own Son to bear it, so that every hard word he speaks to his people now comes from a heart that has already paid the cost of their joy.
verseByVerse.note: This painful visit is not recorded in Acts; it came between 1 and 2 Corinthians.

verseByVerse.quote: And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice, for I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice, for I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.

And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice. Here is the severe letter, and here is what it cost to write. He wrote first, so that when he came, things would already be resolved. A reader who meets the phrase will want to know what it was. Paul refers here and in 7:8 to a letter he wrote between 1 and 2 Corinthians, sent instead of a visit, dealing with the man who had wronged him. We do not have it. Some have suggested it survives as chapters 10 to 13 of this letter, but most scholars think it was a separate letter, and 1 Corinthians does not fit the description of a letter written with many tears. The straightforward reading is that it is simply lost.

A lost letter. That is worth sitting with for a moment. The Spirit of God preserved every word the church would need and did not preserve every word Paul wrote. Scripture is not the complete archive of apostolic correspondence; it is what God intended his people to have, and the canon he gave is complete. Nothing essential has slipped through his fingers.

For I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. Notice the confidence. He wrote the severe letter expecting it to work. Not hoping vaguely: expecting, because he believed that what made him glad and what made them glad were finally the same thing. There is a whole doctrine of the church hidden in that. These are not a minister and his clients with separate interests to be negotiated. They are one body, and when it goes right the joy is not divided between them but shared whole by each.

For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears. Now look at the cost. Much affliction. Anguish of heart. Many tears. The word behind anguish is synochē: a pressing together, a constriction, the feeling of the walls closing in. He did not dash it off. He wrote it the way you write something at one in the morning after four attempts, with your hands shaking. Faithful rebuke is painful for the one who gives it too.

Not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you. He says plainly what the aim was, and that sentence should be printed above every difficult conversation in the church. The letter caused pain; he does not deny it and will admit as much in chapter 7. But pain was not the purpose. Love was the purpose, and the pain was the route it had to take. Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6).

Anger or love? Which gives an unusually clear test for anyone about to say a hard thing. Rebuke that comes out of anger wants the other person to feel what you feel. Rebuke that comes out of love wants the other person to be restored, and would gladly skip the whole episode if there were another way. The two can use identical words. They are not remotely the same act, and the tears are usually where the difference shows. Anyone who has ever been afraid to send the message, and has sent it anyway, and has then lain awake, knows exactly where Paul was standing. He is not writing as a man for whom this comes easily. He is writing as a man who did the hard thing and then had to live through the silence afterwards.

What it does not mean. It does not mean rebuke should be avoided because it hurts. It means rebuke should flow from love and tears.

What if my loving rebuke is rejected? Then you have still done what love required, and the outcome is in God’s hands. Paul did not know, as he wrote, how the letter would be received; he had to wait for Titus. Give it time, keep praying, and do not repeat the rebuke louder or recruit others against the person. Keep the door open, and treat them kindly in the meantime. If the matter is serious sin in the church, Jesus gives further steps involving others (Matthew 18:16–17). But many rebukes do their work slowly, and the person who angrily rejected your words in March may come back to them in September.

In a sentence. Paul wrote as he did so that when he came he would not be grieved by those who should make him glad. He was confident that you would all share his joy. He wrote out of great distress and anguish of heart, with many tears, not to grieve you but to show you how much he loves you.

On a Tuesday. If you must correct someone, pray first, and let them see your love. Before you send the message or knock on the door, write down for yourself what you want for them: not what you want them to feel, but what you want them to become. If the answer is their restoration and joy, go. If the answer is that you want them to hurt, stop and deal with that in yourself first.

For worship. Behind the tears of the apostle stand the tears of his Lord, who wept over the city that would reject him and spoke his hardest words out of a heart breaking for the people who heard them. Every rebuke in Scripture is written in that ink. The Lord disciplines the one he loves (Hebrews 12:6), and his purpose in every wound is that his children should share his joy.
verseByVerse.note: This severe letter is probably lost; some think it is part of 2 Corinthians 10–13.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some measure—not to put it too severely—to all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some measure—not to put it too severely—to all of you.

Now if anyone has caused pain. Watch how carefully Paul handles this. He is the injured party. The man humiliated him in front of the church. And in the one sentence where he could press his own case, he does two remarkable things. He also tactfully avoids naming the man at all.

Who was this man? The older tradition took him to be the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 for living with his father’s wife, and pointed to the punishment by the majority (v. 6) and to Paul’s hope there that he would be saved (1 Corinthians 5:5). The more likely reading is that he was someone who had publicly opposed or insulted Paul during the painful visit. Paul speaks of the wrong as done against himself (v. 10; 7:12), not as sexual sin, and he is far gentler here than he was over the incest. Either way the lesson is the same: discipline aims at restoration, and when a man repents, the church must forgive and welcome him back (vv. 7–8).

He has caused it not to me. The first remarkable thing is that he refuses to make it personal. That is not literally true and everyone reading it knew so; Paul is deliberately declining to stand in the centre of the picture. He will not let the church treat this as a quarrel between two men, because the moment it becomes that, the congregation divides into supporters and the whole thing is lost. The injured leader who insists on his own injury turns a sin into a faction. Paul steps out of the way.

But in some measure, not to put it too severely, to all of you. The second is the extraordinary restraint. He is holding himself back mid-sentence. He could have said far more; the man had earned it. And with the pen in his hand and the entire province about to hear the letter read out, he chooses to understate. That is what it looks like when a wounded man refuses to use his platform to settle a score.

No private sins. But do not mistake the restraint for indifference. Notice what he actually claims: the pain was caused to all of you. This is a genuine and often-missed piece of biblical teaching. There is no such thing as a private sin in the body of Christ. We think of sin the way we think of a personal debt: my business, my conscience, my arrangement with God. Paul thinks of it the way a doctor thinks of an infection in a limb. A church is a body, and what is done in one member is felt in all of them, whether or not they can name what they are feeling (1 Corinthians 12:26; Joshua 7:1). This is why a congregation can become subtly cold, or guarded, or joyless, and nobody can point to a cause. Something was done, and the body registered it.

Whom did it touch? Test it against your own experience. Think of the last time you were harsh at home, or dishonest at work, or nursed a grudge through a Sunday morning. Whom did it touch? The honest answer is never only me. There was a wife who found you difficult that evening, a colleague who learned something about how things are done, a child who was watching. Sin is never contained where it is committed, and this is one of the reasons the New Testament takes church discipline seriously at all: it is not the policing of private morals but the care of a shared body. And it is the reason forgiveness, when it comes in the next verses, has to be shared too. If the whole body was wounded, the whole body must do the healing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was not hurt. It means he will not make his hurt the issue.

When someone wrongs me, should I keep it private or tell the church? Begin privately. Most personal wrongs should be covered by love and never mentioned again (1 Peter 4:8; Proverbs 19:11). If a wrong is too serious to overlook, go to the person alone first (Matthew 18:15), and only if he will not listen involve one or two others, and then the church. Do not talk about it to everyone else in the meantime; that is gossip, and it turns a sin into a faction, exactly what Paul refuses to do here. The exception is crime and abuse: those must be reported to the proper authorities and the church leaders, and a victim is never required to confront an abuser alone.

In a sentence. If anyone has caused grief, he has not so much grieved Paul as he has grieved all of you to some extent, not to put it too strongly.

On a Tuesday. When someone wrongs you, resist making it all about you. Think of the wider good: the church, the family, the team. Before you tell anyone else how you were treated, ask whether telling them will heal the body or divide it. And think honestly about your own recent sins, and the people they touched, and make one thing right.

For worship. There was one who was wronged more than any man has ever been wronged, and he did not make the injury the centre of the story. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). He bore the sin of his people in his own body, so that the wounds of the whole church could be healed by his. The body that is hurt by every sin is joined to a Head who was wounded for all of them.
verseByVerse.note: The offender is unnamed; he is most likely not the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 but someone who had publicly opposed Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough, so you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough, so you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.

For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough. Two words carry this passage, and both cut against the way churches usually behave. The first is enough. “Punishment” is epitimia, a rebuke or penalty: church discipline. By the majority means the church acted together, though perhaps a minority wanted more severity, or none. The discipline had a limit, and the limit has been reached. Paul is not asking whether the man has suffered as much as he deserved; that question, asked honestly, would never be answered yes about anyone, including the people asking it. He is asking whether the discipline has done its work. It has. So it stops.

Hard to start, harder to end. This needs saying because the natural drift of a congregation is the other way. Discipline is difficult to start and far more difficult to end. Once a person has been put outside, a kind of settled respectability attaches to keeping him there; the ones who want him back can be made to look soft on sin, and no one ever gets criticised for being too rigorous. Paul cuts straight through that. A church that cannot say this punishment is enough has not understood what discipline was for.

So you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him. Notice the phrase rather turn. It is a change of direction, and it is required of the same people who administered the discipline. The majority who voted to exclude are the majority who must now go and get him. Forgiveness in the church is not the private decision of the person most offended; it is a shared act, as public as the discipline was. And the instruction is not merely forgive. Forgive is charizomai, to show grace, the word built on grace itself. And comfort is the same word again from chapter 1, parakaleō, to come alongside. The man is to be walked back in, not merely permitted to return. Someone has to sit next to him (Galatians 6:1).

Or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. The second word is overwhelmed. The Greek is katapinō: to swallow down, to gulp whole. It is the word used of the Egyptians drowned in the sea and of death being swallowed up in victory (Hebrews 11:29; 1 Corinthians 15:54). Paul is picturing a man going under. And the thing swallowing him is not his sin. It is his sorrow.

The danger nobody guards against. Sit with that, because it identifies a danger the church almost never guards against. We are alert to the man who repents too little. Paul is alert to the man who is destroyed by grief over what he has done: who has repented, and cannot get up, and has begun to sink under the weight of a guilt that has already been dealt with. Judas is the standing warning: he was sorry, genuinely and violently sorry, and his sorrow killed him (Matthew 27:3–5). Peter denied Christ three times with oaths and was restored over breakfast on a beach (John 21:9–17).

If you are the one who is sinking. Hear the verse aimed at you. There is a sorrow that God uses and a sorrow that Satan uses, and they can feel identical from the inside. The difference is where they end. One drives you to Christ and leaves you lighter. The other drives you in circles round your own failure and leaves you heavier every time (7:10). Paul is so concerned about the second that he writes to an entire province to stop it happening to one man.

What it does not mean. It does not mean discipline should be skipped. It means discipline must end in forgiveness when there is repentance.

What is church discipline, and when is it used? Church discipline is the loving correction of a church member by the church, following Christ’s instructions (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5). Most of it is quiet and private: a brother going to a brother. Formal discipline, up to removal from membership and the Lord’s Table, is for serious, public or persistent sin where the person refuses to repent after patient appeals. Its aims are the restoration of the sinner, the purity of the church and the honour of Christ, never revenge or the protection of a leader’s reputation. And as this verse shows, the moment of genuine repentance is the moment the church turns, wholeheartedly, to forgive.

How can a church tell the repentance is real? Not by a perfect performance, but by fruit: the person owns the sin plainly without blaming others, grieves over the harm done, puts right what can be put right, accepts accountability, and turns from the sin over time (Luke 3:8; 2 Corinthians 7:11). The church should be careful but not suspicious, and should never demand a level of grief that would crush. Where trust has to be rebuilt, as after serious sin, the forgiveness is still full and immediate; the rebuilding of trust follows over time.

In a sentence. The punishment the majority gave him is enough. Now you should forgive and comfort him instead, so that he is not overwhelmed by too much grief.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone who has repented whom you have not fully forgiven: someone you still keep at a distance, still mention in a certain tone, still watch for the next failure? Forgive and comfort them, as Christ has you. Do something concrete this week: a call, an invitation, a word of welcome. And if you are the one who has repented and cannot stop sinking, tell a pastor or a trusted friend that you need help believing you are forgiven. That help is exactly what this verse commands the church to give.

For worship. God himself is the God who says enough. He does not keep his anger for ever (Psalm 103:9); as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us. He did not merely permit the prodigal to return; he ran, and embraced him, and put a ring on his hand (Luke 15:20–22). Every restored sinner in the church is a small picture of that Father, and of the Son who swallowed up the sorrow that would have swallowed us.

verseByVerse.quote: So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him.

So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him. A single line, and two things in it are worth stopping for. The first is the verb beg. It is parakaleō once more, the same root as the comfort of chapter 1, used here in its urgent sense: I appeal to you, I plead with you. An apostle with authority to command is pleading instead. He does this repeatedly in his letters and it is never accidental. Some things cannot be commanded into existence. You can order a church to readmit a man; you cannot order it to love him, and a readmission without love would be a worse cruelty than exclusion.

Reaffirm. The second is the word behind reaffirm: kyroō. It is a legal term. It means to ratify, to validate, to make something officially and publicly binding: the word for confirming a will or ratifying a treaty. Paul is not asking them only to feel warmer toward the man. He is asking them to perform a public act, as public as the discipline was. Not just tolerate, but love.

Forgiveness made public. That distinction matters enormously in practice, and the church has largely lost it. We have made forgiveness an interior condition: something you do in your heart, alone, which the other person may never learn about. Paul makes it a public act. The man was disciplined publicly; he is to be restored publicly. Somebody has to stand up and say, in front of the people who watched him fall, that this man is ours and we love him.

Why it matters. Because a restoration that is never announced is not believed. The man himself will not believe it. He will come back into the room and read every face, and wonder what is being said when he leaves, and carry his disgrace round with him for years like a coat he cannot take off. And the congregation will not believe it either; some will assume the matter is still open, and the whispering will simply move underground. A public sin healed in private is not healed.

What was done for Paul. That is what Paul is begging for, and he is begging for it because it is exactly what was done for him. Saul of Tarsus was not quietly tolerated by the church he had been hunting. Barnabas took him, brought him to the apostles, and vouched for him out loud (Acts 9:27). Someone stood up in the room and put his own name against the man everyone was afraid of. The church has been in the business of ratifying love for former enemies ever since, because that is precisely the business its Lord was in first.

What it does not mean. It does not mean pretending nothing happened. It means welcoming him back fully, in a way he cannot doubt.

Should a restored person go straight back into leadership? Not necessarily. Forgiveness restores a person to the fellowship and the Lord’s Table at once and completely. Restoration to an office of trust is a separate question, governed by the qualifications God gives for leaders, who must be above reproach (1 Timothy 3:2). After serious sin that may take a long time, or may not be wise at all. And where the sin was abuse of any kind, the person must not be placed again in a position of trust over the vulnerable, however sincere the repentance; protecting the weak is itself an act of love. None of this withdraws forgiveness. It is simply wisdom about trust.

In a sentence. So Paul urges you to confirm your love for him publicly.

On a Tuesday. Is there someone among you, in your church or your family, who has repented and been forgiven, and who has never been told so in a way he could not doubt? Not hinted at. Not implied by being allowed to stay. Told: with a hand on the shoulder, a place at the table, or a job to do that only a trusted person would be given. When someone repents, do not keep them at arm’s length. Show them your love clearly, this week.

For worship. Our forgiveness was never a private, unannounced arrangement. God ratified it in public: at the cross before the watching world, in the empty tomb on the third day, in baptism before the congregation, at the Lord’s Table week by week. He has declared it out loud so that his children would never have to wonder. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1), and he has said so where everyone could hear.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is why I wrote, that I might test you and know whether you are obedient in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is why I wrote, that I might test you and know whether you are obedient in everything.

For this is why I wrote, that I might test you. The sentence sounds, on first reading, like something a modern reader will flinch at. Was the severe letter a loyalty test? Did Paul manufacture a crisis to see whether the Corinthians would jump when he said so? Take the objection seriously, because it is the sort of thing a reader wonders and commentaries often glide past. If Paul is testing whether they will do what he says simply because he says it, this is the very domineering behaviour he disclaimed in 1:24. The two verses cannot both be true in that reading.

What is being tested. So look at what the obedience is actually to. The word Paul uses, dokimē, means proving something to see whether it is genuine: character proven by testing, as metal is assayed, not as a student is trapped. And the thing being proved is not their loyalty to him personally. It is whether a church that has received the gospel will act on it when acting is costly and awkward. They had to confront a man many of them liked. Now they have to forgive a man some of them are still angry with. Both are obedience, and neither is comfortable, and the second is harder than the first.

And know whether you are obedient in everything. Note the little phrase in everything. This is the whole issue. Half-obedience is the standing temptation of religious people: we assemble a personal edition of the Christian life out of the commands we already find agreeable and let the others quietly lapse. Nobody does this deliberately. It happens by attrition, one avoided verse at a time. They passed the first test by disciplining the offender. Now obedience means forgiving him.

The command treated as optional. Try answering a narrower question. Not, do I obey God?, which almost everyone answers yes to. Ask instead: what is the command I have been treating as optional? Everyone who has walked with God for any length of time knows the answer within about three seconds: the relationship not repaired, the giving never adjusted, the habit reasoned with rather than killed, the person not forgiven. That immediate answer is the thing this verse is about.

Always working on them. And observe how Paul frames the whole affair. He does not say the letter was written to punish the offender. He says it was written to prove the church. The offender was the occasion; the congregation was the concern. He was always working on them. There is comfort in that as well as challenge, because God does the same. Most of us think of a trial as a thing that has happened to us; Scripture keeps insisting it is also a thing being worked in us. The situation is real, the pain is real, and underneath it something is being assayed and shown to be genuine: the tested genuineness of your faith, more precious than gold that perishes (1 Peter 1:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wanted blind obedience to himself. He wanted obedience to Christ, expressed through apostolic teaching.

Does obeying in everything mean obeying my pastor in everything? No. Paul’s authority as an apostle was unique, and his commands are now in Scripture, which binds every Christian. Your pastors and elders are to be respected and followed as they teach and apply God’s word (Hebrews 13:17), and you should not resist them lightly. But they cannot command what Scripture does not, and you must not obey them if they tell you to sin; we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). Obedience in everything means obedience to Christ in every area of life, including the hard and costly ones like forgiveness.

In a sentence. Another reason Paul wrote was to see whether you would stand the test and be obedient in everything.

On a Tuesday. Name the command you have been treating as optional. Write it down. Then take one step of obedience in it this week, however small: the phone call, the adjusted budget, the apology, the habit cut off. Obedience includes the hard step of forgiveness, and it is usually the hard step that shows whether the rest is real.

For worship. There was one Son who was obedient in everything, to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). He never once treated a command of his Father as optional, and his perfect obedience is counted to everyone who trusts him. And the same God who tests his children does it as a refiner, not a prosecutor: he is not merely getting you through the trial. He is proving something in you, and he intends to show it to you, to his praise, on the day Christ is revealed.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.

Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Paul now binds himself to their decision. Whatever they forgive, he forgives, and the man had wronged him more than any of them. He does not reserve the right to hold on privately to an injury the church has released.

Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ. Paul plays down his own hurt: if I have forgiven anything. And then a phrase that lifts the whole matter off the ground: in the presence of Christ, literally in the face of Christ, under his gaze. Forgiveness in the church is not a social convenience or an agreement to move on. It is transacted in front of the Lord, by his authority, in imitation of what he has already done. Which is exactly the ground Paul gives elsewhere: as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive (Colossians 3:13).

Does forgiving mean feeling differently? No. It means deciding, before Christ, not to hold the debt against the person any longer: not to raise it, not to punish with it, not to run it again in your mind at two in the morning. Feelings usually follow that decision, sometimes slowly, sometimes years later. They are the fruit, not the entry fee. If the old anger rises again, forgive again; that is not failure but the ordinary work of a forgiving heart.

Does forgiving mean restoring trust? Not automatically. Forgiveness is released freely, because that is how it was given to us. Trust is rebuilt over time and by evidence, and it is not unloving to say so. A forgiven embezzler need not be handed the accounts. But notice the direction Paul is pushing this church: they are drifting toward too little restoration, not too much, and he is pushing back hard.

Does it mean pretending nothing happened? No. Paul says what happened in this very paragraph. Forgiveness that requires everyone to lie about the past is not forgiveness; it is suppression, and it always leaks.

What if the person has not repented? Then you are still to forgive in your heart, letting go of bitterness and revenge and leaving judgment to God (Mark 11:25; Romans 12:19), and you are to stand ready to be reconciled the moment he turns. But full reconciliation, the restored relationship, waits on repentance: if your brother sins, rebuke him, and if he repents, forgive him (Luke 17:3). God himself forgives the repentant. So you need not pretend the wrong is resolved, or put yourself back in harm’s way. You can be free of hatred and still wait, praying, for the person to come home.

So that we would not be outwitted by Satan. Then comes the reason, and it is startling. The word is pleonekteō: to take advantage of, to get the better of someone in a transaction, to cheat a man out of what should have been his. Paul is saying that an unforgiving church has been swindled. It thought it was defending righteousness and has been robbed. Satan uses unforgiveness to divide churches, to crush repentant sinners, and to make discipline harsh. Harsh, unending discipline plays into his hands as much as no discipline at all.

For we are not ignorant of his designs. Noēmata: schemes, thought-out plans. This is not a chaotic force of malice but strategy (Ephesians 6:11). And it is worth noticing what Paul, of all people, identifies as one of the enemy’s chief instruments in a church. Not persecution. Not heresy. Not immorality. A congregation that will not forgive a repentant man. That is the door left open, and Paul writes to a whole province to get it shut. Which tells you what forgiveness is really about. It was never merely the settling of a grievance between two people. It is the church displaying, in public, the one thing it exists to announce, and the enemy knows that a body which will not do inside its own doors what it proclaims at them has made the announcement unbelievable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Satan is behind every problem. It means he exploits our sins, including the sin of unforgiveness. He is real and he is clever, but he is a defeated enemy, and his schemes are known to those who read God’s word.

In a sentence. Anyone you forgive, Paul forgives too. And what he has forgiven, if there was anything to forgive, he has forgiven in the sight of Christ for your sake, so that Satan might not outwit us. For we know his schemes.

On a Tuesday. Unforgiveness gives Satan a foothold (Ephesians 4:26–27). Name the person you are still holding something against. Say to God, in the presence of Christ, that you release the debt: you will not raise it, punish with it or rehearse it. If it is right, tell the person. Forgive today, and close the door on him.

For worship. Every forgiveness among Christians is done in the face of Christ, and that face is the face of the one who forgave us first, at the cost of his own blood. He prayed for those who were driving in the nails. He knows Satan’s schemes better than any of us, and he has already crushed the serpent’s head. When his people forgive one another, the accuser is silenced and the gospel is seen, and the glory belongs to the Lamb who made forgiveness possible.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul resumes the story of his journey. At Troas there was an open door for the gospel, but he was too anxious about Corinth to stay when Titus did not arrive, so he went on to Macedonia. Before telling what happened next, he breaks into thanks. He pictures God leading him as a captive in Christ’s victory parade, with the scent of the knowledge of Christ spreading wherever he goes. To some that scent means death, to others life. No one is adequate for such a task, but Paul, unlike those who sell a diluted message, speaks sincerely as one sent by God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The triumphal procession image is rich and theologically precise. In a Roman triumph, captives were led in chains behind the victor — some to be executed at the procession’s end, some to be enslaved. Paul’s use of the image for himself is deliberately surprising: the apostle is not the victorious general but a captive in Christ’s train. Yet this is not degradation — to be a captive of Christ, led in his triumph, is the highest possible dignity. The early church’s constant refrain — “slave of Christ” (doulos Christou) — captures the same paradox: absolute belonging to Christ is absolute dignity.

The double effect of the gospel (life to some, death to others) is grounded in passages like Isaiah 8:14 (the stone of stumbling) and Luke 2:34 (this child is set for the falling and rising of many). The gospel is not universally received, but this is not a failure of the gospel; it is a revelation of the human heart. The same sun that softens wax hardens clay — not because the sun changed but because the materials are different.
verseByVerse.examples: A missionary returns from several years in a largely unresponsive field and struggles with a sense of failure — very few converts, considerable opposition. This passage speaks to him directly: the task is not to produce results but to be the aroma of Christ. The spreading of the fragrance is the mission; the effect — life or death — belongs to God and to the hearts of those who encounter it. Faithfulness is measured by the aroma, not by the response.

verseByVerse.quote: When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord, my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord, my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.

When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ. Two verses of travel narrative, and they contain one of the most honest admissions in the New Testament. Troas was a port on the Aegean coast of Asia, near ancient Troy, and Paul went there after leaving Ephesus. The situation is this. Paul had sent Titus to Corinth with the severe letter and had arranged to meet him, it seems, so as to hear how it had been received. He arrives. Titus is not there.

Even though a door was opened for me in the Lord. And Paul discovers that God has opened a door for the gospel in Troas: the phrase he uses elsewhere for a genuine, God-given opportunity (1 Corinthians 16:9; Colossians 4:3). Preaching is bearing fruit. It is exactly what he lives for.

My spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. And he cannot do it. Not at rest translates a phrase built on anesis: the loosening of tension, the relief of a strap being let out. He had none. Titus was a trusted co-worker who had carried the severe letter, and Paul was desperate to hear how the Corinthians had responded. He could not concentrate for worrying about a letter and a church and a friend who had not arrived.

So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia. So he closed an open door and went to Macedonia to look for Titus. The story resumes in 7:5. Consider how much this admission cost a man whose critics were saying he was weak. He could have left it out. Instead he tells a church that already doubts him that he was so anxious he walked away from fruitful work.

An open door is not always a command. We are often taught that an opportunity is the will of God by definition, and that to walk away is disobedience. Paul walked away from one. He does not apologise for it here, and Luke records that the church at Troas was later flourishing anyway (Acts 20:6–12). God is not so short of workers that the gospel collapses when one exhausted man goes to find his friend. There are seasons where the most spiritual thing available to you is not the open door but the unfinished relationship.

Is anxiety a sin? The anxiety is in the Bible, unrebuked. Paul wrote do not be anxious about anything (Philippians 4:6), and here he is, anxious, and God did not delete it from the record. That should be handled carefully by anyone who has been told that all their worry is simply sin to be repented of and dropped. What Philippians forbids is anxiety left to run: worry that is never brought anywhere, that distrusts God and will not be turned into prayer. What we see here is a man whose distress drove him across a sea to find out how his people were. His agitation had a direction, and the direction was love. Notice too what it was about: not his own reputation, not his safety, not his finances. He could not settle because he did not know how the church was. Paul elsewhere calls it his daily pressure, the anxiety for all the churches (11:28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was wrong to leave. Love for the Corinthians was also gospel work. Nor does it mean that every restlessness is a reason to abandon a task; Paul left for a particular, loving reason, and did not stop preaching in Macedonia.

What do I do with anxiety for someone I love? Bring it to God, specifically and repeatedly; that is what Philippians 4:6 commands, with thanksgiving. Then do what love can rightly do: Paul went to find Titus. Write, call, visit, ask. Where nothing can be done, keep praying and entrust the person to the God who loves them more than you do. Talk to a friend who will pray with you. And if anxiety becomes constant and disabling, seek help from your pastor and your doctor; that is not a lack of faith. Love without news is hard to bear, and God does not despise the sleepless.

In a sentence. When Paul went to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ and found that the Lord had opened a door for him, he still had no peace of mind, because he did not find his brother Titus there. So he said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.

On a Tuesday. Anyone who has lain awake over someone else’s soul, a child who has stopped coming, a friend who will not speak, a congregation in trouble, is in company here. That kind of sleeplessness is not a failure of faith. It is what love feels like when it has no news yet. Bring your anxieties for others to God tonight, by name. And if there is an unfinished relationship that matters more right now than the next opportunity, it may be that the open door can wait.

For worship. The Lord who opened the door at Troas did not withdraw his love from the anxious apostle who walked through another one. He knew the restlessness, he sent Titus at last with good news (7:6), and he went on building his church in Troas without him. Our God comforts the downcast, and his work never depends on the steadiness of our nerves.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast of Asia. Titus was a trusted Gentile co-worker, sent to Corinth with the severe letter.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.

But thanks be to God. Paul has just told us he was too distressed to preach. The sentence has not finished settling before it bursts into one of the great doxologies of the New Testament, as he remembers how God answered his anxiety (7:6). He will not return to the story of Titus until chapter 7. Between here and there stands the most sustained account of Christian ministry he ever wrote, and it begins with a parade.

Who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession. Every reader in the first century knew the picture. A Roman triumph was the highest honour the state could confer, granted only for a decisive victory. The general rode through the city in a chariot; his troops followed; the spoils were carried past; and behind them came the prisoners in chains, some to be sold, some to be executed when the procession reached the temple. Now the surprise. The verb thriambeuō, when it takes an object as it does here, is most naturally taken to mean leading someone as a captive in the procession, not as a fellow victor. Paul has put himself in the chains.

The conquered one. That is not false modesty; it is the whole argument of the letter in one image. His critics looked at the beatings and the imprisonments and saw a defeated man. Paul says: quite so. I am the conquered one, taken on the Damascus road by a Lord I was fighting, and marched ever since wherever he pleases. This is not a picture of Paul’s triumph, but of Christ’s triumph over Paul, which looks like weakness and suffering (1 Corinthians 4:9). What looks like humiliation is participation in someone else’s victory, and there is no higher position available to a human being than to be a trophy of Jesus Christ.

And through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere. Then the incense. All along the route of a triumph, incense burned on altars, so the whole city smelled of the victory for a day. As the captive is led along, the smell of the triumph clings to him, and through Paul’s preaching the knowledge of Christ spreads like a fragrance. Christians carry the atmosphere of the conquering Christ into ordinary rooms without doing anything theatrical. A fragrance cannot be argued with and cannot be kept in. It arrives before the speech does. Most people who come to Christ can name someone whose life simply smelled different.

Always. But the word to hold on to is always. Not usually. Not when the church is flourishing and the preacher is in good voice. He was writing as a man who had recently despaired of life, who had just walked away from an open door because he was too troubled to use it. In that state, anxious, sleepless, criticised, unable to work, he was still being led in triumph. The parade did not pause while he struggled. He was in it the whole time and could not see it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Christian life is constant success. Paul speaks of triumph right after admitting his restless anxiety. The triumph is Christ’s, not ours, and it is often hidden under weakness.

How do I spread the fragrance of Christ in an ordinary week? Mostly by being near Christ, because a fragrance is caught before it is given. Spend time with him in his word and in prayer, and you will carry something of him into the room. Then live in a way that smells of him: honesty when a lie would be easier, kindness to people who cannot repay you, joy that does not depend on circumstances, patience in suffering. And speak of him. The fragrance in this verse is the knowledge of him, and that needs words: what he has done, who he is, why you trust him. Life without words is a scent with no name; words without life are a label on an empty bottle.

In a sentence. But thanks be to God, who always leads us as captives in Christ’s victory parade, and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of knowing him.

On a Tuesday. You are Christ’s captive, and part of his victory. If this week feels like defeat, tell yourself the truth of this verse: you are in the procession, and it has not paused. Then ask God for one opportunity today to let someone catch the fragrance: one honest word, one kindness, one sentence about Jesus.

For worship. Here is the truth to leave unapplied, because it is bigger than any use we could put it to. The procession is not ours and its outcome was never in doubt. Christ went into the one territory nobody had ever come back from, and came out of it in the morning with the keys, and he has been leading his captives home ever since: through prisons, through hospital wards, through the years nothing seemed to be happening.
