Thanks be to God. The triumph is his, the route is his, and not one of the chained is ashamed of the chains.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman triumph was a victory parade through the city; captives were led in chains, and incense was burned along the route.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?

For we are the aroma of Christ to God. The incense keeps burning, and now Paul says something about who smells it first. The word is euōdia, a sweet smell, the word used of sacrifices pleasing to God (Genesis 8:21; Ephesians 5:2). Before the gospel ministry is anything to the world, it is an offering to God, and it pleases him whatever the results. When a faithful Christian speaks of Christ to an empty room or a hostile face, the first one who receives it is the Father, and to him it smells of his Son.

Among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. Now Paul says something uncomfortable. The same smell means opposite things depending on who is breathing it. There are two groups, as in 1 Corinthians 1:18, and the same message is heard by both. In the Roman triumph this was literally true. To the soldiers marching, the incense was the smell of home and reward and a war survived. To the prisoners walking behind them toward execution, the identical smell was the smell of the last hour of their lives. Nobody was neutral, and nobody could avoid smelling it.

To one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. So with the gospel. It is not that the message is unclear, or that the messenger has failed. It is that the same word about the same Christ produces life in one hearer and hardening in another. To those perishing, the gospel smells of death: a crucified man, and their own judgment, and rejecting it leads to final death. To those being saved it is the scent of life, leading to eternal life. Pharaoh heard the word of God again and again and was hardened. Simeon said of the infant Jesus that he was appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel (Luke 2:34). The sun that softens the wax is the sun that bakes the clay; the difference is not in the sun.

A weight lifted. This is worth having straight, because it takes an unbearable weight off the shoulders of ordinary Christians who talk about Jesus and watch nothing happen. If you have shared the gospel with someone you love and they have gone colder rather than warmer, you have not necessarily done it badly. You may have done it exactly right. The aroma is doing what an aroma does. Your job was the fragrance; the response was never in your gift.

Nobody is filed. Notice the tenses too, because they are a mercy. Those who are being saved and those who are perishing are both present participles: processes under way, not finished verdicts announced to us. Nobody reading this has been told which list he is on except by what he does with Christ. The man who hardened last year is not thereby beyond hope; Saul of Tarsus was as far down the second road as a human being can travel, and was stopped in the middle of it.

Who is sufficient for these things? Then the question, and it is a real one, not a rhetorical flourish. “Sufficient” is hikanos: adequate, competent, equal to the task. Stop and feel the weight of it. Paul has just said that when he opens his mouth about Jesus, eternal outcomes are in motion. Who is adequate to carry that? Certainly not the man writing: he has told us in one chapter that he despaired of life and could not preach for anxiety. The honest answer to his question is: nobody, in himself. He does not answer it here. He leaves it hanging for six verses and then says our sufficiency is from God (3:5). That is the only answer there is, and it is enough. The people God uses are not the ones who feel equal to it. They are the ones who have stopped pretending they are, and have therefore started drawing on somebody else’s adequacy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers cause people to perish. The gospel reveals and confirms what people are. Those who perish do so because they refuse the light, not because the light was faulty.

Does God want some people to perish? God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezekiel 33:11), and the gospel is offered sincerely to everyone. Scripture also teaches that God has chosen a people for salvation and that he is sovereign over who believes (Acts 13:48). Both are true, and Scripture does not ask us to resolve them before we preach. Those who perish are never victims of a God who refused them; they are responsible for rejecting the light they were given (John 3:19). Those who are saved can only give thanks that grace opened their eyes. Neither truth is a reason to stop offering Christ to anyone.

Should I keep speaking of Christ to someone who resists? Usually yes, with wisdom. Keep praying for them, keep loving them, and keep the door open. Jesus also told his disciples not to throw pearls before pigs (Matthew 7:6), so there is a time to stop pressing someone who mocks, and let your life and your prayers do the speaking for a while. Do not nag or argue for the sake of winning. But do not conclude from coldness that God has finished with them. Many believers today were once hard and scornful hearers, and somebody kept carrying the fragrance into their lives.

In a sentence. For we are to God the sweet smell of Christ among those being saved and those perishing. To the one we are the smell of death leading to death; to the other, the fragrance of life leading to life. And who is up to such a task?

On a Tuesday. Your faithful witness is pleasing to God, whatever the response. Offer it to him today. Think of the person you have spoken to about Christ who seemed to grow colder. Thank God that your faithfulness was a fragrance to him, and then pray for that person by name. And when you feel inadequate for witness, say so to God: that feeling is the starting point of 3:5, not a disqualification.

For worship. Before ever the gospel reaches a human ear, it rises to the Father as the fragrance of his beloved Son, who gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God (Ephesians 5:2). The Father has never once smelled that aroma without delight. And he has chosen to spread it through weak, inadequate, anxious men and women, so that the life it brings to the dead may be seen to be his work alone, and the sufficiency his alone.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.

For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word. Paul ends the chapter by naming the alternative to the ministry he has just described, and the word he chooses is deliberately insulting. Kapēleuō is what a kapēlos does: a huckster, a small trader working a stall in the market. The word had a settled reputation in the ancient world, and it was not about selling as such but about adulterating: watering the wine, mixing chaff into the grain, weighting the scales. A kapēlos gave you something that was almost the thing you paid for. Plato uses the word for those who hawked teaching the same way.

Selling by diluting. So the charge is not simply that these men made money from the gospel. It is that they altered the product to move it. That is what a peddler does: he finds out what the market will take and adjusts the mixture accordingly. And notice like so many: a pointed reference to the rival teachers in Corinth. Paul does not say a handful. Even in the first generation, with apostles still alive, there were many. Nothing has changed. A message adjusted to what people will pay for is always a growth industry, and it is almost always presented as being about reaching people rather than about the money.

How to recognise a peddled gospel. The signs are not hard to read, and it is worth stating them plainly, because ordinary Christians are the ones who get hurt. Watch what happens to the hard parts. Wrath, judgment, hell, repentance, the cost of following, the call to die to yourself: a peddled gospel does not deny these so much as let them evaporate, until what is left is a message about your potential and your best life, with Jesus attached to it. Watch, too, where the money flows and who is accountable for it. Promises of health and wealth in return for giving are the oldest version of the stall. Paul refused support from Corinth precisely so that nobody could say this of him, and he will spend much of chapters 11 and 12 defending that decision.

But as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God. Against the peddler he sets three phrases. As men of sincerity: eilikrineia again, the thing held up to the sunlight and found sound, pure, unmixed. As commissioned by God, literally as from God: sent, not self-appointed. The message is not his to adjust because it is not his; it comes from God, not from his own ideas.

In the sight of God we speak in Christ. Preaching done in front of an audience of One, by a man who is himself inside Christ. That last phrase is the deepest safeguard there is against handling holy things for gain. Every preacher, teacher, parent and friend who opens their mouth about God speaks with God listening. Not evaluating the performance afterwards: present in the room, hearing every sentence as it is formed, including the ones shaped to be liked. Ministers answer to God for every word.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers should never be paid. Paul taught that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:14), and the labourer deserves his wages (1 Timothy 5:18). It means they must never preach for money, or change the message to please people.

Is it wrong to make the message attractive? No, provided you change the manner and never the message. Paul became all things to all people, adapting his approach to Jews and Gentiles (1 Corinthians 9:22), and he spoke differently in a synagogue and in Athens (Acts 17). Clear language, good illustrations, warmth, even humour can all serve the truth. The line is crossed when the content is altered to make it sell: when sin is renamed, judgment is dropped, the cross is softened, or Christ is offered as a means to something else. A good cook may serve the bread warm. He may not put sawdust in it.

In a sentence. Unlike so many, we do not peddle God’s word for profit. On the contrary, in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as people sent from God.

On a Tuesday. When you speak of Christ, speak sincerely, as before God. Do not water down the message to please others. Before your next conversation about faith, or your next Bible study, ask yourself which part of the truth you are most tempted to leave out with this person, and why. Then ask God for the courage and the kindness to say it. And look honestly at the teachers you listen to and the ministries you fund: do they preach the whole counsel of God, and are they accountable?

For worship. This is a comfort as well as a warning. The faithful man who says the unwelcome thing to a half-empty room is not talking into the air. The one for whom he did it heard every word. God himself is the speaker behind every faithful sermon, his word is never watered down by him, and his Son is the unmixed truth he sends into the world. Every true word about Christ, spoken in his sight, is heard by the Father with delight, and will not return to him empty.
verseByVerse.note: A peddler was a street trader known for watering down his wine to increase profits.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you.<sup>2</sup>For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained?<sup>3</sup>And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice, for I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all.<sup>4</sup>For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.<sup>5</sup>Now if anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some measure—not to put it too severely—to all of you.<sup>6</sup>For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough,<sup>7</sup>so you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.<sup>8</sup>So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him.<sup>9</sup>For this is why I wrote, that I might test you and know whether you are obedient in everything.<sup>10</sup>Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ,<sup>11</sup>so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.<sup>12</sup>When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord,<sup>13</sup>my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.<sup>14</sup>But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.<sup>15</sup>For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing,<sup>16</sup>to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?<sup>17</sup>For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.

3.title: Letters of Recommendation, the New Covenant, and the Unveiled Face
3.overview:
The visiting teachers in Corinth carried letters of recommendation and probably claimed the authority of Moses. Paul answers both claims. He needs no letter: the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts, just as God promised through Jeremiah and Ezekiel that the new covenant would write his law on hearts, not stone. His adequacy comes from God, who has made him a minister of that new covenant, “not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

Then Paul compares the two covenants through the story of Exodus 34. When Moses came down from Sinai with the law, his face shone so that Israel could not look at him, and he put on a veil. Paul argues: if the ministry that brought condemnation came with such glory, a glory that was being set aside, how much greater is the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness, which lasts. To this day a veil lies over the hearts of those who read Moses without Christ; but whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. And all believers, with unveiled faces, behold the glory of the Lord and are being transformed into his image, from one degree of glory to another, by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Ministers of the New Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s rivals came with letters of recommendation. Paul needs none: the Corinthian church is his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts rather than in ink or on stone, just as the prophets promised for the new covenant. His confidence rests not on his own ability but on God, who has made him a servant of that new covenant. The old covenant, written on stone, could only condemn; the Spirit gives life.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between letter and Spirit (v. 6) — “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” — is one of the most misunderstood phrases in Paul. It does not mean that the written word of Scripture is deadly and only spiritual illumination gives life (a Gnostic-leaning interpretation). In context, “the letter” refers specifically to the Mosaic law written on stone — the external commandment that makes demands it cannot empower fulfilling, that reveals sin it cannot remove. The Spirit gives life by doing what the letter could not: writing the law on the heart, enabling obedience from the inside. This is the Jeremiah 31/Ezekiel 36 promise in Paul’s theological shorthand.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation that prides itself on doctrinal correctness — its members can pass any biblical literacy test, articulate the five points of Calvinism, and explain every Confession — but whose relational life is cold and whose evangelistic impact is minimal. The letter/Spirit contrast is not a critique of doctrine or written Scripture; it is a diagnosis of the difference between external knowledge of the truth and inward transformation by it. The new covenant minister’s goal is not to fill heads but to be the instrument through whom the Spirit writes on hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 3 is one of the Bible’s great chapters on the difference between the old covenant and the new. The rival teachers in Corinth arrived with letters of recommendation and perhaps stressed the law of Moses. Paul says the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on their hearts, as Jeremiah and Ezekiel had promised for the new covenant (vv. 1–3). His sufficiency comes from God, who made him a minister of a new covenant, not of the letter that kills, but of the Spirit who gives life (vv. 4–6). Then he compares the two ministries. The old covenant, carved on stone, came with real glory, shining on Moses’ face. But it was a ministry of condemnation and death, and its glory was fading. The new covenant ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness has a far greater, permanent glory (vv. 7–11). Moses veiled his face; a veil still lies over the hearts of those who read the old covenant without Christ. When anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. And all believers, with unveiled faces, behold the Lord’s glory and are being transformed into his image, from glory to glory, by the Spirit (vv. 12–18). The chapter climbs from a dispute about paperwork to the summit of the Christian life: ordinary people looking at Christ and slowly becoming like him.

Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Paul has just said that he speaks as a man commissioned by God, in the sight of God. He hears at once how that could be taken, and he says so: is this Paul recommending himself again? The question is not paranoid. It is what his opponents had been saying. The word again tells us the charge was already in circulation: that his letters were a long exercise in self-promotion, that a man who really had God’s authority would not need to keep asserting it. His defence in chapters 1 and 2 might look like exactly that, and he anticipates the charge.

Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you? Behind the second question lies a real first-century practice. Travel was dangerous, communication slow, and a stranger arriving in a city claiming to teach in the name of Christ could be anyone. So churches wrote letters of recommendation for those they sent. Luke records one: when Apollos wanted to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him (Acts 18:27). Paul himself commends Phoebe to the Romans in exactly this way (Romans 16:1–2), and sent men with letters to carry the collection (1 Corinthians 16:3). There is nothing wrong with the practice and Paul does not attack it.

The credential as currency. What he attacks is what it had become in Corinth. His rivals had arrived carrying impressive documents from somewhere, perhaps from Jerusalem, and the documents had done their work. Notice the second half of his question: or from you? They wanted letters from Corinth as well as to it: the endorsement of a well-known church to carry to the next town. The credential had become a currency. That is a shape worth recognising, because it has not gone away. The modern equivalents are easy to name: the conference platform, the endorsement on a book jacket, the size of a following, the association with a bigger name. None of these is wrong in itself, and all of them can be made to do the job a life is supposed to do. The question is only ever whether the credential is describing something real or standing in for it.

When is it right to speak about your own ministry? There is a genuine tension here that Paul does not dodge. He is about to spend eleven chapters defending himself, and he knows it; he calls it foolishness when he gets there. The answer this chapter gives is that it is legitimate when the people you serve are being taken from you, and illegitimate when your own standing is what is at stake. Paul is not protecting a career. He is protecting a church from teachers who will damage it, and the only thing standing between them is his credibility. A man who defends himself for his own sake is building a reputation; a man who defends himself because his people are in danger is doing something else entirely, and the difference is usually visible in whether he enjoys it. Paul plainly does not. And his answer, when it comes in the next verse, is not another document. It is them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean letters of recommendation are wrong. It means Paul’s ministry needs no paper credentials among people he brought to Christ.

Should churches still check references and credentials? Yes. The early church did, and it is simple wisdom and love. A church should know who is teaching its people and working with its children: it should ask for references from a man’s previous church, test his doctrine against Scripture, and carry out proper safeguarding checks. Leaders should be tested before they serve (1 Timothy 3:10). What Paul warns against is letting paper replace life: being impressed by titles, platforms and endorsements while failing to ask whether a man’s teaching is true and his life is godly. Check the credentials, and then look for the fruit.

In a sentence. Are we starting to recommend ourselves again? Or do we need, like some people, letters of introduction to you or from you?

On a Tuesday. The best recommendation of your faith is not words about yourself but changed lives around you. Notice this week when you are tempted to establish your standing: the name dropped, the achievement slipped into conversation, the book you have read mentioned at just the right moment. Ask what it is standing in for. Then let it go, and let your life and the people you have served speak for you, or let nothing speak for you at all.

For worship. The Lord Jesus came with no letters from the authorities of his day. The religious leaders asked him by what authority he did these things, and he did not produce a document. His credentials were the blind seeing, the lame walking and the poor hearing good news, and at last an empty tomb. He made himself of no reputation, and God gave him the name above every name. Those who belong to him need no other commendation than his.
verseByVerse.note: Letters of recommendation were common for travellers; Paul’s rivals at Corinth came with them.

verseByVerse.quote: You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all. And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all. And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.

You yourselves are our letter of recommendation. Asked for his credentials, Paul points at the people who are asking. Stand in the room and feel the force of it. They wanted parchment. He tells them that the document is the congregation itself: the former idolaters, the reformed swindlers, the slaves and freedmen sitting in that hall who a few years earlier had never heard the name of Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:9–11; 9:2). That is the letter. It is not filed; it walks around Corinth doing business, and the whole city can read it.

Written on our hearts. Before they are a public document they are a private one, carried inside him. Some manuscripts read your hearts, but our is well supported and fits the warmth of the letter (7:3). This is a man who has been criticised, humiliated and dismissed by these people, and he says they are written on his heart. He cannot get them out. Anyone who has loved a difficult congregation, or a difficult child, knows the feeling of carrying people who have cost you a great deal.

To be known and read by all. Everyone can see what God has done in Corinth. A church is a public document, whether it means to be or not.

And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us. Note the correction. In verse 2 they are Paul’s letter; here they are Christ’s, and Paul is downgraded to the courier, or the secretary. Christ is the author. Paul did not write them. He carried them. Every faithful minister eventually discovers this: he is the postman, not the author, and the change he sees in people was not produced by his own hand.

Written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. Then the two great contrasts, and they are not decorative: Paul is echoing the Old Testament without naming it. Ink sits on a surface. It can be scraped off a papyrus with a knife, which is exactly how ancient documents were reused. Something written with the Spirit is not applied to the outside of a person. The Spirit wrote on their lives.

Not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts. Now the reference is unmistakable. Stone tablets were what Moses carried down Sinai, written with the finger of God (Exodus 24:12; 31:18). And centuries later God had promised through Jeremiah, to a nation that had comprehensively failed to keep what was on them: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jeremiah 31:33). Ezekiel put it more bluntly still: I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh, and I will put my Spirit within you (Ezekiel 11:19; 36:26–27).

A promise fulfilled in a Greek port. Paul’s claim is enormous. He is saying that the thing the prophets promised for a far-off day has happened, and that the evidence is sitting in front of him in a difficult church in a Greek port. The new covenant is not only a doctrine he is teaching. It is a group of people he is pointing at.

What has been written on you? Stone can be inscribed and remain stone; that is the whole tragedy of the old covenant. So what has actually been written on you? Not what you can recite: the law on stone could be recited perfectly by people it never changed. The test is whether anything has moved inward: whether you have come to want what you used to merely comply with. That shift is not something a person performs on himself. It is what the Spirit of the living God does with a heart, and it is the only credential any church has ever really had.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law on stone was bad. It was God’s law. But written on stone, it could not change hearts. The Spirit writes the same holy will within.

What if my life does not look much like a letter from Christ? Then look more carefully, and more honestly, in both directions. The letter is still being written, and the Spirit writes slowly; Paul calls the Corinthians Christ’s letter while they are still full of faults. Ask what has changed since you came to Christ, not whether you are finished: a sin you now hate, a person you now love, a hunger for God’s word you once lacked. Those are his handwriting. And if you honestly find nothing at all, do not despair or pretend. Go to Christ now, ask him for the new heart he promised, and keep coming to him in his word and among his people. He has never refused anyone who asked.

In a sentence. You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, known and read by everyone. You show that you are a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on stone tablets but on human hearts.

On a Tuesday. Your life is being read today by people who will never open a Bible: a colleague, a neighbour, your children. Ask what they are reading. Not what you would like them to read; what is actually written. Then thank God for one specific change his Spirit has made in you, and ask him to keep writing, especially in the place where the page still looks blank.

For worship. The God who once wrote with his finger on stone has now written with his Spirit on hearts of flesh, and the ink does not fade. He takes the most unpromising material, idolaters, swindlers, the proud and the broken, and makes of them a letter that carries the name of his Son through the streets of the world. Every believer is his handwriting. The promise of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, waited for through centuries of failure, he has kept in us.

parallels.desc: tablets of stone, written with the finger of God
a heart of flesh

verseByVerse.quote: Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,

Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Paul has just made a very large claim, and he immediately guards it from being heard as self-assurance. The confidence is real: the word is pepoithēsis, settled trust, the state of a man who is not looking over his shoulder. But look where it is anchored: through Christ toward God. It travels along one route and faces in one direction. It is not confidence in himself measured against his rivals. It rests on what God has done through Christ, and it stands before God’s own scrutiny.

Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us. In case anyone should still mishear, verse 5 takes it apart with almost painful precision. Not merely insufficient for the big things; insufficient to claim anything as originating in himself. This is the answer to the question he left hanging at the end of chapter 2, who is sufficient for these things?, and it has taken him six verses to give it. The answer is nobody, in himself.

But our sufficiency is from God. The word running through both verses is hikanos and its noun hikanotēs: adequate, competent, up to the job. It is a word with a history. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, one of the names of God is rendered by this very word, the Sufficient One, translating Shaddai (Ruth 1:20–21). God does not merely have sufficiency. He is it. And the word recalls a line of men who knew they lacked it. When God met Moses at the bush and told him to go to Pharaoh, Moses said, Who am I that I should go? (Exodus 3:11). When God called Jeremiah, he said, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth (Jeremiah 1:6). When Isaiah saw the Lord in the temple he said, Woe is me! For I am lost (Isaiah 6:5). Every one of them was right. Not one of them was adequate. God’s answer in each case was never to argue the point; it was to supply what was missing.

Which sentence do you live in? There is a question here, and it cuts both ways. Ask yourself which of these two sentences you actually live in: I can do this, or, I cannot do this and it is going to be done anyway. The first sounds like faith and is usually self-reliance in good clothes. The second sounds like defeat and is where God does most of his work.

Inadequacy is accurate. There is real comfort in it for anyone who has backed away from something because they did not feel up to it: the class they were asked to teach, the neighbour they were meant to speak to, the parent they have to care for, the marriage they no longer know how to mend. The feeling of inadequacy is not a verdict. It is accurate. Paul felt it and said so in writing. What he learned is that adequacy was never the entry requirement, because it was never going to be supplied from inside him.

On loan, issued daily. Notice, finally, the direction of the preposition: our sufficiency is from God. It comes out of him and arrives in us. It is not that God helps a competent man do a little more than he could alone. The competence itself is on loan, issued daily, and never becomes the property of the person using it. That is why Paul can be bold in the next paragraph and humble in this one at the same time. Both are the same fact seen from two ends.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers need no training or effort. It means their ability to change hearts comes from God alone.

So do I still need to prepare, study and train? Yes. God’s sufficiency does not replace means; it works through them. Paul studied the Scriptures, asked for his books and parchments in prison (2 Timothy 4:13), and told Timothy to do his best to be a worker who rightly handles the word of truth. Prepare the lesson, learn the skills, take advice, practise. But do all of it leaning on God rather than on the preparation. Pray before you study and while you study, and when you have done everything you can, go in knowing that the change in people’s hearts will still be his gift, not your achievement. Hard work and dependence are not rivals; they are the two hands of faithful service.

In a sentence. Such confidence we have through Christ before God. Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim anything as our own; our competence comes from God.

On a Tuesday. You may feel inadequate for what God has called you to. Good. Your sufficiency is from God. Name the task you feel least up to this week, and before you begin it, say to God in plain words: I am not sufficient for this; you are. Then do the work, and watch for what he supplies.

For worship. He is the Sufficient One. Moses at the bush, Jeremiah the youth, Isaiah undone in the temple, Paul despairing in Asia: none of them was adequate, and in every case God was. He has never once called a servant and then left him to supply his own strength. And in Christ he has given us the one in whom all the fullness dwells, so that from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace (John 1:16).

verseByVerse.quote: who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

Who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant. Two enormous things are in this verse: what a minister of the new covenant is, and one of the most abused sentences in the whole Bible. Notice first what Paul says he has been made sufficient to be: a minister of a new covenant. Not a better teacher of the old one. Something the prophets promised and never saw (Jeremiah 31:31–34). When the Lord sat down with his disciples the night before he died and lifted the cup, he said that this cup is the new covenant in his blood (1 Corinthians 11:25; Luke 22:20). The covenant Jeremiah waited for was not inaugurated with tablets on a mountain but with a body given and blood poured out.

Not of the letter but of the Spirit. Now the abuse, because it has done real damage. The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life has been used for centuries to mean that careful attention to the text of Scripture is deadening, while a spiritual impression is where the life is. On that reading, the man who studies the words is quenching the Spirit, and the man who bypasses them is free. Whole movements have been built on it. It cannot mean that, and the context makes it plain. Look at what the two words are set against: not text against feeling, but the letter against a new covenant. And in the very next verse Paul defines his terms: the ministry of death was carved in letters on stone. The letter is the law of Moses, inscribed on tablets, standing outside a person and telling him what to do. The Spirit is the life-giver who writes God’s law on hearts.

For the letter kills. So why does it kill? Not because it is bad. Paul says elsewhere that the law is holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12). It kills because of what it can and cannot do. It can tell you the standard with perfect accuracy; it cannot give you the least power to meet it, and it pronounces death on those who fail (Romans 7:10–11; Galatians 3:10). A speed limit painted on a road has never slowed a single car by itself. A doctor’s diagnosis has never cured anyone. The law describes the disease with total precision and hands you no medicine, and a diagnosis with no cure is a death sentence read aloud.

But the Spirit gives life. And the Spirit gives life by doing the one thing the stone could never do: regenerating a dead heart, and writing the command inside it, so that obedience comes out rather than being demanded in (John 6:63; Romans 8:2, 11).

Where Christians differ: the letter and the spirit. Since Origen, some have read this verse as a principle of interpretation: the literal meaning of Scripture kills, but the spiritual or allegorical meaning gives life. Verdict: Paul is not speaking about methods of reading Scripture, but about two covenants: the law written on stone, which condemns, and the Spirit’s new covenant work, which gives life. The Reformers rightly insisted on the plain, literal-grammatical meaning of Scripture, read in the light of Christ. The law is not abolished as God’s moral standard for believers; but it cannot justify or give life. Only the Spirit, through the gospel, does that.

Backwards. The popular misuse of this verse gets it exactly backwards. Ignoring the words of Scripture is not walking in the Spirit; the Spirit is the one who inspired them. The real warning here is aimed somewhere much closer to home: at the person who knows the Bible thoroughly, keeps the rules scrupulously, and has never been changed by any of it. That is life under the letter, and it can be conducted with a well-marked Bible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law is evil (Romans 7:12). It means the law alone cannot save.

Then how should I read the Bible? For its plain, intended meaning, which is what the Reformers meant by reading it literally. Ask what the human author meant his first readers to understand, paying attention to the kind of writing it is: history read as history, poetry as poetry, parable as parable, prophecy with its images. Read each passage in its context and let clearer passages explain harder ones. Then follow it to Christ, as the apostles did, because the whole Bible is about him (Luke 24:27). Do not hunt for secret meanings no ordinary reader could find. And read prayerfully, asking the Spirit who wrote it to give you understanding and a heart to obey; he works through the words, never around them.

In a sentence. He has made us competent as ministers of a new covenant, not of the written code but of the Spirit; for the written code brings death, but the Spirit gives life.

On a Tuesday. When you obey God this week, where does it come from? Is it a wall you keep running into, or a direction you actually want to go? Both people do the same thing on Sunday. Only one of them has had anything written on the inside. If your obedience feels like the wall, do not throw away the commandments; ask the Spirit to write them on your heart, and look again at the Christ who kept them all for you.

For worship. What the stone could only require, Christ came and supplied, and then wrote into his people by his Spirit. The letter could kill; it took the death of the Lawgiver’s Son to make anything alive. The Spirit who hovered over the waters at creation now breathes on dead hearts, and they live. There is no condemnation left in the new covenant for those who are in him, only the life of God, given freely and never taken back.
verseByVerse.note: The “letter” is the law written on stone, which could condemn but not give life.

parallels.desc: a new covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–18 — The Fading Glory and the Surpassing Glory; the Unveiled Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul compares the two covenants through the story of Moses’ shining face. The law came with real glory, so bright that Israel could not look at Moses. But that ministry brought condemnation and was temporary. The ministry of the Spirit, which brings righteousness and lasts, has a far greater glory. Moses veiled his face; Paul speaks openly. A veil still lies over the hearts of those who read Moses without Christ, but it is removed whenever anyone turns to the Lord. The Lord meets us now by the Spirit, who brings freedom, and all believers, seeing his glory with unveiled faces, are being gradually changed into his likeness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Moses passage (Ex. 34) in Paul’s reading makes a claim that has been debated since the patristic period: Paul appears to say that Moses wore the veil to prevent the Israelites from seeing the glory’s end (v. 13), whereas Exodus dwells on the Israelites’ fear of his shining face. Paul is reading the text through the lens of its fulfilment in Christ: the entire Mosaic economy was a temporary arrangement pointing beyond itself, and the veil that covered Moses’s face symbolises the veil that covers the hearts of those who read him without recognising his Christological pointing.

The transformation passage (v. 18) is the key text for the Reformed understanding of sanctification as a work of the Spirit through the Word. Beholding — katoptrizomenoi (gazing as in a mirror, or reflecting as a mirror) — is the mechanism. The Word presents Christ; the Spirit uses the Word to produce in the believer the image they behold. John Owen, commenting on this verse, says that the primary means of sanctification is not moral effort but contemplation of the glory of Christ as revealed in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: A spiritual director works with a young Christian who is exhausted by the effort of sanctification — constantly striving, measuring, failing, striving again. She introduces him to the practice of deliberate meditation on specific passages that describe the character and glory of Christ, asking him to rest in the image rather than immediately applying it. After several months he reports something shifting in his desires and responses — not through effort but through what this verse would call beholding. The transformation is from the Lord who is the Spirit; the means is the unveiled face gazing at glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?

Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone. Paul now runs an argument he will repeat three times in five verses, and its form is always the same: if the lesser thing had that much glory, think what the greater must have. First, the phrase that startles: the ministry of death. Applied to the law given at Sinai by God himself, it sounds close to blasphemy. But Paul has just explained it. The old covenant, centred on the law given at Sinai, was a ministry of death because, for sinners, its result was condemnation. The commandment is good; what it does to a sinner is fatal, because it can only ever tell him what he has failed to be. Paul is not disparaging the law. He is describing its effect on people like us.

Came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory. Now stage the scene behind the verse, because everything depends on it. Moses has been forty days on the mountain. He comes down carrying the tablets, and he does not know that his face is shining (Exodus 34:29–35). Aaron and the people see him and are afraid to come near. The light is not his; it is residue. He has been standing in the presence of God and has come away carrying some of it on his skin, the way a man who has been near a fire comes back smelling of smoke. And it was so bright that they could not look at him. Note that carefully, because it is Paul’s whole point. That is the glory of the covenant that kills. The old covenant really was glorious, because it came from God.

Which was being brought to an end. Then the phrase he slips in almost quietly. The verb is katargeō: to set aside, to make ineffective, to bring to an end. The shine on Moses’ face was fading even while they were too frightened to look at it, a picture of the temporary nature of the old covenant itself (Hebrews 8:13). It was real glory, and it was temporary, and both things were true at once.

Will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory? So the question answers itself. If a fading light on one man’s face after forty days on a mountain was more than a nation could look at, what is the weight of the ministry that does not condemn but makes righteous, that does not sit on the skin but is written on the heart, and that does not fade?

Does this mean the Ten Commandments are obsolete? No. What is being brought to an end is the old covenant as a ministry: the arrangement under which the law stood outside a person, written on stone, and condemned him. The law itself is holy, and its moral demands still show believers how to love God and neighbour. Paul says we uphold the law (Romans 3:31) and sums up its second table in the commandments (Romans 13:8–10). Some Christians hold that the whole law of Moses has given way to the law of Christ, though the moral teaching it contains is repeated and deepened in the New Testament. Most in the Reformed tradition hold that the moral law summarised in the Ten Commandments still binds, now written on the heart by the Spirit (v. 3). On the fourth commandment Christians differ: the Westminster and 1689 Baptist confessions keep it as the Christian Sabbath, moved to the Lord’s Day; others hold that the Sabbath, like the ceremonial law, is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), while the first day remains the day of worship. Both sides honour the Lord’s Day, and both should do so without judging the other (Romans 14:5).

Short-changed? There is something here for the Christian who reads the Old Testament and feels quietly short-changed. The fire on the mountain, the sea opening, the pillar of cloud, the shining face: it can seem that they got the spectacle and we got the routine of an ordinary Tuesday. Paul says the comparison is real and runs entirely the other way. They had a glory nobody could look at, and it was on its way out. You have a glory that does not fade, in a covenant that cannot be broken, administered by the Spirit of God living inside ordinary people. The reason it looks less impressive is that it has moved inside, where the work needed doing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament has no value. It means its covenant arrangements were preparatory, pointing to Christ.

In a sentence. Now if the ministry that brought death, engraved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not look steadily at Moses’ face because of its glory, fading though it was, will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious?

On a Tuesday. You live under a more glorious covenant than Moses did. Do not settle for less than the Spirit’s life, and do not envy the spectacle of Sinai. When the week feels ordinary, remind yourself what is actually happening inside you and in the believers around you: the Spirit of the living God is at work, and that is a greater glory than the shining of Moses’ face.

For worship. There is one more thing in the picture. The face that shone on Sinai was a borrowed light on a mortal man, and it went out. Centuries later three men watched another face on another mountain, and his face shone like the sun (Matthew 17:2), and that light was not residue from a visit. It was his own, coming out. Moses was there to see it, and this time the glory belonged to the man in the middle. The light Moses carried for a few days, Christ is for ever.

parallels.desc: the skin of Moses’ face shone

verseByVerse.quote: For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.

For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Three verses, and Paul is pressing the same comparison from three directions: what the two ministries do, how they compare when set side by side, and how long each one lasts. First, what they do. One is the ministry of condemnation, the other of righteousness. Both words are courtroom words. The law brings a verdict of guilty, and brings it accurately. The gospel brings a verdict of righteous, and brings it to the same defendant: justification, God’s gift of a right standing through Christ (5:21; Romans 3:21–22). That is the whole distance between Sinai and Calvary in two nouns. Giving righteousness is far more glorious than pronouncing condemnation.

Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. Then the strange sentence of verse 10. Paul is not contradicting himself. He is describing what happens when a real light is put beside a greater one. Anyone who has watched a lamp left burning as the sun comes up has seen it, or the moon at noon. The lamp has not changed and it was never a fraud; it is simply that, in the new light, there is nothing left for it to do. The old covenant’s glory is real, but outshone.

For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory. And in verse 11 the decisive difference: one was being brought to an end, the other is permanent. The word is menō: abiding, remaining, staying put. The new covenant will never be replaced. The old arrangement was always scaffolding: good work, necessary work, put up around a building that was coming.

Why still read the Old Testament? This matters practically for how a Christian reads the first three-quarters of his Bible. It would be easy to conclude from this passage that the Old Testament has been superseded and can be quietly shelved. Paul, who is about to say that the Israelites read Moses with a veil on, is not saying that. He quotes the Old Testament constantly, including in this very argument; his point is not that the old covenant was wrong but that it was never meant to be the end. The scaffolding does not become rubbish when the building appears. It becomes the thing that shows you how the building went up.

Everything else fades. There is also a warning in the fading, aimed at us rather than at Israel. Glory that fades is not only a feature of the old covenant; it is the feature of everything else you might build a life on. Health fades. Beauty fades famously and fast. Careers end, reputations get revised, the house is sold to strangers, and the achievements that took twenty years are summarised in one line at a funeral. None of these things is worthless; the shine on Moses’ face was real. They are simply all being brought to an end, and the only question that matters is whether you have anything that is not.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the moral law has ended. The covenant administration ended; God’s moral will is now written on hearts.

What does the ministry of righteousness mean for me? It means that the verdict over your life, if you trust Christ, is righteous, and that it was given as a gift, not earned. God counts the perfect righteousness of Christ as yours and your sin as his: for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (5:21). You do not stand before God on your record, good or bad, but on Christ’s. This is why a believer can come to God on his worst day with confidence, and why his best days add nothing to his acceptance. The new covenant does not lower God’s standard. It meets it, in Christ, for you.

In a sentence. If the ministry that brought condemnation was glorious, how much more glorious is the ministry that brings righteousness! What was glorious has no glory now compared with the surpassing glory. And if what was fading away came with glory, how much greater is the glory of what lasts!

On a Tuesday. Here is a way to test what you are actually resting on. Take whatever you would find hardest to lose and ask one question of it: in a hundred years, will it still be there? Almost nothing survives that question. Then thank God, by name, for the things that do: his righteousness given to you, his covenant that will not be revised, his Spirit within you.

For worship. What Paul holds out is the one ministry that does not fade: a covenant that will not be revised, a righteousness that will not be reviewed, a glory with no expiry attached to it. Set beside that, the brightest thing this world can put on a face is a lamp at sunrise. Praise God for the ministry of righteousness that declared you right with him. It is more glorious than Sinai, because at its centre stands not a shining servant but the Son, who is himself the Lord our righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have such a hope, we are very bold, not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have such a hope, we are very bold, not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.

Since we have such a hope, we are very bold. The boldness comes first, and notice where it comes from. Not from temperament: Paul has just told us he was too anxious to preach at Troas. Not from success. Since we have such a hope. The confidence is a conclusion drawn from what he has been describing: a glory that does not fade, a covenant that will not be withdrawn. The word is parrēsia, and its root meaning is freedom of speech: the right of a citizen to say everything, to speak openly and frankly, without concealment. It is the opposite of the guarded half-sentence. Paul has nothing to manage and nothing to hide, so he can say it all.

Not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face. Then a comparison that has puzzled readers since the early centuries, and it should be handled honestly rather than smoothed over. Exodus 34:33–35 tells of the people’s fear of Moses’ shining face, and that he wore a veil after speaking to them, removing it when he went in to speak with the LORD.

So that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end. Paul says Moses veiled his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome, the telos or end, of what was being brought to an end: that is, so they would not watch the glory dying away. The veil was a sign that the old covenant was temporary. It also became a symbol that Israel could not see the full meaning of the old covenant, which pointed to Christ.

Is Paul rewriting Exodus? No, and it is worth seeing what he is actually doing. Exodus records what happened; Paul is reading it in the light of what it turned out to mean. The narrative gives the reason at the time, and Paul, standing on the far side of the cross, sees the significance the veil carried in the whole arrangement: an old covenant whose glory was never permanent, and whose end was screened from the people living under it. This is not allegory imposed on the text. It is the same instinct the Lord himself modelled on the Emmaus road, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets to interpret what was said about himself (Luke 24:27).

Managing an impression. But sit with the pastoral picture in it, because it is very human. Moses is covering something that is fading. However tender the motive, and it was tender, the effect is that the people are dealing with a screen rather than a face. That instinct is not confined to prophets. It is one of the most common conditions of religious life. Something has gone quiet inside: the love has cooled, the prayers have dried up, the certainty has thinned. And rather than say so, we put on the veil. We answer fine. We keep the vocabulary, the attendance, the tone of voice. And it works, which is the trouble; nobody can see a fading glory through a cloth, so nobody ever asks.

The open face. Paul’s alternative is not to shine harder. It is boldness: the open face of a man whose glory is not his own and is therefore not running out. That is why he can afford to be seen. The person whose light is borrowed and fading must manage how much of himself is visible. The person who has been given a glory that does not fade has no reason to cover anything, including his weakness. Paul will spend much of this letter telling this church about his weaknesses precisely because he has nothing left to protect.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Moses was deceitful. Paul is drawing out the symbolic meaning of the veil, not accusing the greatest of the prophets of a lie.

Does boldness mean I must tell everyone all my struggles? No. Openness is not the same as broadcasting. Paul chose what to tell, to whom and why, and he wrote of his weaknesses to help the church, not to draw attention to himself. What boldness rules out is the managed mask: pretending to God and to the people closest to you that all is well when it is not. Have at least one or two mature believers to whom you can say the truth about your soul (James 5:16). Be honest with God always; he sees through every veil anyway. And in public, be open about the gospel and about your need of it, without performing either strength or weakness.

In a sentence. Since we have such a hope, we are very open, unlike Moses, who put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from seeing the end of what was passing away.

On a Tuesday. Be open and bold about the gospel. You have nothing to hide. Ask where you are wearing a veil this week: the answer you give when someone asks how you are, the spiritual dryness nobody knows about. Take it off before one trusted friend, and before God in prayer. Then speak of Christ to someone without the guarded half-sentence.

For worship. Our hope rests on a glory that cannot fade, and so we can stand with open faces before God and before the world. The one who gave it to us had nothing to hide either. He spoke openly to the world, he said, and in secret said nothing; and when he was lifted up on the cross the whole city saw him, exposed, so that our shame could be covered and our faces uncovered for ever.

parallels.desc: he put a veil over his face

verseByVerse.quote: But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.

But their minds were hardened. The veil moves. It was on Moses’ face; now it is over the reader’s heart. And Paul says something painful about his own people: that the Scriptures they revere are being read in the synagogue every Sabbath by minds that have been hardened to what they are for. “Hardened” is pōroō: made callous, dulled, as in Romans 11:7. Israel’s unbelief was not just lack of information but hardness of heart.

Two things to say first. This passage has been misused with terrible consequences, so two things must be said before anything else. First, Paul is not writing as an outsider. He is a Jew, a Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5), who says elsewhere that he has great sorrow and unceasing anguish in his heart for his kinsmen, and could wish himself accursed for their sake (Romans 9:2–3). This is not contempt. It is grief. Second, he does not treat the hardening as final. Within a sentence he will say that the veil is removed whenever a person turns: a present possibility, open now, and he himself is the standing proof that it happens to the hardest cases.

For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted. The old covenant here means the Old Testament Scriptures, especially the law, read in the synagogue. This is the first use of the phrase for the Scriptures themselves. Now the substance. The veil is not over the text; the text is fine. It is over the heart. The words are read accurately, translated correctly, memorised, honoured, and the thing they were written to point at is not seen (Luke 24:27; John 5:39). That is what makes this so serious. The problem was never a lack of Bible.

Because only through Christ is it taken away. Christ is the key to the Old Testament. Without him, it remains veiled. And there is a hard truth here about what argument cannot achieve. The veil is not removed by debate. Paul, of all people, could out-argue any man in a synagogue, and he does not say here that the answer is a better case. He says the veil is taken away only through Christ. That is worth knowing if you are the one praying for a relative who knows all the answers and remains cold. You are not up against a shortage of information.

Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts. “Moses” here means the books of Moses, read aloud each Sabbath in the synagogue (Acts 15:21). The veil has moved from Moses’ face to the readers’ hearts.

Closer to home. This passage comes uncomfortably close to home, and it should be allowed to. Christian readers can do exactly the same thing. It is entirely possible to read the Bible through with a plan, to know the names and the dates and the outline of every book, and to have missed the person the whole library was assembled to present. Sacrifices become ancient customs rather than a picture of what it costs to deal with sin. The exodus becomes national history rather than the pattern of every rescue God performs. Reading Scripture without seeing Christ in it is not only a Jewish failing. It is a human one, and any of us can do it in English.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish people are worse than others. Every unbeliever has a veil over the heart (4:3–4). And it does not mean the Old Testament is obscure in itself. It is clear to those who see Christ in it. Nor does it ever justify contempt or hostility toward Jewish people, which the church has too often shown, to its shame.

Will the veil ever be lifted from Israel as a people? Christians who share the same gospel read Romans 11 differently. Many believe Paul promises a future large-scale turning of the Jewish people to Christ before his return, when the fullness of the Gentiles has come in and all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:25–26). Others understand all Israel to mean the full number of God’s elect, Jews and Gentiles together, gathered throughout this age. Both agree that the hardening is partial, that Jewish people are coming to Christ now, and that there is only one way of salvation for Jew and Gentile alike: faith in Jesus the Messiah. Both should lead us to pray, with Paul, for our Jewish neighbours and to share the gospel with them gladly.

In a sentence. But their minds were made dull, and to this day the same veil remains when the old covenant is read. It has not been removed, because only in Christ is it taken away. Even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts.

On a Tuesday. Pray for Jewish friends and all who read the Scriptures without seeing Christ. Ask God to lift the veil. And next time you read the Old Testament, ask one question of the passage before you close it: where is this pointing to Christ? If you cannot see him, ask the Lord to show you, and keep reading.

For worship. Think what did happen to Paul on the Damascus road. He did not lose an argument. He was struck blind, and then something like scales fell from his eyes (Acts 9:18): the veil removed by the one person who can remove it, in a man who had been furiously certain he was reading Moses correctly. Nobody is beyond that. Not the relative you have given up on, and not the version of yourself that has been reading these pages for years without seeing anything. Christ is the light of the Scriptures, and he has never yet failed to be seen by the one he chose to open.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses” here means the books of Moses, read aloud each Sabbath in the synagogue.

verseByVerse.quote: But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.

But when one turns to the Lord. One short sentence, and it is the hinge of the chapter. Paul is once more reaching back into Exodus 34. There is a detail in that chapter easily missed: Moses wore the veil among the people, but whenever Moses went in before the LORD to speak with him, he would remove the veil, until he came out (Exodus 34:34). The covering was for the crowd. In the presence of God it came off. Paul takes that habit of one man and makes it the pattern for anyone: turn to the Lord, and the veil comes off.

Turns. Notice the word. It is epistrephō, the ordinary word for turning round, returning: a change of direction, not only a change of opinion. This is what the Bible means by conversion, repentance and faith together, and the picture is deliberately physical. A man walking one way stops and walks the other. He does not add something to his life; he reverses. And notice what it does not say. It does not say the veil is removed when a person understands enough, or has read enough, or has been convinced by a sufficient weight of evidence. Nor does it say when a person has cleaned himself up first. It says when one turns.

The veil is removed. And it is passive. The verb is periaireō: taken away completely, all round. Not he removes the veil. Nobody pulls the covering off his own heart, any more than a blind man cures himself by deciding to see. Something is done to him. Then the Scriptures become clear, and the glory of Christ is seen. This is the whole difference between religion and the gospel: one tells a man to lift the veil, the other tells him that when he turns he will find it has been taken. And even the turning is God’s gift: God has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ (4:6). The turning is not the achievement that earns the sight; it is the moment the sight is given.

Open at both ends. This makes it the most practical verse in the chapter for anyone reading it from the outside, or from the inside on a cold morning. If the Bible has gone flat, if God has become an idea you defend rather than a person you know, the instruction is not try harder to feel it. It is turn. Stop, face the other way, and speak to him. Paul does not attach conditions to it. He does not say when one turns and has sorted himself out, or when one turns for the first time, or when one turns having not wasted the last ten years. The sentence is open at both ends.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we remove the veil ourselves. Turning to the Lord is itself God’s gift (4:6). Nor does it mean that turning is a single moment never repeated: the Christian life begins with turning and goes on by turning again, every day, to the same Lord.

If the Bible feels veiled to me after years as a Christian, am I not saved? Not necessarily. Believers go through dry seasons, and Scripture can feel flat because of tiredness, grief, unconfessed sin, distraction or simply the way we read. The question is not whether you feel the glory today but whether you are turned toward Christ, trusting him and wanting him. If you are, keep turning. Confess what needs confessing. Read more slowly, and pray before you read: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Read with others, and sit under faithful preaching. The veil does not return over a believer’s heart the way it covers an unbeliever’s; but the eyes of a believer can grow dim, and the Lord delights to brighten them.

What can I do for someone who is still veiled? Pray first, because only the Lord removes the veil, and he does it in answer to prayer. Then do what Philip did for the Ethiopian reading Isaiah: open the Scriptures with them and show them Jesus (Acts 8:35). Do not rely on winning arguments, though you should answer honest questions. Invite them to read a Gospel with you. Live in a way that makes Christ attractive. And keep hoping. You cannot lift the veil, but you can stand beside the person while the Lord does.

In a sentence. But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.

On a Tuesday. If Scripture seems veiled to you, turn to the Lord and ask him to open your eyes as you read. Do it today, before you open the book: stop, face him, and speak to him. Then read one passage slowly, looking for him in it.

For worship. What a thing it is to say about God, that he is that easy to find. There is no antechamber, no delay, no preliminary examination, no queue. A man turns and the covering is gone, and he is looking straight at the Lord. That is what it cost the Son of God to arrange: the curtain of the temple torn in two from top to bottom on the afternoon he died, so that the way in would stand open for everyone who ever turned round (Matthew 27:51). Nobody has ever come and been told to wait.
verseByVerse.note: Paul echoes Exodus: whenever Moses went in before the LORD, he removed the veil.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

Now the Lord is the Spirit. Two claims, tightly joined, and the second is one of the great sentences of the Christian life. The first needs handling with care. The Lord in verse 16, in the Exodus passage Paul is expounding, is Yahweh, the LORD. Paul explains: in the new covenant, turning to the Lord means encountering the Spirit, who applies Christ’s work and removes the veil. The Spirit is the Lord, fully divine; and he is also the Spirit of the Lord, distinct and yet one with him.

Not collapsing the persons. Paul is not merging the persons of the Trinity into one, as though Christ and the Spirit were two names for the same person. He distinguishes them plainly elsewhere, and even in this verse he speaks of the Spirit of the Lord, which requires two. What he is saying is that the Lord to whom a man turns and the Spirit who does the transforming are not rivals or alternatives. To turn to Christ is to come under the working of the Spirit. They are one in operation. You do not get the Son without the Spirit, or the Spirit without the Son.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord the Spirit? Some (modalists) take this verse to mean the Son and the Spirit are the same person. Verdict: Paul distinguishes the Spirit and the Lord in the same verse: the Spirit of the Lord. He is saying that the Lord of the Exodus passage is now encountered through the Spirit, who is himself the Lord, fully God. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three distinct persons, one God (2 Corinthians 13:14).

And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. Then the freedom, eleutheria. And the first question to ask is: freedom from what? From the veil, in the first place: from reading the words of God with the meaning screened off. But the context has been building a bigger answer. Freedom from the covenant that could only condemn. From the standard that made demands and gave no power. From bondage to sin and death (Romans 8:2; Galatians 5:1). From the terrible arithmetic of a religion in which everything depends on your performance and your performance is not good enough. And, given verse 13, freedom from the exhausting business of managing the veil, of maintaining an appearance while something quietly fades underneath. Freedom, above all, of access: the freedom of a child to come into his Father’s presence.

Free on the instrument. What it is not is freedom to do as you please. Paul is emphatic elsewhere: you were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh (Galatians 5:13). A man who defines liberty as the absence of all constraint has never looked honestly at what actually rules him. The heaviest masters people serve are not laws imposed from outside; they are appetites, resentments and fears that were chosen freely and cannot now be put down. Christian freedom is more like the freedom of a musician than the freedom of a man with no commitments. Years under a discipline he did not invent produce someone who can finally play what he hears. He is not free from the instrument. He is free on it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean freedom to sin. Spirit-given freedom is freedom to obey and serve (Galatians 5:13).

Does the freedom of the Spirit mean worship should be unplanned and spontaneous? No. Paul is speaking of freedom from condemnation and the veil, not of a style of worship. The same Spirit who gives freedom is the God of order, not of confusion (1 Corinthians 14:33, 40), and he is as present in a carefully prepared sermon and a written prayer as in an unplanned one. Nor is freedom measured by dramatic experiences or the kind of gifts that marked the apostles’ day; the Spirit’s presence is seen most surely where Christ is exalted, the word is believed and lives are changed. Planned or spontaneous, worship is free when it comes from forgiven hearts that love God and know they are welcome.

In a sentence. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

On a Tuesday. Run a test on yourself. Where is the pressure in your religion? If you obey God mainly to keep something bad from happening, his disappointment, his withdrawal, the sense that you are behind, then whatever you have, the atmosphere of it is not freedom. Something in you is still standing at the foot of Sinai. The mark of the new covenant is not that the commandments have gone soft. It is that the fear has gone out of them, because the verdict was settled before you began. Obey today as a son, not a hired hand.

For worship. That is what the Spirit does where he is. He does not merely help a slave work harder. He makes the slave a son, and then teaches him to cry, Abba, Father (Romans 8:15). The Father planned it, the Son purchased it, and the Spirit pours it into our hearts: the glorious freedom of the children of God, which nothing in heaven or on earth can take away.

verseByVerse.quote: And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.

And we all, with unveiled face. The chapter has been climbing since verse 7, and here it arrives. Nearly every word is load-bearing, so take them one at a time. We all. On Sinai it was one man, and the nation stood at the bottom of the mountain and was warned not to touch it. In the old covenant only Moses saw God’s glory, and he veiled it. Now the whole congregation is on the mountain. There is no spiritual class in the new covenant who see what ordinary members do not. The tired mother, the apprentice, the man who has never been asked to do anything in church: we all. With unveiled face: the covering has been taken off. Nothing stands between the believer and the glory of God; the face is bare and it is safe for it to be bare, which is more than Moses could say of the people.

Beholding the glory of the Lord. The Greek word, katoptrizomai, can mean gazing as into a mirror or reflecting like one, and scholars have argued about it for centuries. The context of Moses looking at God’s glory favours gazing, and the mirror image is worth keeping in mind: we do not see him yet as he is, but truly, as in a good mirror. And where do we see it? In the face of Christ (4:6), as he is revealed in the gospel and in Scripture. Either way the posture is the same. It is looking.

Are being transformed into the same image. The verb is metamorphoō: the word used of the Lord’s own transfiguration, and of the renewing of the mind in Romans 12:2. It is passive: this is being done to us by God. And it is in the present continuous: it is happening now, in the ordinary weeks, whether or not it can be felt. Into the same image: the image of Christ, to which God predestined us to be conformed (Romans 8:29).

From one degree of glory to another. Literally, from glory to glory. By stages. Nobody arrives in a morning. Moses’ glory faded; ours increases. This is sanctification, and it ends in glorification.

We become what we look at. Now put it together, because the practical claim is startling and most of us do not live as though we believed it. We become what we behold. Sanctification, in this verse, is not first a matter of effort, resolutions or accountability, useful as those are. It is a matter of gaze. The transformation flows from contemplation, which is why John Owen, near the end of his life, wrote at length that the great means of holiness is the beholding of the glory of Christ, and why a man can grit his teeth through a list of disciplines for a decade and change very little.
