The other direction. The principle holds in the other direction too, which is where it becomes uncomfortable. Whatever you gaze at is forming you. Look for two hours every evening at people who are richer, and you will become discontented; you will not have decided to. Feed on outrage and you will become an angry person. The mechanism does not care what is in front of it. So the question is not really, am I trying hard enough? It is, what am I looking at?

For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit. And notice how the sentence ends, because it takes the whole weight off the one doing the looking. The Spirit does the transforming. The change is not manufactured by the intensity of your concentration. He is the one doing it, and he has never abandoned a half-finished work (Philippians 1:6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean transformation is instant or that we become perfect in this life. It means steady growth as we look at Christ. Nor does it make effort pointless: the same apostle tells us to put sin to death and to train ourselves for godliness. But all our effort is the effort of looking, and of removing what blocks the view.

How do I actually behold the glory of the Lord? Mainly through the means God has given. Read the Gospels slowly and often, and ask in each scene what it shows you of Jesus: his holiness, his compassion, his authority, his cross. Sit under preaching that sets Christ before you. Take the Lord’s Supper as a looking at his body given and blood shed. Sing hymns full of him. Meditate on a single verse about him through the day. And pray that the Spirit would show you his glory as you look; beholding is not mere reading, but reading with the eyes of faith, asking to see him.

Why do I not feel that I am changing? Because growth is slow and mostly invisible from the inside, like a child’s height measured against the door frame only once a year. The verb is present and passive: it is being done to you, gradually, whether you feel it or not. Look back over years, not days. Ask others who know you well. Often the clearest sign is that you see your sin more clearly than before, which feels like going backwards but is the light growing. Keep looking at Christ, and leave the measuring to the one who is doing the work.

In a sentence. And all of us, with faces unveiled, see the Lord’s glory as in a mirror, and are being changed into his likeness with ever-increasing glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. You become like what you look at. Add up the hours honestly: what is in front of your eyes most in an ordinary week? Then ask where in the week Christ is actually put in front of you long enough for anything to happen: not read about in a hurry, but looked at. Spend time today looking at Christ in his word, and change one habit that keeps your gaze elsewhere.

For worship. From one degree of glory to another, in people who mostly cannot see it happening, the Spirit is quietly making the likeness of the Son. The God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, is painting the face of Jesus on the faces of sinners. And the day is coming when the mirror is taken away, and we shall see him as he is, and being like him will no longer be a process but a fact (1 John 3:2). Moses’ face shone for a season and faded. Ours, in him, will shine for ever.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?<sup>2</sup>You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all.<sup>3</sup>And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.<sup>4</sup>Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God.<sup>5</sup>Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,<sup>6</sup>who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.<sup>7</sup>Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end,<sup>8</sup>will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?<sup>9</sup>For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory.<sup>10</sup>Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it.<sup>11</sup>For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.<sup>12</sup>Since we have such a hope, we are very bold,<sup>13</sup>not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.<sup>14</sup>But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away.<sup>15</sup>Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.<sup>16</sup>But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.<sup>17</sup>Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.<sup>18</sup>And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.

4.title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
4.overview:
Paul has described the surpassing glory of the new covenant ministry. Now he faces the obvious objection: if the ministry is so glorious, why is the minister so unimpressive, so beaten up, so weak? The Corinthians, living in a city that admired polish, power and success, were embarrassed by an apostle who looked like a failure.

Paul answers in three movements. First, he does not lose heart or use tricks; he openly states the truth. If some cannot see it, it is because Satan, “the god of this world”, has blinded them, while the God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” has shone into believers’ hearts with the light of his glory in the face of Christ. Second, this treasure is kept in clay jars, cheap and fragile, so that everyone can see the power is God’s. Paul is afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not in despair, struck down but not destroyed; he carries Jesus’ death in his body so that Jesus’ life may appear. Third, he does not lose heart, because although his outer self is wasting away, his inner self is renewed daily, and this light, momentary affliction is producing an eternal weight of glory. So he looks not at what is seen, which is temporary, but at what is unseen, which is eternal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Light Shining in Darkness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because his ministry is a gift of mercy, Paul does not give up, and he refuses tricks or distortion of God’s word, relying on open truth. If some cannot see the gospel, it is because Satan has blinded them. Paul preaches Christ as Lord, not himself, and regards himself as their servant. Conversion is God’s work, like creation: the God who first commanded light has shone into believers’ hearts so that they see his glory in the face of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The identification of Christ as “the image of God” (v. 4) is one of Paul’s most direct Christological statements, paralleled in Colossians 1:15. Christ is not merely like God or a representative of God; he is the very image — the precise visible representation — of the invisible God. To see Christ is to see God (John 14:9). The glory of God is concentrated in the face of Jesus Christ (v. 6) — not in theophanies or visions or mystical experiences, but in the specific person of Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen.

The parallel between Gen. 1:3 (“Let there be light”) and v. 6 (“God who said Let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts”) is one of the NT’s most striking statements about the nature of conversion: it is a creative act of God, analogous to the original creation. Regeneration is not human spiritual development; it is the same divine fiat that created light from nothing. This is the Reformers’ point: regeneration precedes and enables faith; it is not faith that produces the new birth but the new birth that produces faith.
verseByVerse.examples: A campus minister explains the gospel to a sharp philosophy student who has engaged with every argument and remains unconvinced. He is tempted to find a better argument. This passage suggests a different diagnosis: the issue may not be intellectual but spiritual — a blinding that no amount of superior argument can overcome. The appropriate response includes not abandoning the argument (Paul commends himself to the conscience) but adding sustained prayer for the God who speaks light into darkness to do so in this particular darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart. But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart. But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 4 shows how glorious new-covenant ministry actually looks in practice: like a treasure in a clay jar. First, Paul preaches openly, without trickery or tampering with God’s word. If people do not see, it is because Satan, the god of this age, has blinded them; but God, who said let light shine out of darkness, shines into hearts to show the glory of God in the face of Christ (vv. 1–6). Second, this treasure is carried in weak, breakable human vessels, so that the power is clearly God’s. Paul is pressed, perplexed, persecuted and struck down, but never crushed, despairing, forsaken or destroyed; he carries Jesus’ death in his body so that Jesus’ life may be seen (vv. 7–12). Third, he keeps speaking because he believes in the resurrection (vv. 13–15). So he does not lose heart: the outer self is wasting away, but the inner self is renewed daily, and present troubles are light and brief compared with the eternal weight of glory they are preparing (vv. 16–18). It is a chapter about a cracked pot, and from the first verse to the last it is really about the face it carries.

Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God. The therefore reaches back to the whole of chapter 3: the covenant that does not fade, the veil removed, the glory that transforms. Everything in this chapter about weakness and wasting away is being said by a man who has just described what he has been given. Two phrases come before the main point. This ministry: the new covenant ministry, the staggering thing he has been describing. And by the mercy of God, which is how a man who had hunted Christians to their deaths accounts for holding such a commission (1 Timothy 1:12–16). He never once speaks of it as an achievement.

We do not lose heart. The verb is enkakeō: to grow weary and give up, to run out of nerve, to quit. He will say it again in verse 16, and the two occurrences bracket the whole passage. Everything between them is his answer to the question of why he has not stopped. That is worth naming plainly, because losing heart is one of the commonest and least discussed conditions in the Christian life. It is not usually a crisis of doctrine. It is the slow arrival of a Tuesday on which you cannot see the point of continuing: the class you have taught for eleven years with nothing to show, the marriage you have prayed about since the children were small, the neighbour who is politely unmovable. Nobody announces that they have lost heart. They simply do slightly less, and then a little less than that.

Mercy, not willpower. Paul’s guard against it is not willpower. It is the sentence he has just written: this ministry is not his, and it came by mercy. A man carrying something he earned has to defend it, and will eventually be too tired to. A man carrying something he was given has a different relationship to his own exhaustion. The commission rests on the mercy that gave it, not on the strength of the one who holds it, and mercy does not get tired.

But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. A striking list of things he has ruled out. Disgraceful, underhanded ways are literally the hidden things of shame: whatever a man would not want brought into the light. Perhaps the rival teachers had accused Paul of hidden motives; he answers by naming what he has refused. Cunning is panourgia, readiness to do anything, the word Paul himself will use of the serpent in Eden (11:3). And tamper with God’s word is doloō, a term from the trade in wine and precious metals: to adulterate, to dilute, to alloy. It is the sister of the peddler’s word in 2:17.

What does tampering actually look like? Rarely a denial. Usually a dilution: the doctrine kept but drained of force, the demand quoted but never pressed, the warning read out in a tone that says nobody here need worry. It also runs the other way: the verse hardened past what it says, used to control people. In both directions the operator has decided he knows better than the text what the text should do.

But by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God. Against all of it Paul sets one method. The open statement is phanerōsis, a bringing into the light. Say it plainly, in public, and let it do its own work on the conscience. He appeals to conscience, not to emotion or cleverness, and he does it before God, who sees all. No technique, no leverage, no management of what people are allowed to know. It is a slower way to build anything, and it is the only way anything gets built that will still be standing when the man who built it is gone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persuasion is wrong. Paul persuaded (5:11), reasoned and pleaded. It means persuasion must be honest: the truth set out so that a man’s conscience can see it, never a pressure applied so that his will gives way before his mind has understood.

Losing heart: does it mean I am not a real Christian? No. Paul would not need to say we do not lose heart unless losing heart were a real danger for real believers. Elijah sat under a broom tree and asked to die (1 Kings 19:4); the psalmist told his own soul to hope in God because it was not doing so on its own (Psalm 42:5). Discouragement is a temptation, not a verdict on your standing. The remedy Paul shows is not to feel stronger but to look again at what you were given and who gave it: the ministry, the calling, the salvation itself came by mercy, and mercy is not withdrawn because you are tired. Rest, tell a trusted believer, keep coming to the means of grace, and do the next small faithful thing.

How do I commend the truth to someone’s conscience without pressure? Say what is true, plainly, and say it as one who will stand before God for how you said it. Do not exaggerate to make it more appealing, and do not hide the hard parts to make it more acceptable: sin, judgment, the cost of following Christ. Do not use guilt, flattery or a social debt (I helped you, so you owe me a hearing). Give people time; invite questions; let them see you live it. Then leave the result with God. The conscience is God’s territory, and he is the one who makes the truth land.

In a sentence. So since through God’s mercy we have this ministry, we do not give up. We have rejected secret and shameful ways; we do not use deception or distort God’s word. Instead, by setting out the truth plainly, we commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel, be honest and plain: no tricks, no pressure, no hidden agendas. And when you notice you have begun quietly to do less, ask where your strength has been coming from. If the answer is your own sense of how well it is going, go back to verse 1 and read the two words that hold the rest up: by mercy.

For worship. The ministry is not Paul’s, and the gospel is not ours. It came out of the mercy of God to a man who was holding the coats of those who killed Stephen, and it comes the same way to everyone who has ever carried it since. God does not need to manage anyone into his kingdom. His truth needs no doctoring; it is already more glorious than any improvement we could make to it. He has only to be shown as he is, and he will win the hearts he means to win. Blessed be the God of mercy, who entrusts his treasure to people who had forfeited every right to hold it, and keeps them from giving up.

verseByVerse.quote: And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. Paul has just said he states the truth openly. The obvious objection follows at once: then why does it not work? Why do intelligent, decent people hear the clearest possible presentation of Christ and remain entirely unmoved? Some in Corinth were evidently saying Paul’s gospel was obscure. His answer is not that the message needs improving. The problem is not in the gospel but in the hearers, those on the road to destruction (2:15). And there is a third party in the room.

In their case the god of this world. The phrase is startling, and it needs care, because it must not be heard as though the universe had two gods in it. Paul has already written that there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things (1 Corinthians 8:6). Satan is a creature; he was made, he is on a leash, and he has a date. What the title means is that he is the god people actually serve: the power this age treats as ultimate, worshipped in a thousand forms that never carry his name. This world is literally this age. Jesus called him the ruler of this world and said in the same breath that he would be cast out (John 12:31; compare John 14:30; Ephesians 2:2; 1 John 5:19).

Has blinded the minds of the unbelievers. His method is specific. Not persuaded, not argued: blinded. The verb is a single decisive act. He does not need to make people believe something false about Christ; it is enough that they cannot see him at all. Unbelief is not merely an intellectual position. It is spiritual blindness.

Where Christians differ: the god of this world. Some ancient heretics (Marcion and the Gnostics) took this to mean the God of the Old Testament, a lesser, evil god. Verdict: The god of this age is Satan, who is called god because unbelievers serve him and he holds sway over the present evil age. His power is real but limited and temporary, under God’s sovereign control (Job 1:12), and already defeated at the cross (Colossians 2:15). There is one true God, who made the world and rules it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean unbelievers have no responsibility, or are innocent victims. Paul calls them unbelievers, and blindness of this kind is never against a person’s will; it is the confirmation of a direction already chosen. People love the darkness rather than the light (John 3:19), and Satan blinds those who refuse the truth. Nor does it license writing anyone off. The man writing this was as blind as anyone has ever been, on the Damascus road armed with letters to the synagogues (Acts 9:1–2).

You are up against a blindfold. Here is what it does mean. If you have explained the gospel to someone you love, patiently and well, and nothing has happened, you have not necessarily failed. You are not up against a shortage of argument. You are up against a blindfold, and blindfolds are not removed by better reasoning. That is why the same Paul who reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath (Acts 18:4) also asked churches to pray for him, and why the argument that cannot be won should be followed home with intercession rather than a better book.

To keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. Notice what the blindfold is designed to prevent. Three genitives stacked up, each opening into the next, and they arrive at a person. The image of God is eikōn, the exact visible representation. Not a likeness, not a good approximation. Paul says the same to the Colossians: he is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3). And the Lord himself put it beyond argument to a disciple who wanted a vision of the Father: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). The invisible God has made himself visible in one place only, and that place is a Galilean carpenter who was executed outside a city wall. That is the light the enemy is working so hard to keep from human eyes, and it is worth asking why he should trouble himself so greatly over one face, unless there really is nothing else to see.

Does “perishing” mean my friend is beyond hope? No. Perishing describes the road a person is on now, not a sentence we can read off his life. You cannot know who God has chosen, and Paul did not know either; he simply kept preaching, because some who are blind today will see tomorrow. Every Christian was once on the perishing road (Ephesians 2:1–3). The word should make you urgent, not resigned. The only point at which anyone is beyond hope is death in unbelief, and while your friend is breathing, the God of verse 6 can still speak.

How should I actually pray for someone who is blinded? Pray to God, not at the devil: ask the Father to do what verse 6 says he does, to shine into this heart. Pray specifically, by name, for the one thing that matters most: that they would see the glory of Christ, not merely that their circumstances would improve or their objections be answered. Ask God to send them other believers, and to give you a clear word at the right time. And pray with confidence rather than nervousness, because you are not asking God to do something unusual. Opening blind eyes is what Jesus came to do (Luke 4:18).

In a sentence. And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that they cannot see the light of the gospel that displays the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

On a Tuesday. Choose one person you have more or less given up on. Stop rehearsing the argument you will win next time, and start praying daily, for a month, that God would shine into their heart and show them Christ. Keep being kind, keep being honest, and keep the gospel in plain view. The blindfold is not yours to remove, but the One who removes it hears prayer.

For worship. The devil’s whole strategy against the human race comes down to keeping one face out of sight. He does not mind religion, morality or a great deal of spiritual talk, so long as no one sees Christ. That is the measure of what there is to see. In the face of Jesus is everything God is, made visible for sinners, and the enemy knows that a single clear look would undo him. He has blinded millions, and he did not keep the light out of Saul of Tarsus. The image of the invisible God has stood in the full glare of hell’s hatred and come out risen, and every blindfold in the world is held in place only until he says otherwise.
verseByVerse.note: “The god of this world” is Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.

For what we proclaim is not ourselves. One sentence, and it settles what a Christian minister is for. Begin with the negative, because Paul evidently thought it needed saying. His rivals were promoting themselves: their experiences, their gifts, their success. Not ourselves is a warning about the most natural drift there is. Nobody sets out to preach himself. It happens by increments: the illustration that makes the speaker look perceptive, the anecdote that establishes his credentials, the gradual discovery that a certain kind of story gets a certain kind of response. The message stays orthodox. The subject quietly changes.

The modern shapes. The ancient forms were different in dress only. The ministry organised around one personality. The teaching whose real content is the teacher’s experiences. The platform that requires a photograph. None of these declares itself; each one simply moves the light a few degrees until it is falling on the wrong face. The test is not whether a preacher mentions himself; Paul mentions himself throughout this letter. It is what the hearer goes away thinking about. If people leave impressed with the man, something has gone wrong, however sound the doctrine was.

But Jesus Christ as Lord. That was the earliest Christian confession (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3), three words long, and it cost people their lives, because in the Roman world the sentence Caesar is Lord was the loyalty oath and only one of the two could be true. To say Jesus is Lord was to say that the emperor was not. It has never been a private religious preference. It is a claim about who is actually in charge, of the world and of the hearer.

With ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake. The phrase that turns the whole thing. The word is doulos: not a hired helper but a slave, someone with no independent agenda. The apostle who has spent three chapters defending his authority now defines his relationship to the very people questioning him as slavery to them. It is the opposite of lording it over their faith (1:24).

For Jesus’ sake. The order matters. He is not their slave because they are the customer and the customer is always right; he has just refused to trim the message for them. He is their slave for Jesus’ sake. His Master sends him to serve them, so serving them is obedience to someone else, which is precisely what keeps his service from becoming flattery. A man who serves people for their sake alone will end up telling them what they want. A man who serves them for Christ’s sake will tell them the truth and stay.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers should never share personal experience. Paul does in this very letter, at length. It means preachers must never make themselves the message. Nor does servant mean the congregation sets the agenda: Paul serves them by giving them Christ, whether or not they asked for him.

I am not a preacher. Does this apply to me? Yes. Every Christian speaks about Christ to someone: a child at bedtime, a friend over coffee, a home group, a post online. The same drift threatens all of us. Testimony can become a story about how interesting my journey has been; helping in church can become a way of being needed and noticed; online the temptation is built into the format. The question is the same for you as for Paul: when people have listened to you, are they thinking more about Jesus or more about you? Tell your story, but tell it so that he is the one who acts in it.

In a sentence. For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.

On a Tuesday. When you talk about your faith, make Jesus the hero, not yourself. And look for the menial way to serve someone this week for Christ’s sake: the job nobody thanks you for, done because your Master would have done it, not because anyone is watching.

For worship. Where did the shape of that service come from? From a Lord who “came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45); who on the last night took a towel and washed the feet of the men who were about to abandon him (John 13:4–5). Authority in his kingdom runs downwards. He established it that way by doing it first, and no one has ever found a lower place than the one he took. He is Lord of all, and he knelt. Every faithful servant of the church is only a small copy of the Servant-King, and the copies point, every one of them, to the original.

verseByVerse.quote: For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness.” Verse 4 said the mind is blinded. This verse says what God does about it, and Paul reaches all the way back to the first page of the Bible for the comparison, with an echo too of Isaiah’s promise that the people who walked in darkness would see a great light (Isaiah 9:2). Go back and stand there. The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. There is no dawn coming, because there is no sun. There is nothing to strike a light from and nobody to strike it. Whatever is going to happen must come from outside the situation entirely. And God said, Let there be light, and there was light (Genesis 1:3). Paul says that is what conversion is.

Has shone in our hearts. Conversion is a new creation (5:17). Paul is surely thinking of his own, when a light from heaven flashed around him on the road (Acts 9:3). But he says our hearts: every believer has had God shine into him. Take the parallel seriously, because it decides how a person thinks about his own salvation and about everyone he is praying for. The darkness in Genesis did not cooperate. It did not reach toward the light, or make itself receptive, or take a first small step and get helped the rest of the way. It could not, and it was not asked to. Light arrived because God spoke, and the moment he spoke there was no darkness left to consult.

Where Christians differ: how does conversion happen? Many Christians, in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions, hold that God first gives every person enabling grace, so that they are able to believe, and that new birth follows faith; others believe that God offers light, and humans by their own will choose to open their eyes. They point to the many calls to believe and to John 1:12, where receiving Christ comes before becoming God’s children. But the next verse says those children were born not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:13), and John says that everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God (1 John 5:1). Verdict: The picture is creation. As darkness did not cooperate with God in creating light, the blinded heart does not cooperate in its own illumination. God shines in; the result is sight and faith. This is regeneration, God’s sovereign, effectual work (Ephesians 2:4–5; Westminster 10.1–2). It is not a piece of theological machinery imposed on the text; it is what this verse says. A blinded mind cannot decide to see. But when God says let light shine into a particular human heart, that heart will believe, as certainly as the deep filled with light on the first day. The person then believes freely and gladly, because he now sees.

Two anxieties removed. This takes the anxiety out of two things at once. First, your own standing: if the light in you was lit by God, then the flickering you are so worried about is not evidence against you, because you did not light it and you are not keeping it burning. Second, the person you have given up on. Nothing in their hardness is a problem for a God whose speciality is speaking into a void. He is not looking for a promising surface.

To give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God. Then the destination of the light, and every word of the phrase is deliberate. Not the knowledge of doctrine, though doctrine is how it comes. Not a light that shows you yourself, though it will. God’s glory has been given a location, and the location is a human face. Moses asked to see that glory and was told, “You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exodus 33:20); he was put in a cleft of the rock and shown the back of God going past (Exodus 33:18–23). The thing Moses was refused is what has been given to ordinary believers.

In the face of Jesus Christ. And it is a face that was spat on, that had a crown of thorns pressed above it, that was set toward Jerusalem and would not turn away. There is the glory of God: not in the fire on Sinai, not in the whirlwind, but in the face of a man dying for his enemies. To know Christ is to know the glory of God. Whoever has once seen it never quite recovers, and there is nothing else in the universe that repays looking at in the same way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean conversion is always sudden or dramatic, as Paul’s was. The light may dawn gradually, like a morning rather than a lightning flash, and many who were raised in Christian homes cannot name the day. But it is always God’s work.

If God must shine first, why should I tell anyone the gospel? Because the gospel is the light God shines. Verse 4 calls it the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, and verse 6 is what happens when God makes that same gospel break through. He does not usually shine into hearts apart from the message; he shines through it, when it is spoken (Romans 10:14–17). So your words are the lamp he uses, and his sovereignty is the reason to speak with hope rather than a reason to stay quiet. You cannot open a single eye, but you can hold up the light, and God has promised that his word will not return to him empty (Isaiah 55:11).

How do I know God has shone in my heart? Not chiefly by remembering a moment, but by what you see now. Does Christ look glorious to you, not just true but beautiful and necessary? Do you trust him, rather than yourself, for your acceptance with God? Do you want to know him more, and hate the sin that dims the view? Blind eyes do not see glory at all; they find Jesus dull or irrelevant. If he is precious to you, even when your sight seems dim, that is light, and you did not make it.

In a sentence. For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” made his light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of God’s glory displayed in the face of Christ.

On a Tuesday. When you pray for someone who seems hopelessly hard, pray Genesis 1 over them: Lord, you spoke light into nothing; speak it here. And when your own faith feels faint, do not stare at the flicker. Look again at the face: read a Gospel account of Jesus, slowly, and let the light that first lit you shine again.

For worship. Let light shine out of darkness. He said it over the formless deep, and there was light. He said it over a persecutor on the Damascus road, and there was light. He said it over you, in whatever darkness you were lying, and you saw what you had never seen: the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. The glory Moses could only glimpse from behind has turned toward us, and it is a face full of grace and truth, scarred for our sake. Praise the God of the first creation and the new, who did not wait for the darkness to ask, and against whose word the darkness has never once been able to hold out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Treasure in Jars of Clay
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The treasure of the gospel is carried in fragile, ordinary containers, so that the power is clearly God’s. Paul describes his life as a series of near-defeats that never become defeats: pressed but not crushed, bewildered but not without hope, hunted but not abandoned, knocked down but not destroyed. He shares Jesus’ dying so that Jesus’ life can be seen in him, and his suffering brings life to others. Like the psalmist, he believes and therefore speaks, sure that the God who raised Jesus will raise him too. All of it serves the spread of grace and the increase of thanks to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The four contrasts in vv. 8–9 are not merely biographical observations; they are a theological programme. The pattern of affliction-but-not-destroyed is the pattern of the cross applied to the messengers of the cross. The phrase rendered “the death of Jesus” (v. 10) uses a noun that means the process of dying, death-at-work, rather than the event. Paul is not saying that he dies as Jesus died, but that the same dying-of-Jesus that produced life for the world is at work in Paul’s ministry, producing life for the churches. The apostle’s weakness and suffering is the medium through which resurrection life is communicated. It is worth noting the honesty of v. 8: the verb behind “driven to despair” is the very word Paul used of himself in 1:8, where he says he despaired of life itself. He is describing the normal condition, not issuing an absolute guarantee.

Verse 13 — “I believed, and so I spoke” — quotes Psalm 116:10 in the Greek Old Testament, the psalm of a man who faced death and was delivered, who then declared that he believed and therefore spoke. Paul applies the psalm to the apostolic situation: even in the face of death, the minister speaks because he believes, and the faith of the psalmist and the faith of the Christian are shown to be one and the same pneuma. The resurrection of Jesus (v. 14) grounds this confidence — the same God who raised Jesus will raise us, and bring us with you into his presence.
verseByVerse.examples: A senior pastor of a large church steps down due to a serious health diagnosis and is replaced by a younger, more energetic successor. He struggles with the sense that his fragility is a disqualification. This chapter is addressed precisely to him: the jar of clay is not a disqualification from ministry; it is the precondition for God’s power being unambiguously visible. The question is not whether his vessel is strong enough but whether the treasure is still present — and treasure in a cracked jar leaks light rather than hiding it.

verseByVerse.quote: But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.

But we have this treasure in jars of clay. This is the sentence the whole letter turns on, and it is built out of the most ordinary object in the ancient world. Jars of clay, ostrakina skeuē, were not the household’s good pottery. These were the cheap, unglazed, mass-produced containers used for oil, grain, water and refuse; they cracked, they chipped, they were thrown out and replaced without a thought. Archaeologists find them by the ton because nobody ever bothered to look after one. The word Paul uses is related to ostrakon, the broken shard people scribbled notes on because it was worthless. Treasure was sometimes hidden in such jars, as the Dead Sea Scrolls were, precisely because nobody would look twice at them. The jars are human bodies and lives: weak, mortal, made of dust (Genesis 2:7; Isaiah 64:8).

This treasure. Into that he puts this treasure: the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, straight from the previous verse. The gospel, and the Christ it shows. The most valuable thing in existence, stored in the container you would use once and discard.

To show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us. It is not an accident, and Paul says so. The mismatch is the point. Read it the other way and the logic is obvious. If the apostle had been physically imposing, magnetic, healthy, wealthy and universally admired, then when people came to Christ under his preaching the question of where the power came from would be permanently ambiguous. Some would credit God; many would credit Paul; and Paul himself, being human, would eventually have credited Paul. The cheap jar removes the ambiguity. Nobody looks at a cracked storage pot and concludes that the light is coming from the pottery.

Your weakness is the design. This has enormous pastoral consequences, and they need saying plainly to the people who most need them. If you have ever thought that your weakness disqualifies you, the health that limits what you can commit to, the temperament that makes you dread the door, the education you did not get, the failure everybody remembers, the age you have reached, this verse is aimed directly at you. Your fragility is not an obstacle God is working around. It is the design. He chose the container precisely because nobody would mistake it for the treasure.

A warning folded into the comfort. A church, a ministry or a Christian can work very hard at not looking like a clay pot: the polished presentation, the projected confidence, the careful concealment of anything that might suggest struggle. The trouble is that the strategy succeeds. People are impressed, and being impressed is not the same as seeing God, and they go away thinking well of us. The gospel travels furthest through people who are visibly unequal to carrying it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean weakness is good in itself, or that we should want to be weak for its own sake. It means God uses weakness to display his strength: my power is made perfect in weakness (12:9).

Should I then make a show of my weaknesses, or stop trying to do things well? Neither. Displaying your weakness can become another way of drawing attention to yourself, a clay pot that wants to be admired for being so honestly cracked. And Scripture commends work done heartily, as for the Lord (Colossians 3:23); preparing well, practising, and taking care are not pride. The point is where you put your confidence and whom you want people to see. Do your best, be honest about your limits when it helps others, never hide behind a polished image, and then give God the credit openly for whatever good comes of it.

In a sentence. But we have this treasure in clay jars, to show that this all-surpassing power is from God and not from us.

On a Tuesday. Name the weakness you most wish God had not given you. Then ask, not how to hide it, but how God might show his power through it this week: in a conversation where you have to say I cannot do this alone, in a task you take on in dependence, in a prayer you pray because there is nothing else. Do not be discouraged by your weakness. God has chosen to carry his treasure in a jar like you.

For worship. Consider how far this pattern goes. God had a Son to send and no shortage of options for how to send him. He chose a village nobody rated, a manger, a working man’s hands, and finally an instrument of execution used on slaves and rebels. The treasure has always come in the cheapest possible container, and the reason has always been the same: so that when the light gets out, there can be no argument about whose it is. The Lord of glory was content to be carried in earthenware, and to be himself the jar that was broken on the cross, so that the light would pour out over the world. All the power is his. All the glory is his. And he is pleased to put both into hands like ours.
verseByVerse.note: Clay jars were cheap, fragile, everyday containers.

verseByVerse.quote: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;

We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed. Four pairs, hammered out in the same shape each time: a real blow, then a limit. Paul is describing what it is actually like to be a clay jar with a treasure in it. Take them one at a time, because each pair says something different. The first word, thlibō, is the pressing weight of affliction again; the second, stenochōreō, means squeezed into a corner with no room left. The pressure is real and total, in every way, but there is always still room to move. Not comfort. Room.

Perplexed, but not driven to despair. This is the most interesting pair in the list, and it is a small masterpiece of honesty. The two Greek words are the same verb, one of them intensified: aporoumenoi all’ ouk exaporoumenoi, at a loss, but not at an utter loss. And exaporeomai is precisely the word Paul used in 1:8 about the affliction in Asia, where he says he despaired of life itself. So he is not claiming that a believer never goes under. He has already told us that he did, though he despaired of life, not of God. What he is describing here is the normal condition, not an absolute guarantee against dark seasons: usually bewildered, not usually finished. Anyone who has been through the worse thing will notice that Paul does not pretend it cannot happen.

Persecuted, but not forsaken. The word is the ordinary one for being hunted or chased. Men pursue him; God does not abandon him. Behind it stands the promise repeated all through Scripture and quoted to nervous Christians ever since: “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

Struck down, but not destroyed. The picture is of a man knocked to the ground, like a wrestler thrown. He does go down. What does not happen is the finishing blow.

Where Christians differ: suffering and the prosperity gospel. Some teach that faith brings health, wealth and success, and that suffering shows weak faith. Verdict: The greatest apostle was constantly afflicted, perplexed, persecuted and struck down. Suffering is normal in the Christian life (Acts 14:22; 2 Timothy 3:12). God’s promise is not to remove suffering but to sustain us in it and bring us through. The prosperity gospel contradicts the cross and the apostles’ experience.

What it does not mean. Notice what this list does not promise, because misreading it has hurt people. It does not say a Christian will be spared affliction; all four blows land. It does not say he will feel calm; he is perplexed. It does not even say he will stay standing. It does not mean Christians never feel crushed or despairing. It says something narrower and far more durable: that in every case there is a floor, and the floor holds. They are never finally overcome.

But what about Christians who are killed for their faith? Were they not destroyed? No, and this is exactly Paul’s point. He himself would be executed. The body can be killed, but the believer cannot be destroyed, because his life is hidden with Christ and the God who raised Jesus will raise him (v. 14). Jesus said not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul (Matthew 10:28). The martyr is struck down in the most final way this world has, and the floor still holds: he goes straight into the presence of the Lord (Philippians 1:23), and his body waits for the resurrection. Destroyed would mean lost, cut off from God; that is the one thing that cannot happen to those who are his (Romans 8:38–39).

Test it against your own history. Test it against your own history rather than against a theory. Think of the year you were sure you would not survive. You are reading this. That is not luck and it is not your resilience; you know how thin that was at the time. Something held, and it was not you.

In a sentence. We are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed; at a loss, but not in despair; persecuted, but not abandoned; knocked down, but not destroyed.

On a Tuesday. Write the four pairs out with your own circumstances in the first half of each: pressed by this, but not crushed; at a loss about that, but not in despair. Do not falsify the first half; it is allowed to be as hard as it is. Then read the second half aloud as a statement about God, not about your strength. When a fellow believer is in the first half, do not hurry them to the second; sit with them in it, and be one of the ways God keeps them from being forsaken.

For worship. There is one more thing to see, and it is the reason the list has this shape. Paul is describing his own life in the pattern of somebody else’s. His Lord was afflicted, perplexed in Gethsemane, persecuted from Bethlehem onwards, struck down at Calvary, and in his case the last blow fell. He was crushed. He was forsaken; he said so out loud in the dark. He was destroyed, and buried, and the stone was rolled across. That is why there is a floor under his people. The one place the sequence ran all the way to the end, it ran to the end for us, and came back out on the third day. Every but not in this list was bought at a cross where there was no but not at all. Glory to the Son who was forsaken so that we never will be.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay: “perplexed” (aporoumenoi) but not “driven to despair” (exaporoumenoi) — at a loss, but not utterly at a loss.

verseByVerse.quote: always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.

Always carrying in the body the death of Jesus. Paul now names what the four blows amount to. This is not simply a hard life. It is the death of Jesus being carried about in a human body. The word behind death here is nekrōsis, and it means the process rather than the event: the dying, the putting to death, death at work. Paul is not saying he re-enacts Calvary. He is saying that his sufferings for the gospel are a kind of ongoing dying, a share in Jesus’ sufferings (Galatians 6:17; Philippians 3:10). And notice always, twice. Not in seasons of persecution only. Continuously, as the settled condition of the life.

So that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. Then the purpose, also twice. The verb means to be made visible, brought into the open. The risen life of Jesus is seen in Paul’s survival, endurance and joy. Here is the mechanism at the heart of this whole letter. The dying is not the price paid for the ministry; it is the medium of it. Resurrection life becomes visible in a human being at exactly the points where that human being is being emptied out.

Where people actually see it. That is why it is nearly always the wrong question to ask only why God has not removed the difficulty. Watch where people actually see the life of Jesus. Not in the Christian whose life has gone well; there is nothing to explain there, and the world explains it easily. They see it in the man who lost the job and did not become bitter. In the widow who still sings. In the couple who buried a child and are still in church, still kind, still able to sit with someone else who is grieving. Something is showing through, and it is not personality, because personality does not survive that.

For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake. Notice the phrase being given over. It is paradidōmi, handed over, and it is passive, and in Paul the passive normally has God behind it. He is not merely suffering the consequences of a dangerous job. He is being handed over: the same verb used of Christ himself, delivered up for our trespasses (Romans 4:25). Someone is administering this. That should be said carefully, because it is not a sentence to be tossed at a person in fresh pain. But it is the truth Paul is living on. He is not the victim of circumstance. He is in the hands of a God who is doing something deliberate with a life, and who is not being careless with what it costs.

So that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh. The second half of the pair changes the wording in a way that repays attention. Not in some spiritual compartment. In the body that gets tired, ill and old. The place where the dying is most obvious is the place where the life is to be displayed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must seek suffering, or that pain is holy in itself. It means suffering for Christ’s sake displays his life.

Is every hardship the dying of Jesus, or only persecution? Paul’s first meaning is suffering that comes because of Jesus: the beatings, the dangers, the costs of the gospel. But the principle reaches further. Illness, loss and weariness are part of the outer self wasting away (v. 16), and when a believer carries them in union with Christ, trusting him and refusing bitterness, they become the place where his life is seen. What does not qualify is suffering we bring on ourselves by sin or folly (1 Peter 4:15). Even then, confessed and borne humbly, God can use it; but it is not suffering for his sake.

Does God cause my suffering, then? God is sovereign over all of it, and he is never the author of evil. The person who wrongs you is responsible for the wrong; the illness is part of a fallen world. Yet nothing reaches you that your Father has not permitted and does not intend to use for your good and his glory (Romans 8:28; Genesis 50:20). That is why Paul can say he is being handed over and not merely knocked about. It is not a philosophy to answer every why. It is a refuge: the hands that hold the situation are the hands that were pierced for you.

In a sentence. We always carry around in our bodies the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our bodies. For we who are alive are always being handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that his life may be seen in our mortal bodies.

On a Tuesday. When following Jesus costs you something today, the honest word you did not soften, the evening given up, the loss you are carrying without complaint, remember: his life is being shown through your dying. You may never know who saw it. You need only not waste it by grumbling or by hiding it behind a show of strength.

For worship. It is a good deal easier to bear when you see whose pattern it is. He carried his cross through the streets before any of his people carried anything. The dying that is at work in them is his dying, and it is going the same way his did: through a Friday nobody could explain, to a morning nobody expected. The life of Jesus is not a memory. It is a risen life, strong enough to shine through bodies that are wearing out, and one day it will raise those bodies too. Praise the Lord who was handed over for us, and who now hands out his own life through the cracks in ours.

verseByVerse.quote: So death is at work in us, but life in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So death is at work in us, but life in you.

So death is at work in us, but life in you. One short sentence. Paul has said something like it before in this letter and he will say it again, but never this starkly. The two halves are held apart deliberately: death here, life there. The apostles absorb one and the church receives the other. His losses are their gains, and the transaction is not a figure of speech: the beatings that took the skin off his back were the price of the gospel arriving in Corinth at all. Like Christ, whose death brought life to others, the minister spends himself so that others may live.

At work. The verb is energeitai, from which we get energy: something operating, exerting force. Death is not merely present in Paul. It is busy. And so, in Corinth, is life.

No invoice. Stop and consider what it takes for a man to write this to that church. They had questioned his credentials, compared him unfavourably with better speakers, and complained about his travel arrangements. He tells them that death is doing its work in him so that life can do its work in them, and he says it without a trace of self-pity or invoice. There is no after all I have done for you. It is simply the arrangement, and he is content with it. He is not shaming them into gratitude; this is not a bill. He is telling them how the kingdom moves, and he is glad to be where he is.

Ground that was bought. The principle is far wider than apostles, and once you see it you will see it everywhere. Nearly everything good in your life came to you because it cost somebody else something. The parents who went without so there would be school fees. The missionaries who are buried in the country they went to. The believers who were burned so that the Bible could be read in English in an ordinary house. Whoever it was who prayed for you for years and died before it worked. Life in you; death in them. You are, all of you, standing on ground that was bought.

Whose life is your death producing? That turns the question round. It is a hard question because most of us have arranged our lives to keep the cost low. But if the pattern of the kingdom is that death here produces life there, then a life that costs nothing is producing correspondingly little, and no amount of activity disguises that. The people whose ministry outlives them are almost always the ones who were spent.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Corinthians should not suffer. They share in sufferings too (1:6–7). It means Paul’s suffering serves their life.

Does Paul’s suffering, or my pastor’s, pay for anything? No, not in the way Christ’s death does. Only Christ’s death atones for sin; his sacrifice was once for all and nothing can be added to it (Hebrews 10:14). Paul’s suffering brought the Corinthians life because it was the cost of bringing them the message about the One whose death saves. He travelled, was beaten, stayed, wrote and wept, and through all that the gospel reached them. The minister’s sacrifice is the delivery, never the payment. That is why Paul can be content with it: he is not trying to save anyone by his pain, only to get the news of Christ to them at any cost.

How do I spend myself for others without burning out? Paul was spent, but he was not driven. He did not lose heart because he drew daily on a renewal not his own (v. 16), and he lived in prayer and in the Scriptures. Being spent for others is not the same as never saying no, never resting, or carrying burdens God has given to others. Jesus himself withdrew to pray (Luke 5:16). Give yourself gladly where God has placed you, accept help, share the load with the church, and remember that the life you are passing on is Christ’s, not yours to manufacture.

In a sentence. So death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.

On a Tuesday. Write down the names of two or three people whose sacrifice brought the gospel to you, and thank God for them; if any are still living, thank them too. Then ask where your own life might be spent for someone else’s good this week: an hour with someone lonely, a generous gift, a costly conversation. Do it without keeping an account.

For worship. Paul is glad because he did not invent the arrangement. He is standing inside it at second hand. There was a death that was at work in one man on one afternoon, and the life it produced runs out to every believer who has ever lived and will not be exhausted when the last of them is raised. Paul only ever says at a small scale what his Lord did at the largest scale there is, and it is the deepest logic of the universe: someone goes down so that someone else comes up. Christ went all the way down, into death and the grave, so that a people beyond counting might come up into life. Blessed be the Lamb who was slain, whose death is the life of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak, knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak, knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.

Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke.” Paul has just said that death is at work in him. The obvious question is why he keeps talking. Here is the answer, and it comes in two parts: because he believes, and because of what he knows about the end. The quotation is from Psalm 116 (Psalm 115:1 in the Greek numbering), and the whole psalm is worth having in view. It is the song of a man who had been at the edge, “The snares of death encompassed me; the pangs of Sheol laid hold on me” (Psalm 116:3), who called on the Lord and was heard. In the Greek version Paul used, the line runs: I believed, and so I spoke. The psalmist was in mortal danger and he opened his mouth about God anyway.

The same spirit of faith. Paul says he has the same spirit of faith. Not the same opinions: the same disposition, the same instinct, the same inability to keep quiet. It is one of the clearest statements anywhere that the faith of the Old Testament saint and the faith of the Christian are the same thing, worked by the same Spirit, separated by centuries and no difference in kind.

We also believe, and so we also speak. Note the logic. Speech is not an extra that follows faith for the more confident sort of believer. It is faith surfacing. What a man truly believes will eventually get out of him, and when it does not, that is worth thinking about rather than merely regretting. Paul keeps preaching despite suffering, because he believes.

A sight problem, not a technique problem. That is a kinder way into the subject than the usual one. Most Christians carry a low-grade guilt about not speaking of Christ more, and the usual remedy is a course on how to do it. This verse suggests looking further upstream. Silence is very often not a technique problem but a sight problem: we have stopped seeing him clearly enough to have anything pressing to say. Fix the gaze, and the tongue tends to follow. Nobody needs to be taught how to talk about something they cannot get over.

Knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus. Then the second reason, and it is the ground under everything. Not hoping: knowing. The resurrection is not merely a doctrine Paul holds; it is the fact that makes his arithmetic work. If death is genuinely at work in him and there is nothing on the other side, then he is simply being consumed. If there is a resurrection, he is being invested. Even if he is killed, God will raise him.

And bring us with you into his presence. The verb is paristēmi, to present, to stand someone before another. Then the phrase that shows what he is really looking forward to: not bring us home, not even raise us in glory, but with you. After everything, the humiliating visit, the letters, the men who despised him, what he pictures at the end is arriving in the presence of God with these very people beside him, raised and glorified together. He expects to see the ones who wounded him there, and the thought gives him pleasure. That is what resurrection hope does to a quarrel. It puts everyone concerned in the same room, standing in front of the same face, and makes the present disagreement look exactly as large as it is going to look then.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only preachers should speak. All who believe should speak of Christ, each in the place and manner God gives.

I am shy and tongue-tied. Do I have to speak like Paul? You do not have to speak like Paul, but you will want to speak of what you believe, and you can. Speaking of Christ is not only preaching or knocking on doors. It is saying, when a colleague asks how you cope, that you pray and why; offering to pray for a friend; telling your children what God has done for you; inviting someone to church; giving a book with a brief word. Start where faith is already surfacing: what has Christ been to you this week? Say that, simply, to one person. The Spirit who gave the psalmist his voice is the same Spirit in you.

Will we know one another in the resurrection? Yes. Paul expects to be presented with the Corinthians, which means he expects to recognise them and be glad of them. Our Lord spoke of sitting at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Matthew 8:11), and Paul comforts the Thessalonians by saying they will be with their departed loved ones and with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). We will be changed, but not into strangers. Every redeemed relationship will be healed and made what it should have been, and the centre of it all will be the face of Christ.

In a sentence. It is written, I believed; therefore I have spoken. With that same spirit of faith we also believe and therefore speak, because we know that the one who raised the Lord Jesus from the dead will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you to himself.

On a Tuesday. If you believe, speak. The resurrection gives you courage to tell others about Christ, because nothing they can do to you is final. And think of the believer you find hardest to love. Picture the two of you standing together, raised, before the face of Christ. Let that picture shape what you say to them, and about them, this week.

For worship. He who raised the Lord Jesus. That is God’s name in the New Testament, the way he is known now: the God who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus. Death did its worst to the Son, and God undid it on the third day, and the same power stands under every believer who is being worn down for his sake. The psalmist sang it from the edge of the grave, Paul preached it under the lash, and the whole church will sing it on the day when he presents us all together, faultless and glad, to himself. Faith speaks because there is a God like this to speak about.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes the Greek form of the psalm.

parallels.desc: I believed, even when I spoke

verseByVerse.quote: For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.

For it is all for your sake. Here Paul tells us where the whole thing is going, and the destination is not what most people would guess. All of it: the afflictions, the perplexity, the daily handing over to death, the dying at work in his body. Every bit of it is aimed at them. He has said this three times now in four chapters (1:6; 4:12; and here), and the repetition is not accidental. He wants them in no doubt about whom the suffering is for.

A chain with three links. Then a chain with three links, and it is worth following them in order, because each one produces the next. First, grace extends to more and more people. The verb suggests something spreading outward, gaining ground. The suffering of one man is not a closed loop; it is how the gospel gets to the next town.

So that it may increase thanksgiving. Second, every new person reached is a new voice added. Grace multiplies, and gratitude multiplies with it, because a person who has been given something he could not earn will say so.

To the glory of God. Third, and this is the terminus: to the glory of God. That is what all of it is finally for. Not Paul’s vindication, not even the Corinthians’ comfort; those are real, and they are on the way to something else. Ministry serves people, and people’s thanksgiving serves God’s glory.

A larger question than what God is teaching me. Sit with that for a moment, because it quietly rearranges the way most of us think about our own troubles. The usual Christian question in hardship is what is God teaching me? It is a good question and it has a real answer. But it is a smaller question than this verse is asking. Paul’s question is not what he is getting out of his affliction. It is how many mouths will end up thanking God because of it. That is a genuinely different way to hold a hard season, and it is available to ordinary people, not only apostles. The illness that has made you dependent has given several people the chance to serve, and some of them are praying for the first time in years. The redundancy that humiliated you is being watched by your children, who are learning what a man does when the money stops. You may never see the accounting. Paul, writing this, could not see most of his either.

What it does not mean. It does not mean people are only a means to an end. God’s glory and people’s good go together: the Corinthians are blessed in the very act of giving thanks.

Is it not selfish of God to want his own glory? It would be selfish in us, because we are not the greatest good and our seeking glory robs others. But God is the greatest good there is. For him to seek anything less than his own glory would be to point us away from the only thing that can satisfy us. When God draws out our thanks, he is drawing us into joy in himself, which is what we were made for; that is why the Shorter Catechism puts glorifying God and enjoying him in the same answer. His glory and our happiness are not rivals. Thanksgiving is the moment they become one thing.

In a sentence. All this is for your benefit, so that the grace reaching more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow to the glory of God.

On a Tuesday. Take the hardest thing in your life just now and ask not only what God is teaching you, but whose thanksgiving it might produce. Then add your own voice: name three specific graces God has given you this week and thank him for each, aloud. Your thanksgiving glorifies him.

For worship. Notice the shape of what Paul expects at the end. Not a report on results. A rising volume of thanks. And that is the note the passage lands on, because it is the note the universe lands on. God is not accumulating servants or achievements. He is gathering worship: voice after voice, from places nobody planned, most of them belonging to people who were given something they never earned and could not repay. Every grace that goes out comes back as thanksgiving, and the whole long enterprise of the gospel exists so that the number of people who have reason to praise him should be as large as it can possibly be made. To him be the glory, from every mouth his grace has reached.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–18 — The Outer and Inner; the Seen and Unseen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So Paul does not lose heart. His body is wearing out, but his inner life is renewed daily. Present troubles, heavy as they are, are light and brief beside the lasting glory they are preparing. So he keeps his attention on what cannot yet be seen, because the visible things are temporary and the unseen ones eternal.
verseByVerse.theology: The seen/unseen contrast (v. 18) is not Platonic dualism — Paul is not saying that the material world is bad and the spiritual world is good, or that the body is a prison from which the soul escapes. He is making an eschatological point: what is currently visible (the suffering, the wasting body, the opposition) is temporary; what is currently invisible (the renewed inner person, the weight of glory being prepared) is permanent. The resurrection of the body (ch. 5; 1 Cor. 15) will make the invisible visible — the glory will become physical and permanent in the resurrection.
verseByVerse.examples: An elderly woman in a nursing home, her body failing, tells her pastor that she has never felt closer to God. She cannot explain it; the outer self is clearly wasting away. But there is something else. This verse names what she is experiencing: while the outer is being destroyed, the inner is being renewed day by day. The renewal is not despite the physical decline but somehow through it — the loosening grip of the outer on the inner’s attention, the daily reminder that this is not home, the intensified gaze at the unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.

So we do not lose heart. The phrase from verse 1 comes back as Paul’s conclusion, and now we can see what it cost him to say it. He does not lose heart, and he is telling us in the same breath that he is falling apart.

Though our outer self is wasting away. Take the honesty of it first. The outer self, literally the outer man, is the body and visible earthly life, subject to ageing, sickness, wear and suffering. The verb, diaphtheirō, means to be ruined, corrupted, destroyed by degrees; it is present tense, happening now. Paul is not talking merely about persecution. He is talking about the body: the eyes that are worse than they were, the strength that does not come back after a hard week, the accumulating record of what has been done to him. He is no longer young and he is running out. Christian faith does not require anyone to be brave about this or to pretend it is not happening. There is no verse here about ageing gracefully. There is a blunt admission that the jar is cracking, written by a man who could see it happening to himself.

Our inner self is being renewed day by day. Set against it, in the same sentence, is a second process. The inner self is the inner person, the heart and spirit united to Christ. The verb, anakainoō, is passive and continuous: it is being done, and it is being done now, by the Spirit. Not restored to what it was; the word means made new, made afresh (Colossians 3:10). And day by day, in the ordinary increments in which the other process is also happening. Two things are going on in the same person at the same time, in opposite directions. One is visible and everybody can see it. The other is invisible, and it is the one that is going to last.

The verse for a hospital chair. This is the verse for a hospital chair, and it should be given away freely. Anyone who has sat with an elderly believer knows the strange thing it describes: a body plainly failing and something else plainly not failing. The conversation goes somewhere unexpected, or a hymn surfaces from sixty years ago, or the person says with complete simplicity that they are not afraid, and you leave the room having received rather than given. The outer self was telling the truth about the outer self and nothing else.

The mind too. This belongs as much to the mind as to the body. Depression and long mental illness are part of the outer self that is wasting away, and not losing heart is not a feeling to be produced on demand. It is a direction to face, even when the feelings will not follow. The psalmist argued with his own soul, “Why are you cast down, O my soul?” (Psalm 42:5); Elijah asked to die (1 Kings 19:4); Paul himself says he despaired of life itself (1:8). None of them was rejected for it. A believer in that darkness should seek help, from the church and from doctors, and know that the inner renewal goes on even when it cannot be felt.

What the renewal runs on. It is worth asking what the renewal actually runs on, because it is not automatic. Nothing in this verse suggests that decline by itself produces spiritual growth; plenty of people grow old and merely become more themselves. The next two verses give the answer: a way of counting the affliction, and a direction of gaze. The renewal happens in people who are looking at something.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the body does not matter, or that the real you is only a soul trapped in a shell. The body will be raised (v. 14). It means its present decay is not the whole story.

What exactly is the inner self, and how is it renewed? The inner self is you as God sees you from within: your heart, mind and will, joined to Christ by the Spirit. It is not a separate person, and it is not something you can see in a mirror. It is renewed as the Spirit applies Christ to you through the means God has appointed: his word read and preached, prayer, the Lord’s Supper, the fellowship of believers, and obedience in ordinary things. None of these is magic, and none is optional for someone who wants to be renewed. They are simply where God has promised to meet his people, day by day.

In a sentence. Therefore we do not lose heart. Though outwardly we are wasting away, inwardly we are being renewed day by day.

On a Tuesday. Here is the honest question for anyone still healthy enough to ask it. Both processes are already running in you; the first began some years ago whether or not you have noticed. The only real question is whether the second one is running too, because the day is coming when it will be the only thing you have left, and it is not built in an afternoon. Spend time with God each day, not as a duty to tick but as the place your inner self is fed. As you grow older or weaker, ask him for daily renewal, and expect it.

For worship. Everything given now to the inner self is provision laid down for a season we cannot yet imagine, and every believer who has arrived there has found the supply was already waiting. That is the faithfulness of God: the One who never grows weary renews the weary every morning (Isaiah 40:28–31). The world sees an old body failing; heaven sees a new creation nearly finished. Praise the Spirit who does his quiet work in us day after day, while the jar cracks, until the day when outer and inner are made new together and nothing will waste away again.

verseByVerse.quote: For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,

For this light momentary affliction. Read that sentence beside the man who wrote it and it becomes almost outrageous. By the time he reaches this letter Paul had been flogged five times with thirty-nine lashes, beaten with rods three times, stoned and left for dead, shipwrecked three times, and had spent a night and a day adrift at sea (11:23–27; Acts 14:19). He had been hungry, cold, sleepless and betrayed. He had recently despaired of life itself. And he calls it light. He calls it momentary. Not because it was easy, but because of what it is compared with.

Nobody may say this for him. Nobody may say this sentence to a sufferer on Paul’s behalf. It is a thing a man may say about his own troubles and nobody may say about another’s. Handled carelessly it becomes the cruellest verse in the New Testament: cheer up, it is only light and momentary, said to a woman who has buried a child. Paul is not minimising anything. He has spent four chapters refusing to minimise it.

Weighing, not minimising. What he is doing is weighing. Both key words are comparative. Light means light in comparison; momentary means brief in comparison. Put a real weight on a scale with nothing on the other side and it is heavy. Put the glory on the other side and the same weight rises. The affliction has not changed. Something has been added to the other pan.
