Is preparing for us. The verb is katergazomai, to work out, to produce as a result. The suffering is not merely followed by glory; it is doing something. There is a line running from the hardest thing in your life to the weight of glory, and it is a line of cause. Nothing is being wasted and nothing is merely being endured.

An eternal weight of glory. The word weight is the point of the whole verse. Behind it lies the Hebrew kabod, the ordinary Old Testament word for glory, which comes from a root meaning heavy, and Paul may well be playing on it. Glory in the Bible includes brightness, but its root idea is weight: substance, mass, the sheer solidity of God. So Paul sets a weight against a weight: light affliction against heavy glory, momentary against eternal. This is not a promise of something airy to compensate for something painfully solid. What is coming is heavier than what is happening.

Beyond all comparison. The phrase is built by piling one intensifier on another, literally according to excess unto excess (compare Romans 8:18). He has run out of Greek. It is the same expression that gave him the utterly of 1:8 when he was describing how far past his strength he had been pushed, and here he uses it twice in a row, straining language at the other end of the scale. He is not saying the glory will be worth it, as though it were a fair exchange narrowly won. He is saying the two things cannot be put on the same scale at all: that the heaviest grief a human being can carry will one day be found to have been the lighter object in the comparison, and that we do not currently have the vocabulary to say why.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering earns glory. Glory is God’s gift, purchased by Christ. But suffering endured in faith prepares us for it.

My trouble has lasted decades. How can it be momentary? Measured against your life, it is not momentary, and Paul does not ask you to pretend it is. Many of his own troubles lasted for years, and the thorn in 12:7 was never removed. Momentary is measured against eternity. Thirty years of pain, set beside ten thousand years of glory and then ten thousand more, becomes what Paul calls it, without ceasing to be real. You are not asked to feel it as light today. You are invited to believe that God will one day show you it was, and to let that hope hold you up while it is still heavy.

Will those who suffer more receive more glory? Scripture does speak of reward, and of God’s noticing what was borne for his sake (Matthew 5:11–12; Romans 8:17). But the reward is grace, not wages: no one will stand in glory because he suffered enough to deserve it, and the believer who suffered little is not second class. What the verse promises every believer is that nothing endured in faith is wasted. Leave the measuring to God. He will be generous beyond anything we can imagine, and nobody in heaven will be envious.

In a sentence. For our light and brief troubles are achieving for us an eternal glory that far outweighs them all.

On a Tuesday. Put your present troubles on the scales. Write them down honestly, every one, in full weight. Then, on the other side, write what God has promised: to be with him, to see the face of Christ, a body that will not fail, no more tears. Do not argue with your feelings; simply look at both columns, and ask God to let the second one grow heavier in your sight.

For worship. Paul had more on his side of the scale than most people ever carry, and he is the one calling it light. He could, because he knew Someone had carried the full weight of what we deserved, and found it anything but light. Christ bore the wrath that would have crushed us, so that the only weight left for his people at the end is the weight of glory. Blessed be the God who turns affliction into an instrument of joy, and who has prepared for those who love him a glory so heavy that every grief of this life will be found, in his presence, to weigh nothing at all.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew the word for “glory” comes from a root meaning “heavy” — glory has weight.

verseByVerse.quote: as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

As we look not to the things that are seen. The verse begins with as, and it is doing real work. This is the condition. The affliction prepares a weight of glory as we look; the renewal of verse 16 and the weighing of verse 17 both happen in people whose eyes are pointed somewhere particular. The verb is not the ordinary word for seeing. Skopeō means to fix attention on, to take aim at; it is the root of our word scope. It describes the deliberate, sustained look: a man sighting down a line, not a man glancing. Not on visible circumstances: sickness, opposition, loss.

But to the things that are unseen. God, Christ at his right hand, the resurrection, the world to come (Hebrews 11:1, 27; 12:2). Then the obvious objection, which any honest reader raises at once: how do you look at something you cannot see? The answer is not mysticism, and it is not pretending. Paul has already told us where the unseen is made visible. The glory of God is in the face of Jesus Christ (v. 6), and it is beheld in the gospel (3:18). You look at the unseen by looking at what God has said about it, until it becomes as real to you as the things in the room. That is what faith actually is in practice: not a feeling, but attention paid to the invisible on the authority of God’s word about it.

Done in ordinary places. That makes this an intensely practical verse rather than an airy one. The looking is done in ordinary places: a Bible open at a kitchen table before anyone else is awake, a hymn sung on the way to work, a truth deliberately turned over during a hospital wait instead of the phone. The word behind look implies aim, and aim implies effort. Nobody drifts into this. The seen presses itself on you free of charge; the unseen has to be attended to.

For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal. Then the reason, and it is where the argument lands. Transient is proskaira: for a season, temporary, on a timer. Everything visible will pass. Notice how completely this reverses the ordinary way of counting. We call the visible real and the invisible abstract. Paul says the opposite. The mortgage, the diagnosis, the argument at work, the state of the nation: these are the things with an expiry date on them. The unseen things, which feel thin because we cannot get our hands on them, are the ones with no end.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring present realities or responsibilities. It means seeing them in eternal perspective. Nor is this the old idea that matter is bad and spirit is good. Paul believes in the resurrection of the body and is about to spend a chapter on it. He is not saying the physical is unreal. He is saying the present arrangement is temporary, and that what is now invisible will one day be the most solid thing there is.

Will fixing my eyes on heaven make me careless about this life? The opposite. The people who have done most good in this world have usually been those most sure of the next, because they had nothing to lose and nothing to prove. Abraham looked for a city with foundations, and so could live as a generous stranger (Hebrews 11:10). A believer who knows his treasure is safe can give money away, forgive debts, serve the unthankful, care for creation and work hard at an ordinary job, all without anxiety, because none of it has to be his heaven. It is the man who looks only at the seen who must cling to it.

In a sentence. So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen, since what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.

On a Tuesday. Where are your eyes fixed today? Notice what you look at first in the morning and last at night, and what you turn to in every spare minute. Then give the unseen a fixed time and place: one passage about Christ or his coming kingdom, read slowly, before the news or the messages. Look up from your problems to the unseen and eternal, and do it again tomorrow.

For worship. So the whole chapter comes to rest on where a person is looking. The jar is cracking; the treasure is not. The outer is going; the inner is being made new. What can be seen is on its way out, and behind it, entirely steady, is a glory with a face: the one thing in the universe that will still be there when everything currently visible has finished happening. He is the same yesterday and today and for ever. Kingdoms rise and fall, bodies fail, the stars themselves will be rolled up like a garment, and the Lamb on the throne remains, and his people will see his face.

4.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart.<sup>2</sup>But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.<sup>3</sup>And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing.<sup>4</sup>In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.<sup>5</sup>For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.<sup>6</sup>For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.<sup>7</sup>But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.<sup>8</sup>We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair;<sup>9</sup>persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;<sup>10</sup>always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies.<sup>11</sup>For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.<sup>12</sup>So death is at work in us, but life in you.<sup>13</sup>Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak,<sup>14</sup>knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.<sup>15</sup>For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.<sup>16</sup>So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.<sup>17</sup>For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,<sup>18</sup>as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

5.title: The Heavenly Dwelling, the Judgment Seat, and the Ministry of Reconciliation
5.overview:
Paul has just said that his outer self is wasting away and that he looks to what is unseen. Now he explains why death does not frighten him. If this tent, our present body, is taken down, we have a building from God, eternal in the heavens. We groan now, longing not to be stripped bare but to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, so that what is mortal is swallowed up by life; and God has given the Spirit as a down payment. So Paul is courageous: he would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. Either way, his aim is to please him, because all must appear before the judgement seat of Christ.

That fear of the Lord, and above all the love of Christ, drives his ministry. One died for all, so all died, so that the living should live for him. Anyone in Christ is a new creation. God has reconciled us to himself through Christ, not counting our sins against us, and has made Paul an ambassador with a message: be reconciled to God. The chapter ends with one of the greatest sentences in Scripture: God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Heavenly Dwelling and the Judgment Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why death does not frighten him. The present body is like a tent that will one day be taken down, but God has a permanent dwelling ready. Believers long to receive it, not to be left without a body but to have mortality swallowed up by life, and the Spirit is God’s guarantee. So Paul is confident: to leave the body is to be at home with the Lord, which he would prefer. Either way, his ambition is to please Christ, because everyone will stand before Christ’s judgement seat and give account for their life in the body.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment seat of Christ (v. 10) is a significant and sometimes neglected doctrine. Reformed theology insists on two distinct judgments: the justification that settles the believer’s eternal standing (entirely by grace, through faith, in Christ — Rom. 8:1: “no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”) and the assessment of the believer’s life and works (1 Cor. 3:10–15; 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 22:12). At the bēma, salvation is not at stake; stewardship is. This distinction protects the gospel of grace while maintaining genuine accountability for the quality of the Christian life.
verseByVerse.examples: A Christian professional justifies a series of ethical compromises in his career with the thought that “grace covers everything.” He is not wrong about grace — but he is using it as a licence rather than a motivation. The judgment seat of Christ does not threaten his justification; it does call him to account for the quality of his stewardship. Paul says the knowledge of the judgment seat motivates him to “persuade others” (v. 11) — it is a motivating, not a threatening, reality for the justified believer.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 5 carries on from the unseen, eternal glory of 4:18 and then rises to the heart of the gospel. First, Paul speaks of death and the future. The present body is a tent that will be taken down; God has prepared a permanent building, the resurrection body. We groan now, longing not to be unclothed but to be clothed with life, and God has given the Spirit as a guarantee (vv. 1–5). So we are of good courage: to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord. Whether here or there, we aim to please him, for all will appear before the judgement seat of Christ (vv. 6–10). Second, Paul explains what drives his ministry: the fear of the Lord and the love of Christ. One died for all, so that those who live might live for him. Anyone in Christ is a new creation (vv. 11–17). Third, the message itself: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting trespasses. So we are ambassadors, pleading: be reconciled to God. For God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (vv. 18–21). Verse 21 is one of the clearest statements in Scripture of the great exchange at the heart of the gospel, and the whole chapter climbs toward it: from a tent coming down, to a Judge on his seat, to a King pleading with rebels, to the Son made sin in their place.

For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed. Paul has just said his outer self is wasting away. Now he says what happens when the wasting finishes its work, and he does it with two buildings. The tent first. He is a tentmaker; this is the trade he worked at in Corinth beside Aquila and Priscilla (Acts 18:3). He knows exactly what a tent is worth. It goes up in a morning and comes down in an afternoon. It keeps out most of the weather. The stitching fails, the goat hair stretches, and one season it will not be worth mending. Nobody grows attached to a tent, and nobody expects one to last (compare 2 Peter 1:13–14). That is the body, and notice he does not despise it. A tent is a real shelter and a good one for the journey. It is simply not a house.

Destroyed. The word should not be softened. It is katalyō: taken down, dismantled, what you do to a tent when the camp moves. Paul is not pretending death is gentle. He is saying it is a dismantling, and that a dismantling is not the end of the story when there is a house already standing.

We have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. Three things about it, and each answers something about the tent. It is from God rather than run up by human hands (Mark 14:58; Hebrews 9:11). It is a building, permanent, with foundations. And it is eternal, so the question of how many more seasons it will take never arises. What is this house? Not, in Paul’s mind, a heavenly location instead of a body. He is about to spend three verses insisting that he does not want to be unclothed. Most take the building to be the resurrection body, the same reality he described at length to this church already: it is sown in dishonour and raised in glory, sown in weakness and raised in power (1 Corinthians 15:42–54). What is promised is not escape from embodiment but the exchange of a temporary body for a permanent one.

We know. Notice how the sentence opens. Not we hope, not we like to think. It is the settled knowledge of a man who has staked his life on it, and the ground of the knowledge is that it has already happened once, in a garden, to a body that had been in a tomb for three days.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we receive the resurrection body at the moment of death. Some think believers receive a new body at death, others an interim body until the resurrection. But Paul speaks of being unclothed between death and resurrection (vv. 3–4), and elsewhere places the new body at the last trumpet, at Christ’s return (1 Corinthians 15:52). The more likely reading is that we have expresses certainty: the resurrection body is as good as ours, prepared by God and waiting, so certain that it can be spoken of as present. Between death and that day the soul of the believer is at home with the Lord (v. 8), without the body but not without Christ.

Does it matter what happens to my body after I die? Not to God’s power: he will raise his people whether they were buried, lost at sea or burned, because the resurrection depends on him and not on what is left. But the body matters to God, and Christians have long buried their dead as a sign of that hope, laying the body down like a seed (1 Corinthians 15:36–38) and treating it with honour. Families may differ on practical choices, and none of them can hinder the resurrection. What matters is that we speak of the body as Scripture does: not a shell to be discarded, but a tent that God will replace with a house.

In a sentence. For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is taken down, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands.

On a Tuesday. Your body is a tent. Care for it, but do not cling to it. When you look in the mirror and see it ageing, or sit beside someone whose body is failing, say to yourself what Paul says: we know. What is happening is real, and it is being described accurately here: a shelter coming apart. Nobody is being asked to call it something else. But a better home is waiting.

For worship. The same sentence that describes the tent coming down says that the person inside is not homeless. The building is not being built when the tent falls; the verb is present tense: we have a building. It is standing now, in the heavens, waiting, because the God who made it has already raised one body from the grave and seated it at his right hand. The Son pitched his tent among us (John 1:14), let it be torn down at Calvary, and rose in a body that will never be dismantled again. Every believer’s house is built on that one. Blessed be the God who does not leave his children out in the weather.
verseByVerse.note: Paul, a tentmaker by trade, pictures the present body as a tent — temporary — and the resurrection body as a permanent building.

parallels.desc: houses of clay

verseByVerse.quote: For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling, if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling, if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.

For in this tent we groan. Paul groans. It is worth pausing there before anything else, because a great deal of Christian talk about death is bright in a way this verse is not. The word stenazō is a deep, inarticulate sound: the noise a person makes under a weight, not a complaint formed into words. He uses it in Romans 8 of believers who groan inwardly as they wait for the redemption of their bodies, alongside a whole creation groaning as in the pains of childbirth (Romans 8:22–23). It is the sound of something that knows it was made for more than this.

Hope does not require pretending. So Christian hope does not require pretending to be comfortable. Anyone who has been ill for a long time, or has watched someone they love become someone they have to care for, knows the groan. This verse says it is not unbelief. It is the correct response to a tent in a storm.

Longing to put on our heavenly dwelling. But look what the groaning is for. Not for release, not for the end of consciousness, not even simply for heaven. Paul mixes his pictures, building and clothing: the house has become a garment, and the desire is to have it on. He longs to be clothed with the resurrection body.

If indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked. This half-line has puzzled readers for centuries and it deserves a straight answer rather than a shrug. The image is consistent with everything around it. To be naked is to be without a body: a self with no dwelling, exposed, uncovered. In the Greek world that was the goal: the soul at last free of the flesh, the immortal escaping the mortal. Plato would have called it salvation. Paul calls it nakedness, and shrinks from it. A bodiless state is not the goal; resurrection is. (A textual note: some manuscripts read taking it off instead of putting it on, and the ESV margin mentions this. The point is not affected: Paul does not want to be found without a body.)

A correction we still need. That is a deeply important correction, because Christians have absorbed far more of the Greek idea than they realise. Ask most believers what happens at death and the answer will be about the soul going to heaven, and there it stops. That is real and it is precious; Paul will say in six verses that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord. But it is not the hope of this chapter, and it is not the end. It is the interval. The Christian hope is a body: a real one, on a real new earth, standing up out of a grave. And the reason Paul recoils from nakedness is that God made us to be embodied and called it very good. Human beings are not souls temporarily inconvenienced by flesh. The body is not the problem; death is the problem, and the answer to death is not escape from the body but the resurrection of it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the soul without the body is unhappy. Being with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23). But it is incomplete until the resurrection.

What will the resurrection body be like? It will be like Christ’s risen body (Philippians 3:21). It will be truly you, recognisable, as the risen Jesus was known by his friends and even ate with them (Luke 24:39–43). It will be physical, not ghostly. But it will be imperishable, glorious, powerful and fully suited to the Spirit (1 Corinthians 15:42–44): no more decay, disease, disability or death, no more tiredness that sleep cannot cure. Scripture does not answer every curious question, such as age or appearance, but it says enough: the body you will have is the one God always meant you to have, and it will never be taken down.

In a sentence. Meanwhile we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, because when we are clothed we will not be found without a body.

On a Tuesday. Check what your own longing is actually aimed at. If it is chiefly to be finished with pain, that is honest and God is not offended by it. But there is a larger thing to want, and it will bear more weight: not to be rid of the tent, but to be at last properly clothed. When you groan in your body, bring the groan to God and turn it into hope: Lord, I am waiting for what you have promised.

For worship. Everything necessary for that clothing has already been done in the body of a man who came out of a grave in one piece. The Son of God did not despise our flesh; he took it, carried it to the cross, and raised it, and he wears it still at the Father’s right hand. The groan of the creation and the groan of the believer are not the sounds of a lost cause. They are birth pangs, and the One who made bodies and called them very good has promised to finish what he began. Praise him for a hope that is as solid as an empty tomb.

verseByVerse.quote: For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened. He says the groan again, and this time he says why. Being burdened is bareō: weighed down, pressed by a load. It is the same root Paul used in chapter 1 of the affliction in Asia, when he was so utterly burdened beyond his strength (1:8).

Not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed. Then he corrects a misunderstanding before it can form, and the correction is the heart of the verse. Two different desires, and the difference matters enormously. To want to be unclothed is to want to be finished: to have the thing taken off and nothing put in its place. To want to be further clothed, ependyomai, is to want something put on over the present one. The Greek carries that quite literally: a garment drawn on top of what is already being worn. Paul would prefer to be alive at Christ’s return and have the resurrection body put on over the present one, without dying at all (1 Corinthians 15:51–53). He is not longing for the end of his existence, nor even chiefly for relief. He is longing for the moment when the mortal thing he is wearing is covered by something so much more alive that the mortality disappears inside it.

So that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. One of the great images in Scripture. The verb is katapinō: to gulp down, to swallow whole. It is the word used in chapter 2 of a man in danger of being overwhelmed by sorrow (2:7), and it is the word of Isaiah’s promise that God will swallow up death forever (Isaiah 25:8), which Paul quotes in triumph at the end of 1 Corinthians 15 (15:54). Notice which way round it runs. We speak of death swallowing people; every funeral has that shape, the person going down and the ground closing over. Paul reverses it. Life is the mouth. Mortality is what gets swallowed.

Two candles. Picture the difference. A candle blown out is unclothed: the light removed, dark where it was. A candle carried outside at sunrise is swallowed up by life: nothing has been taken away, and there is so much more light that the flame is no longer needed. That is the Christian hope, and it is worth getting straight, because most of us instinctively imagine death as the first picture and hope for the best.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul feared death. He longed for the fullness of life, which only resurrection brings.

Is it wrong to wish I could just stop? No; Paul was carrying that weight when he wrote this, and so did Elijah and Job. If you have ever caught yourself wanting simply to stop, the tiredness that is deeper than sleep, the private wish to be finished, this verse does not condemn you. What it does is take the desire and correct its aim. What you actually want is not to be switched off. It is to be so thoroughly alive that everything currently wearing you out is swallowed and gone. But if the wish begins to turn into thoughts of ending your own life, tell someone today: a pastor, a friend, a doctor. That darkness lies to you, and God has given you people and help for exactly this.

In a sentence. For while we are in this tent, we groan and are burdened, not because we want to be unclothed but to be clothed over with our heavenly dwelling, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

On a Tuesday. Death is not the goal; life is. When you think about dying, your own or someone else’s, stop picturing the candle blown out. Picture the sunrise. Then hold on to the hope of resurrection by saying it aloud in the words of Scripture: death is swallowed up in victory.

For worship. There is only one place in the universe where life has ever been offered like this, by a Lord who went into the ground himself and came out with mortality swallowed whole. Death opened its mouth for him on Friday and found on Sunday that it had swallowed something it could not keep down. Now the direction has changed for ever. The grave is not the mouth; life is. Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ, and who will one day swallow up in life every weary, burdened tent that belongs to him.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.

He who has prepared us for this very thing is God. Everything in the previous four verses has been about longing. Now Paul says where the longing came from. The verb, katergazomai, means to work something up, to fashion it for a purpose. The homesickness is not a temperament and not wishful thinking; it was made. God fashioned you for the building, and then he made you want it. This is your destiny, and it was designed.

The ache that nothing satisfies. That is worth turning over, because it explains something most people notice and few can account for. There is a restlessness in human beings that no arrangement of circumstances satisfies. Get the house, the health, the family, the settled work, and there remains a thin persistent ache that something is not yet right. We usually treat it as a fault to be corrected by acquiring one more thing. Paul says it is a fitting, deliberately made, and it corresponds to something real.

Who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee. Then the evidence. The word is arrabōn again, met already at 1:22 (and Ephesians 1:14): the down payment that legally commits the payer to hand over the rest. Not a token of goodwill. The first instalment, in the same currency as the balance. The Spirit is the first part of our future life, given now, guaranteeing the rest, and the Spirit who raised Jesus will raise us (Romans 8:11). So the argument runs like this. You were built for the resurrection body. You can tell, because you groan. And to prove that the groaning is not a cruel joke, God has put a deposit in your hands, and the deposit is not a thing but a Person.

The first instalment. Take that seriously and it changes how a believer reads his own spiritual experience. The moments when Scripture has come alive; the peace that arrived when there was no reason for it; the affection for people you would once have avoided; the fact that you want God at all: those are not the whole payment and they were never meant to satisfy you. They are the first instalment, deliberately given so that you would know what is coming and be unable to settle for less. That is why a Christian who is spiritually alive is often more homesick rather than less. The deposit does not quiet the longing. It confirms it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean resurrection is uncertain. The deposit guarantees it.

Can that guarantee be lost? No. The one who gave it is God, and he does not default on what he has pledged. Paul says the Spirit is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it (Ephesians 1:14). A believer can grieve the Spirit (Ephesians 4:30), but in the same verse Paul says he was sealed for the day of redemption. And the fear of having lost the Spirit is not evidence that one has; it is usually the evidence of a conscience he is still at work in.

Do I need a special experience to know I have the Spirit? No. Every believer has the Spirit; anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him (Romans 8:9). Scripture does not tie his presence to a dramatic sign, a particular feeling or a gift of tongues. The marks it gives are quieter and surer: you call God Father from the heart (Romans 8:15–16), you confess Jesus as Lord (1 Corinthians 12:3), you love his people, you fight your sin, and his fruit, love, joy, peace, patience, slowly grows in you (Galatians 5:22–23). Look for those, not for fireworks.

In a sentence. Now the one who has fashioned us for this very purpose is God, who has given us the Spirit as a deposit, guaranteeing what is to come.

On a Tuesday. When assurance is thin, you will be tempted to look for proof in the strength of your feelings, which rise and fall with sleep and circumstance. Look instead for the deposit. Is there anything in you that was not there before: any hunger for God, any grief over sin that is more than embarrassment, any love for his people that has no natural explanation? Name it, and thank God for it.

For worship. That deposit is not your achievement. It is money already paid into the account by Someone who does not default, and every penny of it is a promise about the rest. The Father who fashioned us for glory, the Son who rose as the first instalment of the new creation, the Spirit who lives in us as the down payment: the whole Trinity is engaged in getting us home. God does not make a down payment on something he means to abandon. Praise him that the ache in us is his handiwork, and that he has already begun to answer it with himself.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “guarantee” was used for a deposit or first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.quote: So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.

So we are always of good courage. Paul has been groaning for four verses. Now, without contradiction, he says he is always of good courage. Both are true at once, and any account of the Christian life that has to choose between them has gone wrong somewhere. The word is tharreō: to be confident, cheerful, to take heart. And always: not on good days. The courage does not depend on the groaning having stopped. It rests on the Spirit’s guarantee.

We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord. Then a startling admission. The two words are endēmeō and ekdēmeō: to live in one’s own country, and to be abroad. Paul is saying that the present life, even at its best, is a kind of absence. He has had the Damascus road, the third heaven, revelations he is not permitted to describe, and he still calls this away from the Lord. In this life we are with Christ by the Spirit, but not yet face to face.

No guilt about the distance. Nobody should be told to feel guilty about it, then. Every Christian knows the frustration: the prayers that feel like speaking into the next room, the sense that the best moments were glimpses rather than sight. That is not a defect in your discipleship. It is the address you are currently living at.

For we walk by faith, not by sight. Here is the reason, in one of the most quoted and most misused sentences in the New Testament. Take the misuse first. It is regularly used to mean that Christians should act on impressions without evidence, or that asking sensible questions is a lack of faith, or that the less you know the more spiritual your decision. That is not what the words mean. Sight here translates eidos: appearance, form, the visible thing itself. Paul is not contrasting faith with thinking. He is contrasting faith with seeing Christ face to face, which is what verse 8 goes on to describe. The believer walks now on the testimony of a Lord he has not yet seen; one day faith will become sight and the walking by faith will be over (1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 Peter 1:8).

A description before a command. That makes the sentence a description before it is a command. This is simply the condition of every Christian who has ever lived. Nobody in the church has seen him now. Even Paul, after the road to Damascus, is walking the same way you are. Note the verb too. Not we stand by faith or we feel by faith. We walk. It is the ordinary word for daily conduct, one foot in front of the other, going somewhere on a road you cannot see the end of. Faith is not primarily a state of certainty; it is a way of moving in the dark on the word of Someone who can see.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is absent from believers now. He is with us always (Matthew 28:20), by his Spirit. But not visibly.

How do I make decisions by faith, not by sight? Not by waiting for a sign or an inner voice. Walking by faith means trusting what God has said and acting on it when you cannot see how it will turn out. So decide in the light of Scripture first: what does God command, forbid or commend here? Then use the wisdom God gives: pray, think carefully, ask mature believers, weigh your circumstances honestly (Proverbs 15:22; James 1:5). Where Scripture leaves you free, choose what seems wisest and most loving, and trust God with the outcome. Faith is not a leap away from reason; it is obedience that does not need to see the end of the road first.

In a sentence. Therefore we are always confident, knowing that as long as we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord. For we live by faith, not by sight.

On a Tuesday. Walk by faith today. Pick the thing you are most anxious about and find one promise of God that speaks to it. Act on the promise, not on the anxiety: do the duty, make the call, give the gift, rest when you should rest, and leave what you cannot see with the One who can.

For worship. That is why the courage is possible while the groaning continues. A man walking a mountain path at night with a guide he trusts is not comfortable and is not lost. He may say both things in the same breath, and Paul does. Our Guide has walked the whole road before us, through death and out the other side, and he holds our hand in the dark. We have not seen him, yet we love him; and the day is coming when the walking by faith will end, and we will see the One we have trusted all along, and find that he was exactly as good as he said.

verseByVerse.quote: Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. The two words are swapped round. In verse 6 he was at home in the body and away from the Lord; now he says he would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. This verse is where a Christian goes when someone he loves has died. So take the question directly, because it is the one people actually ask at a graveside: what happens to a believer at the moment of death?

Immediately at home. Paul’s answer here is as plain as it could be. Away from the body, and immediately at home with the Lord. There is no gap, no waiting room, no period of unconsciousness. He says the same thing to the Philippians from prison: his desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better (Philippians 1:23). And the Lord himself said it to a dying criminal who had nothing to offer and no time left: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). Today. This is what theologians call the intermediate state: the condition of a believer between dying and the resurrection of the body. It is conscious, it is with Christ, and it is better than here; and it is not the end, because the body is still to be raised.

Where Christians differ: what happens at death? Some teach soul sleep, an unconscious state until the resurrection; Roman Catholics teach purgatory for most believers. Verdict: To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, immediately and consciously. There is no purgatory and no soul sleep. It is difficult to see how being asleep for centuries could be called far better, or how it could be described as being at home with the Lord at all; the New Testament’s language is of presence, and of presence now. Nor is there an interval of purging for believers who died imperfect. Paul, who knew what he still was, expects to be at home the moment he is away. The reason is not that he had reached a standard. It is verse 21, thirteen verses further on: the exchange has already been made. The souls of believers, made perfect in holiness, are received into heaven, where they behold God’s face in light and glory, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies (Westminster 32.1).

Two things at a Christian funeral. Hold together, though, what this chapter holds together. Being with Christ without a body is far better, and it is still not the end. Verses 3–4 called that state nakedness, and Paul did not want it for its own sake. The full hope is further clothing: the resurrection body, the new creation, the dead raised. So a Christian funeral is properly two things at once. The person is with the Lord today, and there is a morning coming when they will be given back their body and it will never fail again.

Home. Notice the one word Paul uses for it: home. Not a reward, not a destination, not even a place. Home is where a person stops being a stranger. The whole of this life he has described as living abroad. Death, for a believer, is the end of the foreign posting.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should seek death. It means they need not fear it. Paul stays, gladly, as long as his Lord has work for him (Philippians 1:24–25).

Can my loved one who has died see me, or can I speak to them? Scripture does not tell us that the dead in Christ watch over us, and it firmly forbids trying to contact the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). The great cloud of witnesses in Hebrews 12:1 are witnesses in the sense of those who testify by their lives of faith, not spectators sent to guard us. So speak to God about them, not to them. Thank him for them; tell him your grief. You have not lost them; you have been separated from them for a while, and they are where you are going.

What if they died with sins they never confessed? A believer is not saved by having confessed every sin, but by Christ, whose blood cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7). Every believer dies with sins he did not know about or never named; if forgiveness depended on a complete list, no one would be home. Paul expects to be with the Lord because of what Christ did, not because his accounts with God were tidy at the last moment. If your loved one trusted Christ, the unfinished conversations, the last weak years, the failures you remember, do not keep them out. They are at home.

In a sentence. We are confident, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

On a Tuesday. If someone you love has died in Christ, say it plainly to yourself and to those grieving with you: they are at home with the Lord. And if you are afraid of dying, do not try to argue yourself out of the fear; look at where death takes a believer. Then live today as someone whose worst outcome is going home.

For worship. The last enemy has been made into a door. That was not true before a certain Friday. It cost the Lord of glory his own descent into the ground to change what death is for everyone who belongs to him, and now the worst thing that can happen to a Christian is that he goes home. Into the hands of the Lord who said today to a thief, every believer is received at the moment of death, welcomed, made perfect, and kept until the morning of the resurrection. Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints, because he paid for every one of them himself.

verseByVerse.quote: So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.

So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. Having settled where he is going, Paul says what he intends to do in the meantime. Whether we are at home or away, living or dead, in the body or out of it, the aim does not change: to please him. The word for aim is philotimeomai, a term of ambition: to count something an honour, to make it your driving purpose. Paul was an ambitious man. This was his ambition.

For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. Then the reason, and it is one many Christians are surprised to find in their Bibles. The word is bēma. Anyone in Corinth knew what one looked like; there was a stone platform in their own marketplace where Paul had once stood before Gallio (Acts 18:12). A bēma was the raised seat from which a magistrate gave verdicts, and also the platform at the games from which the judge awarded the crowns. And appear is phaneroō: to be made manifest, laid open. It is not merely to show up, but to have a life brought fully into the light.

So that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. Notice what he has done in the body. Not what he intended, not what he believed about doing. The body is where the Christian life is actually conducted: the hands, the diary, the money, the tongue. This is the same body Paul has just called a tent that is coming down, and here he says it is the very place where a life is either laid up or wasted. Our deeds in this bodily life matter for ever, and all of them will be assessed.

Where Christians differ: judgement of believers. How can believers, who are justified and free from condemnation (Romans 8:1), be judged by their works? Verdict: Believers will not be condemned; their sins are covered by Christ. But their lives will be revealed and evaluated, and their works rewarded according to God’s grace (1 Corinthians 3:12–15; Matthew 25:21). Good works do not earn justification, but they are the evidence of true faith, and God graciously rewards them (Westminster 33.1). The judgement will also openly vindicate God’s people and show his justice. Both statements are true because two different things are in view. The verdict on whether you belong to Christ is not reopened; it was settled at the cross. What is assessed at the bēma is what you did with the life you were given after that verdict was passed. Paul wrote about this to this same church a letter earlier: the foundation is Christ and cannot be relaid, but what a man builds on it is tested by fire, and some of it burns, though he himself will be saved (1 Corinthians 3:15).

What does good or evil mean for a believer? His sins will not be held against him for condemnation; their penalty was paid at the cross. But his life will be brought into the light, what was done in faith and love and what was not, for the Lord will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of the heart (1 Corinthians 4:5). What he receives is not a verdict on his salvation but on his service. Scripture speaks of reward, of commendation from God (1 Corinthians 4:5), and of work that survives the fire (1 Corinthians 3:14); some will suffer loss, though they themselves are saved. That loss is real, and it is a reason to live well; but it never touches the believer’s standing in Christ.

Should that frighten a believer? Paul does not seem frightened; he moves straight from it to ambition, not to dread. But he plainly does not treat it as nothing either. The honest position is that a Christian may lose a great deal there, the years spent on things that turned out to be nothing, the gifts unused, the reputation protected instead of spent, and will lose nothing of Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on our works. It means our works matter.

Is it selfish to want rewards? No, as long as the reward is what Scripture says it is. Jesus himself urged us to lay up treasure in heaven (Matthew 6:20), and the chief reward is not a prize separate from God but the joy of his approval: well done, good and faithful servant, enter into the joy of your master (Matthew 25:21). Wanting that is not mercenary; it is love wanting to please the one it loves. And the reward is grace on grace: God crowns in us the works he himself worked in us. No one in heaven will boast in his reward; everyone will cast it at the feet of the Lamb.

In a sentence. So whether we are at home in the body or away from it, our aim is to please him. For we must all appear before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each of us may receive what is due for what we have done in the body, good or bad.

On a Tuesday. Take this week as it actually was: the hours, the conversations, the things you gave your attention to. That is what will be looked at, by Someone who loves you and who died for the failures in it. A Christian who lives with that in view does not become anxious. He becomes deliberate. Make it your ambition today to please Christ in one specific thing you would otherwise have done carelessly.

For worship. The Judge on that seat is the same Jesus who was once made to stand before Pilate’s bēma and was condemned there in our place. Everyone who belongs to him will stand before a Judge who has already been judged for them. He knows every hidden thing, and he is not looking for reasons to reject his people; he is looking for every cup of cold water, every unseen act of faithfulness, so that he can praise it. How kind is the Lord, who saves us freely and then rewards us for the very works his grace produced, and who will make even the judgement day a day of joy for those who are his.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat (bema) was the raised platform where a Roman official gave judgment; Paul had stood before one in Corinth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Ministry of Reconciliation and the Great Exchange
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Knowing the fear of the Lord, Paul tries to persuade people, and he hopes the Corinthians can see his sincerity and answer those who boast in appearances. What drives him is Christ’s love: one died for all, so all who are his have died with him and now live for him. Paul no longer judges anyone, Christ included, by worldly standards; whoever is in Christ belongs to the new creation. God has reconciled people to himself through Christ, not counting their sins against them, and has made Paul his envoy, pleading with people to accept that reconciliation. The ground of it all is an exchange: the sinless Christ was treated as sin for us, so that in him we might be counted righteous before God.
verseByVerse.theology:
“In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself” (v. 19) — the agency is God’s. Reconciliation is initiated, accomplished, and offered by God, not by humanity. The word order matters and is often misquoted: it is not that God was waiting to be reconciled to humanity, as if he needed to be persuaded or appeased by a more merciful Son. Rather, God himself was the reconciler — the one who, in Christ, removed the obstacle that prevented humanity from being reconciled to him. The obstacle is sin; the removal is the cross, and v. 21 states its cost.

Verse 21 — “he made him to be sin who knew no sin” — requires precise handling. “Made him to be sin” does not mean Christ became a sinner or had sinful desires. It means God treated Christ as the sin-bearer — the one who stood in the place of sinners, receiving the judgment that sin deserves. The Old Testament background is the sin offering: in Leviticus the offering itself is called by the same word as the sin it carried, the animal becoming the sin-bearer, and Isaiah says it without a picture at all — “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isa. 53:6). The result: we “become the righteousness of God” — not merely receive a righteous verdict but are constituted righteous in him, which is why the standing cannot be damaged by a bad week.
verseByVerse.examples: An evangelism trainer teaches his church that the goal of evangelism is to persuade people to make a decision for Christ. This passage suggests a deeper framework: the goal is to implore people, on Christ’s behalf, to be reconciled to God — as ambassadors of a reconciliation that God himself has already accomplished and is already offering. The difference is not merely semantic: the ambassador does not create the peace; he announces and conveys the peace that the King has already made.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.

Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. The judgement seat has an immediate effect on Paul, and it is not the one we might expect. It does not send him into anxious self-examination. It sends him out to talk to people. First, that phrase, because it is badly worn and often emptied out. The fear of the Lord is not terror of a God who might turn on you; that is precisely what the gospel removes. Nor is it merely respect, which is how it is usually softened. It is the awe of a creature who has grasped what God actually is: that this is the One before whom the nations are like a drop from a bucket (Isaiah 40:15), and that one day every person will stand before his Son’s seat (v. 10). A man who has felt that does not treat other people’s eternity as a conversational risk.

We persuade. So he persuades. The word is peithō, the ordinary one for winning someone over by argument. Paul is not manipulating and not merely announcing; he is reasoning with people, pleading, working to change their minds (Acts 17:4; 18:4), because he believes what he has just said about the bēma. There is a quiet challenge in the connection. Most Christian silence about Christ is not really shyness. It is that we have stopped believing anything much is at stake. Recover the seriousness and the awkwardness stops being decisive.

But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. The word known is again phaneroō, made manifest. God already sees Paul’s heart completely; Paul hopes the Corinthians, in their consciences, will recognise his sincerity too. He lives now as a man already laid open before God, which is the best preparation there is for the day when every life will be.

We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us. Then Paul turns back to his critics, and verse 12 is delicately done. He knows how the previous chapters have sounded; he raised the objection himself at 3:1. So he says it again: we are not commending ourselves. His purpose is not to be admired. It is to put something in their hands, so that they can answer the others. That is a generous piece of pastoral strategy. The Corinthians were caught between two sets of teachers and had nothing to say when Paul was disparaged in front of them. He is arming them, not defending himself.

Those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart. Notice the fault line he draws. Literally, boasting in the face rather than the heart. The rival teachers had presence, polish, credentials, visions and delivery. Paul had a wasting body and a speaking manner his critics thought contemptible. The church has never stopped needing that line drawn. We assess by the face still: the platform manner, the confidence, the numbers, the production. And God has said from the beginning how he assesses, in the words spoken to Samuel while he was busy admiring the wrong brother: “For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). The awkward implication is that the most impressive Christian you know may not be the one God is most pleased with, and neither of you can currently tell.

What it does not mean. It does not mean evangelism should be driven by fear tactics. It means the reality of judgement makes evangelism urgent.

Should a Christian fear God or not? Both answers in Scripture are true, because there are two kinds of fear. The fear that expects punishment is cast out by God’s perfect love (1 John 4:18): a believer need not dread that God will condemn him, because Christ bore the condemnation. But the fear of the Lord, reverent awe at his holiness, majesty and power, is the beginning of wisdom and never leaves the believer; it grows as we know him better (Proverbs 9:10; Hebrews 12:28–29). A child who adores his father and would not dream of grieving him has the right kind. It is the fear that makes us take sin seriously, take people’s souls seriously, and take God at his word.

In a sentence. Since we know what it is to fear the Lord, we try to persuade others. What we are is plain to God, and Paul hopes it is plain to your conscience too. We are not commending ourselves again, but giving you reason to be proud of us, so that you can answer those who take pride in appearance rather than in what is in the heart.

On a Tuesday. Think of one person you see regularly who does not know Christ, and remember that they too will stand before his judgement seat. Let that move you, not to a speech, but to the next honest step: a question about what they believe, an invitation, a word about what Christ means to you. And the next time you size up a Christian by how impressive they are, stop and remember whose eyes see the heart.

For worship. The Lord who looks on the heart is the same Lord who made a way for hearts like ours to be accepted. He is holy enough to be feared by angels and kind enough to be loved by sinners, and in the gospel these are not two moods but one glory. Blessed be the God before whom we are already wholly known, and who, knowing everything, sent his Son to make us his own.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.

For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God. A short verse, and it lets us hear one of the accusations being made about Paul. Beside ourselves translates existēmi: literally to stand outside oneself, the word for being out of one’s mind. Somebody had said Paul was unhinged. It was not a new charge; Festus would later shout it across a courtroom: “Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind” (Acts 26:24). His own Lord had the same thing said about him by his family, who went out to seize him, for they were saying, “He is out of his mind” (Mark 3:21).

What lay behind it. What lay behind it in Corinth we cannot be certain of. Perhaps his ecstatic experiences; he will mention being caught up to the third heaven in chapter 12 (12:1–4), and clearly did not talk about it often. Perhaps simply the shape of his life: a man of formidable training who could have had a comfortable career, who instead crossed provinces on foot, took beatings, and refused payment. To a sensible observer that looks like a man who has lost his balance. And Paul does not deny it. He allocates it. Whatever in him goes past what people find reasonable is between him and God, and God is the One it is for.

If we are in our right mind, it is for you. Then the other half, which is just as important. The word is sōphroneō: sober, self-controlled, sane. He is not choosing between the two. He is saying that when he is measured and careful, that too is a service; it is for their sake, so that they can be taught. Either way, his life is not for himself.

The right way round. There is real pastoral wisdom in that division. Christians frequently feel pulled between two accusations: from one side, that they are excessive, fanatical, disproportionate about religion; from the other, that they are too restrained, too ordinary, not zealous enough. Paul’s answer is that both intensity and sobriety have their place, and that what determines the place is whom each is for. There is a passion that belongs between you and God and does not need an audience: the hours in prayer nobody knows about, the tears over Scripture, the extravagance in giving that would embarrass you if it were discussed. And there is a sober, patient, unremarkable steadiness that belongs to the people you serve, because they need teaching more than they need to watch you burn. The failure comes when the two are swapped: the intensity performed in public where it can be seen, and the sobriety kept for private life, where zeal quietly cools. The Lord warned about exactly that: the giving and praying and fasting done to be seen, which has already had its reward (Matthew 6:1–6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was unstable. It means everything he did was for God and others.

My family thinks I have gone too far with my faith. What should I do? First, be glad you are in good company: they said it of Paul and of Jesus. Then ask honestly whether there is anything in their complaint you should hear. Are you neglecting them, lecturing them, or making your faith a reason to be unkind? If so, put it right; a sober, loving life is itself for them. But if what they object to is simply that Christ comes first, that you worship, give, pray and will not join in sin, do not argue and do not retreat. Love them more visibly than before, keep your private devotion private, and let the steadiness of your life answer the charge over time (1 Peter 3:1–2, 15–16).

In a sentence. If we are out of our mind, as some say, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.

On a Tuesday. Do not be afraid of looking foolish for God. Give him something this week that no one else will know about, and do not mention it. And when you speak to others, speak sensibly and patiently for their good, with the kind of steadiness that helps rather than impresses.

For worship. They said it of Jesus first. The Son of God was thought mad by his own family, because he would not stop healing and teaching long enough to eat. He was extravagant toward his Father, rising before dawn to pray, and he was patient and plain with his disciples, teaching them over and over what they could not grasp. Both were love. His whole life was for God and for us, and none of it for himself. Praise the Lord who was counted out of his mind for our sake, and whose holy zeal for his Father’s house consumed him all the way to the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.

For the love of Christ controls us. Here is the engine of Paul’s life, and he names it in a single phrase. First, whose love? The love of Christ can grammatically mean Paul’s love for Christ or Christ’s love for Paul, and the sentence itself decides it. Look at what follows the word because: not a description of Paul’s devotion but of Christ’s death. It is Christ’s love for him, shown at the cross, that is doing the driving. That distinction is not academic. A ministry powered by how much you love Christ will run exactly as far as your affections do, which on a bad week is not far. A ministry powered by how much he loved you has a fixed and finished event underneath it.

Controls. The word is synechō: to hold together, to press in from both sides, to hem in. It is used of a crowd pressing round a man (Luke 8:45). The picture is not a whip driving him forward but walls preventing him going anywhere else. A river between banks is not restricted; it is given force. Take the banks away and you have a swamp.

Because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died. Then the conclusion he has reached. This is representation, the great Pauline idea. Christ died as the representative and substitute of his people, and what happens to the one counts as having happened to those he stands for, as Adam’s act counted for the race that came from him (Romans 5:18–19). So when Christ died, those who are in him died with him, in union with him (Romans 6:3–8; Galatians 2:20). His death counts as theirs. The old self, the old account, the old standing, went into the grave with him.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Two words in that sentence have been argued over for centuries, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise: for all. Some take all here to mean that Christ died for every human being equally, making salvation possible for all, and applied on believing. Both sides are trying to protect something real: one the sufficiency and freeness of the offer, the other the effectiveness of the cross. Verdict: Paul says the all for whom Christ died have died with him, and live for him. That describes those united to Christ, not every human. Christ died effectively for all his people, of every nation, securing their salvation, not merely making it possible (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). This is definite atonement. The gospel is offered sincerely to every person, and Christ’s death is sufficient for all, but it was designed to save his people (Canons of Dort 2.3, 8). What is beyond argument in this verse is its logic: that his death was for people, in their place, and that it did something to them and not merely for them.

And he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves. Then the purpose, which is where the passage lands. Those who live are those who now have new life in Christ. That is the whole Christian ethic in one line, and it is not first a rule but a consequence. A man who has died is finished with running his own affairs. The only question left is whose he now is. His death frees them from self-centred living.

But for him who for their sake died and was raised. The new life is lived for Christ, and notice both halves: died and was raised. The cross ends the old life; the resurrection gives the new one its Master. The cross and resurrection change the direction of a life.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s love is limited in its sincerity. His love for his people is infinite. And the gospel call goes to all.

Can I tell an unbeliever that Christ died for them? You can tell every person, without hesitation, that Christ died for sinners, that he is a full and sufficient Saviour, that he offers himself freely to them, and that whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). That is the gospel the apostles preached to unbelievers: they proclaimed Christ crucified and called all to repent and believe (Acts 2:38; 17:30). Many in the Reformed tradition prefer that wording to Christ died for you, because the personal assurance belongs to the one who believes. But the offer is utterly sincere. No one who comes will find that Christ did not die for him.

So what does living for him look like on a Monday? It looks like asking, in ordinary decisions, what would please the one who died for me, and not only what I want. It reaches the diary (how I use my time), the bank account (where my money goes), the tongue (what I say about others), the body (what I do with it), the home (how I treat the people closest to me), and work (doing it as for him). It does not mean a life with no rest or enjoyment; it means a life whose centre has moved. The test is not dramatic sacrifice but small daily choices where self used to sit on the throne.

In a sentence. For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that one died for all, and therefore all died. And he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and was raised again.

On a Tuesday. Here is the plainest question in the chapter. Whose life are you living for? Not what you would say: what the diary and the bank statement say. Almost every human being alive is living for himself and has never noticed, because there is nothing unusual about it. Look at one hour of your day, one item of your spending, one relationship, and ask how it would change if it were lived for him.

For worship. The strange thing, the thing that needs explaining, is a person who is not living for himself. And there is only one event in history with the power to produce it. One died. The Son of God went down into death as the head of his people, and they went down with him; he rose, and they rose too. His love does not merely invite us; it hems us in on every side, like banks around a river, until we flow in only one direction, toward him. Glory to the Lord Jesus, whose love was strong enough to die for us and is strong enough now to carry us.

verseByVerse.quote: From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.

From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. If one died for all and all died, then everything has to be looked at again. Paul begins with how he looks at people. According to the flesh means by the world’s standards of assessment: appearance, status, ethnicity, success, the face rather than the heart, exactly the fault line drawn in verse 12. It is the reflex by which we file a person within seconds of meeting them: the accent, the clothes, the job, the health, the usefulness. Paul says that reflex has been retired. The cross changes how we see everyone.

Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. He then gives the decisive example, and it is himself. Saul of Tarsus had assessed Jesus of Nazareth by exactly those criteria: an executed provincial with no standing, a blasphemer, crucified and therefore cursed by God, obviously nothing. He had been completely confident and completely wrong. Now he sees Christ as the risen Lord. A man who has made that mistake about that person never trusts his own first assessment of anyone again.

Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. One of the best-known sentences in the New Testament and one of the most misheard. The Greek is even more abrupt than the English: if anyone in Christ, new creation! There is no verb. And the phrase kainē ktisis, new creation, was not, in Paul’s world, a term for personal improvement. It was the great promise of the prophets about the world itself: behold, I create new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17; Galatians 6:15). Paul takes that cosmic vocabulary and says it has already begun, and where it has begun is inside people. Not just a new person, but part of God’s new creation, the age to come breaking in. Conversion is creation, not renovation.

The old has passed away; behold, the new has come. The words echo Isaiah 43:18–19, where God tells his people to stop dwelling on the former things, because he is doing a new thing. The old order of sin and death is passing; the new has arrived in Christ. And notice the little word at the centre: behold. It is a word for pointing at something. Paul is not describing an inward process; he is drawing attention to an event that has already happened: the new creation begun, in Christ, in the middle of an old world that does not yet know it has been superseded.

The misheard part. This verse has quietly wounded a great many honest Christians. Read as a description of how you feel, it is crushing: the old has passed away, and yet the temper is still there, the same fears, the same failure on a Thursday afternoon that has been there for thirty years. Many conclude the verse cannot be true of them. But look at what the sentence actually says. It does not say if anyone feels new. It says if anyone is in Christ. The newness is first a matter of location, not of sensation. It describes what is true of a person who has been transferred into Christ, on the authority of God who transferred him, and it was as true on the day it happened as it will be on the last day.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never sin or struggle. The old nature still fights (Galatians 5:17). But the believer’s identity is new. What has passed away is the old order you belonged to: the guilt, the condemnation, the ownership, the dominion of sin over you. What remains is the mopping up, and the mopping up is real work that takes a lifetime. But a man does not stop being a citizen because he still has an accent from the old country.

If I am a new creation, do the consequences of my past disappear? The guilt does; not always the consequences. In Christ you are fully forgiven, and God will never hold your past against you. But a debt may still need repaying, a broken trust may take years to rebuild, a prison sentence may still need serving, and a damaged body may not be restored in this life. Zacchaeus, newly saved, repaid what he had taken (Luke 19:8). Face those consequences without despair, because they no longer define you; make right what you can, humbly; and do not let anyone, including yourself, call you by your old name. God does not.

In a sentence. So from now on we regard no one from a worldly point of view. Though we once regarded Christ that way, we do so no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: the old has gone, the new is here!

On a Tuesday. You are a new creation. Do not let your past define you. When old guilt resurfaces, answer it with this verse: that is who I was, not who I am in Christ. And look at others, not by worldly standards, but as people for whom Christ died: the colleague you find dull, the neighbour you have written off, the believer whose background makes you uneasy. Ask what God may be making of them.

For worship. Behold. God is pointing at something, and it is the new creation. The God who said let there be light in Genesis 1 has begun the new heavens and the new earth, and he has begun them in the risen body of Jesus and in the hearts of those who are in him. Every believer is a first piece of a world to come, a down payment on a renewed universe. The old has passed away. Praise the Creator who does not patch up what we ruined, but makes all things new, and has started with us.

parallels.desc: behold, I am doing a new thing

verseByVerse.quote: All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.

All this is from God. Paul now names what has happened, and the word is one of the warmest in the New Testament. But first he says where it came from: all this, the new creation, the death of the one for all, everything from verse 14 onward, is God’s work, from start to finish.

Who through Christ reconciled us to himself. Reconcile, katallassō, is not a religious term at all. It belongs to ordinary life: the ending of a quarrel, the restoration of a relationship that had broken down, a change from enmity to friendship. It is what happens when two people who could not be in the same room are in the same room again. That tells you what the human problem is, underneath everything else. Not chiefly ignorance, or unhappiness, or unrealised potential. Estrangement. We were God’s enemies (Romans 5:10). There is a relationship that is broken, and it is the one every other relationship was hanging from.

The offended party crossed the room. Now watch the direction, because it is everything. God is the one who reconciles. He is not the party being talked round. In every human quarrel, the offended person is the one who has to be approached, and the offender does the approaching. Here the offended party crossed the room. Notice: God reconciled us to himself. The barrier was on both sides: our rebellion, and God’s just wrath. Christ removed both.

That is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself. The world here means people from every nation, not just Israel: God acted in Christ for a world in rebellion. And note carefully what this does and does not mean. It does not mean there was nothing to settle. Paul will say in two verses exactly what it cost, and the cost is the measure of how real the estrangement was.
