Human sin is not a misunderstanding that God waved away; it met the full weight of his opposition to it, and the meeting happened at the cross. What the verse rules out is the picture of a reluctant God being softened by a merciful Son. God himself is the reconciler. He was in Christ doing it.

Not counting their trespasses against them. The phrase carries the whole gospel in six words. Counting is logizomai, an accounting term: reckoning, crediting, entering the item in the ledger. The debts are real and they are not being recorded against those who are reconciled, because God put them on Christ (v. 21). Paul says the same thing in Romans by quoting David: blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin (Romans 4:8).

The ledger inside you. Stop there for a moment, because most people carry a version of that ledger inside them. There is a page in you with things on it you would not want read out: words to a parent now dead, a year you would give anything to have back, something nobody knows. You have been keeping the account even if God is not. This says the entry was not made. Not excused, not minimised, not forgotten in the sense of being overlooked. Charged to somebody else.

And entrusting to us the message of reconciliation. Then, astonishingly, the last clause of each verse: gave us the ministry of reconciliation, entrusting to us the message of reconciliation. God did the work and then handed the announcement to human beings, to the very people who had been on the wrong side of the quarrel. He could have written it in the sky. He chose to say it through the mouths of the reconciled, which means that the ordinary Christian talking awkwardly to a colleague is carrying something that was placed in his hands on purpose.

Where Christians differ: is the whole world reconciled? Universalists read this as saying every person is already reconciled. Some other Christians read it as a reconciliation achieved for every person, which each must then accept; Reformed Christians read it as the world of those God actually reconciles in Christ, drawn from every nation. Verdict: If everyone were already reconciled, Paul would not need to plead: be reconciled to God (v. 20). God accomplished reconciliation in Christ for the world of his people from every nation, and it is received by faith. The message goes to all, calling all to receive it, and no one is reconciled who does not come.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God needed to be persuaded to love us. His love sent Christ. But his justice needed to be satisfied, and Christ satisfied it.

If God has reconciled me, do I have to be reconciled with people? Yes, and the one leads to the other. A person who has been forgiven an unpayable debt cannot keep a ledger against others (Matthew 18:21–35). Jesus told his disciples to leave their gift at the altar and go to be reconciled with a brother first (Matthew 5:23–24). Take the first step, whether you are the offender or the offended, just as God did. Reconciliation is not always fully possible: the other person may refuse, and where there has been abuse, safety comes first and trust must be earned. But forgiveness from the heart, and readiness for peace as far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18), are always required.

In a sentence. All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: that God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ, not counting people’s sins against them. And he has committed to us the message of reconciliation.

On a Tuesday. Think of the page in your own ledger you least want read out, and say to God: this was not counted against me, because it was counted against your Son. Then think of one person with whom you are not at peace, and take one step toward them this week: a message, an apology, a kindness.

For worship. You were God’s enemy, and he made you his friend. He did not wait for you to come round, or ask you to make the first move; he came in the person of his Son, into the middle of the quarrel, and settled it in his own body. There has never been a peacemaker like him. The One we wronged took the cost of the wrong, tore up the record, and then trusted the news to people like us. Praise the God of reconciliation, whose love found a way to be both just and the justifier, and who has made enemies into children.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.

Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ. Paul now names the office. An ambassador, presbeuō, the verb used of an imperial legate, is the personal representative of a sovereign in foreign territory. He does not compose the message; he carries it, exactly. His authority is entirely borrowed, and it is absolute while he is carrying it, because to hear him is to hear the one who sent him. Three things follow from that, and they matter for anyone who has ever felt unqualified to speak about Christ.

Three things about an ambassador. The message is not yours to adjust. An ambassador who improved on his instructions would be recalled. This is the safeguard against every attempt to make the gospel more agreeable, and also the relief, because you are not responsible for whether it is well received. The authority is not yours either, and that is the encouragement. The dignity of an ambassador has nothing to do with his personal impressiveness. A shy man with a letter from a king has more standing in that room than a magnificent man without one. And the posting is foreign. Christians live in a country that is not theirs, representing a King the locals do not acknowledge. That accounts for a good deal of the strangeness of the Christian life. You were not meant to feel entirely at home here.

God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ. The tone of the sentence is remarkable. Both verbs are words of entreaty: appeal is parakaleō, to urge, to beg; implore is deomai, to plead. God does not summon; he appeals. Paul does not command; he implores. When the gospel is preached, God himself is pleading. This is the Almighty, the offended party, the one who was in the right throughout, pleading with the people who wronged him to accept the peace he has already made at his own expense. There is nothing else like it in the history of religion, and it ought to stop us. We think of God as the one who must be approached carefully. Here he is the one doing the approaching, and not with terms but with entreaty.

Be reconciled to God. Accept the reconciliation God has provided. Stop fighting him. Receive his peace. And notice who is being addressed. This is written to a church. Paul is imploring people who are already in the pews, perhaps because some were drifting, and the reason is worth sitting with. It is entirely possible to be inside the congregation, holding the doctrine, doing the duties, and never to have made peace: to be at church and not at home. If the whole thing has been an arrangement you inherited rather than a quarrel that was ended, then this verse is not about the neighbours. It is addressed to you, and it is not a threat; it is a plea.

A passive verb. The word be reconciled is passive. Nobody reconciles himself. It has all been done; the only thing left is to stop refusing it. That is what the King is pleading for, through the mouths of his own ambassadors, barely a generation after his Son died to make it possible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we reconcile ourselves by effort. It means we receive what God has done.

I have been in church all my life. How do I know I have actually been reconciled? Not by your attendance or your family, but by whether you have personally come to Christ. Ask yourself honestly: have I seen my sin as an offence against God, not just a mistake? Have I stopped relying on my good record and trusted Christ alone, his death in my place? Do I now want to belong to him and follow him? If you are unsure, do not wait until you are sure; respond to the plea now. Tell God plainly that you have been at war with him, that you trust his Son’s death for you, and that you give yourself to him. Then speak to your pastor. Whoever comes to Christ is never turned away.

In a sentence. So we are Christ’s ambassadors, as though God were making his appeal through us. We beg you on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God.

On a Tuesday. You are Christ’s ambassador at work, at home, with friends. You are not responsible for results, only for carrying his message faithfully and in his tone: pleading, not scolding. Pray this week for one opportunity to speak of the peace God has made, and when it comes, say it simply.

For worship. The King pleads. The Lord of heaven and earth, who could have demanded our surrender, sends messengers to beg us to accept a peace he paid for himself. He stands at the door and knocks. He stretches out his hands all day to a rebellious people. He wept over the city that would kill him. No one has ever been more patient with his enemies, or more eager to be friends with them. Blessed be the God who implores, and whose pleading is the sound of grace that will not give up.
verseByVerse.note: An ambassador spoke with the authority of the king who sent him.

verseByVerse.quote: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin. Fifteen words in Greek, and there is nothing in Scripture more densely packed. Luther called what it describes the joyous exchange. Take it apart slowly. He made him to be sin. The subject is God the Father; the object is his Son. And the verb is deliberate and terrible: not he allowed, not it happened to him. God did this. What can it mean? Not that Christ became sinful; the next clause forbids it, and so does the whole New Testament. It means that God treated him as sin: laid our sins on him, and punished sin in him (Isaiah 53:6, 10; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). Everything that the sin of his people deserved was laid on him and dealt with there.

The shape of it in the Old Testament. The Old Testament had been teaching the shape of it for fifteen centuries: a hand laid on the head of an animal, guilt transferred, the innocent dying in the place of the guilty. Some understand the word sin here to mean a sin offering, as it sometimes does in the Greek translation of Leviticus 4. Either way, he bore our sin. And Isaiah had said it without a picture at all: “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).

Who knew no sin. The one phrase in the sentence that could be said about no other human being who has ever lived (Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22; 1 John 3:5). Not merely that he did not commit sins, but that he had no acquaintance with it from the inside: no divided motive, no private version of himself. His enemies watched him for three years looking for something and in the end had to find false witnesses who could not agree (Mark 14:55–56). Only a sinless one could bear others’ sin; a sinner would have had his own to answer for.

What being made sin sounds like. And it is this one, the only person in history with nothing whatever owing, who is made sin. That is why the cry from the cross is what it is. “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34) is not a moment of confusion. It is what being made sin sounds like from the inside, in the one relationship that had never had a shadow across it since before the world was made.

So that in him we might become the righteousness of God. Now the exchange completes, and notice how far it goes. It does not say we might be forgiven, though we are. It does not say we might be treated as though we had not sinned, though we are. It says we become the righteousness of God: the right standing God gives, credited to us (Romans 3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). As Christ was treated as a sinner though he was not, we are treated as righteous though we are not. Feel the two halves against each other. He got what was ours: the guilt, the charge, the abandonment. We get what was his: the standing, the welcome, the Father’s pleasure. Nothing was averaged; each side received the other’s whole account.

In him. And everything turns on the last two words. This is not a transfer of a substance into the believer, as though righteousness were now a quality you possess and might mislay on a bad week. It is true of you because of where you are: in union with Christ. That is why a Christian at his worst is no less righteous before God than at his best. The standing was never generated by the performance, and cannot be damaged by it.

Where Christians differ: imputation. Some deny that our sin was legally credited to Christ and his righteousness legally credited to us, saying instead that we are made righteous only by inner transformation. Verdict: The parallel is exact. Christ was made sin, not by becoming sinful inside, but by having our sin counted to him. So we become righteous, not first by inner change, but by having his righteousness counted to us. This is double imputation, the heart of justification by faith alone (Westminster 11.1; Heidelberg Catechism Q. 60). Inner transformation follows in sanctification, but it is not the ground of our acceptance with God. And it shows the cross as penal substitution.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ ever stopped being holy, or that God the Father hated the Son. Christ was beloved even as he bore the Father’s wrath against sin. Indeed, the Son was never more pleasing to the Father than in that act of obedience (Philippians 2:8–9).

How can it be just for God to punish an innocent person in our place? It would be unjust if an unwilling stranger were seized and punished for someone else. But that is not the cross. The Son came willingly, laying down his life of his own accord (John 10:18). He came as the head of his people, joined to them, as Adam was joined to the race. And he is God himself: the Judge did not lay the penalty on a third party but bore it in his own person. At the cross God is both just and the one who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:26). Justice is not set aside; it is fully satisfied, by God, for us.

If I am counted righteous, does it matter how I live? It matters more than ever, though not as payment. Paul anticipated the question: shall we go on sinning so that grace may increase? By no means (Romans 6:1–2). The same union with Christ that gives you his righteousness also joins you to his death and resurrection, so that sin no longer rules you. Those who are in him become a new creation (v. 17) and live for him who died for them (v. 15). Holiness is not the price of your standing; it is the shape of your new life. You obey because you are accepted, not in order to be accepted.

In a sentence. God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

On a Tuesday. When your conscience accuses you today, do not answer it with your recent performance, good or bad. Answer it with this verse: my sin was counted to him, and his righteousness is counted to me. Then, freed from earning, go and do the good works God has prepared for you, gladly.

For worship. There is nothing to add here, and nothing that could be added. He was made what he was not, so that we might be made what we could never be. The sinless one hanging in the place of the guilty, and the guilty walking away wearing his righteousness: this is what the Father planned, what the Son bore, and what the Spirit was sent to seal, and it will be the subject of the singing when this world is over. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain. He took my sin; he gave me his righteousness. Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, for an exchange so unequal that heaven will never finish praising it.

parallels.desc: he was pierced for our transgressions

5.text: <sup>1</sup>For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.<sup>2</sup>For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling,<sup>3</sup>if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.<sup>4</sup>For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.<sup>5</sup>He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.<sup>6</sup>So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord,<sup>7</sup>for we walk by faith, not by sight.<sup>8</sup>Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.<sup>9</sup>So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him.<sup>10</sup>For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.<sup>11</sup>Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience.<sup>12</sup>We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.<sup>13</sup>For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.<sup>14</sup>For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died;<sup>15</sup>and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.<sup>16</sup>From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer.<sup>17</sup>Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.<sup>18</sup>All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation;<sup>19</sup>that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.<sup>20</sup>Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.<sup>21</sup>For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

6.title: The Open Heart, the Catalogue of Hardships, and the Unequal Yoke
6.overview:
Having said that God makes his appeal through his ambassadors, Paul makes it: do not receive God’s grace in vain, for now is the day of salvation. Then he shows the Corinthians what a true servant of God looks like, in one of the most powerful passages he ever wrote. It is not a list of successes but of endurance: beatings, prisons, riots, sleepless nights and hunger, and alongside them purity, kindness, the Holy Spirit and genuine love. He lives in paradoxes: treated as an impostor yet true, dying yet alive, sorrowful yet always rejoicing, poor yet making many rich, having nothing yet possessing everything. He has opened his heart wide to them; he asks them to open theirs.

Then a sudden, sharp section (6:14–7:1): do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. Light has nothing in common with darkness, nor Christ with Belial, nor God’s temple with idols. The church is the temple of the living God, as the prophets promised, so it must come out and be separate from idolatry and impurity, and God will be a Father to his sons and daughters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Open Heart and the Catalogue of Hardships
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God’s fellow workers, Paul urges the Corinthians not to let God’s grace come to nothing in them: the time of God’s favour that Isaiah promised has arrived. He takes care that his conduct puts no obstacle in anyone’s way. His credentials are not successes but endurance in hardship, beatings, prison, riots, overwork and hunger, together with purity, patience, kindness, the Spirit, love and truthful speech. His life is full of paradox: dishonoured yet honoured, called a fraud yet genuine, dying yet alive, grieving yet always glad, poor yet enriching many, owning nothing yet possessing everything. He has opened his heart to them and asks them to open theirs in return.
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue of hardships (vv. 4–5) is one of several in 2 Corinthians (cf. 4:8–9; 11:23–29; 12:10). Together they constitute Paul’s theology of the cross applied to ministry: the authentic apostle is identified not by spectacular results or impressive presence but by the pattern of cruciform suffering. This does not glorify suffering for its own sake; it identifies the shape that kingdom advance takes in a world that crucified its King. Those who carry the message of the cross will bear in their bodies the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: A young minister enters a hard urban church plant with ambitions of rapid growth and visible impact. After three years, he has a small congregation, many failures, and a life that looks more like Paul’s catalogue than his vision board. He questions his calling. This passage is the specific word for him: the catalogue of hardships is not evidence of failed ministry but of authentic ministry. The question is not whether ministry is fruitful by visible metrics but whether the minister is conducting himself with the character described in vv. 6–7.

verseByVerse.quote: Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 6 continues Paul’s appeal from 5:20. First, he urges the Corinthians not to receive God’s grace in vain, for now is the day of salvation (vv. 1–2). Second, he describes his ministry, to show that it gives no one cause to stumble: through endurance in every kind of hardship, through the fruit of the Spirit, through honour and dishonour, appearing as an impostor, dying, sorrowful and poor, yet true, alive, rejoicing, and making many rich (vv. 3–10). Third, he opens his heart to them and asks them to open theirs in return (vv. 11–13). Finally, he warns them not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers. Light and darkness, Christ and Belial, the temple of God and idols cannot be partners. We are the temple of the living God, so come out and be separate, and God will be our Father (6:14–7:1). The chapter that begins with the day of salvation ends with the Lord Almighty calling former idolaters his sons and daughters.

Working together with him, then. He has just implored them, on Christ’s behalf, to be reconciled to God. Now the second half of the appeal: having received grace, do not let it lie there. The word is synergeō, one Paul made his own: a fellow worker, a colleague on the same job (1 Corinthians 3:9). It is a staggering way to describe the relationship between an apostle and God in the ministry of reconciliation, and it should not be softened into a mere figure of speech. God does the work; he does it through people; and the people are genuinely working.

We appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. The phrase is eis kenon, to emptiness: to no purpose, a gift that arrives and produces nothing. Do not let God’s grace be wasted on you. Some in Corinth were in danger of drifting after false teachers (11:3–4) and back into unholy living (12:21).

Can grace come to nothing? This raises a question honest readers ask and deserve a straight answer to. Does this passage threaten someone’s salvation? Take it carefully. Paul has just told this church that they are a new creation, sealed and guaranteed by the Spirit; he does not now suggest that God’s work in them might quietly fail. What he is warning against is a life in which the grace received makes no difference: grace treated as a transaction completed rather than a relationship begun. That can describe two different people. It can describe a believer who is wasting years he will not get back. It can also describe someone who has all the appearance of faith and has never actually come. Paul does not sort them here, and neither should we; the warning is addressed to everyone in the room and is meant to be taken personally rather than assigned to somebody else.

For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Then he quotes Isaiah 49:8, and it repays knowing where the words come from. In Isaiah, God is speaking to his Servant: the one who will be a light for the nations (Isaiah 49:6) and whose salvation will reach to the end of the earth. God tells the Servant that his cry has been heard and his day of help has come, promising salvation and the restoration of his people. Paul takes that promise, made to Christ, and says it is being handed on to everyone who is in him.

Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Then he does something with it that should stop the reader. Twice behold, twice now. The day Isaiah foresaw has arrived in Christ. The prophecy is not approaching. It is here, and it is here today. That is worth saying plainly, because almost everyone reading has a version of later. Later, when work settles. Later, when the children are older. Later, when I have got a few things straightened out. Scripture never speaks about God’s dealings in the future tense of convenience. It says, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Hebrews 3:15; compare 3:7–8, 13), and it says it because a heart that intends to respond eventually is already hardening while it waits.

What it does not mean. It does not mean true believers can lose their salvation. It means that professing believers must show that grace has truly taken hold, and that the call to respond is urgent.

If God does the work, why does Paul call himself God’s fellow worker? Because God chooses to work through means, and the means are people. Paul is not saying he helps God save anyone: regeneration is God’s work alone (4:6), and no one contributes to his own new birth. But in the ministry of reconciliation, the preaching, praying, pleading and serving, God gives real work to real people and lets them share in it. That is not a burden placed on you; it is an honour. You cannot open one blind eye, but you can carry the message, and God is pleased to call you his co-worker when you do.

What does receiving grace in vain look like in a church member? It looks like years of hearing about forgiveness without ever forgiving anyone. Singing about Christ’s love while nursing the same resentment. Knowing the gospel well and never speaking of it. Receiving comfort and never comforting. Treating Sunday as complete in itself and Monday as unaffected. None of these is a single dramatic fall; each is grace landing on ground that does not let it grow. The remedy is not to try harder in general, but to ask: what has God given me that I am sitting on? Then take one step of obedience in that place today.

In a sentence. As God’s co-workers we urge you not to receive God’s grace in vain. For he says, “At the right time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” Now is the right time; now is the day of salvation.

On a Tuesday. Is there a step of obedience you have been putting off: a sin to confess, a person to forgive, a conversation to have, a gift to give, a commitment to make? Today is the day. Do not waste God’s grace by saving it for later.

For worship. Nobody has been promised the favourable time twice. And notice, before that thought is allowed to become merely frightening, what the word actually is. Not now is the day of warning. Now is the day of salvation: the door standing open at this moment, on the authority of a promise made to the Servant and kept. The Father heard his Son’s cry, raised him and gave him a people, and now the same Father hears and helps everyone who comes in his name. This is the acceptable year of the Lord, and it is still today. Praise the God of the open door, who holds back the night so that more may come in.

parallels.desc: in a time of favour I have answered you

verseByVerse.quote: We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry,

We put no obstacle in anyone’s way. A short verse, and a discipline that costs more than it looks. The word for obstacle is proskopē: something you strike your foot against, a stumbling block. Paul’s concern is not that he might be criticised. It is that something about him might become the reason a person does not come to Christ. Note the range: in anyone’s way. Not just the sympathetic, not just the congregation. Anyone.

He was fiercely practical about this. It is why he refused financial support from Corinth, working at a trade so that nobody could say he was in it for money (1 Corinthians 9:12–15; 2 Corinthians 11:7–9). It is why he arranged for the collection to be carried by men the churches themselves had chosen, so no accusation could be made about the handling of it (8:20–21). It is why he became all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9:22; 10:32): not to be liked, but to remove every avoidable barrier between a person and the gospel.

Two kinds of obstacle. Distinguish two things here, because confusing them has done harm in both directions. Some obstacles must not be removed. The cross is a stumbling block by nature; Paul says so (1 Corinthians 1:23). A gospel adjusted until nobody trips over it has been tampered with, the very thing he renounced in 4:2. If people are offended by sin being called sin, or by Christ being the only way, that offence is the gospel doing its work and it is not to be smoothed away. But every other obstacle is ours to deal with, and there are more of them than we like to count. The manner that makes people feel small. The money question that was never explained. The political opinion nailed to the pulpit as though it were doctrine. The way we speak about people who are not in the room. The reputation for being unreachable, or unforgiving, or slightly dishonest about small things. None of these is the gospel. All of them can be, and regularly are, the reason somebody stops listening.

So that no fault may be found with our ministry. Notice how the sentence ends. The verb, mōmaomai, means to find fault, to blame, to ridicule. Not with him: with the ministry. He is not protecting his name. He is protecting the message from being discredited by its messenger, because the ministry represents Christ, and that is the only reason a Christian’s reputation is worth anything at all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean avoiding the offence of the gospel itself. The cross offends; the messenger should not add offence.

What if I already have been an obstacle to someone? Then go and move the stone. Name what you did, without excuses: I was harsh with you, I was dishonest about that, I mocked what you believe, I never paid you back. Apologise plainly, put right what can be put right, and do not make the apology a sermon. Many unbelievers have never heard a Christian say I was wrong, and a humble confession can do more to open a door than years of argument. Then leave it with God, and keep living in a way that does not lay the stone down again.

In a sentence. We put no stumbling block in anyone’s path, so that our ministry will not be discredited.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone you know who is not a Christian and who knows you are. Is there anything in how you have behaved toward them that gives them a legitimate reason not to take you seriously? Not an excuse: a reason. Something you would have to explain away. The answer usually arrives at once, which is the uncomfortable part. If there is, that is a stone in the road, and it is yours to move rather than theirs to climb over.

For worship. The apostle worked half the night with his hands for years to avoid leaving one stone in anyone’s road, and he learned it from his Master. The Son of God paid a temple tax he did not owe so as not to give offence (Matthew 17:27); he ate with tax collectors, touched lepers and welcomed children, removing every barrier but one. The only stumbling block he left standing was himself, crucified, the stone the builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone. Blessed be the Lord who cleared the way to himself at such cost, and who is himself the way.

verseByVerse.quote: but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger;
verseByVerse.commentary:
but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger;

But as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way. His rivals came with letters. Paul offers a different sort of credential: not letters but a life (3:1). He is a servant, diakonos, of God, and this is the first of the great hardship catalogues in the letter.

By great endurance. Notice the heading he puts over the whole list. The word is hypomonē, met already at 1:6: a remaining under, staying put beneath a weight. It is not the ability to avoid trouble but the refusal to walk out from under it. Everything that follows is offered as evidence of that one thing. The list comes in three groups of three, and they move from the general to the sharply particular.

In afflictions, hardships, calamities. First, three broad words for pressure. Afflictions are thlipseis, pressures. Hardships are anankai, the distress of necessity, constraints you cannot get out of. Calamities are stenochōriai, literally a narrow place: being wedged where there is no room. This is the shape of the life: pressed, hemmed in, cornered.

Beatings, imprisonments, riots. Second, three things done to him by other people. Each of these has a face attached to it. Someone swung the rod. Someone turned the key. A crowd gathered and decided. Paul had been beaten and imprisoned at Philippi (Acts 16:22–23) and had faced the mob at Lystra and at Ephesus (Acts 14:19; 19:29). In chapter 11 he will give the numbers, and they are appalling: five times thirty-nine lashes, three beatings with rods, one stoning (11:23–25).

Labors, sleepless nights, hunger. Third, three things he took on for the sake of the work. The word for labours means toil to the point of exhaustion. The sleepless nights are not insomnia but nights deliberately spent: travelling, working at his trade, praying, sitting up with people (1 Thessalonians 2:9). The word for hunger is the one used for fastings: going without food, whether by choice or because there was nothing.

What is missing from the list. What is striking is what is missing. There are no results. No church-planting statistics, no numbers converted, no cities won. If a man today were asked to commend his ministry, this is not the document he would produce. And that is exactly Paul’s point, aimed at a church that had begun assessing ministers the way the world assesses anyone. His credential is not what he has achieved but what he has absorbed and not quit.

Faithful, not successful. There is a word here for the person whose service has produced very little that can be counted. The years in a small church that never grew. The teaching of eight children, six of whom moved away. The praying for a family member across two decades with nothing to show. On this list, none of that is failure. Endurance is the credential, and it is the one thing in Christian service that cannot be faked, borrowed, or produced quickly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering proves a ministry is true. False teachers can suffer too. But true ministry is marked by endurance in suffering, not escape from it.

So how should I judge a pastor or a ministry? Not by size, celebrity, polish or how much you enjoy it. Ask the questions Scripture asks. Does he preach the true gospel plainly, Christ crucified and risen, without trimming it (4:2, 5)? Is his life consistent with what he preaches: honest with money, faithful in marriage, gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of status (1 Timothy 3:1–7)? Does he stay when it is hard, and serve when no one sees? Are people being built up in Christ rather than attached to him? A faithful ministry may be small and unremarkable for years. It will be marked by truth, love and endurance.

In a sentence. Rather, as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: in great endurance; in troubles, hardships and distresses; in beatings, imprisonments and riots; in hard work, sleepless nights and hunger.

On a Tuesday. Pray for persecuted Christians who know these hardships today, by name if you can: the imprisoned, the beaten, the driven out. Ask God to give them endurance. And if your own service feels fruitless, stop measuring it by results. Ask instead whether you are still under the weight, still faithful, and ask God for the grace to remain.

For worship. The Lord said the same to a church under pressure at Smyrna, promising nothing about outcomes and everything about the end: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Revelation 2:10). Faithful, not successful. The two are frequently confused, and only one of them is ever commanded. And the great Servant of God commended himself the same way: afflicted, beaten, imprisoned, sleepless in Gethsemane, hungry in the wilderness, enduring the cross and despising its shame. He stayed under the whole weight until it was finished. Glory to the enduring Christ, whose faithfulness is the strength of every faithful servant.

verseByVerse.quote: by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; by truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;
verseByVerse.commentary:
by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; by truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;

By purity, knowledge, patience, kindness. The list continues, and it turns inward. Paul has said what has been done to him; now he says what has been produced in him. This is the more searching half, because a man can endure a great deal and remain unpleasant. Purity, hagnotēs, heads it: moral cleanness, sincerity of motive, the state of a man with nothing to keep out of sight. Knowledge is not cleverness but the true understanding of God and his gospel; warmth without content is no credential. Patience is makrothymia, literally long-temperedness: the fuse that takes a very long time to burn. It is used of God himself, and it means the ability to be wronged by the same person repeatedly and not retaliate. Kindness, chrēstotēs, is the practical, unglamorous form of love: the useful act, the small mercy. It is possible to be doctrinally impeccable and unkind, and this list forbids it. Compare the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22).

The Holy Spirit. Then, in the middle of a list of virtues, something that is not a virtue at all. Some take the phrase as a holy spirit, a holy attitude, but the Holy Spirit fits best. Paul does not explain the intrusion, and the absence of explanation is the point. None of the qualities on either side of him is native to a human being. He is named among them because he is the one producing them.

Genuine love. Literally love without hypocrisy, anypokritos (Romans 12:9). The word for hypocrite was the word for a stage actor. There is a way of doing all the right things for people while performing, and everybody can eventually tell.

By truthful speech, and the power of God. Then two more: truthful speech, the word of truth, the gospel and honest speaking, saying what is so; and the power of God, the Spirit working through it, without which the whole list is a moral programme and not a ministry.

With the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left. Finally the image that gathers them up. A Roman soldier carried the sword in the right hand and the shield on the left. So this is armament for attack and for defence, and the material of both is righteousness: right living, and the righteousness of God in Christ. It is one of Paul’s recurring pictures; he will give it in full to the Ephesians, where the belt is truth and the shield is faith (Ephesians 6:13–17). Paul’s weapons are spiritual and moral, not manipulation.

Defending yourself with righteousness. Take the picture seriously and it changes how a Christian handles opposition. When you are misrepresented, the instinct is to defend yourself by the means being used against you: the counter-story, the quiet word to the right person, the version that puts you in a better light. Paul says the shield in the left hand is righteousness. Not cleverness, not the better argument, not a well-placed friend. You defend yourself by continuing to live rightly, and you attack by the same means, and there is nothing else in either hand. It is slower than the alternative and it is very much harder. It is also the only defence that does not have to be maintained, because a life is a great deal more difficult to answer than an argument.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was perfect in all of these. It means they characterised his ministry.

Should I never set the record straight when I am falsely accused? You may, and sometimes you should; Paul spends much of this letter doing exactly that. The difference is in the weapons. Speak the truth plainly, to the people who need to hear it, without exaggeration, without attacking the other person’s character, and without a campaign behind their back. Where wrong has been done that needs addressing, use the proper channels: go to the person first (Matthew 18:15), involve church leaders, and where a crime has been committed, the authorities. Then leave your reputation with God. Your job is to tell the truth and keep living rightly; vindication is his.

In a sentence. In purity, understanding, patience and kindness; in the Holy Spirit and in sincere love; in truthful speech and in the power of God; with weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left.

On a Tuesday. Read the list slowly and ask which quality is thinnest in you this week: purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, genuine love, truthful speech. Ask the Holy Spirit to produce it, and then look for the place today where you will need it. It is usually with the person who tries you most.

For worship. Every word of this list was first true of Jesus. He was pure, with nothing to hide; he knew the Father; he was patient with slow disciples and kind to the despised; he was full of the Holy Spirit, loved without pretence, spoke only truth, and did everything in the power of God. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; he carried no weapon but righteousness, and by it he overcame the world. Praise the Spirit who takes the life of Christ and slowly writes it into ordinary people, until the list begins to describe them too.
verseByVerse.note: Weapons “for the right hand and for the left” are weapons for attack (the sword) and defence (the shield).

verseByVerse.quote: through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;

Through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. Now the paradoxes begin, and they are among the most compressed things Paul ever wrote. Each one has the same shape: what people see, then what is actually so. First the pairs that come at him from outside. Note that he does not say he receives one and not the other; he passes through both. In the same week a man may be admired in one town and vilified in the next, and both reports concern the same person doing the same work. Paul’s ministry goes on whether people praise or insult him. He is not controlled by reputation.

Governed by opinion. That is worth holding on to, because most people are governed by these two more than they know. We adjust ourselves, often without noticing, toward whatever produces praise and away from whatever produces criticism, and after twenty years of small adjustments a life has been shaped by other people’s opinions. Paul walks through both without changing direction, which is only possible for a man who is expecting to give his account somewhere else (5:10).

We are treated as impostors, and yet are true. The word, planoi, means deceivers, frauds: people pretending to be what they are not. This was actually being said about him, as Jesus’ enemies called him that deceiver (Matthew 27:63). And his answer is not an argument; it is a fact: and yet are true.

As unknown, and yet well known. Nobody in the imperial capital had heard of him. He was a provincial of no standing, and in most rooms he entered he would have had to explain who he was. Unknown and insignificant to the world. And he is well known: known to the churches, and known by God, which is the knowing that counts. There is real comfort here for anyone who has spent a life doing something no one notices. The question is never whether you are known; it is only ever by whom.

As dying, and behold, we live. The behold is a note of astonishment; he is surprised himself. By every reasonable assessment he should be dead: the stoning at Lystra (Acts 14:19), the night and day adrift at sea, the affliction in Asia. Always near death, yet kept alive (4:10–11). And here he is, writing.

As punished, and yet not killed. The word is paideuō: disciplined, chastened, corrected. Behind it lies a psalm Paul knew well: “The LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death” (Psalm 118:18). The floggings had not been random cruelty only; a Father had been at work in them, and had set the limit himself.

The second half of the sentence. That is the thread running through all four. The world’s assessment of a Christian is not merely unkind; it is working with incomplete information. It reads the visible half of the sentence and stops. And the second half, in every case, is supplied by a God who is not impressed by appearances and has never once mistaken one of his servants for a fraud.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the world’s view is unimportant. It means God’s view is what counts.

How do I stop living for other people’s opinions? Not by ceasing to care about people, but by caring more about God’s verdict. Notice where approval and criticism steer you: what you post, what you avoid saying, which friends you keep, which convictions you go quiet on. Bring those to God and ask what pleases him. Remember that in Christ you already have the only verdict that finally matters: accepted, beloved, righteous (5:21). Then listen to criticism humbly, because it may be true, without being ruled by it; and receive praise gratefully, without needing it. A person secure in God’s love can afford both.

In a sentence. Through glory and dishonour, bad report and good report; genuine, yet regarded as impostors; known, yet regarded as unknown; dying, and yet we live on; beaten, and yet not killed.

On a Tuesday. When people misjudge you for following Christ, remember: God knows you, and his verdict stands. And when you are praised, do not let it change your direction any more than the criticism would. Pick one thing you would do differently today if only God were watching, and do it.

For worship. They called the Lord Jesus an impostor, and he was the Truth. They counted him unknown, the carpenter’s son from Nazareth, and he is the One by whom all things were made. He died, and behold, he lives for evermore. He was smitten by God and afflicted, and the Father did not give him over to death for ever. Every paradox in Paul’s life is a reflection of his Lord’s. Praise the God who reads the whole sentence, who knows his own, and who will one day show the world the second half of every line it misjudged.

verseByVerse.quote: as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.

As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. Three more paradoxes, and they go deeper than the four before them, because these are not about how others see him. They are about what is true inside. This may be the most useful sentence in the chapter for ordinary Christians, and it is regularly flattened by being read as though one cancels the other. It does not say sorrowful, but cheering up. It does not say the sorrow was a misunderstanding to be corrected by better theology. Both verbs stand, and the second has always attached to it. Paul is describing a man who is genuinely grieving, over sin, over suffering, over the lost (Romans 9:2), and genuinely rejoicing in the Lord (Philippians 4:4), at the same time, in the same hour, about different things.

Two floors in one house. Anyone who has stood at a Christian funeral has seen it. The grief is not reduced; a real person is gone and the loss is exactly as large as it feels. And underneath it, not instead of it, there is something that will not go out, because the person who is being buried is with the Lord, and the God who arranged that is still what he was last week. Two floors in one house. That is possible because Christian joy was never built on circumstances and therefore is not demolished when they collapse.

Grief is not a failure of faith. This frees the believer from a cruel expectation. Christians are frequently made to feel that grief is a failure of faith, that a really trusting person would be at peace by now. That is not in the Bible. Jesus wept at a grave he was about to empty (John 11:35). What the gospel promises is not the absence of sorrow but a joy that runs at a level sorrow cannot reach.

As poor, yet making many rich. Paul owned almost nothing: a cloak, some books, the parchments (2 Timothy 4:13). And whole provinces were made rich through him, in the only currency that survives. The pattern is his Lord’s: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (8:9), a sentence Paul is two chapters away from writing.

As having nothing, yet possessing everything. The last one is the largest. A man with no property, no security and no home says he possesses everything, and he is not being brave. He had already told this church why: all things are theirs, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas, the world, life, death, the present or the future, because they are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). The God who did not spare his own Son will with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32). That is the arithmetic of the kingdom, and it is not consolation for people who have missed out. The Christian is the richest person in the world.

What it does not mean. It does not mean poverty is holier than wealth. It means riches in Christ outweigh all earthly wealth.

May a Christian work to improve his circumstances, or should he be content with little? Both, rightly understood. Scripture commends honest, diligent work that provides for your family and lets you give to others (1 Thessalonians 4:11–12; Ephesians 4:28; 1 Timothy 5:8). There is nothing unspiritual about a better job or a sound budget. What Scripture forbids is the love of money and the anxious craving for more (1 Timothy 6:6–10), and what it teaches is contentment: Paul learned to be content in plenty and in want (Philippians 4:11–12). Work hard, give generously, hold everything loosely, and never think that what you own is what you are.

In a sentence. Sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything.

On a Tuesday. If you are grieving, do not hurry yourself out of it or pretend; let the sorrow be real, and look for the floor beneath it. Name one reason for joy in Christ that your grief cannot touch. And if you have little, write down what you possess in him: forgiveness, the Father’s love, the Spirit, a future, a family in the church. Then ask whom you might make rich this week with what God has given you.

For worship. The One who owns everything gave himself to his people, and everything he owns came with him. He was a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief, and for the joy set before him endured the cross. He had nowhere to lay his head, and he is heir of all things. There is no Christian anywhere, however little he has, who is not an heir of the world with him, and no one outside Christ, however much he holds, who owns anything he will still have in a hundred years. Blessed be the Lord who became poor to make us rich, and whose joy no one can take from us.

verseByVerse.quote: We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.

We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians. The rhetoric stops. For the first time in the letter he uses their name, the only time he addresses them directly as Corinthians, and it is the sound of a man dropping his voice. We have spoken freely is literally our mouth is open to you. Nothing has been withheld, nothing said behind a hand. He has told them about the affliction in Asia, about despairing of life, about being unable to preach at Troas for anxiety. A man defending his authority has spent five chapters admitting weakness.

Our heart is wide open. The verb is platynō: widened, enlarged, made spacious. There is room in him for all of them; whatever they have done, they have not been shut out.

You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections. Then the diagnosis, and it is put with great delicacy. The word for restricted, stenochōreō, means to be cramped, confined in a narrow space; it is the opposite of the widened heart. And the word for affections is splanchna, the inward parts. Hebrew and Greek alike located deep feeling in the gut rather than the chest, and the word is not decorative; its verb is the one used of the Lord’s compassion when he saw the crowds (Matthew 9:36). So the trouble in this relationship is named exactly. It is not that Paul has withdrawn. It is that they have narrowed. There is a cramped place in them where he used to be.

A cooled relationship. Anyone who has been on either side of a cooled relationship knows how precisely this describes it. Nothing is formally wrong. The greetings still happen. But something has closed, and the person on the outside can feel the reduced room without being able to point to a moment. Notice how Paul handles it. He does not accuse them of sin, though something is wrong. He does not demand an explanation. He describes what is true, his heart open, theirs narrow, and leaves it in front of them. That is remarkably hard to do. The instinct is either to pretend not to notice or to make an accusation that forces a defence, and both close the door further.

A narrowed heart. And the deeper point: constriction of heart is a real spiritual condition, not merely a social awkwardness. A narrowed heart cannot receive much, which is why the Corinthians could not take in what Paul was giving them. Their capacity had shrunk. Suspicion does that; so does resentment held for a long time; so does the quiet decision to protect yourself after being hurt once. It always feels like prudence and it always costs the same thing: the ability to be loved.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was sentimental. He was honestly asking for reconciliation.

But what if my heart closed because I was really wronged? Then your hurt is real, and God takes it seriously. Opening your heart does not mean pretending nothing happened, or putting yourself back in harm’s way. Where there has been abuse or ongoing danger, wisdom and safety come first, and trust is something the other person must rebuild over time. But even then, you can refuse to let bitterness have the room: forgive from the heart before God (Ephesians 4:31–32), stop rehearsing the wrong, pray for the person, and remain willing for peace if they repent. A heart can be open toward God and toward reconciliation while still being careful.

In a sentence. We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians, and opened wide our hearts to you. We are not withholding our affection from you, but you are withholding yours from us.

On a Tuesday. Turn this on yourself. Where has your heart narrowed? There is usually a name attached to the answer, and there is usually a good reason, and the reason has never yet made anybody less confined. Is your heart narrow toward someone who loves you: a parent, a pastor, a spouse, an old friend? Open it, this week, by one concrete act.

For worship. Paul’s open heart is only a small copy of a larger one. The Lord Jesus spoke freely to us: he withheld nothing the Father gave him, and told us plainly of his love, his sorrow and his coming death. His heart has never been narrow toward his people; he looked on the crowds and was moved in his inmost being, and he stretched out his arms on the cross wide enough to take in the world. If there is a cramped place between us and him, it is never on his side. Praise the Saviour whose heart is wide open still.

verseByVerse.quote: In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.

In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also. The whole appeal comes to one request, and there is not a trace of authority in it. He could have commanded. He is an apostle; he founded this church; he has just spent ten verses laying out what it has cost him. Instead: widen your hearts also. The same word as verse 11: make room, open up, be enlarged. Love me back. Reconciliation needs both sides.

An exposed moment. It is one of the most exposed moments in Paul’s letters. He is asking to be loved, by people who have not been loving him, and he is asking without leverage. Anyone who has done this knows the risk: a request for affection can be refused, and the refusal costs more than never having asked.

I speak as to children. Then the parenthesis, and it is doing careful work. Two things at once. It is affectionate: he is their father in the faith, as he told them plainly in the earlier letter (1 Corinthians 4:14–15), and a father may say things to his children that a colleague could not say. And it is a small, deliberate reduction of the pressure. By flagging that he is speaking as a parent speaks, he lets them off the formality of an adult negotiation. He is not building a case. He is asking.

What he is not asking for. Notice also what he is not asking for. Not an apology. Not agreement about the past. Not for the offenders to be dealt with. Only for room in their affections. There is a lesson here for anyone in a damaged relationship, and it works in families as well as churches. We tend to make the reopening of a relationship conditional on settling the history: who was right, what was said, who should speak first. Paul, who had by any reckoning the stronger case, sets all of it aside and asks for the one thing that would actually change anything. Widen your heart. The record can be sorted out later, or never; a heart that has opened usually finds the record matters less than it did.

Widening is an act. And observe that the widening is something he asks them to do. A heart does not enlarge by itself, and it does not enlarge by waiting to feel differently. It is an act: the visit made, the message sent, the deliberate refusal to run the grievance through your mind one more time, the choice to think the better explanation of what they did.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul needed their approval for his ministry. He wanted their love for their own good and his joy.

What if I widen my heart and they still refuse? Then you have done what God asked, and the rest is theirs and his. Paul could not make the Corinthians love him; he could only open his heart and ask. Scripture says, if possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18), which admits that sometimes it will not be possible. Keep the door open without forcing it. Do not punish them with coldness, and do not keep score of your efforts. Pray for them. Some relationships are restored years later; some only in heaven. Either way, a heart that stays open is free, and it is like God’s.

In a sentence. As a fair exchange (Paul speaks as to his children), open wide your hearts also.

On a Tuesday. Think of one relationship that has cooled. Without waiting to settle the history, do one thing that makes room: a message, a visit, an invitation, a kind word about them to someone else. Ask God to enlarge your heart toward the people he has given you, and then act as though he has.

For worship. Behind it all is the pattern that made Paul’s heart wide in the first place. He had been the enemy. He had watched Stephen die and gone looking for more (Acts 7:58–8:3). And the room made for him in the church of God was not made because he apologised his way in; it was made by the One whose heart was so wide that it took in the man who was hunting him. Nobody who has been received like that can plead a shortage of room. Praise the Father who ran to meet the prodigal, and the Son who went to the cross for his enemies, and whose open arms are the measure of every widened heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–7:1 — Do Not Be Unequally Yoked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to bind themselves in partnerships with unbelievers that compromise their loyalty to Christ. Righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness, Christ and Satan, God’s temple and idols have nothing in common. The church is God’s temple, the place where he has promised to live among his people. So, drawing on several prophetic promises, Paul calls them to leave idolatry and impurity behind, and God will welcome them as his sons and daughters. Holding such promises, they should cleanse themselves from everything that defiles body and spirit and pursue holiness in reverence for God.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage has been applied to several specific situations: (1) Marriage between believers and unbelievers — the most common application, supported by the principle if not the primary context. 1 Cor. 7:39 (she is free to marry “only in the Lord”) is the direct marriage prohibition. (2) Formal religious partnerships — interfaith worship, ecumenical agreements that require treating fundamental doctrinal differences as unimportant. (3) Business partnerships that require ethical compromise. The principle is: any relationship of primary spiritual allegiance that requires pulling in the same direction as one who is opposed to Christ creates an incompatible yoke. Ordinary friendship, working relationships, and engagement with unbelievers are not in view — Paul explicitly says in 1 Cor. 5:9–10 that he did not mean to avoid all contact with the immoral of the world.
verseByVerse.examples: A senior pastor receives an invitation to co-host a community prayer service with leaders from several faiths, including those who explicitly deny the Trinity and the uniqueness of Christ as Saviour. He must decide whether this is a civic engagement (speaking to the community) or a spiritual partnership (worshipping together). This passage suggests the distinction matters: representing the church’s concern for the community is different from implying that all faith traditions are pulling the same spiritual yoke toward the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?

Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. The subject changes abruptly, and the abruptness has led some to think this paragraph was originally somewhere else. But the connection is there. He has just asked them to widen their hearts toward him; now he tells them there is one direction in which the heart must not be opened. A church that has room for everything has room for nothing in particular.

The picture from the farm. The image comes from farming. Heterozygeō is built from different and yoke: to be yoked with a different kind. Behind it stands the old law: you shall not plough with an ox and a donkey together (Deuteronomy 22:10). The reason is practical rather than ceremonial. Two animals of different height, strength and stride, fastened to the same beam, cannot work. Each is pulled off its line by the other, the furrow wanders, and both are injured by the harness. It is not that the donkey is wicked. It is that they cannot pull together.

For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? Then five questions, of which these are the first two, each expecting the answer none. Partnership is metochē, sharing; fellowship is koinōnia. They are not really questions. The second answers itself in a way anybody can test. Light and darkness do not negotiate, and they do not blend (John 3:19–21; Ephesians 5:8–11). One of them simply ends where the other begins.

Where Christians differ: what is an unequal yoke? Some apply this only to marriage; others to any contact with unbelievers. Verdict: In context, Paul’s main concern is probably Corinthians joining in pagan temple worship and following false teachers. The principle applies to any binding partnership that pulls a believer away from Christ: most clearly marriage (1 Corinthians 7:39), and also business partnerships or alliances that compromise faith and obedience. It does not forbid friendship, work or ordinary life with unbelievers, which Paul assumes (1 Corinthians 5:10; 10:27).

Precision matters. It is important to be precise, because this verse has been used to justify things Paul explicitly refused. It does not mean avoiding unbelievers. Paul had already had to correct exactly that misunderstanding in his earlier letter: when he told them not to associate with the immoral, he did not mean the people of this world, since then they would need to go out of the world (1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Friendship, employment, neighbourliness, hospitality, business dealings, marriage to an unbeliever already entered: none of these is forbidden, and a Christian who withdraws from the world has misread the whole New Testament and disqualified himself from the ministry of chapter 5. What is in view is a yoke: a binding of your direction to someone whose direction is opposed to Christ, in a way you cannot easily undo. The clearest applications are the obvious ones: a Christian choosing to marry someone who is not one (Paul gives the rule elsewhere: a widow is free to marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord, 1 Corinthians 7:39); a partnership that requires you to serve two masters; a formal religious alliance that treats the identity of God as a detail.

Does this apply to dating? Yes, where dating means looking for a husband or wife. If a Christian should not marry an unbeliever, he should not begin a romance that is heading that way; hearts follow where time and affection go. Ordinary friendship with unbelievers is not what Paul forbids, and it is often how they come to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer already married to an unbeliever should leave (1 Corinthians 7:12–13). It means do not enter such a yoke. A word must be said straight to the person for whom this is not a decision but a situation. If you are already married to someone who does not believe, this verse is not about you, and no one should be allowed to use it against you. Paul’s instruction in that case could not be plainer: “If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him” (1 Corinthians 7:13), and the reason he gives is hope: “For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?” (1 Corinthians 7:16). The command here is about yokes you are choosing. It is never a reason to break one you are already carrying, and God has used a great many such marriages to save the other half of them.

I knowingly married an unbeliever after I became a Christian. Am I living in sin? You may need to confess that the choice was disobedient, but the marriage itself is real, binding and honourable before God, and staying in it is obedience, not sin. Do not torment yourself by treating every day of it as a fresh offence. Love your spouse well, pray for them, and let your conduct speak more than your words (1 Peter 3:1–2). If the unbelieving spouse insists on leaving, Paul says the believer is not bound (1 Corinthians 7:15; Westminster 24.6). And if there is abuse, seek safety and help from your church at once; God never asks anyone to remain in danger.

In a sentence. Do not be yoked together with unbelievers. For what do righteousness and wickedness have in common? Or what fellowship can light have with darkness?

On a Tuesday. Before you enter any binding commitment, a marriage, business, or alliance, ask: will this pull me with Christ, or against him? Ask it early, before your heart is already fastened, and ask a mature believer to help you answer honestly. And if you are single and hoping to marry, settle now, before anyone is in view, that you will marry only in the Lord.

For worship. The Lord who forbids the unequal yoke offers his own: take my yoke upon you, he says, for my yoke is easy and my burden is light (Matthew 11:29–30). He does not ask us to give up a partner and pull alone. He asks us to be fastened to him, the One who walks in step with us, carries the heavier side, and never pulls us off the line. Blessed be Christ, who yoked himself to our humanity so that we might walk with God, and who shares the furrow with every one of his people until the field is done.
verseByVerse.note: The picture comes from the law forbidding an ox and a donkey to be yoked together at the plough.

verseByVerse.quote: What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?

What accord has Christ with Belial? The questions keep coming, and this one is sharper than the rest, because Paul now names the opposition. Belial is a Hebrew word, and it is not really a name to begin with. It means worthlessness: something with no profit in it, a thing that yields nothing. The Old Testament uses it as a description: the men of Gibeah who surrounded the house were worthless men, sons of Belial (Judges 19:22). By the time of Paul, Jewish writers, including those of the Dead Sea Scrolls, had turned the word into a title for the chief adversary, Satan. It is the only place the New Testament uses it.

Everything against nothing. He could have written Satan, as he does elsewhere in this letter. He chose the word that means worthless, and the choice is doing something. Set the names side by side: Christ, the Anointed One, in whom every promise of God is Yes (1:20), and Belial, the one whose entire estate is worth nothing. That is the actual comparison. It is not two powers of comparable weight dividing the world between them. It is everything, against a name that means nothing.

Accord. The word is symphōnēsis, the one behind our symphony: sounding together, in tune. Christ and Belial do not make a chord. Anything that tries to hold both will be, quite literally, discordant, and everybody listening will hear it.

Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever? The last question of the pair is put in the plainest terms. The word portion, meris, is a word for an allotted share: the piece of land a family received in Israel, what falls to a person by right. It is about what you have in common at the deepest level. In the deepest things, believers and unbelievers have no common share. Their destinies differ.

What Paul is not saying. Here the honest reader must be careful not to hear more than is said. Paul is not saying believers and unbelievers have nothing in common; they share a world, a workplace, a street, a humanity, and Christians who forget that become insufferable. He is saying that at the level of ultimate allegiance, what your life is finally for, there is no shared portion. Two people can share a house and a mortgage and thirty years of affection, and still be walking in opposite directions on the one road that goes anywhere.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are better people. It means they belong to a different kingdom.

Does this mean my unbelieving relative has no hope? No. The portion describes where a person stands now, not where God may bring him. Every believer once had no share in Christ; such were some of you, Paul told this church, but you were washed (1 Corinthians 6:11). The difference between you and your relative is not that you are better but that grace reached you. So the verse should make you more prayerful and more tender, not more distant. Keep loving them, keep the gospel in view, and pray that God would give them a share in Christ too.

In a sentence. What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? Or what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever?

On a Tuesday. Put the question to yourself about the partnerships you are actually in. Not is this person pleasant? They often are. Ask instead: if this arrangement is pulling in a direction, where does the direction go, and am I free to stop? Then thank God that your portion is Christ, and let your life sound in tune with him.

For worship. Take the comfort in the name he chose. Whatever is on the other side of the yoke, it is not a rival to Christ. It is Belial: a name meaning nothing at all, wearing the borrowed authority of an age that is passing. He has already been judged, and the One who judged him is the One every believer is joined to. The LORD is my portion, says my soul. We have no share with worthlessness because we have been given a share in Christ, who is worth more than the world. Praise him that the lines have fallen for us in pleasant places.
verseByVerse.note: Belial (“worthlessness”) was a Jewish name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

What agreement has the temple of God with idols? The last of the five questions arrives, and it turns out to be the one the others were climbing toward. Agreement is synkatathesis, a joint decision, a vote cast together. Idols in God’s temple were the ultimate sacrilege; it was what Manasseh did, and what Ezekiel saw in his vision of the abominations in the temple (2 Kings 21:4–7; Ezekiel 8). The reason a believer cannot be yoked to the darkness is not chiefly a rule about company. It is a fact about what he now is.

For we are the temple of the living God. Stop and take that in, because the Corinthians would have heard it against a skyline. Corinth had temples: to Apollo, to Aphrodite on the height above the city, to half a dozen others. A temple was a building, and what made it a temple was that the god was understood to live there. Paul says the temple is the congregation (1 Corinthians 3:16). Not the building they met in; there was no building. The people. God has moved out of architecture and into a group of former idolaters, labourers and freedmen in a Greek port. So the church cannot join itself to idol worship.

As God said. Then he supports it with the Old Testament, and it is worth seeing what he does. The quotation weaves together several promises: Leviticus 26:11–12, where God says he will make his dwelling among his people and walk among them; Ezekiel 37:27, the promise of a dwelling place in the middle of them; and the covenant refrain, sounded in Jeremiah too, that he will be their God and they shall be his people. Every one of those was given to Israel, about a tabernacle and a temple and a land. Paul says they have landed here, fulfilled in the church by the Spirit. This is the heart of the covenant: God living among his people.

I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them. The words repay slowing down. Behind make my dwelling stands the promise of God’s tabernacle, his tent, set in the middle of the camp, and John reaches for the same picture when he says the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). God pitches his tent in the camp. And walk among them: not visit, but walk about among them, at home, as he walked in the garden in the cool of the day before anything went wrong.

Someone already resident. Now the practical force of it, which is what Paul is after. If you are the place where God lives, then what you join yourself to is not a private matter of preference. You are not deciding what to do with your own life; you are deciding what to bring into his house. That is why the questions have been getting steadily more serious. It is not that idols are intellectually silly. It is that there is Someone already resident.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s presence is limited to church buildings. His people are the temple.

What counts as an idol today? Anything you look to for what only God can give: security, identity, worth, comfort, meaning. It is often a good thing made into an ultimate thing: money, career, a relationship, children, reputation, health, a political cause, pleasure, even ministry.
