A useful test is to ask what you most fear losing, what you daydream about, where your spare money and time go, and what makes you angry when it is threatened. Idols rarely look like statues now. But they still demand sacrifices, and they still cannot save. Little children, keep yourselves from idols (1 John 5:21).

Is my own body God’s temple too? Yes, though that is not Paul’s main point here. In this verse the temple is the church together, we, plural. Elsewhere he applies the same truth to each believer’s body, in the context of sexual immorality: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, so glorify God in your body (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). So both are true. Care for your body and keep it from sin, not because it is your own, but because it is his house. And treat your church with the same reverence: when believers gather, God is in the midst.

In a sentence. What agreement is there between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God. As God has said: “I will live with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.”

On a Tuesday. You are part of God’s temple. Keep your life free of idols. Name the one thing most likely to compete with God for your heart this week, and decide in advance what you will do when it calls. And on Sunday, walk into church remembering that you are not entering a building where God lives; you are joining the people in whom he does.

For worship. There is a comfort in it larger than the warning. The whole story of the Bible has been God working out how to live with people who could not survive his presence: a garden lost, a tent in the wilderness with a curtain across it, a temple with a room nobody could enter but once a year with blood. Then a body, and the curtain torn from top to bottom. And now, an ordinary congregation of unremarkable people, and the living God at home in the middle of them, walking about. He has wanted this from the beginning, and he paid what it cost to have it. Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. Praise him who has made us his home.

parallels.desc: I will walk among you and be your God

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,

Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord. The quotation continues, now from Isaiah 52:11: words originally spoken to the exiles as they left Babylon, carrying the vessels of the temple home. Paul applies them to a church living inside a pagan city. Believers must separate themselves from idolatry and the corrupting practices of the world. And the first thing to establish is what the words cannot mean, because this verse has done a great deal of damage in the hands of people who wanted a reason to withdraw.

Not withdrawal. They cannot mean physical separation from unbelievers. The same apostle wrote that avoiding the immoral of this world would require going out of the world altogether (1 Corinthians 5:10), and the same Lord prayed for his disciples, “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one” (John 17:15). The Christian is not withdrawn from society; he is planted in it, as light is planted in a dark room. Every retreat into a Christian enclave, every version of the faith that measures holiness by how few outsiders you know, has misread this sentence.

And touch no unclean thing. What then is being commanded? Look at this phrase, which controls the other two. Uncleanness here is moral and spiritual now, rather than ritual. It is not people who are to be avoided but defilement. The exiles leaving Babylon were not told to hate Babylonians; they were told not to carry Babylon home with them.

A line through your own life. So the separation is real, and it runs along a different line from the one we usually draw. It is not a line between us and them. It is a line through the middle of your own life, and it falls at every point where the surrounding culture would make itself at home in the temple of God: what you watch, what you are willing to laugh at, how you get money, what you do with your private hours, the ambitions you have absorbed without ever examining them. That is a harder command than physical withdrawal, which is why physical withdrawal has always been the more popular option. It is entirely possible to live in a Christian bubble and be thoroughly Babylonian inside it, and possible to work in the least Christian environment imaginable and touch nothing unclean.

Where Christians differ: separation. Some interpret separation as withdrawing from all association with the world, or even from other Christians who associate with unbelievers. Verdict: Separation here means refusing to take part in idolatry and sin, not physical withdrawal from the world (John 17:15; 1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Christians are to be in the world but not of it. Separating from other true believers over secondary matters is not what Paul teaches; he calls for separation from false worship and from those who teach a false gospel (Galatians 1:8–9; Romans 16:17).

Then I will welcome you. At the end of the verse, from Ezekiel 20:34, comes the thing that turns a command into gospel. The verb is the word for taking someone in: receiving a guest, gathering someone to yourself. God receives those who come out from idolatry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God only welcomes us after we have cleaned ourselves up. He welcomes sinners. But those he welcomes leave their idols. Note the order, and do not get it backwards. This is not make yourself clean and then God may accept you; the whole letter has said the opposite, and chapter 5 ended with the righteousness of God given to people who had none. The welcome is what God does for his own. But he says it here because a life divided between two houses does not feel welcomed, whatever is true of it, and the way back into the enjoyment of what you already have is to stop carrying Babylon into the room where he lives.

How do I decide what is unclean in entertainment and daily life? Start with what Scripture plainly calls sin, and do not make it entertainment: sexual immorality, cruelty enjoyed for its own sake, mockery of God, greed held up as glory (Ephesians 5:3–12). Then ask honest questions about the rest. Does this make sin attractive to me? Does it leave me colder toward God and people? Would I be comfortable watching it with Christ in the room, because he is? Am I free in this, or does it have a grip on me (1 Corinthians 6:12)? Christians will draw some lines differently in matters of conscience (Romans 14), and should not judge one another for it. But each of us must draw them, and be willing to give something up.

In a sentence. Therefore, “Come out from them and be separate, says the Lord. Touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you.”

On a Tuesday. Is there something unclean you have been carrying into the temple: a habit, a screen, a way of making money, a resentment you feed? Name it before God. Leave it, not in order to be accepted, but because you already are, and run to the God who welcomes you.

For worship. Then I will welcome you. The Lord who calls his people out of Babylon is the same Lord who went out to meet them on the road. He touched the leper and was not defiled, but made the leper clean. He ate with sinners and they went home changed. His holiness is not fragile; it is contagious. Blessed be the God who separates us from our idols by drawing us to himself, and who always has his arms open for the one coming home.

parallels.desc: depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing

verseByVerse.quote: and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”

And I will be a father to you. The chain of quotations ends here, and Paul has saved the greatest for last. The words come from 2 Samuel 7:14, and it is worth knowing exactly who they were spoken to. David wanted to build God a house. God refused, and turned the whole thing round: David would not build him a house; he would build David one. And of David’s son he said, I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son. That promise belonged to the royal line. It was the charter of the house of David, the sentence that stood behind every king of Judah and finally behind the Messiah himself. It was not a promise for the general population, and it was certainly not a promise for Gentiles in a port city on the far side of the Aegean. Paul hands it to them. He applies it to all believers.

And you shall be sons and daughters to me. Notice the main alteration Paul makes, because it is not carelessness. Where 2 Samuel says a son, singular, Paul writes sons and daughters, echoing Isaiah’s promise that God would bring his sons from afar and his daughters from the end of the earth (Isaiah 43:6). The promise made to one royal heir has become a promise to a family, and the family includes women, which needed saying in a world where inheritance ran through sons. Women are fully God’s children, equal heirs of the promise. In Christ, a slave woman in Corinth stands in the sentence that was spoken over the throne of David.

How can that be? Only one way. The Son to whom the promise properly belonged took his inheritance and shared it. He is the firstborn among many brothers (Romans 8:29), and everyone joined to him is inside his standing. This is adoption into God’s family (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:5–7). It is why the Christian may say Father at all, and it is why the word is not a figure of speech: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1).

Says the Lord Almighty. Then the title Paul chooses for God in the same breath, and the collision is deliberate. Almighty is pantokratōr, ruler of all; in the Greek Old Testament it often renders the Hebrew Lord of hosts: the God of armies, commander of everything that exists. That is the One who has just said he will be your Father. Hold the two together and do not let either soften the other. A father who is not almighty can love you and be unable to help; an almighty God who is not a father can help and have no particular interest in doing so. Here is one Person who is both, saying so under his own name. The Almighty becomes our Father. It is the greatest privilege imaginable.

Where the argument was going. This is where the argument about yokes has been going the whole time. Paul is not fencing them in. He is telling them what they would be trading, and whom they belong to.

What it does not mean. It does not mean adoption is earned by separation. It is God’s gracious gift, which calls us to holy living.

My earthly father was absent or cruel. How can I relate to God as Father? Slowly, honestly, and by letting God define the word rather than your memories. Your father showed you what a father should not be; God shows you what a father is. He is never absent (Hebrews 13:5), never cruel, never fickle; he disciplines only in love and for your good (Hebrews 12:10); he gave his own Son for you. You may need to tell him plainly that the word is hard for you; he will not be offended. Read how Jesus speaks of the Father (Luke 15:11–32; Matthew 6:25–33). Over time, the true Father heals what the false one wounded, and the church can be part of that, as older believers become fathers and mothers in the faith to you.

In a sentence. And, “I will be a Father to you, and you will be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.”

On a Tuesday. The Lord Almighty is your Father. Live today as his son or daughter, secure and loved. When you pray, begin with the word Father and stop there for a moment before asking for anything. When you are afraid, remember who has taken you as his own. And when you are tempted to go back to the idols, remember what you would be trading.

For worship. The Lord of hosts has taken the promise he made to a king and given it away to fishermen and slaves and idolaters who came in late, and he calls them sons and daughters, and he means it. The Son of David, the only Son by right, stood under the Father’s wrath so that we might stand under the Father’s smile. The Ruler of all, who commands the stars by name, bends down to be called Abba by the weakest of his children. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has made us his own, and who will never be anything less than a Father to us.

parallels.desc: I will be to him a father
bring my sons and my daughters

We are treated as impostors, and yet are true;<sup>9</sup>as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;<sup>10</sup>as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.<sup>11</sup>We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open.<sup>12</sup>You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.<sup>13</sup>In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.<sup>14</sup>Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?<sup>15</sup>What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?<sup>16</sup>What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.<sup>17</sup>Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,<sup>18</sup>and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”

7.title: Godly Grief and the Joy of Reconciliation
7.overview:
Chapter 7 finishes two things. First, the call to holiness: since God has promised to live among his people and be their Father, they must cleanse themselves from everything that defiles body and spirit (7:1). Second, the story Paul broke off at 2:13. He had left Troas in anxiety and gone into Macedonia, where he found no rest: fighting outside, fear inside. Then Titus arrived with news from Corinth. The severe letter had hurt them, but the hurt had led to repentance. They had grieved, longed for Paul, and dealt with the offender.

So Paul explains the difference between two kinds of sorrow. Godly grief produces repentance that leads to salvation and leaves no regret; worldly grief produces death. He lists what their godly grief produced: earnestness, eagerness to clear themselves, indignation, fear, longing, zeal and readiness to see justice done. Titus has been refreshed by them, Paul’s boasting about them has proved true, and he rejoices that he can have complete confidence in them.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 7 brings the long defence of Paul’s ministry (2:14–7:4) to a close and returns to the story of Titus. Verse 1 concludes the call to separation in chapter 6: since God has promised to dwell among us and be our Father, let us cleanse ourselves and pursue holiness. Then Paul asks again for open hearts (vv. 2–4). He tells how, in Macedonia, harassed and afraid, he was comforted by the arrival of Titus with news that the Corinthians had responded to his severe letter with grief, longing and zeal (vv. 5–7). He does not regret the letter, because their grief was godly grief, which leads to repentance and salvation, unlike worldly grief, which leads to death. He describes the marks of their repentance: earnestness, eagerness to put things right, indignation, fear, longing, zeal and justice (vv. 8–12). Titus’s joy and Paul’s confidence in them complete his comfort (vv. 13–16). The chapter is one of Scripture’s best descriptions of true repentance.

Since we have these promises, beloved. Key words. The promises of 6:16–18: God dwelling among his people, being their God and Father.

Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit. Key words. “Cleanse” (katharizō). “Defilement” (molysmos, stain, pollution). Of body: sexual sin, idolatrous feasts. Of spirit: inner sins of pride, bitterness and false worship. Holiness covers the whole person. Notice “let us”: Paul includes himself.

Bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God. Key words. “Bringing to completion” (epiteleō, carrying through to the end). Holiness is a lifelong pursuit, motivated by reverent fear of God.

Where Christians differ: who does the cleansing? Some say sanctification is entirely God’s work, with believers passive; others say it is entirely up to our effort. Verdict: Paul calls believers to cleanse themselves, yet it is God who sanctifies by his Spirit (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Sanctification is God’s work in which we actively cooperate: we work out what God works in (Philippians 2:12–13; Westminster 13.1, 3). It is never complete in this life; perfect holiness comes at glorification.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn God’s promises by cleansing ourselves. We already have the promises; holiness is our response.

In a sentence. Since we have these promises, dear friends, let us purify ourselves from everything that contaminates body and spirit, perfecting holiness out of reverence for God.

On a Tuesday. Name one defilement of body or spirit in your life. Confess it, and take a practical step to clean it out today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–16 — Godly Grief, Worldly Grief, and Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks again for a place in their hearts, insisting he has wronged and exploited no one, and assuring them he says this in love, not accusation. He takes up the story from chapter 2: in Macedonia he had no rest, with conflict outside and fear inside, until God comforted him through Titus’s arrival and his news. The Corinthians had been grieved by the severe letter, and Paul briefly regretted sending it, but their grief led to repentance. He contrasts sorrow that turns to God and leads to salvation with worldly sorrow that leads to death, and lists the earnest, practical fruits their repentance produced. Titus was refreshed by them, Paul’s confidence in them proved justified, and he rejoices.
verseByVerse.theology: The distinction between godly grief and worldly grief is pastorally crucial. Worldly grief can look like repentance: tears, distress, self-accusation. But its focus is on the pain caused to oneself (loss of reputation, loss of relationships, loss of comfort) rather than on the offence against God. Judas displays worldly grief — he is distraught over what he has done, even returns the money, but cannot receive forgiveness; he destroys himself. Peter displays godly grief — the same tears, the same self-accusation, but directed toward the face of Jesus, resolved by Jesus’s restoration. The direction of the grief determines its outcome.
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor is confronted with evidence of long-term financial dishonesty. He weeps, expresses remorse, describes how devastated he is — by the damage to his reputation, the pain to his family, the end of his ministry. He never directly addresses the harm done to those he stole from, or the offence against God. His leadership team recognises, with the categories of this passage, that they are witnessing worldly grief — real grief, but pointed in the wrong direction. Genuine repentance would ask different questions: not “what have I lost?” but “against whom have I sinned, and what must I do to make it right?”

verseByVerse.quote: Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.

Make room in your hearts for us. Key words. “Make room” (chōreō, give space). Picking up 6:11–13.

We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. Key words. Three denials, probably answering accusations. Wronged (adikeō, treated unjustly). Corrupted (phtheirō, ruined, led astray morally or doctrinally). Taken advantage (pleonekteō, exploited, cheated), perhaps a charge about the collection (12:17–18).

I do not say this to condemn you. Key words. He is not accusing them.

For I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together. Key words. A pledge of unbreakable loyalty, like friends who swore to live and die together. Paul’s love will not let go of them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was sinless. It means his conduct toward them had been honest.

In a sentence. Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, corrupted no one, exploited no one. Paul does not say this to condemn you; he has said before that you have such a place in our hearts that we would live or die with you.

For worship. Thank God for friends who are committed to you in life and death. Be that kind of friend.

verseByVerse.quote: I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.

I am acting with great boldness toward you. Key words. “Boldness” (parrēsia, frankness, confidence).

I have great pride in you. Key words. After all the trouble, Paul boasts of them.

I am filled with comfort. Key words. The theme of chapter 1 returns.

In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy. Key words. “Overflowing” (hyperperisseuomai, super-abounding). Joy in the middle of affliction, not after it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean affliction ended. It means joy can overflow even in it.

In a sentence. Paul speaks to you with great frankness; he takes great pride in you. He is greatly encouraged; in all our troubles his joy knows no bounds.

On a Tuesday. Tell someone today that you are proud of them in the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,

For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest. Key words. Paul picks up the story he broke off in 2:13: waiting anxiously for Titus. “Bodies” (literally flesh): his whole human self.

But we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. Key words. Outward conflicts: opposition, perhaps persecution in Macedonia. Inward fears: anxiety for the Corinthians, and perhaps for Titus’s safety. Paul is honest about fear.

But God, who comforts the downcast. Key words. From Isaiah 49:13: God comforts his afflicted ones. “Downcast” (tapeinos, lowly, depressed). God is especially near the downhearted.

Comforted us by the coming of Titus. Key words. God’s comfort came through a person. God often comforts us through friends.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fear is always sin. Paul felt fear. Faith brings it to God.

In a sentence. For when we came into Macedonia, we had no rest, but were harassed at every turn: conflicts on the outside, fears within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,

For worship. If you are downcast, the God who comforts the downcast is near. Ask him to send you comfort, perhaps through a friend.
verseByVerse.note: Paul picks up the story he broke off in 2:13: waiting anxiously for Titus.

verseByVerse.quote: and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.

And not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you. Key words. Titus had been encouraged by the Corinthians’ response, and passed it on to Paul. Comfort flows around the body of Christ (1:4).

As he told us of your longing. Key words. They longed to see Paul again.

Your mourning. Key words. They grieved over the offence and over hurting him.

Your zeal for me. Key words. They were eager to defend him and put things right.

So that I rejoiced still more. Key words. Paul’s joy was even greater than his relief.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all problems were solved. Chapters 10–13 show some opposition remained.

In a sentence. and not only by his coming but also by the comfort you had given him. He told us about your longing for us, your deep sorrow, your eager concern for Paul, so that Paul’s joy was greater than ever.

On a Tuesday. Pass on good news about other believers. It comforts and encourages.

verseByVerse.quote: For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.

For even if I made you grieve with my letter. Key words. The severe, tearful letter (2:3–4).

I do not regret it—though I did regret it. Key words. Honest about mixed feelings. After sending it, Paul worried whether he had been too harsh. Now he sees it was right.

For I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while. Key words. The pain was real, but temporary, and led to good.

What it does not mean. It does not mean inspiration removes all human emotion. Paul felt doubts. God’s word came through a real person.

In a sentence. Even if Paul caused you sorrow by his letter, he does not regret it. Though he did regret it at first, he sees that the letter hurt you, but only for a little while,

For worship. If you have had to say something hard in love, leave the results with God.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.

As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. Key words. Paul does not enjoy their pain. He rejoices in its fruit: repentance (metanoia, a change of mind and direction).

For you felt a godly grief. Key words. Literally, grief according to God: sorrow that God approves, that sees sin as God sees it.

So that you suffered no loss through us. Key words. The letter hurt, but did them only good.

For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret. Key words. Godly grief leads to repentance, which leads to salvation, and is never regretted. “Without regret” (ametamelētos): no one ever regrets true repentance.

Whereas worldly grief produces death. Key words. Worldly sorrow: regret over consequences, embarrassment, self-pity, being caught, without turning to God. It leads to despair, bitterness and death. Judas felt remorse and despaired (Matthew 27:3–5); Peter wept and was restored (Luke 22:62; John 21:15–19).

Godly and worldly grief. Godly grief is sorry for sin because it offends God; worldly grief is sorry for the consequences. Godly grief runs to God; worldly grief runs from him. Godly grief changes behaviour; worldly grief only feels bad. The Westminster Shorter Catechism defines repentance unto life as a sinner’s grief and hatred of sin, turning from it to God, with full purpose of new obedience (Q. 87).

What it does not mean. It does not mean repentance earns salvation. It is the fruit of grace and the way into salvation’s blessings.

In a sentence. Yet now Paul is happy, not because you were made sorry, but because your sorrow led you to repentance. For you became sorrowful as God intended and so were not harmed in any way by us. Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation and leaves no regret, but worldly sorrow brings death.

For worship. Ask God for godly grief over your sin: not mere regret, but sorrow that turns you back to him.

parallels.desc: Peter’s tears and Judas’s remorse

verseByVerse.quote: For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.

For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you. Key words. Seven marks of true repentance. Earnestness (spoudē): seriousness, no longer indifferent.

But also what eagerness to clear yourselves. Key words. Literally, defence (apologia): eagerness to put things right and show they did not approve of the wrong.

What indignation. Key words. Anger at the sin and at themselves for tolerating it.

What fear. Key words. Reverent fear of God, and perhaps of Paul’s discipline.

What longing. Key words. Longing for restored fellowship.

What zeal. Key words. Zeal for what is right, for Paul, for God’s honour.

What punishment! Key words. “Punishment” (ekdikēsis, justice, vindication): they disciplined the offender (2:6). Repentance acts to put wrongs right.

At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter. Key words. “Innocent” (hagnos, pure, clear). By their response, they showed they were not complicit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they were never at fault. It means their repentance cleared them.

In a sentence. See what this godly sorrow has produced in you: what earnestness, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what concern, what readiness to see justice done. At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in this matter.

On a Tuesday. Test your repentance by these marks. Is it earnest? Does it want to put things right? Does it act?

verseByVerse.quote: So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.

So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong. Key words. Not mainly to punish the offender.

Nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong. Key words. Not mainly to vindicate the one offended, probably Paul himself.

But in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God. Key words. The main purpose: that the Corinthians would discover, before God, how much they really did care about Paul and the truth. Sometimes we do not know our own hearts until tested.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the wrong did not matter. It means Paul’s deepest concern was the church’s spiritual health.

In a sentence. So even though Paul wrote to you, it was neither on account of the one who did the wrong nor on account of the injured party, but rather that before God you could see for yourselves how devoted to us you are.

For worship. Ask God to show you your own heart, and to make your love for him and his people sincere.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.

Therefore we are comforted. Key words. The outcome.

And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus. Key words. Paul delights in his friend’s happiness.

Because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. Key words. “Refreshed” (anapauō, rested). Titus went expecting trouble and found warmth.

For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. Key words. Before sending Titus, Paul had told him good things about the Corinthians, perhaps to encourage him. They proved true.

But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true. Key words. Paul’s word is reliable, whether to them or about them (1:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul flattered them. He spoke the truth both ways.

In a sentence. By all this we are encouraged. In addition to our own encouragement, we were especially delighted to see how happy Titus was, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you. Paul had boasted to him about you, and you have not embarrassed him. Just as everything we said to you was true, so our boasting about you to Titus has proved true as well.

On a Tuesday. Speak well of other believers to others, and live in a way that makes others’ good words about you true.

verseByVerse.quote: And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.

And his affection for you is even greater. Key words. “Affection” (splanchna, deep inner feelings). Titus loves them more now.

As he remembers the obedience of you all. Key words. They obeyed the apostolic instructions.

How you received him with fear and trembling. Key words. With reverence and humility, taking his message seriously as from God (Philippians 2:12; Ephesians 6:5).

I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you. Key words. “Complete confidence” (tharreō en panti, take courage in everything). This prepares for his appeal about the collection in chapters 8–9.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul thought them perfect. Chapters 10–13 show remaining concerns. But he rejoices in their present response.

In a sentence. And his affection for you is all the greater when he remembers that you were all obedient, receiving him with fear and trembling. Paul is glad he can have complete confidence in you.

For worship. Receive God’s word, and those who bring it, with humble reverence. Thank God for faithful messengers.

7.text: <sup>1</sup>Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.<sup>2</sup>Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one.<sup>3</sup>I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.<sup>4</sup>I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.<sup>5</sup>For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within.<sup>6</sup>But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,<sup>7</sup>and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.<sup>8</sup>For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.<sup>9</sup>As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us.<sup>10</sup>For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.<sup>11</sup>For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.<sup>12</sup>So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.<sup>13</sup>Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all.<sup>14</sup>For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.<sup>15</sup>And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling.<sup>16</sup>I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.

8.title: The Grace of Giving: Christ Became Poor
8.overview:
Chapters 8 and 9 are about money: the collection Paul was gathering from his Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Some background helps. The Jerusalem church had been poor for years. There was a famine under the emperor Claudius (Acts 11:28–30), many believers had lost work or family support for following Jesus, and the church had many widows (Acts 6:1). When Paul’s apostleship was recognised in Jerusalem, the leaders asked him to “remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10). For Paul the collection was more than relief. It was a sign that Jews and Gentiles were one body: the Gentiles, who had shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings, were sharing material blessings in return (Romans 15:25–27). Corinth had started eagerly a year earlier (1 Corinthians 16:1–4), but the quarrel with Paul had stalled it.

In chapter 8 Paul encourages them to finish. He points to the poor, persecuted churches of Macedonia, who gave beyond their means and begged to take part, because they first gave themselves to the Lord. Above all he points to Christ, who though he was rich became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich. Giving should be willing, proportionate to what one has, and aimed at fairness between churches. Then Paul introduces the team who will collect the money, Titus and two trusted brothers, chosen so that the handling of the gift will be above suspicion before God and people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Macedonian Example and Christ Who Became Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He describes the Macedonian churches, who in severe trials and deep poverty gave joyfully and beyond their means, even begging to be allowed to take part, because they had first given themselves to the Lord. He urges the Corinthians, who excel in so much, to excel in this generosity too. It is not a command; it is a test of genuine love, measured against the example of Christ, who was rich yet became poor for their sake so that they might become rich. They began a year ago; now they should finish, giving in proportion to what they have. The aim is not to burden them but fairness between churches, as with the manna in the wilderness, where no one had too much or too little.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is one of the key NT texts for the kenosis of the incarnation (alongside Phil. 2:5–8 and John 1:1–14). “Though he was rich” describes the pre-incarnate state of the Son — possessing all the resources of divine glory, honour, and power. “He became poor” describes the incarnation and more specifically the cross: the Son laid aside the exercise of divine prerogatives and took on the condition of creaturely poverty, ultimately the poverty of crucifixion and cursed death. “That you by his poverty might become rich” — the result is the enrichment of believers: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, the inheritance of the new creation.
verseByVerse.examples: A church board is considering its annual budget and the portion allocated to mission outside its own walls. One member argues that they should ensure their own facilities and staff are well-funded before giving generously abroad. This passage holds before him the Macedonian model: churches in deep poverty begging to give. And the Christological ground: the Son of God did not ensure his own comfort before giving to others. The board’s question is not merely financial but spiritual: does this budget reflect the grace described in v. 9?

verseByVerse.quote: We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.

Meaning first. Chapters 8–9 concern the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, which the Corinthians had begun a year earlier but not finished (1 Corinthians 16:1–4). These two chapters are the Bible’s fullest teaching on Christian giving. Chapter 8 makes three points. First, the example of the Macedonian churches, who, though desperately poor and afflicted, begged to give, beyond their means, because they first gave themselves to the Lord (vv. 1–5). Second, the supreme example and motive: the grace of the Lord Jesus, who though rich became poor so that we might become rich (vv. 6–9). Third, practical principles: finish what you started; giving is measured by willingness, not amount; and the goal is fairness, so that abundance meets need, as with the manna in the wilderness (vv. 10–15). Then Paul commends Titus and two trusted brothers who will handle the collection, so that everything is done honourably in the sight of God and people (vv. 16–24). Notice that Paul never uses the word money in these chapters; he calls the gift grace, fellowship, service, blessing and generosity.

We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia. Key words. Macedonia: northern Greece, with churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. “Grace” (charis): generosity is a gift of God’s grace at work. The word appears ten times in chapters 8–9.

For in a severe test of affliction. Key words. The Macedonian churches faced persecution from the start (Acts 16:19–24; 17:5–9; 1 Thessalonians 1:6; 2:14).

Their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty. Key words. “Extreme poverty” (literally poverty down to the depths). Yet they had abundant joy. Joy and poverty together produced generosity.

Have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part. Key words. “Generosity” (haplotēs, simplicity, single-heartedness, liberality). Giving without calculating or holding back.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only the poor can be truly generous. It means generosity comes from grace and joy, not from having plenty.

In a sentence. And now, brothers and sisters, we want you to know about the grace God has given the Macedonian churches. In the middle of a very severe trial, their overflowing joy and their extreme poverty welled up in rich generosity.

On a Tuesday. You do not need to be rich to be generous. Give out of joy in God, whatever you have.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 8–9 concern the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The Macedonian churches — Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea — were poor and persecuted.

verseByVerse.quote: For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—

For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means. Key words. They gave what they could, and then more than seemed possible. Sacrificial giving, like the widow’s two coins (Mark 12:41–44).

Of their own accord. Key words. “Of their own accord” (authairetoi, self-chosen, voluntary). No pressure was needed.

Begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints. Key words. Astonishing: they begged to be allowed to give. Paul may have hesitated to ask such poor churches. “Favour” (charis, grace, privilege). “Taking part” (koinōnia, fellowship, partnership). “Relief” (diakonia, service, ministry). Giving is a privilege of partnership, not a burden.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should give irresponsibly, neglecting their families (1 Timothy 5:8). It means giving should be generous and joyful.

In a sentence. For Paul testifies that they gave as much as they were able, and even beyond their ability. Entirely on their own, they urgently pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the Lord’s people.

For worship. See giving as a privilege. Thank God for the chance to share in what he is doing.

parallels.desc: the widow gave out of her poverty

verseByVerse.quote: and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.

And this, not as we expected. Key words. Their response exceeded all expectations.

But they gave themselves first to the Lord. Key words. The secret of their generosity. Before giving money, they gave themselves. When the heart belongs to the Lord, the wallet follows. Giving begins with consecration (Romans 12:1).

And then by the will of God to us. Key words. Then they gave themselves to Paul and his mission, as God willed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving money can replace giving yourself. God wants you first, and then your gifts.

In a sentence. And they went beyond what we expected: they gave themselves first of all to the Lord, and then, by the will of God, to us as well.

On a Tuesday. Before you decide what to give, give yourself again to the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.

Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started. Key words. Titus had begun organising the collection in Corinth, perhaps on an earlier visit.

So he should complete among you this act of grace. Key words. “Act of grace” (charis): giving is grace in action. “Complete” (epiteleō, finish, as in 7:1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Titus would pressure them. He would help them complete what they wanted to do.

In a sentence. So we urged Titus, just as he had made a beginning earlier, to bring this act of grace on your part to completion.

For worship. Pray for those in your church who organise giving and generosity. Thank God for them.

verseByVerse.quote: But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.

But as you excel in everything. Key words. “Excel” (perisseuō, abound). The Corinthians were richly gifted (1 Corinthians 1:5–7).

In faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you. Key words. Their gifts and their recent earnest repentance (7:11). Some manuscripts read your love for us; the ESV notes this.

See that you excel in this act of grace also. Key words. Generosity is a grace to excel in, as much as faith or knowledge. A church rich in spiritual gifts should also be rich in giving.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving is more important than faith. It means it is part of a complete Christian life.

In a sentence. But since you excel in everything, in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in complete earnestness and in the love we have kindled in you, see that you also excel in this grace of giving.

On a Tuesday. If you are strong in knowledge and faith, ask: am I also strong in generosity?

verseByVerse.quote: I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.

I say this not as a command. Key words. Paul does not order them to give. Christian giving must be voluntary (9:7).

But to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine. Key words. “Prove” (dokimazō, test). The Macedonians’ example tests the Corinthians’ love. Genuine love gives (1 John 3:17–18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving is optional for Christians. It means it must be willing, not forced.

In a sentence. Paul is not commanding you, but testing the sincerity of your love by comparing it with the earnestness of others.

For worship. Let your giving be a test you are glad to pass: a proof of genuine love.

verseByVerse.quote: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.

For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. The supreme motive for giving: Christ’s grace. You know it: you have experienced it.

That though he was rich. Key words. Rich in the glory he shared with the Father before the world began (John 17:5; Philippians 2:6). He owned everything.

Yet for your sake he became poor. Key words. The incarnation and the cross. He laid aside the privileges of glory, was born in a stable, had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58), and died stripped naked on a cross. “Became poor” (ptōcheuō, became a beggar).

So that you by his poverty might become rich. Key words. Rich in salvation: forgiveness, righteousness, adoption, the Spirit, eternal life, an inheritance (Ephesians 1:3, 18). A great exchange, like 5:21.

Where Christians differ: what did the Son give up? Some (kenotic theories) teach that the Son gave up some of his divine attributes, such as omniscience, when he became man. Verdict: The Son did not stop being God or lose any divine attribute. He became poor by taking a human nature and the humble life and death of a servant, veiling his glory and not using his divine privileges for himself (Philippians 2:6–8). He remained fully God while becoming fully man (Chalcedonian Definition; Westminster 8.2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s poverty promises believers material wealth. The riches are spiritual and eternal, as the prosperity gospel forgets.

In a sentence. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that through his poverty you might become rich.

For worship. Meditate on Christ, rich, becoming poor for you. Then give, in gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.

And in this matter I give my judgment. Key words. Advice, not command (v. 8).

This benefits you. Key words. Giving is good for the giver: it frees from greed and grows the soul (Acts 20:35).

Who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. Key words. The Corinthians were the first to begin, and to want to (1 Corinthians 16:1–2). But they had stalled, perhaps because of the troubles.

So now finish doing it as well. Key words. Good intentions must become action.

So that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have. Key words. Out of what you have: according to your means. Not beyond what you possess.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they had failed completely. It means they needed to follow through.

In a sentence. Here is Paul’s judgement about what is best for you: last year you were the first not only to give but also to want to give. Now finish the work, so that your eager willingness may be matched by your completion of it, according to your means.

On a Tuesday. Is there a generous intention you have not followed through on? Finish it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.

For if the readiness is there. Key words. “Readiness” (prothymia, eagerness, willingness). God looks first at the heart.

It is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have. Key words. God measures the gift by what the giver has. A small gift from little is as acceptable as a large gift from much (Mark 12:43–44). No one is expected to give what they do not have.

What it does not mean. It does not mean willingness is enough without action. Paul has just said: finish it. It means God does not demand the impossible.

In a sentence. For if the willingness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have.

For worship. Thank God that he looks at the heart, and accepts the willing gift of the poor as gladly as the rich.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.

For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened. Key words. Paul is not asking the Corinthians to impoverish themselves for others’ comfort.

But that as a matter of fairness. Key words. “Fairness” (isotēs, equality, balance). The aim is that no believer lacks the necessities while others have plenty.

Your abundance at the present time should supply their need. Key words. Corinth had more; Jerusalem had less. Now the Corinthians share.

So that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness. Key words. Circumstances change; one day the Corinthians may be in need, and others will help them. The church is a family that shares.

Where Christians differ: Christian sharing and economics. Some use this passage to support enforced redistribution of wealth by the state. Others ignore it. Verdict: Paul is speaking of voluntary giving within the body of Christ, not compulsory state action (v. 8; 9:7). He does not call for absolute equality of possessions, but for generous sharing so that no believer lacks basic needs. Christians remain owners of their goods as stewards, but are called to deep generosity, especially to fellow believers (Acts 4:32–35; Galatians 6:10; 1 John 3:17). Christians may disagree on public policy, but they cannot neglect personal generosity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean wealth is evil or that all Christians must have exactly the same. It means abundance carries responsibility.

In a sentence. Our desire is not that others might be relieved while you are hard pressed, but that there might be fairness. At the present time your plenty will supply what they need, so that in turn their plenty will supply what you need. The goal is fairness.

On a Tuesday. Look at your abundance. Whose need could it meet? Share it.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”

As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.” Key words. From Exodus 16:18, about the manna in the wilderness. Some gathered more, some less, but when measured, everyone had enough. Hoarding was pointless, since extra manna rotted (Exodus 16:20). God provided for all. Paul applies this to the church: through generous sharing, God’s provision reaches everyone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there will be no differences in wealth. It means that in God’s family, no one should be left in need.

In a sentence. As it is written: “The one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little.”

For worship. Thank God for his daily provision. Trust him enough to share, rather than hoard.

parallels.desc: whoever gathered much had nothing left over

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Titus and the Brothers; Transparency in Giving
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God for Titus’s eagerness to return to Corinth and introduces two companions: a brother well known among the churches for his gospel work and chosen by the churches to travel with the gift, and another brother proven in many tests. The arrangement is deliberate. Paul wants the handling of the money to be honourable not only before the Lord but in the eyes of people, so that no one can accuse him. He commends these representatives of the churches and asks the Corinthians to show them openly the love that Paul has boasted of.
verseByVerse.theology: The principle of handling ministry finances with transparent accountability applies directly to all Christian organisations. Paul, who could have simply trusted his own integrity, insists on multiple overseers and transparent processes — because the integrity of the ministry is at stake not only in God’s sight but in the sight of the watching world. Financial scandal in Christian ministry has consistently damaged the gospel’s credibility; Paul’s precaution (v. 20) is prophylactic wisdom.
verseByVerse.examples: A mission organisation implements a new policy requiring two-signature approval for all expenditures over a certain threshold, and annual independent financial audits reported to the whole organisation. Some staff feel this implies distrust. This passage gives the theological rationale: the precautions are not about distrust of individuals but about protecting the honour of the Lord and the integrity of the ministry in the sight of those who would use any irregularity to attack the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.

But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. Key words. God gave Titus a love for the Corinthians like Paul’s. Good desires in our hearts come from God (Philippians 2:13).

For he not only accepted our appeal. Key words. Paul asked him to go.

But being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord. Key words. He wanted to go anyway. God’s will and his own desire coincided.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Titus had no choice. God worked in his heart, and he freely chose.

In a sentence. Thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same concern Paul has for you. For Titus not only welcomed our appeal, but he is coming to you with much enthusiasm and on his own initiative.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the good desires he puts in your heart. Act on them.

verseByVerse.quote: With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.

With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. Key words. The famous brother is unnamed; some early writers guessed Luke, others Barnabas, Silas or Apollos. His fame was for gospel ministry.

And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us. Key words. “Appointed” (cheirotoneō, elected, chosen by show of hands). The churches chose him as their representative.

As we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us. Key words. The collection.

For the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will. Key words. The collection glorifies Christ and shows the eagerness of all involved.

What it does not mean. It does not mean his name is important for us to know. God knows him; that is enough.

In a sentence. And we are sending along with him the brother who is praised by all the churches for his service to the gospel. What is more, he was chosen by the churches to accompany us as we carry this gift, which we administer to honour the Lord himself and to show our eagerness to help.

For worship. Thank God for unnamed, faithful servants of the gospel. Most of God’s best workers are unknown to history.
verseByVerse.note: The famous brother is unnamed; some early writers guessed Luke.

verseByVerse.quote: We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.

We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us. Key words. Paul’s critics might accuse him of stealing from the collection (12:16–18). So he has independent, church-appointed people travel with the money.

For we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man. Key words. From Proverbs 3:4 in the Greek. It is not enough to be honest before God; we must also be seen to be honest. Financial accountability protects both the gospel and the ministers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean reputation matters more than integrity. Integrity comes first, and transparency shows it.

In a sentence. We want to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift. For we are taking pains to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord but also in the eyes of people.

On a Tuesday. In handling money, at church or work, be transparent. Make it easy for others to see you are honest.

verseByVerse.quote: And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.

And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters. Key words. A third person, proven in faithfulness.

But who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. Key words. He believes in the Corinthians.

As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. Key words. Partner (koinōnos) and fellow worker (synergos).

And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches. Key words. The ESV notes that “messengers” is literally “apostles”: men sent by the churches as their delegates. Not apostles of Christ like the Twelve and Paul, but representatives sent on a mission.

The glory of Christ. Key words. Such faithful servants bring honour to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean these men held the apostolic office. The word is used in its general sense, sent ones.

In a sentence. In addition, we are sending with them our brother who has often proved to us in many ways that he is zealous, and now even more so because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is Paul’s partner and co-worker among you; as for our brothers, they are representatives of the churches and an honour to Christ.

For worship. Thank God for faithful co-workers in his kingdom. Be one yourself.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “messengers” is literally “apostles” — men sent by the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.

So give proof before the churches of your love. Key words. Show these representatives, and through them all the churches, that your love is real.

And of our boasting about you to these men. Key words. Paul has praised the Corinthians to others. Let your actions confirm it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving for show. It means letting genuine love be seen.

In a sentence. Therefore show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our pride in you, so that the churches can see it.

On a Tuesday. Let your love be visible in action, especially in welcoming and supporting those who serve.

9.title: Sowing Generously: The Cheerful Giver
9.overview:
Paul continues on the collection for Jerusalem. He has boasted to the Macedonians that Corinth was ready a year ago, and their eagerness stirred the Macedonians to give. Now he is sending the brothers ahead so that the Corinthian gift is ready when he arrives with Macedonian companions, as a willing gift and not something extracted under pressure.

Then he gives the principles of Christian giving. A farmer who sows sparingly reaps sparingly. Each should give what he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to make every grace overflow, so that his people always have enough and plenty left for every good work; he supplies seed to the sower and will multiply it, enriching them so that they can be generous in every way. And the result goes far beyond meeting needs in Jerusalem: it overflows in thanksgiving to God, proves the Gentiles’ obedience to the gospel, and binds Jewish believers to them in prayer and love. The chapter ends with praise for the gift behind every gift: “Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Sowing and Reaping; the Cheerful Giver; the Inexpressible Gift
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says he hardly needs to write about the collection, since he has boasted of Corinth’s readiness to the Macedonians and it has spurred them on. He is sending the brothers ahead so that the gift is ready when he arrives with Macedonian companions, and is a generous gift rather than something extracted. Then come the principles. Giving is like sowing: the harvest matches the sowing. Each should give what they have decided in their heart, willingly, for God loves a cheerful giver. God is able to supply everything needed and more, so that his people can be generous in every good work; he provides seed and will multiply it. The gift will meet needs in Jerusalem, but it will also overflow in thanks to God, prove the Corinthians’ faith, and draw the Jerusalem believers to pray for them. Paul ends by thanking God for his gift, too great for words.
verseByVerse.theology:
The sowing-reaping principle in v. 6 must be held in tension with the warning against prosperity theology, and the passage itself supplies the correction three times over. Paul is not promising that generous financial giving will result in financial wealth. The reaping he describes is named in v. 10 as “the harvest of your righteousness” — moral integrity and fruitfulness in God’s sight. The supply God gives in that same verse is “seed to the sower and bread for food” — resources to live on and resources to give again — and it is the seed, not the bread, that he undertakes to multiply. Verse 11 then adds that the enriching is “to be generous in every way.” The giver is not made wealthy; he is kept supplied so that generosity can continue. The decisive counter-example is in the previous chapter: the man held up as the supreme giver at 8:9 became poor.

Verse 9 quotes Psalm 112:9. The psalm is a portrait of the man who fears the LORD, and it places distributing freely and giving to the poor among his identifying marks, alongside steadiness and courage — generosity as a feature of godliness rather than an optional extra of temperament. The clause Paul is after is “his righteousness endures forever”: the money is gone and cannot be pointed to, and what it produced does not go anywhere.

“God loves a cheerful giver” (v. 7) comes from the Greek Old Testament at Proverbs 22:8, which carries a line the Hebrew text does not — a blessing on the cheerful and generous man. Paul’s citation focuses the divine pleasure on the disposition of the giver: the motivation and the manner of giving are as important to God as the amount.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation uses a pledge campaign with carefully designed giving targets and social dynamics (recognising top givers, publishing goals) that effectively apply social pressure to giving. Many give generously as a result. But the pastor wonders whether the giving is cheerful or compelled. This passage challenges not the amount raised but the mechanism: “not reluctantly or under compulsion” (v. 7). The goal is not merely generous giving but the formation of cheerful givers — people who give because they have been gripped by the inexpressible gift of God and cannot hold back.

verseByVerse.quote: Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints, for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 9 continues the appeal about the collection. Paul first explains why he is sending the brothers ahead: so that the gift the Corinthians promised will be ready when he arrives with Macedonians, and will be a willing gift, not something squeezed out (vv. 1–5). Then he gives the principles of generous giving: whoever sows generously reaps generously; each should give as he has decided, not reluctantly or under pressure, for God loves a cheerful giver; and God is able to make all grace abound so that his people always have enough for every good work (vv. 6–11). Finally, he shows the wider results of giving: it meets needs, it overflows in thanksgiving to God, it proves the reality of the Corinthians’ confession of the gospel, and it binds Jewish and Gentile believers together in prayer and love. And he ends with praise for God’s inexpressible gift, Christ himself (vv. 12–15).

Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints. Key words. A tactful opening: you hardly need me to tell you. “Ministry” (diakonia, service).

For I know your readiness. Key words. Their willingness to give.

Of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. Key words. Achaia was southern Greece, including Corinth; Macedonia was northern Greece. Paul used the Corinthians’ example to inspire the Macedonians, and the Macedonians’ example to inspire the Corinthians (8:1–5).

And your zeal has stirred up most of them. Key words. Their early enthusiasm encouraged others. Generosity is contagious.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was manipulating them. He spoke honestly of both churches.

In a sentence. There is no need for Paul to write to you about this service to the Lord’s people. For he knows your eagerness to help, and he has been boasting about it to the Macedonians, telling them that since last year you in Achaia were ready to give; and your enthusiasm has stirred most of them to action.

On a Tuesday. Your generosity can inspire others. Let it be seen, humbly, for God’s glory.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was southern Greece, including Corinth; Macedonia was to the north.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.

But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter. Key words. The brothers of 8:16–24.

So that you may be ready, as I said you would be. Key words. Good intentions need preparation.

Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident. Key words. Paul gently points out the embarrassment it would cause. Honest pastoral motivation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they should give to avoid shame. It means they should follow through on what they promised.

In a sentence. But Paul is sending the brothers so that our boasting about you in this matter will not prove hollow, but that you may be ready, as he said you would be. For if any Macedonians come with him and find you unprepared, we, not to mention you, would be ashamed of having been so confident.

For worship. Ask God to help you keep your commitments, including your commitments to give.

verseByVerse.quote: So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.

So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you. Key words. To prepare.

And arrange in advance for the gift you have promised. Key words. “Gift” (eulogia, blessing). Giving is a blessing to others.

So that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction. Key words. “Willing gift” is literally a blessing; “exaction” (pleonexia, greediness, something extracted). Paul wants it to be generous blessing, not something reluctantly squeezed out. If it is collected last minute under pressure, it would feel extracted.

What it does not mean. It does not mean planned giving is less spiritual. Planning makes giving free and generous.

In a sentence. So Paul thought it necessary to urge the brothers to visit you in advance and finish the arrangements for the generous gift you promised. Then it will be ready as a generous gift, not as one grudgingly given.

On a Tuesday. Plan your giving ahead, so that it is generous and willing, not last-minute and reluctant.

verseByVerse.quote: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
