The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.

The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. Key words. A farming proverb (Proverbs 11:24–25; 22:9; Galatians 6:7). A farmer who plants few seeds harvests little.

And whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully. Key words. “Bountifully” (literally with blessings). Generous sowing brings a generous harvest. The harvest is described in verses 8–14: God’s abundant grace, the means to keep giving, righteousness, thanksgiving to God, and the love and prayers of others.

Where Christians differ: the prosperity gospel and seed faith. Some teach that if you give money to God (often to a particular ministry), he will return far more money to you, so giving is an investment for personal wealth. Verdict: Paul does promise that God rewards generosity. But the harvest is mainly spiritual: grace, righteousness, thanksgiving, and the means to be generous again (vv. 8, 10–11). God supplies enough for every good work, not luxury. Giving in order to get is the opposite of the cheerful, self-forgetting generosity Paul describes. Christ became poor to make us rich spiritually (8:9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God never blesses materially. He supplies our needs (Philippians 4:19). But giving is not a scheme for wealth.

In a sentence. Remember this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.

For worship. Sow generously today, not to get, but because God has sown so generously in you.

parallels.desc: one gives freely, yet grows all the richer

verseByVerse.quote: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

Each one must give as he has decided in his heart. Key words. “Decided” (proaireō, chosen beforehand, purposed). Personal, prayerful, deliberate decision. No fixed amount is imposed.

Not reluctantly. Key words. Literally, not out of grief: not with a heavy heart.

Or under compulsion. Key words. Not because of pressure from others or guilt.

For God loves a cheerful giver. Key words. From Proverbs 22:8 in the Greek translation. “Cheerful” (hilaros, from which hilarious): glad, joyful. God delights in those who give gladly. He is himself the most cheerful giver of all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean you should only give when you feel like it. It means ask God to make you glad to give.

In a sentence. Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under pressure, for God loves a cheerful giver.

On a Tuesday. Pray before you give. Decide in your heart. Then give with a smile.

parallels.desc: from every man whose heart moves him
the Greek Old Testament adds a line about God blessing a cheerful giver

verseByVerse.quote: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.

And God is able to make all grace abound to you. Key words. God’s ability to provide. All grace: every kind of blessing, material and spiritual.

So that having all sufficiency in all things at all times. Key words. Notice “all” four times. “Sufficiency” (autarkeia, contentment, self-sufficiency): the Stoic word for being independent of circumstances. Paul transforms it: having enough because God provides (Philippians 4:11–13; 1 Timothy 6:6).

You may abound in every good work. Key words. The purpose of God’s provision is not hoarding but more giving and serving. God gives to us so that we can give through us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians will always be wealthy. It means they will have enough to do the good God calls them to.

In a sentence. And God is able to bless you abundantly, so that in all things at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work.

For worship. Trust that God will give you enough for every good work he calls you to. Then do them.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”

As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor.” Key words. From Psalm 112:9, describing the righteous person who fears the LORD. “Distributed freely” (skorpizō, scattered, like a sower scattering seed). The righteous scatter their goods generously.

“His righteousness endures forever.” Key words. The generous person’s righteousness, shown in giving, lasts. Its fruit is eternal. Psalm 111:3 says the same of God; the righteous person reflects God’s character.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving makes us righteous before God. It means generosity is a mark of the righteous life.

In a sentence. As it is written: “They have freely scattered their gifts to the poor; their righteousness endures for ever.”

On a Tuesday. Scatter your gifts generously to the poor this week. It has eternal value.

parallels.desc: he has distributed freely; he has given to the poor

verseByVerse.quote: He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.

He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food. Key words. From Isaiah 55:10. God gives the farmer seed to plant and bread to eat. He is the source of all provision.

Will supply and multiply your seed for sowing. Key words. God will give the generous person more to sow, more resources for giving.

And increase the harvest of your righteousness. Key words. From Hosea 10:12. The harvest is righteousness: good works, a godly life, and its eternal fruit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God multiplies seed so that we can eat it all. Seed is for sowing.

In a sentence. Now he who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will also supply and increase your store of seed and will enlarge the harvest of your righteousness.

For worship. Thank God for everything he supplies. Ask him to multiply your seed so you can sow more.

parallels.desc: seed to the sower and bread to the eater

verseByVerse.quote: You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.

You will be enriched in every way. Key words. God will make you rich, but for a purpose:

To be generous in every way. Key words. Enriched in order to be generous. God’s blessings are given to flow through us, not to stop with us.

Which through us will produce thanksgiving to God. Key words. When Paul delivers the gift, the recipients will thank God. Giving ends in worship.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s purpose is our comfort. It means his purpose is generosity and thanksgiving.

In a sentence. You will be enriched in every way so that you can be generous on every occasion, and through us your generosity will result in thanksgiving to God.

On a Tuesday. Ask: what has God enriched me with, so that I can be generous with it?

verseByVerse.quote: For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,

For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints. Key words. “Service” (leitourgia, priestly service, from which liturgy). Giving is worship.

But is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. Key words. The gift meets needs and multiplies praise.

By their approval of this service. Key words. Literally, by the proof (dokimē) of this service. The gift proves the reality of the Corinthians’ faith.

They will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ. Key words. The Jewish believers in Jerusalem, who might have doubted Paul’s Gentile converts, will see that their faith is real: their generosity is obedience flowing from confessing the gospel. Giving is evidence of genuine faith (James 2:15–17).

And the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others. Key words. “Contribution” (koinōnia, fellowship, sharing). The gift expresses unity with all believers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving saves. It shows salvation.

In a sentence. This service you perform not only supplies the needs of the Lord’s people but also overflows in many expressions of thanks to God. Because of the proof this service gives, others will praise God for the obedience that accompanies your confession of the gospel of Christ, and for your generosity in sharing with them and with everyone else.

For worship. Let your giving be worship, offered to God, overflowing in others’ thanksgiving.

verseByVerse.quote: while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.

While they long for you and pray for you. Key words. The Jerusalem believers, receiving the gift, will love and pray for the Gentile Corinthians they have never met. The collection builds bridges between Jewish and Gentile Christians.

Because of the surpassing grace of God upon you. Key words. They will see God’s grace at work in the Corinthians, and love them for it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean prayer can be bought. It means generosity creates bonds of love and prayer.

In a sentence. And in their prayers for you their hearts will go out to you, because of the surpassing grace God has given you.

On a Tuesday. Give to believers in another place or culture. It will bind you together in love and prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!

Thanks be to God. Key words. Paul ends two chapters on giving with praise.

For his inexpressible gift! Key words. “Inexpressible” (anekdiēgētos, indescribable, beyond telling). The gift is Christ himself, God’s Son, given for us (John 3:16; Romans 8:32). All our giving is a small response to God’s infinite gift. This is the ultimate motive for generosity (8:9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the collection is the inexpressible gift. The collection is a small echo of it.

In a sentence. Thanks be to God for his gift, too wonderful for words!

For worship. Stop and thank God for his inexpressible gift: Jesus. Let your giving flow from that thanks.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints,<sup>2</sup>for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.<sup>3</sup>But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be.<sup>4</sup>Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.<sup>5</sup>So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.<sup>6</sup>The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.<sup>7</sup>Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.<sup>8</sup>And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.<sup>9</sup>As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”<sup>10</sup>He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.<sup>11</sup>You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.<sup>12</sup>For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God.<sup>13</sup>By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,<sup>14</sup>while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.<sup>15</sup>Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!

10.title: Divine Weapons and Boasting in the Lord
10.overview:
With chapter 10 the tone changes sharply. Chapters 1–9 are warm and relieved; chapters 10–13 are a fierce defence against the visiting teachers Paul will call “super-apostles” and “false apostles”. Some scholars therefore think these chapters were a separate letter, either the earlier tearful letter (2:4) or a later one written after fresh bad news. No manuscript divides the letter, and Paul may simply turn here from the repentant majority to the minority still under the rivals’ influence. Either way, these chapters are Scripture and their meaning is clear.

The rivals mocked Paul: bold in letters but feeble in person, a poor speaker, an unimpressive man. Paul answers that he appeals by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, but he is not powerless. His weapons are not worldly ones (rhetoric, manipulation, status), but divine power that demolishes strongholds of false reasoning and takes every thought captive to obey Christ. What he writes when absent he will do when present. He refuses to measure himself against others who commend themselves. He keeps to the field God assigned him, which reached as far as Corinth, and hopes to go beyond it. The only boast that counts is in the Lord, and the only commendation that counts is the Lord’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Weapons of Divine Warfare
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tone sharpens as Paul answers rivals who mock him as timid in person and bold only on paper. He appeals to them with the gentleness of Christ, hoping he will not have to act firmly against those who accuse him of worldly motives. He does live as a weak human being, but he does not fight with worldly methods. His weapons have God’s power to demolish fortresses of the mind: arguments and proud ideas raised against the knowledge of God. He aims to bring every thought under Christ’s rule, and is prepared to discipline persistent disobedience once the church as a whole is obedient.
verseByVerse.theology: The “weapons of warfare” in v. 4 are the weapons of gospel ministry: the proclaimed word, prayer, the demonstration of transformed lives, the power of the Spirit. These are not powerful by worldly standards (rhetorical brilliance, social influence, political power) but divinely powerful for pulling down strongholds. This is the consistent NT theology of ministry: God chooses the weak and foolish things to shame the strong and wise (1 Cor. 1:27), precisely so that the power is unmistakably his. The church that abandons the means God has ordained in favour of worldly methods of influence has swapped divinely powerful weapons for humanly impressive ones.
verseByVerse.examples: A church in a university town hires a communications consultant to help them “win the argument” with the secular culture. The consultant advises them to lead with culturally acceptable values rather than with gospel claims. This passage challenges the strategy: taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ is the goal, but the weapons for achieving it are not strategic communication management — they are the divinely powerful weapons of the gospel, prayer, and the demonstration of transformed lives. The strongholds that prevent the knowledge of God are spiritual, and only spiritual weapons can pull them down.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away!— I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness with such confidence as I count on showing against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away!—I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness with such confidence as I count on showing against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh.

Meaning first. Chapters 10–13 answer rival teachers at Corinth who belittled Paul. The tone changes sharply: from relief and warmth to warning and irony. These intruders, whom Paul will call super-apostles and false apostles, boasted of their credentials, eloquence and visions, and mocked Paul as weak in person and unimpressive in speech. Chapter 10 begins Paul’s answer. First, he appeals to them by the meekness of Christ, asking them not to force him to be severe when he comes. His warfare is spiritual, with divine weapons that demolish strongholds of proud thinking and take every thought captive to Christ (vv. 1–6). Second, he answers the charge that he is bold in letters but weak in person: he will be the same in action when present as in writing when absent (vv. 7–11). Third, he refuses to compare himself with those who measure themselves by themselves. He boasts only within the field God assigned him, which includes Corinth, since he brought them the gospel first. Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord, for only the Lord’s commendation counts (vv. 12–18).

I, Paul, myself entreat you. Key words. Emphatic and personal. Some think Paul took the pen himself here.

By the meekness and gentleness of Christ. Key words. “Meekness” (prautēs, strength under control, humility). “Gentleness” (epieikeia, reasonableness, forbearance). Christ described himself as gentle and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29). Paul’s gentleness, which his opponents mocked as weakness, is Christlike.

I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away! Key words. Paul quotes his critics’ accusation. “Humble” (tapeinos, lowly), which they meant as servile, timid.

I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness. Key words. He would rather not have to be severe.

Against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh. Key words. Some accused Paul of acting by merely human motives and methods: self-interest, weakness, manipulation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean meekness is weakness. Christ was meek and yet overturned the tables in the temple.

In a sentence. By the humility and gentleness of Christ, Paul appeals to you, Paul who is said to be timid when face to face with you but bold toward you when away! He begs you that when he comes he may not have to be as bold as he expects to be toward some people who think that we live by the standards of this world.

On a Tuesday. Be gentle like Christ. And do not let others mistake your gentleness for weakness.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 10–13 answer rival teachers at Corinth who belittled Paul.

parallels.desc: Moses was very meek

verseByVerse.quote: For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.

For though we walk in the flesh. Key words. Paul lives in a human body, with human weakness.

We are not waging war according to the flesh. Key words. But he does not fight by worldly methods: manipulation, force, rhetoric, political power.

For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh. Key words. The weapons are spiritual: the word of God, prayer, truth, righteousness, faith (6:7; Ephesians 6:13–18).

But have divine power to destroy strongholds. Key words. Strongholds were fortified towers or citadels. Proverbs 21:22 speaks of a wise man bringing down the stronghold in which the mighty trust. The strongholds here are explained in verse 5: proud arguments and ideas that resist God.

Where Christians differ: what are the strongholds? Some popular teaching takes strongholds to mean territorial demons over cities, to be bound by special prayer, or demonic footholds in a believer’s life to be cast out. Verdict: Paul defines the strongholds himself in verse 5: arguments and lofty opinions raised against the knowledge of God. The battle is for minds and hearts, fought with the truth of the gospel. Spiritual forces are real (Ephesians 6:12), but Scripture never teaches us to map or bind territorial spirits. Our weapons are the word, prayer and holy lives.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should use physical force to spread the faith. That is warfare according to the flesh.

In a sentence. For though we live in the world, we do not wage war as the world does. The weapons we fight with are not the weapons of the world. On the contrary, they have divine power to demolish strongholds.

For worship. Pray for strongholds of unbelief in your culture to be pulled down by the truth of the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Strongholds were fortified towers or citadels.

verseByVerse.quote: We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ,

We destroy arguments. Key words. “Arguments” (logismoi, reasonings, philosophies). The strongholds are intellectual and moral systems that resist God.

And every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God. Key words. “Lofty opinion” (hypsōma, high thing, a tower raised up). Pride lifted up against God, like the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:4).

And take every thought captive to obey Christ. Key words. “Take captive” (aichmalōtizō, take prisoner of war). Every thought is brought under Christ’s lordship. The Christian mind is not neutral; it bows to Christ in everything: science, art, ethics, politics, relationships.

Where Christians differ: how should Christians argue for the faith? Some approaches to apologetics try to meet unbelievers on neutral ground, reasoning from shared premises toward God. Verdict: No thought is neutral; all thinking either submits to Christ or rebels against him. Christians should reason carefully and use evidence (Acts 17:2–3; 1 Peter 3:15), but from a standpoint of submission to God’s revelation, not as if human reason were the final judge. The aim is not merely to win arguments, but to bring every thought captive to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be anti-intellectual. It means the mind is to be used fully, and in obedience to Christ.

In a sentence. We demolish arguments and every proud idea that sets itself up against the knowledge of God, and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ.

On a Tuesday. Notice the thoughts in your own mind that rebel against God: worry, pride, lust, bitterness. Take one captive today and bring it to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: being ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
being ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete.

Being ready to punish every disobedience. Key words. “Punish” (ekdikeō, bring justice). Paul is prepared to exercise church discipline against the rebels when he comes (13:2, 10).

When your obedience is complete. Key words. First the church as a whole must fully return to obedience. Then Paul can deal with the remaining troublemakers, with the church on his side.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wants to punish. He wants obedience. Discipline is a last resort.

In a sentence. And we will be ready to punish every act of disobedience, once your obedience is complete.

For worship. Pray for your church leaders as they guard the church. And ask God to make your own obedience complete.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges them to look at the facts. He belongs to Christ as much as anyone, and his authority was given to build them up, not tear them down. Some say his letters are impressive but he is feeble in person and a poor speaker; they will find him the same in action as on paper. He will not join those who rate themselves by comparing themselves with each other. His boasting stays within the field God assigned him, which included Corinth, where he was first to bring the gospel. He does not claim credit for others’ work, and hopes their growth will free him to preach further afield. In the end only one boast counts, boasting in the Lord, and only one approval, the Lord’s.
verseByVerse.theology: The criterion of the Lord’s commendation (v. 18) is the basis of all genuine ministerial authority in the NT. The super-apostles derive their authority from letters of recommendation (3:1), impressive personal presence, rhetorical skill, and visions and revelations (12:1). Paul derives his from the divine call (Gal. 1:1), the fruit of his ministry (the transformed Corinthians — 3:2), and ultimately from the Lord’s own assessment. This does not make Paul self-certifying; it means his legitimacy is determined at the bar of heaven, not at the bar of human opinion.
verseByVerse.examples: A minister with a large platform cultivates an online presence that constantly showcases his ministry’s results — attendance figures, conversion stories, speaking engagements, endorsements from well-known figures. He tells himself he is building credibility for the gospel. This passage asks a harder question: is he building the gospel’s credibility or his own? The test is not whether he mentions God in his self-promotion but whether his confidence is ultimately in the Lord’s assessment or in the metrics of human comparison.

verseByVerse.quote: Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you, I will not be ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you, I will not be ashamed.

Look at what is before your eyes. Key words. Or: you look only at outward appearances. Either way: face the facts.

If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s. Key words. The rival teachers claimed a special connection to Christ, perhaps through Jerusalem, or visions.

Let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. Key words. Paul belongs to Christ just as much.

For even if I boast a little too much of our authority. Key words. Paul has real apostolic authority from Christ.

Which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you. Key words. The purpose of all church authority: to build up, not tear down (13:10). Authority that destroys people is abused authority.

I will not be ashamed. Key words. His claim will be vindicated.

What it does not mean. It does not mean authority never corrects. Correction is part of building up.

In a sentence. You are judging by appearances. If anyone is confident that they belong to Christ, they should consider again that we belong to Christ just as much as they do. So even if Paul boasts somewhat freely about the authority the Lord gave us for building you up rather than tearing you down, he will not be ashamed of it.

For worship. Pray for leaders to use their authority to build up, never to destroy.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.”

I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. Key words. Paul does not want his letters seen as threats from a safe distance.

For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong.” Key words. Even his critics admitted his letters were powerful. They are still read today.

“But his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.” Key words. Greek culture prized impressive physical presence and polished oratory. Paul apparently was not physically imposing and lacked the rhetorical polish of professional speakers (11:6; 1 Corinthians 2:1–4). An ancient description, perhaps reliable, pictured him as short, bald and bow-legged.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul could not speak well. Acts shows him as a powerful speaker. It means he refused the showy techniques the Corinthians admired.

In a sentence. Paul does not want to seem to be trying to frighten you with his letters. For some say, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but in person he is unimpressive and his speaking amounts to nothing.”

On a Tuesday. Do not judge Christian leaders by charisma or appearance. Judge them by faithfulness to Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized impressive physical presence and polished oratory.

verseByVerse.quote: Let such a person understand that what we say by letter when absent, we do when present.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let such a person understand that what we say by letter when absent, we do when present.

Let such a person understand. Key words. A warning to the critics.

That what we say by letter when absent, we do when present. Key words. Paul is consistent. When he comes, they will find him as firm in action as in writing. His gentleness is not weakness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul will be harsh. It means he will do what is necessary.

In a sentence. Such people should realise that what we are in our letters when we are absent, we will be in our actions when we are present.

For worship. Ask God to make you consistent: the same in private and in public, in writing and in person.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.

Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. Key words. Irony. Paul would not dare to put himself in the same class as these impressive self-promoters.

But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another. Key words. They use each other as the standard, a closed circle of mutual admiration.

They are without understanding. Key words. Foolish. The only true measure is God’s standard, not comparison with others.

What it does not mean. It does not mean learning from others is wrong. It means comparison is a false measure of spiritual worth.

In a sentence. We do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they are not wise.

On a Tuesday. Stop comparing yourself with other Christians. Measure yourself by Christ and his word.

verseByVerse.quote: But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.

But we will not boast beyond limits. Key words. Paul keeps within bounds.

But will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us. Key words. “Area of influence” (kanōn, measuring rod, assigned field, from which canon). God gave Paul a field of ministry: the Gentiles (Galatians 2:7–9).

To reach even to you. Key words. Corinth is within that field.

For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. Key words. Paul is not claiming territory that is not his.

For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ. Key words. Paul founded the Corinthian church (Acts 18:1–11). The rival teachers came later and tried to take over his work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean churches belong to their founders. They belong to Christ. But Paul had a God-given responsibility for them.

In a sentence. We, however, will not boast beyond proper limits, but will confine our boasting to the sphere of service God himself has assigned to us, a sphere that also includes you. We are not going too far in our boasting, as would be the case if we had not come to you, for we did get as far as you with the gospel of Christ.

For worship. Thank God for the field of service he has assigned you. Work faithfully within it.

verseByVerse.quote: We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged, so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged, so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.

We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. Key words. Unlike the intruders, who took credit for Paul’s work.

But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged. Key words. As the Corinthians grow and settle down, Paul will be free to go further.

So that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you. Key words. Paul hoped to go on to Rome and Spain (Romans 15:23–24, 28). Pioneer missions was his passion.

Without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence. Key words. Paul did not want to build on another’s foundation (Romans 15:20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean only pioneer work matters. Others water what pioneers plant (1 Corinthians 3:6).

In a sentence. Neither do we go beyond our limits by boasting of work done by others. Our hope is that, as your faith continues to grow, our sphere of activity among you will greatly expand, so that we can preach the gospel in the regions beyond you. For we do not want to boast about work already done in someone else’s territory.

On a Tuesday. Do not take credit for others’ work. And pray for the gospel to reach the regions beyond.
verseByVerse.note: Paul hoped to go on to Rome and Spain.

verseByVerse.quote: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

“Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” Key words. From Jeremiah 9:24, quoted also in 1 Corinthians 1:31. All legitimate boasting is in what the Lord has done.

For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved. Key words. “Approved” (dokimos, tested and genuine). Self-promotion proves nothing.

But the one whom the Lord commends. Key words. Only the Lord’s verdict counts (1 Corinthians 4:4–5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never speak of what God has done through them. Paul does. It means all the credit goes to the Lord.

In a sentence. But, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

For worship. Seek the Lord’s commendation above all. Boast in him today.

parallels.desc: let him who boasts boast in this

10.text: <sup>1</sup>I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away!—<sup>2</sup>I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness with such confidence as I count on showing against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh.<sup>3</sup>For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh.<sup>4</sup>For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.<sup>5</sup>We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ,<sup>6</sup>being ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete.<sup>7</sup>Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we.<sup>8</sup>For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you, I will not be ashamed.<sup>9</sup>I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters.<sup>10</sup>For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.”<sup>11</sup>Let such a person understand that what we say by letter when absent, we do when present.<sup>12</sup>Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.<sup>13</sup>But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you.<sup>14</sup>For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.<sup>15</sup>We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged,<sup>16</sup>so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.<sup>17</sup>“Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”<sup>18</sup>For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

11.title: The Fool's Speech and the Catalogue of Suffering
11.overview:
In this chapter Paul does something he finds distasteful: he boasts. The rival teachers in Corinth commended themselves loudly, with their Jewish pedigree, eloquence, visions and fees, and the Corinthians were impressed. So Paul plays “the fool” for a while, borrowing their method to expose it. He fears the church is being seduced away from Christ, like Eve by the serpent, by teachers who bring a different Jesus, a different spirit and a different gospel. He defends his practice of preaching free of charge, which they took as a sign of inferiority, and unmasks the rivals as false apostles, servants of Satan disguised as servants of righteousness.

Then comes the “fool’s speech” proper. Paul matches their credentials, Hebrew, Israelite, descendant of Abraham, and then lists not his successes but his sufferings: floggings, beatings, a stoning, shipwrecks, dangers on every road, hunger, cold and the daily weight of care for all the churches. The climax is deliberately absurd: his greatest exploit was being lowered in a basket through a window to escape from Damascus. If he must boast, he will boast of his weakness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Jealousy for the Corinthians and the False Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks the Corinthians to put up with a little foolishness from him, because he loves them with God’s own jealousy: he promised them to Christ like a bride to her husband, and fears they are being led away from simple, pure devotion to Christ, as Eve was deceived by the serpent. They tolerate teachers who preach another Jesus and another gospel, yet Paul is in no way inferior to these so-called super-apostles, even if he is no polished speaker. Was it wrong of him to preach to them free of charge, taking support from other churches instead? He will keep refusing their money, to cut the ground from under those who want to claim equal status with him. These men are false apostles disguised as apostles of Christ, which is no surprise, since Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light; they will end as their deeds deserve.
verseByVerse.theology: The identification of false apostles as servants of Satan (v. 15) is one of Paul’s most severe theological statements. It raises the question of how to identify false apostles — since they come disguised as servants of righteousness. The test that Paul has been applying throughout the letter is: what is the content of the message? What is the character of the minister? Does the ministry bear the cruciform pattern of genuine apostolic suffering? Paul’s opponents fail all three tests: their message is a different gospel; their character is self-promotional; their lives show no evidence of the suffering that authentic ministry requires.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation is attracted to a visiting teacher who is eloquent, radiantly confident, and preaches a message of spiritual empowerment, prosperity, and supernatural experience — all framed in Christian language. The pastor is concerned but cannot point to an obviously heretical statement. This passage gives him the categories: the test is not merely whether Jesus is mentioned but which Jesus is being presented, which spirit is being invoked, which gospel is being preached. The angel-of-light disguise means the most dangerous false teaching often looks impressively spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 11 is Paul’s fool’s speech. The super-apostles at Corinth boasted of their credentials, and the Corinthians were impressed. Paul hates boasting, but to rescue the church he plays the fool and boasts, in order to expose the emptiness of their boasting. First, he explains his motive: a godly jealousy, like a father who has promised his daughter to one husband, Christ, and fears she will be seduced, as Eve was, by another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel (vv. 1–6). Second, he answers their complaint that he refused payment: he did it out of love, to show the difference between himself and the false apostles, who are Satan’s servants disguised as servants of righteousness (vv. 7–15). Third, he boasts as a fool. He matches their pedigree: Hebrew, Israelite, offspring of Abraham. But as a servant of Christ he outdoes them, not in triumphs but in sufferings: imprisonments, beatings, lashings, stoning, shipwrecks, dangers of every kind, hunger, cold, and daily anxiety for the churches. If he must boast, he will boast of his weakness, like the time he escaped Damascus in a basket (vv. 16–33).

I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Key words. “Foolishness” (aphrosynē): boasting about himself, which Paul considers foolish (v. 17). He asks them to put up with it.

Do bear with me! Key words. Or: you are already bearing with me.

For I feel a divine jealousy for you. Key words. Literally, I am jealous over you with God’s jealousy. Not selfish possessiveness, but the holy zeal God has for his people’s exclusive love (Exodus 20:5; Hosea 2:19–20).

Since I betrothed you to one husband. Key words. In a Jewish betrothal the bride was already bound to her husband, though the wedding came later. Breaking it was like divorce. The father’s duty was to guard the bride’s purity until the wedding. Paul, the church’s spiritual father, promised the Corinthians to Christ when they believed.

To present you as a pure virgin to Christ. Key words. At Christ’s return, the wedding day, the church will be presented to him (Ephesians 5:27; Revelation 19:7–9). Paul wants her faithful until then.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wants the Corinthians’ loyalty to himself. He wants their loyalty to Christ.

In a sentence. Paul hopes you will put up with a little of his foolishness; yes, please put up with him! He is jealous for you with a godly jealousy. He promised you to one husband, to Christ, so that he might present you as a pure virgin to him.

On a Tuesday. You are betrothed to Christ. Guard your heart’s loyalty to him today.
verseByVerse.note: In a Jewish betrothal the bride was already bound to her husband-to-be, and her purity was guarded until the wedding; Paul pictures himself in that guardian role.

parallels.desc: I will betroth you to me forever

verseByVerse.quote: But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.

But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning. Key words. From Genesis 3:1–6, 13. The serpent (Satan, v. 14; Revelation 12:9) deceived Eve with clever words that twisted God’s word. “Cunning” (panourgia, craftiness, as in 4:2).

Your thoughts will be led astray. Key words. “Led astray” (phtheirō, corrupted, seduced). The danger is to the mind, through false teaching.

From a sincere and pure devotion to Christ. Key words. “Sincere” (haplotēs, simplicity, single-minded). “Pure” (hagnotēs, chaste). Some manuscripts omit and pure, as the ESV notes. The danger is not just wrong ideas, but a divided heart, adding something to Christ or replacing him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean simple devotion means simplistic thinking. It means undivided loyalty.

In a sentence. But Paul is afraid that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may somehow be led astray from your sincere and pure devotion to Christ.

For worship. Ask God to keep your devotion to Christ simple, single-hearted and pure.

parallels.desc: the serpent deceived me

verseByVerse.quote: For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.

For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed. Key words. Same name, different person. The rivals preached a Jesus without the cross, perhaps a triumphant wonder-worker, or a Jesus who required law-keeping.

Or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received. Key words. A spirit of pride, power and spectacle, not the Holy Spirit who produces humility and love.

Or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted. Key words. A message other than the gospel of grace through Christ crucified (Galatians 1:6–9).

You put up with it readily enough. Key words. Irony: you put up with them, so put up with me!

Where Christians differ: another Jesus. Many groups use the name of Jesus while teaching a different person: a created being, a mere prophet, a spirit brother of Satan, a teacher of self-improvement. Verdict: The true Jesus is the one the apostles proclaimed: eternal Son of God, fully God and fully man, crucified for our sins, risen bodily, Lord of all. Any Jesus who differs from the apostolic Jesus is another Jesus, and any gospel that adds to or subtracts from grace through faith in him is another gospel (Galatians 1:8). Christians must test teachers by Scripture (1 John 4:1–3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every disagreement among Christians is a different gospel. It means the core identity and work of Christ are non-negotiable.

In a sentence. For if someone comes to you and preaches a Jesus other than the Jesus we preached, or if you receive a different spirit from the Spirit you received, or a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it easily enough.

On a Tuesday. Test what you hear about Jesus by Scripture. Is it the Jesus of the apostles?

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.

Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles. Key words. “Super-apostles” is Paul’s ironic name for the rival teachers: “extra-super” apostles (hyperlian apostoloi). Probably not the Twelve, but the false apostles of verse 13, who claimed superior status.

Even if I am unskilled in speaking. Key words. “Unskilled” (idiōtēs, amateur, untrained). Paul admits he lacked professional rhetorical training, or refused to use it.

I am not so in knowledge. Key words. He knows the truth of God (Ephesians 3:3–4).

Indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things. Key words. His teaching among them proved it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean polished speaking is wrong. It means content matters more than style.

In a sentence. Paul does not think he is in the least inferior to those super-apostles. He may indeed be untrained as a speaker, but he does have knowledge. We have made this perfectly clear to you in every way.

For worship. Thank God for preachers who may not be polished but who know and teach the truth.
verseByVerse.note: “Super-apostles” is Paul’s ironic name for the rival teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.

Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted. Key words. Irony. Paul worked with his hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), a lowly trade in Greek eyes. The Corinthians thought a real teacher would charge fees.

Because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge? Key words. Was that a crime? (1 Corinthians 9:12–18).

I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you. Key words. “Robbed” (sylaō, plundered, stripped, a military word). A deliberate exaggeration: he took support from poorer churches (Macedonia) so that he could serve the richer Corinthians free.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul stole. It means he accepted gifts that made his Corinthian ministry possible.

In a sentence. Was it a sin for Paul to lower himself in order to lift you up by preaching the gospel of God to you free of charge? He robbed other churches by receiving support from them so as to serve you.

On a Tuesday. Are you willing to be humbled so that others may be lifted up?

verseByVerse.quote: And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.

And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone. Key words. “Burden” (katanarkaō, be a dead weight). Even in need, he did not ask the Corinthians.

For the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. Key words. Silas and Timothy brought gifts from Macedonia (Acts 18:5; Philippians 4:15–16).

So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way. Key words. He will continue this policy.

As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia. Key words. A solemn oath. His boast of free ministry will not be taken away (1 Corinthians 9:15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean accepting support is wrong. Paul accepted it from others.

In a sentence. And when Paul was with you and needed something, he was not a burden to anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied what he needed. He has kept himself from being a burden to you in any way, and will continue to do so. As surely as the truth of Christ is in him, nobody in Achaia will stop this boasting of his.

For worship. Thank God for those who support gospel workers, like the Macedonians.

verseByVerse.quote: And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.

And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do! Key words. Some said Paul refused their money because he did not care about them. Paul calls God as witness to his love.

And what I am doing I will continue to do. Key words. He will keep preaching free of charge.

In order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do. Key words. The rivals took payment and wanted to say Paul was no different. By refusing payment, Paul cut the ground from under them. “Undermine” (ekkoptō, cut off).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was being stubborn. He had a strategic reason.

In a sentence. Why? Because he does not love you? God knows he does! And he will keep on doing what he is doing in order to cut the ground from under those who want an opportunity to be considered equal with us in the things they boast about.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes love means refusing what is offered, so that the gospel is not compromised.

verseByVerse.quote: For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

For such men are false apostles. Key words. “False apostles” (pseudapostoloi). Paul names them plainly.

Deceitful workmen. Key words. “Deceitful” (dolioi, crafty, treacherous). They work, but for themselves, by trickery.

Disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. Key words. “Disguising” (metaschēmatizō, changing outward form, masquerading). They look like apostles, but are not.

And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light. Key words. Satan does not usually appear as obvious evil, but as something beautiful, spiritual, enlightening. His most dangerous tactic is to imitate truth.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every teacher we disagree with is a false apostle. These men preached another Jesus and another gospel (v. 4).

In a sentence. For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.

For worship. Ask God for discernment. Not everything that looks bright and spiritual is from him.

verseByVerse.quote: So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.

So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Key words. “Servants” (diakonoi, ministers). Satan has his ministers. They talk of righteousness, perhaps law-keeping, morality or holiness, but they are his.

Their end will correspond to their deeds. Key words. Their end (telos): final judgement. God will judge them by what they truly are and did (Philippians 3:19; 2 Peter 2:1–3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean they knew they were Satan’s servants. Deceivers can be deceived. But they are accountable.

In a sentence. It is not surprising, then, if his servants also masquerade as servants of righteousness. Their end will be what their actions deserve.

On a Tuesday. Look past the outward appearance of teachers. Test their message and their fruit (Matthew 7:15–20).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — The Fool’s Boast and the Catalogue of Sufferings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says again that he is not really a fool, but if they insist on thinking so, they can let him boast a little like one. He admits that this kind of boasting is not how the Lord would speak; it is the way of the flesh, which the rivals practise. The Corinthians, so wise in their own eyes, happily put up with fools, and even with leaders who enslave, exploit, take advantage, act superior and slap them in the face. Paul confesses, ironically, that he was too weak for that. Then he matches the rivals’ claims: like them he is a Hebrew, an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, and as a servant of Christ he outdoes them, in labours, imprisonments, beatings and near-deaths. He lists floggings in the synagogues, Roman beatings, a stoning, three shipwrecks and a night and day adrift, and every kind of danger on his travels, along with toil, sleeplessness, hunger, thirst, cold and exposure. On top of all that comes the daily pressure of concern for all the churches; he feels every believer’s weakness and burns over every one who is made to stumble. If he must boast, he will boast of his weakness, and he swears before God that he is telling the truth. He ends with an anti-climax: at Damascus, when the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city to arrest him, he escaped by being let down through a window in a basket.
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue of sufferings is Paul’s primary credential. In his opponents’ world, apostolic legitimacy was demonstrated by impressive spiritual experiences (visions, tongues, miraculous signs) and social credibility (letters of recommendation, personal charisma, philosophical sophistication). Paul’s credential is precisely the opposite: a body broken by service, a life spent in the pattern of the cross. This is not masochism; it is the coherence of messenger and message. The one who preaches a crucified Christ must bear in his body the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: A church’s senior pastor has served for 25 years in a difficult context: modest attendance, a neighbourhood in decline, countless crises with little visible breakthrough. When a search committee from a larger church comes to interview him, they ask about his “greatest ministry successes.” He does not know what to say. This passage suggests a different category: the 25-year record of faithfulness in hardship, the daily anxiety for the congregation, the pattern of showing up — this is the apostolic credential. The question “what have you built?” is not the only or even the primary question.

verseByVerse.quote: I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.

I repeat, let no one think me foolish. Key words. Paul is not really a fool; he is playing a part.

But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little. Key words. Paul adopts the rivals’ style of boasting to expose it, calling it foolishness. In ancient drama, the fool could say things others could not.

What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool. Key words. Boasting about oneself is not Christlike. Paul does it under protest.

Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast. Key words. According to the flesh: about worldly credentials and achievements.

What it does not mean. It does not mean this passage is less inspired. Paul is deliberately using irony, under the Spirit’s guidance.

In a sentence. Paul repeats: let no one take him for a fool. But if you do, then tolerate him just as you would a fool, so that he may do a little boasting. In this self-confident boasting he is not talking as the Lord would, but as a fool. Since many are boasting in the way the world does, he too will boast.

For worship. Ask God to free you from the need to boast about yourself.
verseByVerse.note: Paul adopts the rivals’ style of boasting to expose it, calling it foolishness.

verseByVerse.quote: For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.

For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves! Key words. Biting irony. You are so wise, you happily put up with fools.

For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you. Key words. The false apostles were enslaving them, controlling their lives.

Or devours you. Key words. Eating up their resources, demanding payment.

Or takes advantage of you. Key words. “Takes advantage” (lambanō, takes, catches, exploits).

Or puts on airs. Key words. “Puts on airs” (epairō, lifts himself up), arrogance.

Or strikes you in the face. Key words. Possibly literally; or a figure for public humiliation. Either way, abusive leadership.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Corinthians were stupid. It means they had been impressed by dominating personalities and mistook abuse for authority.

In a sentence. You gladly put up with fools since you are so wise! In fact, you even put up with anyone who enslaves you or exploits you or takes advantage of you or puts on airs or slaps you in the face.

On a Tuesday. Spiritual abuse is real. If a leader controls, exploits or humiliates people, that is not Christlike authority. Seek help.

verseByVerse.quote: To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!
verseByVerse.commentary:
To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!

To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that! Key words. Heavy irony. Paul was too weak to abuse them as the false apostles did. If that is weakness, he admits it. The Corinthians called Paul weak (10:10); he turns the charge around. His weakness was Christlike gentleness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul regretted being gentle.

In a sentence. To Paul’s shame he admits that we were too weak for that!

For worship. Thank God for leaders who are too weak to abuse, who serve gently like Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.

Are they Hebrews? So am I. Key words. The rivals were Jewish Christians who boasted of their pedigree. Hebrews: perhaps Hebrew- or Aramaic-speaking Jews, from Palestine. Paul was a Hebrew of Hebrews (Philippians 3:5).

Are they Israelites? So am I. Key words. Members of the covenant people (Romans 9:4; 11:1).

Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I. Key words. Heirs of the promises.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish ancestry gives spiritual superiority. Paul counts it as rubbish compared with knowing Christ (Philippians 3:7–8). He matches their boasts only to show they mean nothing.

In a sentence. Are they Hebrews? So is Paul. Are they Israelites? So is he. Are they Abraham’s descendants? So is he.

On a Tuesday. Your background, whatever it is, does not make you better or worse before God. Christ is all.

verseByVerse.quote: Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.

Are they servants of Christ? Key words. Here Paul does not merely match them. They claim to serve Christ.

I am a better one—I am talking like a madman. Key words. “Madman” (paraphroneō, out of one’s mind). Paul is uncomfortable even saying it.

With far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death. Key words. The surprise: his proof is not success, but suffering. Labours: hard work. Imprisonments: at Philippi (Acts 16:23), and others not recorded. Beatings: countless. Near death: often (1:8–10). The marks of a true servant of Christ are the marks of the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering earns status. It means faithful service of a crucified Lord involves suffering.

In a sentence. Are they servants of Christ? (Paul is out of his mind to talk like this.) He is more. He has worked much harder, been in prison more often, been flogged more severely, and been exposed to death again and again.

For worship. Thank God for the sufferings of those who brought the gospel to the world, and pray for those suffering now.

verseByVerse.quote: Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;

Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one. Key words. The law allowed up to forty lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3); the synagogues gave thirty-nine to avoid going over by mistake. A brutal punishment that could kill. Paul submitted to synagogue discipline five times, rather than abandon his people. None of these are in Acts.

Three times I was beaten with rods. Key words. The Roman punishment, by officials called lictors. Once at Philippi (Acts 16:22–23), even though Roman citizens were exempt by law.

Once I was stoned. Key words. At Lystra, he was stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:19).

Three times I was shipwrecked. Key words. Before the shipwreck of Acts 27, which came later.

A night and a day I was adrift at sea. Key words. Twenty-four hours in the open sea, clinging to wreckage.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Acts is incomplete or wrong. Acts selects only some events. Paul’s list shows how much more he endured.

In a sentence. Five times he received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. Three times he was beaten with rods, once he was pelted with stones, three times he was shipwrecked, and he spent a night and a day in the open sea,

On a Tuesday. When you think the Christian life is hard, read this list. Then thank God for his sustaining grace.
verseByVerse.note: The law allowed up to forty lashes; the synagogues gave thirty-nine to be sure of not exceeding it. Beating with rods was a Roman punishment. The shipwrecks were before the one described in Acts 27.

parallels.desc: Paul stoned at Lystra
beaten with rods at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers; in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.

On frequent journeys. Key words. Paul travelled perhaps ten thousand miles, mostly on foot.

In danger from rivers, danger from robbers. Key words. Rivers without bridges could be deadly in flood; roads through the mountains of Asia Minor were notorious for bandits.

Danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles. Key words. Jewish opponents plotted against him (Acts 9:23; 20:3); Gentile mobs attacked him (Acts 16:19–22; 19:23–41).

Danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea. Key words. No place was safe.

Danger from false brothers. Key words. Perhaps the most painful: betrayal by those who claimed to be Christians (Galatians 2:4).

In toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure. Key words. Physical deprivation. “Without food” may mean voluntary fasting. Cold and exposure: lacking clothing and shelter (4:11; 2 Timothy 4:13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every Christian must suffer like this. It means faithfulness may cost greatly.

In a sentence. He has been constantly on the move. He has been in danger from rivers, from bandits, from his fellow Jews, from Gentiles; in danger in the city, in the country, at sea; and in danger from false believers. He has laboured and toiled and often gone without sleep; he has known hunger and thirst and often gone without food; he has been cold and without enough clothing.

For worship. Pray for Christians who travel to dangerous places for the gospel. Ask God to protect them.
verseByVerse.note: Rivers without bridges could be deadly in flood; roads through the mountains were infested with robbers.

verseByVerse.quote: And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.

And, apart from other things. Key words. Besides the outward sufferings.

There is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches. Key words. “Pressure” (epistasis, a crowding in, a burden pressing every day). “Anxiety” (merimna, care, concern). The inner burden of pastoral care: worrying about churches being led astray, divided, persecuted. For Paul, this was as heavy as the beatings.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul disobeyed the command not to be anxious (Philippians 4:6). This is the godly concern of love, which he brought to God in prayer.

In a sentence. Besides everything else, he faces daily the pressure of his concern for all the churches.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your pastor, who carries a daily burden of care for your church.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.

Who is weak, and I am not weak? Key words. Paul identifies with weak believers. He feels their weakness with them (1 Corinthians 9:22).

Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant? Key words. “Indignant” (pyroō, burn, inflamed). When someone is led into sin, Paul burns with grief and anger at those who caused it.

If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness. Key words. The turning point. Unlike the rivals, Paul boasts in his weakness, because there God’s power is seen (12:9–10). This is the theology of the cross.

What it does not mean. It does not mean weakness is a virtue in itself. It means God’s strength is displayed in it.

In a sentence. Who is weak, and Paul does not feel weak? Who is led into sin, and he does not inwardly burn? If he must boast, he will boast of the things that show his weakness.

For worship. Thank God that his strength shows in your weakness. Boast in that.

verseByVerse.quote: The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me, but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me, but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.

The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying. Key words. A solemn oath, because the story is so humiliating.

At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me. Key words. Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, whose kingdom lay south and east of Damascus; he ruled from about 9 BC to AD 40. Soon after Paul’s conversion, his preaching in Damascus provoked a plot (Acts 9:23–25).

But I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands. Key words. Roman soldiers received a crown for being first up the wall of an enemy city. Paul boasts of being first down the wall, in a basket, fleeing. The opposite of a hero’s story. His Christian life began in humiliating weakness. That is his boast.

What it does not mean. It does not mean escape from danger is cowardice. Jesus told his followers to flee persecution when possible (Matthew 10:23).

In a sentence. The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, who is to be praised for ever, knows that Paul is not lying. In Damascus the governor under King Aretas had the city guarded in order to arrest him. But he was lowered in a basket from a window in the wall and slipped through his hands.

On a Tuesday. You do not have to be the hero of your story. Christ is. Let him have the glory, even through your humbling moments.
verseByVerse.note: Aretas IV was king of the Nabataeans, whose kingdom lay south and east of Damascus; he died around AD 40.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me!<sup>2</sup>For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.<sup>3</sup>But I am afraid that as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your thoughts will be led astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ.<sup>4</sup>For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus than the one we proclaimed, or if you receive a different spirit from the one you received, or if you accept a different gospel from the one you accepted, you put up with it readily enough.<sup>5</sup>Indeed, I consider that I am not in the least inferior to these super-apostles.<sup>6</sup>Even if I am unskilled in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; indeed, in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.<sup>7</sup>Or did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I preached God’s gospel to you free of charge?<sup>8</sup>I robbed other churches by accepting support from them in order to serve you.<sup>9</sup>And when I was with you and was in need, I did not burden anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my need. So I refrained and will refrain from burdening you in any way.<sup>10</sup>As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.<sup>11</sup>And why? Because I do not love you?
