God knows I do!<sup>12</sup>And what I am doing I will continue to do, in order to undermine the claim of those who would like to claim that in their boasted mission they work on the same terms as we do.<sup>13</sup>For such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ.<sup>14</sup>And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.<sup>15</sup>So it is no surprise if his servants, also, disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will correspond to their deeds.<sup>16</sup>I repeat, let no one think me foolish. But even if you do, accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.<sup>17</sup>What I am saying with this boastful confidence, I say not as the Lord would but as a fool.<sup>18</sup>Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.<sup>19</sup>For you gladly bear with fools, being wise yourselves!<sup>20</sup>For you bear it if someone makes slaves of you, or devours you, or takes advantage of you, or puts on airs, or strikes you in the face.<sup>21</sup>To my shame, I must say, we were too weak for that!<sup>22</sup>Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they offspring of Abraham? So am I.<sup>23</sup>Are they servants of Christ? I am a better one—I am talking like a madman—with far greater labors, far more imprisonments, with countless beatings, and often near death.<sup>24</sup>Five times I received at the hands of the Jews the forty lashes less one.<sup>25</sup>Three times I was beaten with rods. Once I was stoned. Three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I was adrift at sea;<sup>26</sup>on frequent journeys, in danger from rivers, danger from robbers, danger from my own people, danger from Gentiles, danger in the city, danger in the wilderness, danger at sea, danger from false brothers;<sup>27</sup>in toil and hardship, through many a sleepless night, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and exposure.<sup>28</sup>And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.<sup>29</sup>Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to fall, and I am not indignant?<sup>30</sup>If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.<sup>31</sup>The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying.<sup>32</sup>At Damascus, the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus in order to seize me,<sup>33</sup>but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.

12.title: The Thorn in the Flesh and Power in Weakness
12.overview:
The rivals in Corinth boasted of visions and revelations. Paul reluctantly matches them, and then turns the boast inside out. He tells, in the third person as if about someone else, of a man taken up into the third heaven, into paradise, fourteen years earlier, where he heard things no human may repeat. But he will not build his reputation on that. To keep him from pride after such revelations, he was given a “thorn in the flesh”, a messenger of Satan to torment him. Three times he begged the Lord to take it away. The Lord answered: my grace is enough for you, for my power is brought to completion in weakness. So Paul now gladly boasts of his weaknesses, because when he is weak, then he is strong.

The rest of the chapter returns to the relationship. Paul has been forced into this foolish boasting because the Corinthians failed to stand up for him, though the signs of an apostle were done among them. He is coming a third time, and still will not take their money: he wants them, not their possessions, and will gladly spend himself for them. He denies trickery through his co-workers, insists that everything he has said was for building them up, and confesses his fear that when he comes he will find quarrelling, immorality and unrepented sin, and will be humbled and grieved over them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Thorn in the Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says he must go on boasting, though nothing is gained by it, and turns to visions and revelations from the Lord. He describes, as if speaking of another man, someone in Christ who fourteen years before was taken up into the third heaven, into paradise, whether in the body or not he does not know, and heard words too sacred for any human to speak. He will boast about that man, but about himself only of his weaknesses. If he did boast he would be telling the truth, but he holds back, so that no one rates him higher than what they see and hear from him. To keep him humble after such extraordinary revelations, he was given a painful thorn in his body, Satan’s messenger to beat him down. He pleaded with the Lord three times to remove it, and the Lord replied that his grace was sufficient and that his power reaches its full strength in weakness. So Paul will gladly boast of his weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may rest on him. For Christ’s sake he accepts weakness, insults, hardship, persecution and distress, because when he is weak, then he is strong.
verseByVerse.theology:
The phrase “power is made perfect in weakness” is the theological summit of the letter. The verb is from the word for a goal: brought to completion. Divine power achieves its intended perfection/completion in the context of human weakness. This is not simply a compensation for weakness (“when you can’t do it, God will”) but a statement about the natural habitat of divine power: it is when human resources are exhausted that the divine power is most purely displayed. The implication is not that Christians should cultivate weakness artificially but that they should not be surprised or ashamed when their weakness becomes the occasion for the display of a power that is clearly not theirs.

The three-fold prayer (v. 8) and the divine refusal is one of the clearest statements in the NT that God’s answer to prayer is sometimes “no, but here is something better.” Paul prayed earnestly, repeatedly, and specifically. The thorn was not removed. But what was given instead — a word of grace, an experience of Christ’s power — was worth more than the removal would have been. The “no” was a deeper “yes.”
verseByVerse.examples: A woman with a chronic pain condition has prayed for healing for years. She has been to healing services; she has been told that her lack of healing indicates insufficient faith. This passage speaks directly to her: the greatest apostle prayed three times for the removal of his thorn and was refused. The word he received instead was not a failure of faith but a revelation of grace. “My grace is sufficient for you” is not a consolation prize; it is a gift that the removal of the thorn would not have given him.

verseByVerse.quote: I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 12 continues Paul’s fool’s speech, now turning to the kind of thing the super-apostles most loved to boast of: visions and revelations. First, Paul tells, in the third person and with great reluctance, of being caught up to paradise fourteen years earlier and hearing things that cannot be told. But he will not boast of it (vv. 1–6). Second, to keep him from pride, he was given a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan. He pleaded three times for it to go, but the Lord answered: my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness. So Paul boasts of weakness, because when he is weak, then he is strong (vv. 7–10). This is the heart of the whole letter. Third, Paul ends the fool’s speech: the signs of an apostle were done among them; his only offence was not burdening them. He is coming a third time, seeking not their money but them, and gladly spending himself for their souls (vv. 11–18). Finally, he warns that he fears finding quarrelling, immorality and unrepentance when he arrives (vv. 19–21).

I must go on boasting. Key words. Paul feels compelled, because the Corinthians are being misled by the rivals’ boasts.

Though there is nothing to be gained by it. Key words. Boasting does no spiritual good.

I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord. Key words. Visions (optasiai) and revelations (apokalypseis) from the Lord, or about the Lord. The rivals claimed spiritual experiences as proof of their authority.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul despised spiritual experiences. He had many (Acts 16:9; 18:9; 22:17–18). It means they are not the basis for authority.

In a sentence. Paul must go on boasting. Although there is nothing to be gained, he will go on to visions and revelations from the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Do not measure your faith, or anyone else’s, by spectacular experiences.

verseByVerse.quote: I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows. And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—
verseByVerse.commentary:
I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows. And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—

I know a man in Christ. Key words. Paul speaks of himself in the third person, out of modesty and reluctance (v. 7 makes clear it was him). “In Christ”: a believer.

Who fourteen years ago. Key words. About AD 42, during Paul’s “silent years” in Syria and Cilicia before his missionary journeys (Galatians 1:21; Acts 11:25). He had kept quiet about it for fourteen years. Those who constantly talk of their visions should note that.

Was caught up to the third heaven. Key words. “Caught up” (harpazō, snatched up, the word used in 1 Thessalonians 4:17). The “third heaven” means the dwelling place of God, beyond the sky (first heaven) and the stars (second). Some Jewish writings spoke of seven heavens; Paul uses the simpler scheme.

Whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows. Key words. Paul honestly does not know the mode of the experience. He refuses to speculate.

And I know that this man was caught up into paradise. Key words. Paradise (paradeisos, a Persian word for a garden or park): the presence of God, where the dying thief went with Jesus (Luke 23:43; Revelation 2:7). The same place as the third heaven.

Where Christians differ: visits to heaven today. Many popular books and speakers today claim detailed visits to heaven. Verdict: Paul, an apostle, was taken to paradise and was forbidden to describe what he heard (v. 4). He waited fourteen years to mention it, and then only to rebuke boasting. Claims today to have toured heaven and brought back detailed descriptions do not match Paul’s reticence, add to Scripture, and often contradict it. Scripture is sufficient to tell us what we need to know about heaven (2 Timothy 3:16–17; Westminster 1.6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s experience was imaginary. It was real, and he insists it was true (v. 6).

In a sentence. Paul knows a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven. Whether it was in the body or out of the body he does not know; God knows. And he knows that this man, whether in the body or apart from the body he does not know, but God knows, was caught up to paradise

For worship. Paradise is real, and believers will be there with Christ. Rest in that hope.
verseByVerse.note: Paul speaks of himself in the third person. The “third heaven” means the highest heaven, the presence of God; fourteen years before this letter would be in the early 40s AD.

verseByVerse.quote: and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter. On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—
verseByVerse.commentary:
and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter. On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—

And he heard things that cannot be told. Key words. “Cannot be told” (arrēta, inexpressible, unspeakable). Things too holy for human words.

Which man may not utter. Key words. Not permitted. God forbade Paul to repeat them. Not every revelation was meant for publication.

On behalf of this man I will boast. Key words. Paul distances himself from the experience, as if it happened to someone else. It was God’s gift, not his achievement.

But on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses. Key words. His own boasting is only of weakness.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul had secret teaching that the church needs. Everything necessary for faith and life is revealed in Scripture.

In a sentence. and heard inexpressible things, things that no one is permitted to tell. Paul will boast about a man like that, but he will not boast about himself, except about his weaknesses.

On a Tuesday. If God gives you a special experience of his presence, treasure it humbly. You need not broadcast it.

verseByVerse.quote: though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.

Though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth. Key words. If he boasted of his revelations, it would be true, unlike the rivals’ exaggerations.

But I refrain from it. Key words. He chooses not to.

So that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me. Key words. Paul wants to be judged by what people can see in his life and hear in his teaching, not by claimed experiences that cannot be checked. A healthy test for every leader.

What it does not mean. It does not mean experiences are irrelevant. It means character and teaching are the tests of ministry.

In a sentence. Even if he should choose to boast, he would not be a fool, because he would be speaking the truth. But he refrains, so no one will think more of him than is warranted by what he does or says.

For worship. Ask God to make your visible life and words the true measure of your faith.

verseByVerse.quote: So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.

So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations. Key words. “Conceited” (hyperairomai, lifted up too high, exalted). Great revelations bring the danger of pride.

A thorn was given me in the flesh. Key words. “Thorn” (skolops, a stake, a sharp splinter). No one knows what the thorn was; suggestions include a chronic illness (perhaps eye disease, Galatians 4:13–15; 6:11; or malaria, migraines, epilepsy), a speech impediment, or relentless opposition and persecution. Paul does not say, which allows every believer with a thorn to apply the passage. “Was given”: passive, implying God gave it.

A messenger of Satan to harass me. Key words. “Messenger” (angelos, angel, messenger). Satan meant it for harm. “Harass” (kolaphizō, beat with fists, as Jesus was beaten, Matthew 26:67). Present tense: an ongoing torment.

To keep me from becoming conceited. Key words. Repeated for emphasis. God used Satan’s weapon for Paul’s good, as with Job (Job 1–2). Satan intended to hinder; God intended to humble. The same event can serve two purposes.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is the author of evil. Satan is responsible for his evil intent. But God rules over even Satan’s actions for his people’s good (Romans 8:28; Genesis 50:20).

In a sentence. Or because of these surpassingly great revelations. Therefore, in order to keep Paul from becoming conceited, he was given a thorn in his flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment him.

On a Tuesday. What is your thorn? Ask God how he might be using it to keep you humble and dependent on him.
verseByVerse.note: No one knows what the thorn was; suggestions include a chronic illness, poor eyesight, or persistent opposition.

parallels.desc: thorns in your sides

verseByVerse.quote: Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.

Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this. Key words. “Pleaded” (parakaleō, begged, appealed). The Lord here is probably Jesus. Jesus too prayed three times in Gethsemane (Mark 14:32–41), asking that the cup pass, and submitted to the Father’s will. Paul’s prayer was earnest, persistent and honest.

That it should leave me. Key words. He asked for healing or removal. It was right to ask.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul lacked faith. He prayed in faith, and God said no.

In a sentence. Three times he pleaded with the Lord to take it away from him.

For worship. Bring your thorn to the Lord in prayer, honestly and persistently. He listens.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus too prayed three times in Gethsemane.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

But he said to me. Key words. Perfect tense: he has said, and it stands. Christ’s answer is permanent.

“My grace is sufficient for you.” Key words. Not removal, but grace. “Sufficient” (arkeō, enough). Christ’s grace is all Paul needs to bear the thorn and serve faithfully. The answer is better than the request.

“For my power is made perfect in weakness.” Key words. “Made perfect” (teleō, brought to completion, fully displayed). Christ’s power is seen most clearly where human strength is weakest. This is the principle of the whole letter (4:7).

Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses. Key words. Paul does not just tolerate weakness; he boasts in it, gladly.

So that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Key words. “Rest upon” (episkēnoō, pitch a tent over, dwell upon). An echo of God’s glory dwelling in the tabernacle. Christ’s power settles on the weak.

Where Christians differ: healing and faith. Some teach that it is always God’s will to heal believers who have enough faith, and that remaining sick shows lack of faith. Verdict: Paul, the great apostle, prayed in faith three times for his thorn to be removed, and the Lord said no. God does heal in answer to prayer, and we should pray for healing (James 5:14–15). But he sometimes chooses not to, for purposes better than healing: humility, dependence, and the display of his power in weakness. Paul left Trophimus sick (2 Timothy 4:20) and advised Timothy to take wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean weakness is good in itself, or that we should not seek relief. It means God’s grace is enough when relief does not come.

In a sentence. But he said to Paul, “My grace is all you need, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” So Paul will boast all the more gladly about his weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may rest on him.

For worship. Hear Christ say to you: my grace is sufficient for you. Thank him for it, today, in your weakness.

parallels.desc: he gives power to the faint

verseByVerse.quote: For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.

For the sake of Christ, then, I am content. Key words. “Content” (eudokeō, take pleasure in, be well pleased). Not resigned, but glad.

With weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. Key words. Five kinds of suffering: physical weakness, verbal abuse, deprivation, persecution, distress.

For when I am weak, then I am strong. Key words. The great paradox of the Christian life. When we are weak and know it, we depend on Christ, and his strength works through us. Self-reliance is real weakness; dependence on Christ is real strength.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should seek out weakness or suffering. It means they can embrace it when it comes.

In a sentence. That is why, for Christ’s sake, he delights in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when he is weak, then he is strong.

On a Tuesday. When you feel weak today, say it: when I am weak, then I am strong. Then lean on Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — Signs of Apostleship and Pastoral Fears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul says he has made a fool of himself, but they drove him to it; they should have been speaking up for him, since he is in no way inferior to the super-apostles, even though he is nothing. The marks of a true apostle were done among them with great perseverance: signs, wonders and mighty works. The only way they have been treated worse than other churches is that he never burdened them, and he asks them, ironically, to forgive him that wrong. He is ready to come a third time and still will not be a burden, because he wants them, not their money; parents save for their children, not children for parents. He will gladly spend everything, himself included, for them, even if loving them more means being loved less. Some say he was cunning and tricked them, but did he or Titus or the brother he sent ever exploit them? Everything he has said has been spoken before God in Christ to build them up. He fears that when he comes he will find them not as he hopes, full of quarrelling, jealousy, anger, rivalry, slander, gossip, arrogance and disorder, and that God will humble him among them as he mourns over those who have not repented of their impurity and immorality.
verseByVerse.theology: The “signs of a true apostle” (v. 12) — signs, wonders, mighty works — are offered not as the primary credential of Paul’s apostleship but as evidence that the Corinthians have already received from him what a true apostle gives. His primary credential, as the entire letter has argued, is the cruciform pattern of his ministry. The miraculous signs are additional evidence, not the foundation. This ordering matters: making miraculous signs the primary criterion for apostolic authenticity is precisely the error of the super-apostles.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation’s governing board is reviewing the annual ministry assessment and focusing entirely on measurable outcomes — attendance, baptisms, giving — as indicators of pastoral effectiveness. This passage suggests a broader criterion: has the ministry demonstrated the signs of true apostolic work (transformed lives, gospel truth, pastoral care), and has the minister borne the cruciform character that authentic ministry requires? The absence of spectacular growth does not disqualify; the absence of gospel integrity does.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.

I have been a fool! You forced me to it. Key words. The fool’s speech ends. The Corinthians’ failure to defend Paul forced him to defend himself.

For I ought to have been commended by you. Key words. They should have spoken up for him.

For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. Key words. In himself, nothing (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). By God’s grace, not inferior.

The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience. Key words. “Patience” (hypomonē, endurance). The marks of a true apostle include perseverance in suffering.

With signs and wonders and mighty works. Key words. Three words for miracles. Paul did miracles in Corinth (Romans 15:19). They were signs confirming his apostleship.

Where Christians differ: the signs of an apostle today. Some argue that miracles should be normal in every church today. Verdict: Paul calls signs and wonders the signs of an apostle: marks that distinguished true apostles from false. If they were common to all believers, they could not mark out apostles. This supports the view that the miraculous sign gifts were tied to the apostolic foundation of the church (Hebrews 2:3–4; Ephesians 2:20) and are not the norm today. God remains free to do wonders.

What it does not mean. It does not mean miracles alone prove truth. False prophets can do signs (Matthew 24:24). Doctrine and character must agree.

In a sentence. Paul has made a fool of himself, but you drove him to it. You ought to have commended him, for he is not in the least inferior to the super-apostles, even though he is nothing. The things that mark an apostle, signs, wonders and miracles, were done among you with great perseverance.

For worship. Speak up for faithful servants of Christ who are criticised unfairly.

verseByVerse.quote: For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong! Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong! Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Key words. They received everything other churches did, except the privilege of supporting Paul.

Forgive me this wrong! Key words. Biting irony.

Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. Key words. First visit: founding the church. Second: the painful visit. Third: coming soon (13:1).

And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. Key words. The heart of a true pastor. Not their money, but them: their souls, their good.

For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children. Key words. Paul is their spiritual father. Fathers provide for children, not the other way round.

What it does not mean. It does not mean children have no duty to care for aging parents (1 Timothy 5:4). Paul is speaking of normal provision for children.

In a sentence. How were you inferior to the other churches, except that Paul was never a burden to you? Forgive him this wrong! Now he is ready to visit you for the third time, and he will not be a burden to you, because what he wants is not your possessions but you. After all, children should not have to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

For worship. Thank God for pastors who seek you, not what is yours.

verseByVerse.quote: I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?

I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. Key words. “Spend” (dapanaō): spend his money, time, energy. “Be spent” (ekdapanaomai, be utterly spent, used up): give his very life. Gladly. Like Christ, who gave himself (Galatians 2:20).

If I love you more, am I to be loved less? Key words. A heartbreaking question. The more Paul loved them, the less they seemed to love him in return. Love does not always receive love back.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul served in order to be loved. He loved regardless.

In a sentence. So Paul will very gladly spend for you everything he has and expend himself as well. If he loves you more, will you love him less?

On a Tuesday. Spend yourself for others gladly, even if they do not love you back. Christ did.

verseByVerse.quote: But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?

But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Key words. A new accusation: Paul refused money directly but was skimming it through the collection.

Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? Key words. Paul invites them to check the record.

I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Key words. No. Titus’s conduct had been honest, as they knew.

Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps? Key words. Paul and his co-workers behaved with the same integrity. Literally, walk in the same footprints.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should not be accountable. Paul welcomes scrutiny.

In a sentence. Be that as it may, Paul has not been a burden to you. Yet, crafty fellow that he is, he caught you by trickery! Did he exploit you through any of the men he sent to you? He urged Titus to go to you and sent our brother with him. Titus did not exploit you, did he? Did we not walk in the same footsteps by the same Spirit?

For worship. Ask God to keep you honest in all your dealings, especially with money.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.

Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? Key words. The Corinthians might think Paul was trying to win their approval.

It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ. Key words. Paul’s court is God’s, not theirs (1 Corinthians 4:3–4).

And all for your upbuilding, beloved. Key words. The purpose of everything he has written: to build them up (10:8; 13:10). And he calls them beloved.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was unconcerned about what they thought. He cared, for their sake.

In a sentence. Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? We have been speaking in the sight of God as those in Christ; and everything we do, dear friends, is for your strengthening.

On a Tuesday. Speak and act before God, for others’ good, not to win approval.

verseByVerse.quote: For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.

For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish. Key words. Not yet repentant.

And that you may find me not as you wish. Key words. Severe instead of gentle.

That perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. Key words. Eight sins of community life, the kind that tear churches apart. Quarrelling (eris), jealousy (zēlos), anger (thymoi, outbursts), hostility (eritheiai, selfish ambition, factions), slander (katalaliai, speaking against), gossip (psithyrismoi, whisperings), conceit (physiōseis, puffings-up), disorder (akatastasiai, tumult).

I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you. Key words. Their sin would humiliate Paul as their father.

And I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented. Key words. Grieve, as over the dead (1 Corinthians 5:2).

Of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced. Key words. Sexual sins (1 Corinthians 5–6). Some had not repented.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the whole church was unrepentant. Many had repented (7:9–11). But not all.

In a sentence. For Paul is afraid that when he comes he may not find you as he wants you to be, and you may not find him as you want him to be. He fears there may be discord, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish ambition, slander, gossip, arrogance and disorder. He is afraid that when he comes again his God will humble him before you, and he will be grieved over many who have sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual sin and debauchery in which they have indulged.

On a Tuesday. Look at the list of sins in this verse. Are any of them in your relationships at church? Repent and make peace.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>I must go on boasting. Though there is nothing to be gained by it, I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.<sup>2</sup>I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows.<sup>3</sup>And I know that this man was caught up into paradise—whether in the body or out of the body I do not know, God knows—<sup>4</sup>and he heard things that cannot be told, which man may not utter.<sup>5</sup>On behalf of this man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except of my weaknesses—<sup>6</sup>though if I should wish to boast, I would not be a fool, for I would be speaking the truth; but I refrain from it, so that no one may think more of me than he sees in me or hears from me.<sup>7</sup>So to keep me from becoming conceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming conceited.<sup>8</sup>Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.<sup>9</sup>But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.<sup>10</sup>For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.<sup>11</sup>I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing.<sup>12</sup>The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.<sup>13</sup>For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong!<sup>14</sup>Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.<sup>15</sup>I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?<sup>16</sup>But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit.<sup>17</sup>Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you?<sup>18</sup>I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?<sup>19</sup>Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.<sup>20</sup>For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder.<sup>21</sup>I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.

13.title: Self-Examination, Final Warnings, and the Grace Benediction
13.overview:
The letter ends with a warning and a blessing. Paul is about to make his third visit, and he will deal with unrepented sin properly, on the evidence of witnesses, as the law requires. The Corinthians have demanded proof that Christ speaks through him; they will have it. Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by God’s power, and Paul, weak in him, will live with him by God’s power in dealing with them. But the real test is theirs: they must examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith, whether Christ is in them. Paul would rather appear to fail than see them do wrong; his authority is for building up, not tearing down, and he writes now so that he will not need to be severe when he arrives.

Then the tone softens into final appeals: rejoice, aim for restoration, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you. After greetings, the letter closes with the fullest Trinitarian blessing in the New Testament: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. The letter that began with the God of all comfort ends with the triune God present with a troubled church.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul announces his third visit. Any charge will be settled by two or three witnesses, and he warns those who sinned before, and everyone else, that this time he will not spare them. They wanted evidence that Christ speaks through him: Christ is not weak towards them but powerful among them. He was crucified in weakness yet lives by God’s power, and his servants, weak in him, will live with him by that same power in their dealings with the church. Paul turns the test round: they should examine themselves to see whether they are really in the faith, and recognise that Christ is in them, unless they fail the test. He hopes they will see that he has not failed. His prayer is that they do no wrong, not so that he looks good, but so that they do right even if he seems to have failed. He can do nothing against the truth, only for it. He is glad to be weak if they are strong, and prays for their restoration. That is why he writes before coming: so that he will not have to use his authority harshly, since the Lord gave it to him to build up, not to tear down.
verseByVerse.theology: The call to self-examination (v. 5) has been used in Reformed tradition as the basis for the practice of self-examination before the Lord’s Supper (1 Cor. 11:28–31). Genuine self-examination is not the cultivation of paralyzing doubt but the honest assessment of the soul before God: am I in the faith? Is Christ in me? Is my trust in Christ or in my own religious performance? The examination that produces assurance is the examination that finds Christ as the ground of hope, not the examination that finds sufficient personal righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation prepares for a communion service and the pastor leads a five-minute self-examination period before the elements are distributed. Some members treat it as a routine; others spiral into anxiety. This passage clarifies the goal: not to find sufficient personal holiness to “qualify” for the table, but to find whether Christ is there — whether the faith that receives him is genuine. The person who comes to the table trusting Christ is examining themselves correctly; the person who comes evaluating their performance has missed the point of both the examination and the table.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 13 closes the letter with a final warning and a final blessing. First, Paul announces his third visit. He will act with justice, establishing every charge by witnesses, and will not spare the unrepentant. The Corinthians want proof that Christ speaks through him; they will get it. Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by God’s power, and Paul, weak in him, will deal with them by that power (vv. 1–4). Second, he turns the test around: examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Paul hopes they will pass, and prays that they will do right, even if he seems weak, because his authority is for building up, not tearing down (vv. 5–10). Finally, he gives brief commands: rejoice, aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree, live in peace. He sends greetings, and ends with the fullest Trinitarian blessing in the New Testament: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit (vv. 11–14).

This is the third time I am coming to you. Key words. After the founding visit and the painful visit (2:1).

Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. Key words. From Deuteronomy 19:15, also Jesus’ rule for church discipline (Matthew 18:16) and for accusations against elders (1 Timothy 5:19). Paul will not act on rumour. Due process and justice in the church.

I warned those who sinned before and all the others. Key words. He warned them on the second visit.

And I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them. Key words. A clear final warning. He will exercise discipline.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is eager to punish. He has given many warnings and much time.

In a sentence. This will be Paul’s third visit to you. Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. He already gave you a warning when he was with you the second time. He now repeats it while absent: on his return he will not spare those who sinned earlier or any of the others,

On a Tuesday. Never act on rumour against a fellow believer. Insist on clear evidence and fair process.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three

verseByVerse.quote: since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.

Since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. Key words. “Proof” (dokimē, test result). The Corinthians demanded evidence that Paul really spoke for Christ.

He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you. Key words. Christ himself has shown his power among them: in their conversion, the gifts, the miracles. They should not doubt Christ’s power in Paul’s ministry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s power is always visible as human strength. It is often displayed through weakness (12:9).

In a sentence. since you are demanding proof that Christ is speaking through Paul. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.

For worship. Thank Christ for his power at work in your church, often in quiet ways.

verseByVerse.quote: For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.

For he was crucified in weakness. Key words. The cross looked like utter weakness (1 Corinthians 1:25). Christ chose weakness.

But lives by the power of God. Key words. The resurrection displayed God’s power (Romans 1:4; Ephesians 1:19–20).

For we also are weak in him. Key words. Paul shares Christ’s weakness, in suffering and humility.

But in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God. Key words. And he shares Christ’s resurrection power, which will be seen when he comes to deal with them. The pattern of cross and resurrection shapes all Christian ministry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean weakness and power are opposites to choose between. In Christ, they go together.

In a sentence. For to be sure, he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by God’s power. Likewise, we are weak in him, yet by God’s power we will live with him in our dealing with you.

On a Tuesday. Your weakness is not the end of the story. In Christ, resurrection power follows.

verseByVerse.quote: Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!

Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Key words. The Corinthians were testing Paul. He turns it around. “Examine” (peirazō, test, put to the proof). “In the faith”: truly believing, united to Christ.

Test yourselves. Key words. “Test” (dokimazō, prove, as metal is tested).

Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Key words. The sign of a true believer: Christ dwells in them by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10; Galatians 2:20; Colossians 1:27).

Unless indeed you fail to meet the test! Key words. “Fail the test” (adokimos, disqualified, counterfeit). If they find Christ is in them, then their faith came through Paul, which proves his apostleship. If not, they have bigger problems than Paul.

Where Christians differ: self-examination and assurance. Some say believers should never doubt their salvation; others make constant introspection the mark of true faith. Verdict: Self-examination is commanded, especially for those whose lives contradict their profession. Assurance rests first on God’s promises in Christ, confirmed by the inner witness of the Spirit and the fruit of a changed life (1 John; Westminster 18.2). Self-examination should lead not to endless morbid introspection but to looking at Christ, and to repentance where needed. Those who find Christ in them can rest assured.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on perfect performance. It means real faith shows itself, and should be checked.

In a sentence. Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Do you not realise that Christ Jesus is in you, unless, of course, you fail the test?

For worship. Take time to examine yourself before God. Is Christ in you? If so, rest in him. If not, come to him now.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.

I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. Key words. Paul hopes they will see that he is genuine.

But we pray to God that you may not do wrong. Key words. His real concern: their holiness, not his reputation.

Not that we may appear to have met the test. Key words. He is not praying for his own vindication.

But that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed. Key words. If they repent and do right, Paul will have no need to show his authority in discipline, and may look weak again. He is happy with that, as long as they do right. Selfless love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul did not care about the truth of his apostleship. He cared more about their good.

In a sentence. And Paul trusts that you will discover that we have not failed the test. Now we pray to God that you will not do anything wrong, not so that people will see that we have stood the test, but so that you will do what is right even though we may seem to have failed.

On a Tuesday. Pray for others’ holiness, even if it means you look less impressive.

verseByVerse.quote: For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.

For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth. Key words. The truth: the gospel and God’s will. Paul’s authority can only be used in the service of truth. If they are doing right, he has no grounds to discipline them. Church authority has limits: it cannot act against God’s truth.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul could not sin. It means apostolic authority was given only to serve the truth.

In a sentence. For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.

For worship. Ask God to make you someone who always stands for the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.

For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Key words. Paul rejoices if he appears weak because they are strong in faith and holiness. Their strength is his joy.

Your restoration is what we pray for. Key words. “Restoration” (katartisis, being put right, mended, equipped, as nets are mended). Paul prays for the church to be made whole again.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wanted to be weak for its own sake. He wanted them strong.

In a sentence. We are glad whenever we are weak but you are strong; and our prayer is that you may be fully restored.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church’s restoration and strength, even above your own reputation.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.

For this reason I write these things while I am away from you. Key words. The purpose of the letter.

That when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority. Key words. “Severe” (apotomōs, sharply, cuttingly). He writes now to avoid severity later.

That the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down. Key words. Repeated from 10:8. The Lord gave the authority, and its purpose is construction, not destruction. Echoes Jeremiah 1:10 and 24:6.

What it does not mean. It does not mean authority never corrects. Sometimes building up requires tearing down what is false.

In a sentence. This is why Paul writes these things when he is absent, that when he comes he may not have to be harsh in his use of authority, the authority the Lord gave him for building you up, not for tearing you down.

For worship. Thank God for leaders who correct in order to build up. Respond to correction quickly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Final Greetings and the Trinitarian Benediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul closes with brief appeals: rejoice, put things right, encourage one another, think alike, and live at peace, and the God of love and peace will be with them. They are to greet one another with a holy kiss, and he passes on greetings from all the believers with him. The final words are a blessing naming the Lord Jesus Christ, God the Father and the Holy Spirit together: may the grace of the Lord Jesus, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit be with them all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The benediction is not a formula but a theology: it presents the three persons in distinct but coordinated action, each contributing uniquely to the believer’s life. The order (Christ, Father, Spirit) is unusual — the more common Pauline order puts the Father first — possibly because the letter’s concerns have centred on the grace of Christ (the atonement of ch. 5, the self-giving of ch. 8). The coordinated action of all three persons in the single benediction is an implicit trinitarian claim: to receive grace, love, and fellowship from these three distinct persons is to receive from one God in three persons.

Koinōnia of the Holy Spirit — three possible meanings, all theologically valid: (1) the fellowship that the Spirit creates among believers; (2) participation in the Spirit — sharing in the Spirit’s life; (3) the Spirit as the one who communicates fellowship with the Father and Son. These are not mutually exclusive; the Spirit’s work achieves all three simultaneously. Those who are indwelt by the Spirit share in the divine koinōnia — the mutual love and life of the Trinity — and that sharing is expressed in genuine community with one another.
verseByVerse.examples: A church that closes every service with this benediction has been pronouncing it for decades as a familiar liturgical ending. A new pastor stops before pronouncing it and asks the congregation: do you know what you are about to receive? Each phrase is unpacked slowly — the grace that flows from Christ’s cross, the love that originated in the Father’s heart before creation, the fellowship that the Spirit creates both with God and among the gathered community. The familiar words suddenly land with the weight they have always carried. The benediction is not a farewell; it is a sending into the world with the fullness of the Triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.

Finally, brothers, rejoice. Key words. “Rejoice” (chairō): this can also mean farewell, as a greeting. Both fit: goodbye, and be glad in the Lord.

Aim for restoration. Key words. “Restoration” (katartizō, be mended, as in v. 9). Work toward putting things right.

Comfort one another. Key words. Or: listen to my appeal. Either way, encouragement (parakaleō), the theme of chapter 1.

Agree with one another. Key words. Literally, think the same thing: be of one mind (Philippians 2:2).

Live in peace. Key words. End the quarrels (12:20).

And the God of love and peace will be with you. Key words. The only time this title, God of love and peace, appears in the New Testament. As they live in love and peace, they will know the God who is love and peace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s presence is earned. It means a church living in peace experiences his presence.

In a sentence. Finally, brothers and sisters, rejoice! Strive for full restoration, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you.

On a Tuesday. Pick one of these commands and do it today: rejoice, mend a relationship, encourage someone, agree, make peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. Key words. A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends in that culture. In the church, it expressed love, reconciliation and family belonging (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20). After all the conflict, a pointed command.

All the saints greet you. Key words. The believers with Paul in Macedonia. The wider church cares about them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a literal kiss is required in every culture. It means warm, pure, family affection.

In a sentence. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All God’s people here send their greetings.

For worship. Greet your fellow believers warmly this Sunday, especially anyone you have been at odds with.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. The free, undeserved favour shown in Christ, who though rich became poor for us (8:9). Grace comes first, because it is through Christ that we come to know the Father’s love.

And the love of God. Key words. The Father’s love, the source of everything (John 3:16; Romans 5:8).

And the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Key words. “Fellowship” (koinōnia): sharing, communion. Either our fellowship with the Spirit, or the fellowship among believers that the Spirit creates. Both are true.

Be with you all. Key words. All: including those who opposed Paul. The letter ends with blessing for everyone.

The Trinity. This blessing names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, and is one of the clearest witnesses to the Trinity in Scripture. Each person is distinct, each gives a distinct blessing, and they are named side by side as equal sources of divine blessing. Written about twenty-five years after the resurrection, it shows that the early church worshipped one God in three persons. It has been used as a benediction in Christian worship ever since.

What it does not mean. It does not mean each blessing belongs to one person only. Grace, love and fellowship come from the one God. But each is especially associated with one person.

In a sentence. May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

For worship. Pray this blessing over yourself, your family and your church today.
verseByVerse.note: This blessing names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, and is still widely used to close Christian worship.

parallels.desc: the priestly blessing

13.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>2</sup>I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—<sup>3</sup>since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.<sup>4</sup>For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.<sup>5</sup>Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!<sup>6</sup>I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test.<sup>7</sup>But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.<sup>8</sup>For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.<sup>9</sup>For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.<sup>10</sup>For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.<sup>11</sup>Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.<sup>12</sup>Greet one another with a holy kiss.<sup>13</sup>All the saints greet you.<sup>14</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
